entries.title: The succession question after the Prophet's death (632 CE)
questions: What happened after Prophet Muhammad died?
Who was supposed to lead the Muslims after the Prophet?
Why did Muslims disagree about succession in 632?
How did Sunni and Shia Islam first divide?
Did the Prophet name a successor?
What was the first crisis in the Muslim community?
Why do Shia Muslims say Ali should have led after the Prophet?
What is the difference between caliph and imam at the start?
entries.answer:
The Prophet Muhammad died in 632 CE, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies describes this moment as the first crisis of the young Muslim community: who should lead now that revelation had ended?

Two broad answers emerged. One group held that the Prophet had left no designated successor, and that leadership should pass to a caliph chosen by the community; over time this view crystallised into the majority Sunni position, the Ahl al-Sunna wa'l-Jama'a, 'the people of the Sunna and the community'. The other group, who became known as the Shi'at Ali, the 'Party of Ali', held that the Prophet had, under divine command, designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib (d. 661 CE) to lead after him.

IIS scholarship stresses that for the Shia this was not simply a political quarrel. Their position rested on a conviction that, although prophecy ended with Muhammad, the community's continuing need for spiritual and moral guidance did not. Someone had to go on interpreting the Qur'an and the Prophet's message for new circumstances, and the Shia believed that this responsibility had been entrusted to the Prophet's family.

IIS writers also caution against reading modern categories into the period. In seventh-century Arabia the distinction between 'religious' and 'political' authority that we take for granted did not exist, so describing the dispute as merely political distorts it. What was at stake was what kind of authority could best preserve the Islamic message and realise it in the life of the community.

These attitudes hardened only gradually. Shia and Sunni doctrines took shape over generations rather than being fixed in 632.

entries.title: Ghadir Khumm (632 CE)
questions: What is Ghadir Khumm?
What did the Prophet say at Ghadir Khumm?
Where is Ghadir Khumm?
Why is Ghadir Khumm important to Shia Muslims?
What is Eid al-Ghadir?
Did Sunnis also record the Ghadir Khumm event?
What does mawla mean in the Ghadir hadith?
When is Ghadir Khumm commemorated?
entries.answer:
Ghadir Khumm means roughly 'the pond of Khumm'. It was a watering place between Mecca and Medina, in what is now Saudi Arabia. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that in 632 CE, returning to Medina from his farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet Muhammad stopped there and delivered a sermon in which he declared Imam Ali to be the mawla of the believers. Mawla is a rich Arabic word that can mean patron, lord, master or protector. Hadith collections preserve the Prophet's words along the lines of: whoever has me as his mawla, Ali is his mawla too.

IIS notes that in the same sermon the Prophet spoke of leaving behind 'two weighty things' (al-thaqalayn) for the community's future guidance: the Qur'an and his family.

Both Shia and Sunni sources record the event. What distinguishes the Shia reading is the meaning given to it. For Shia Muslims, including Ismailis, Ghadir Khumm is the public designation (nass) of Ali as the Prophet's successor and as the first Imam of guidance. Other Muslims have understood the words as an expression of affection and respect rather than an appointment to leadership.

The event falls on the 18th of Dhu'l-Hijja in the Muslim lunar calendar and is commemorated by Shia Muslims as Eid al-Ghadir.

Early Shia teaching leaned heavily on Ghadir Khumm. The fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, treated the sermon and its hadith as among the most important proofs of the Imamate, and the Fatimid jurist al-Qadi al-Nu'man built on it in his exposition of walaya, devotion to the Imam.

entries.title: The Ahl al-Bayt, the Prophet's household
questions: Who are the Ahl al-Bayt?
What does Ahl al-Bayt mean?
Why do Shia Muslims revere the Prophet's family?
Which Qur'anic verses do Shia cite about the Prophet's family?
Who was Fatima al-Zahra?
Did the meaning of Ahl al-Bayt change over time?
What is the event of mubahala?
Do all Muslims honour the Prophet's family?
entries.answer:
Ahl al-Bayt means 'People of the House', that is, the Prophet Muhammad's household. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that Shia Muslims believe the Prophet's legacy was entrusted to this family, in whom he had invested authority.

Shia readings ground this in the Qur'an. IIS cites verses describing how God chose the family of Abraham and the family of Imran and gave their descendants 'the book, the authority and prophethood' (Qur'an 3:33-34; 6:84-89), and the verse asking that impurity be removed from the People of the House (33:33). Another commonly cited verse asks for no reward except love for those near to the Prophet (42:23).

A historical episode is often linked to this. When Christian leaders from Najran in Arabia challenged the Prophet, both sides agreed to a mutual imprecation, which the Christians in the end declined. According to the tradition, those referred to as the Ahl al-Bayt on that occasion were the Prophet, Ali, Fatima, and Ali and Fatima's sons Hasan and Husayn.

Fatima al-Zahra, the Prophet's daughter and only surviving child, married Ali; the Imams are descended from the two of them, and IIS describes the Imamat as a hereditary office in succession from the first Imam, Ali.

IIS notes that the sense of the term shifted. In the earliest, tribal usage the Prophet's family was understood broadly, so that Shia Imams were recognised not only in the main branches of the Alid family but in other branches of the Prophet's clan of Banu Hashim. Only later, after the Abbasids came to power, did the Shia define Ahl al-Bayt more narrowly as the descendants of the Prophet through Fatima and Ali. All Muslims hold the Prophet's family in great reverence.

entries.title: Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (d. 661 CE)
questions: Who was Imam Ali?
What was Ali's relationship to the Prophet?
When was Ali caliph?
How did Imam Ali die?
Why is Ali the first Imam for Shia Muslims?
What happened during Ali's caliphate?
Where is Imam Ali buried?
What does asas mean in early Ismaili thought?
entries.answer:
Ali ibn Abi Talib was the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and, through his marriage to the Prophet's daughter Fatima, his son-in-law. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that according to most traditions he was the first male to accept the message of Islam, and that he earned the Prophet's admiration by championing that message even at risk to his life. He was close to the Prophet from the beginning of the mission.

For Shia Muslims he is the first Imam: the figure the Prophet designated, most publicly at Ghadir Khumm, to carry on the work of guidance and interpretation. Ismaili writers of the early period gave him a particularly high place. He was called the asas, the 'foundation', both because he founded the line of the Imamate and because the Imams after him drew their knowledge of the inner meaning of revelation from him. He was also described as the wasi, the heir or legatee who unfolds the esoteric sense of what the Prophet had proclaimed.

Ali's early partisans included Qur'an reciters, close Companions, prominent people of Medina and respected tribal chiefs. Pro-Alid feeling revived during the troubled caliphate of Uthman (d. 656 CE). After Uthman was murdered, Ali succeeded to the caliphate in very difficult circumstances, and the first civil war in Islam followed. His supporters were centred on Kufa in southern Iraq, and it is from this period that they were designated Shi'at Ali, the Party of Ali. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria and Uthman's cousin, used the demand to avenge Uthman as grounds for claiming the caliphate.

Ali was murdered in 661 CE. His tomb at Najaf in Iraq became a major place of pilgrimage.

entries.title: How Shia Islam began
questions: How did Shia Islam start?
What does the word Shia mean?
Who were the Shi'at Ali?
Was the Shia-Sunni split political or religious?
When did Shia Islam become a distinct community?
What do Shia Muslims believe about guidance after the Prophet?
Why did Shia Islam appeal to people under the Umayyads?
Is Shia Islam a departure from 'orthodox' Islam?
entries.answer:
The word Shia means 'partisan' or 'adherent'. In Islamic history it came to mean those Muslims who held that Ali and his descendants were the rightful authorities for the community. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the designation Shi'at Ali, 'the Party of Ali', settled on his supporters in Kufa during his own caliphate.

IIS presents the origins of Shia Islam as a question of authority rather than of party politics. All Muslims affirm the shahada: the unity of God and the guidance given through His Messenger. What the Shia added was the conviction that God instructed the Prophet to designate a figure of authority to succeed him, because the community's need for spiritual and moral guidance, through continuing interpretation of the Islamic message, did not end when revelation ended.

This conviction developed into a doctrine of the Imamate: the Imam, descended from Ali and Fatima, possesses a divinely given knowledge ('ilm) not obtained by ordinary study or reasoning, and it is through him that the divine purpose is worked out on earth.

Two historical currents fed the movement. One was resistance to Umayyad rule (661-750 CE), which many Muslims saw as a betrayal of Islam's ethical principles, especially after Karbala. The other was widespread social and economic grievance, which gave force to the Shia claim that justice and equality could only be realised under the guidance of the Ahl al-Bayt.

IIS scholars stress two cautions. The Shia are internally diverse, and they are best understood not as a sect breaking away from an original orthodoxy but as one of several 'communities of interpretation' that took shape gradually over the first Islamic centuries.

entries.title: Imam Hasan and the treaty with Mu'awiya
questions: Who was Imam Hasan?
What happened after Imam Ali was killed?
Why did Hasan give up the caliphate?
Did Hasan make a treaty with Mu'awiya?
Do Ismailis count Hasan as an Imam?
When did Imam Hasan die?
What is the Nizari Ismaili view of Hasan's role?
entries.answer:
After Imam Ali was murdered in 661 CE, the Shia of Kufa recognised his eldest son Hasan (d. 669 CE) as his successor. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that Hasan chose not to take up the role of caliph. He made a peace treaty with Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, who then assumed the caliphate and founded Umayyad rule, and Hasan withdrew to Medina and kept out of political life. The Shia nonetheless continued to regard him as their Imam after Ali.

Ismaili sources describe the position slightly differently from other Shia accounts. IIS explains that the Ismailis hold that after Ali the full authority of the Imamate was inherited by his son Husayn, while acknowledging Hasan as a successor whose role the Nizari Ismailis regard as custodial, that is, holding the office in trust until Husayn assumed it.

Hasan's withdrawal did not end Shia hopes. When he died, the Shia of Kufa revived their aspiration to restore the caliphate to the Prophet's family and turned to his younger brother Husayn, whom they now regarded as their Imam, inviting him to rise against Umayyad rule. That invitation led, after Mu'awiya's death and the succession of his son Yazid, to the journey that ended at Karbala.

This is one of the points where Ismaili and Twelver reckonings of the Imams diverge slightly, which is part of why the numbering of Imams differs between Shia communities.

entries.title: Imam Husayn and Karbala (680 CE)
questions: What happened at Karbala?
Who was Imam Husayn?
Why did Husayn refuse to accept Yazid?
When was the battle of Karbala?
What is Ashura?
Why is Karbala so important to Shia Muslims?
What effect did Karbala have on Shia identity?
Where is Imam Husayn buried?
entries.answer:
Husayn ibn Ali was the Prophet Muhammad's grandson, the younger son of Imam Ali and Fatima, and for the Shia the Imam of his time. When Mu'awiya died and his son Yazid succeeded him (r. 680-683 CE), Husayn refused to acknowledge Yazid's rule. Responding to appeals from supporters in Kufa, he set out for that city.

He never reached it. On 10 Muharram 61 AH, which the Institute of Ismaili Studies gives as 10 October 680 CE, Husayn and his small group of relatives and companions were intercepted by an Umayyad army at Karbala, some distance from Kufa, and killed.

IIS describes Karbala as the climax of Umayyad persecution of the Ahl al-Bayt. The killing of the Prophet's grandson caused shock and revulsion among Muslims generally and spread the feeling that the Umayyad leaders had wholly betrayed the ethical principles of Islam. For the Shia it did something more: it gave their cause new fervour, consolidated a distinct Shia ethos and identity, and encouraged activist trends. Scholars associated with IIS describe Karbala as a religio-political symbol that supplied meaning and emotion to a whole series of later Shia movements.

The martyrdom is commemorated on the tenth of Muharram, known as Ashura. IIS notes that this is a remembrance of tragedy rather than a festive celebration, marked by Twelver Shia communities with processions, majalis (commemorative sessions), sermons and dramatic re-enactments. Husayn's tomb at Karbala in Iraq became one of the holiest Shia pilgrimage sites; Cairo also holds a site believed to be where his head was kept.

sources.title: Imam al-Baqir and the Doctrine of Imamate

entries.notes: The Ashura practices described by IIS in this material are those of Twelver Shia communities; the sources consulted do not describe how Ismailis mark Muharram.

entries.title: Early Shia movements: Kaysaniyya, Zaydis and the Imamiyya
questions: Were there other Shia groups besides Ismailis and Twelvers?
Who were the Kaysaniyya?
Who were the Zaydis?
Why did early Shia groups disagree about the Imam?
What is the difference between an activist and a quietist imam?
Who was Zayd ibn Ali?
Who were the mawali and why did they support Shia causes?
What did early Shia groups have in common?
entries.answer:
Under Umayyad rule (661-750 CE) the Shia were not a single organised body. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes a landscape of groups, made up of Arab Muslims and of new non-Arab converts, backing different candidates for the Imamate from among the Prophet's wider family, the Banu Hashim.

One cluster was the Kaysaniyya, who traced the Imamate through Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, a son of Imam Ali by a wife other than Fatima. Disagreements about who held the office after him split them further. A feature of these groups was their appeal to nass, explicit designation of a successor, an idea that later became central to mainstream Shia thought.

Another group formed around Zayd, a son of Imam Zayn al-Abidin and half-brother of Imam Muhammad al-Baqir. They became known as the Zaydiyya. Their distinctive position was that a true Imam had to be willing to rise in arms against illegitimate rulers, which in their time meant the Umayyads. They defined leadership in political and military terms and, unlike other Shia, attached no particular importance to hereditary succession or to nass.

A large body of Shia, known as the Imamiyya, took the opposite path, staying politically quiet and concentrating on intellectual and religious development. They traced authority through Husayn's surviving son, Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin.

IIS observes that for many early sympathisers it mattered less who the leader was than that he belonged to the Banu Hashim, and that these groups' differing conceptions of the Imamate partly reflected the needs of the people whose support they sought. Discontented groups such as the mawali, non-Arab Muslims who resented their low status, often expressed their grievances through Shia causes.

entries.title: Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin (d. 712 CE)
questions: Who was Zayn al-Abidin?
What happened to Husayn's family after Karbala?
What does Zayn al-Abidin mean?
Who was the Imam after Husayn?
Why is Zayn al-Abidin called the Ornament of the Worshippers?
When did Imam Zayn al-Abidin die?
Where did Zayn al-Abidin live?
entries.answer:
Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin (d. 712 CE / 94 AH) was Imam Husayn's sole surviving son and, in the Ismaili and wider Shia reckoning, the Imam who followed his father after Karbala.

His title, Zayn al-Abidin, means 'Ornament of the Worshippers'. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he was held in great esteem in the pious circles of Medina, where he lived. His Imamate belongs to a period when a large section of the Shia, later called the Imamiyya, adopted a deliberately quietist stance in political matters and concentrated instead on the intellectual and religious development of Islam, tracing their authority through him.

IIS describes this early stretch of Shia history, from Husayn through Zayn al-Abidin to Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq, as significant precisely because none of these Imams exercised political power. It was around the Imamate as a spiritual and teaching office, rather than around a state, that Shia identity consolidated within the wider Muslim community.

When he died in 94 AH / 714 CE by the reckoning used in one IIS reading guide, there was disagreement among the Shia about who should succeed him, with several groups pressing the claims of different descendants of Ali. One of his sons, Zayd, became the figure around whom the Zaydiyya organised; another, Muhammad al-Baqir, was recognised by the Imamiyya as the next Imam.

entries.title: Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (d. 731 CE)
questions: Who was Muhammad al-Baqir?
What does al-Baqir mean?
Why is al-Baqir important in Shia history?
Was al-Baqir a political leader?
What did Imam al-Baqir teach?
When did Imam al-Baqir live?
How did al-Baqir shape the idea of hadith for the Shia?
Why did al-Baqir oppose armed revolt?
entries.answer:
Imam Muhammad al-Baqir was born in 57 AH / 677 CE and, according to Shia tradition, succeeded to the Imamate in 94 AH / 714 CE at Medina after his father Imam Zayn al-Abidin. The Institute of Ismaili Studies gives his death as 731 CE.

His title, baqir al-ilm, means something like 'one who splits open knowledge'. A study published with IIS suggests the image draws on the old comparison of knowledge to a tree, and implies that he was regarded as one who could reach the roots or first principles of a subject. It fits his approach: he was, above all, a teacher during an Imamate of nearly twenty years.

IIS describes him as no revolutionary. He opposed armed revolt against the Umayyads and advocated what one IIS author calls a 'non-rebelling' Imamate, seeking followers through the pen rather than the sword. With hindsight this looks like a realistic reading of a period in which the Umayyads were militarily unassailable, but it was also a positive claim: that the Imam's role was spiritual and intellectual rather than political.

His Imamate coincided with the growth of Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), and his own role was chiefly as a reporter of hadith and a teacher of law. He is credited with shaping the Shia approach to hadith: where Sunni collections confined themselves to the sayings and doings of the Prophet, the Shia came to define hadith as statements of the Prophet and of the Imams. He is also unanimously respected in non-Shia circles as a trustworthy authority on Prophetic traditions. He introduced the principle of taqiyya, and after his death his eldest son Ja'far was recognised as Imam.

entries.title: Imam al-Baqir's doctrine of the Imamate
questions: How did the Shia doctrine of the Imamate develop?
What is nass?
What is ilm in Shia thought?
What does nur mean in relation to the Imams?
What does masum or isma mean?
How did al-Baqir argue for the Imamate?
Why did al-Baqir's theory of the Imamate last?
Did Ismailis and Twelvers share this doctrine?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies presents Imam Muhammad al-Baqir as a decisive figure in turning Shia sentiment into a worked-out doctrine of the Imamate.

In summary, his theory ran like this. The Qur'an and hadith establish that the Prophet appointed Imam Ali as his successor. That explicit designation, nass, was accompanied by the Prophet bequeathing to Ali his knowledge ('ilm) and his light (nur). The 'ilm and nur that an Imam holds by virtue of nass render him masum, protected from error and sin.

Al-Baqir built the case in two ways. He commented on particular Qur'anic verses, offering interpretations that supported the claim, and he drew on Prophetic traditions, of which he regarded the Ghadir Khumm sermon and its hadith as the most important. Studies published with IIS point out that these were contested readings at the time, and set the Shia and Sunni understandings of the same verses and traditions side by side.

IIS also explains why this formulation carried weight. Al-Baqir's emphasis on nass suited his unusually strong genealogy, since both of his grandfathers were grandsons of the Prophet, and at a time when descent largely defined status this gave him an advantage over rival claimants. More importantly, resting legitimacy on designation rather than on the ability to lead a revolt brought order to a confused situation and provided a stable foundation for authority. Instead of the sword, legitimacy flowed from the pen and the intellect.

Both of the main Shia branches, Ismaili and Twelver, trace their doctrine of the Imamate through al-Baqir and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq, and his interpretations were taken up by later writers including the Ismaili jurist al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 974) and the Twelver scholar al-Kulayni (d. c. 940).

entries.title: Taqiyya: precaution under hostile rule
questions: What is taqiyya?
Why did Shia Muslims conceal their beliefs?
Who introduced the principle of taqiyya?
Is taqiyya the same as lying?
How did taqiyya affect Ismaili history?
Why is early Ismaili history hard to reconstruct?
What does taqiyya mean in practice?
entries.answer:
Taqiyya is the precautionary concealment of one's true religious belief and practice. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that Imam Muhammad al-Baqir introduced the principle, as a way of protecting the Imams and their followers when circumstances were dangerous.

It is best understood as a survival measure rather than as deception for advantage. The Shia, and the Ismailis in particular, repeatedly lived under regimes that treated them as enemies, and IIS notes that they found it necessary at many points simply to conceal their beliefs in order to survive. Framed as a formal principle, this practice became taqiyya.

The principle has consequences for how the history is written. IIS writers observe that taqiyya is one reason the early history of the Ismailis is unusually hard to reconstruct: the community's own sources often avoid explicit historical discussion, and much of what survives was written by hostile outsiders. Ismaili teaching also held that some aspects of doctrine could be grasped only by those whose capacity for understanding had been sufficiently developed, so such material was deliberately withheld from general circulation. On top of this, later Ismaili writings, like other retrospective traditions, tend to project a later self-image back onto the early past.

This combination means that historians working on the first Ismaili centuries face problems that do not arise to the same degree with other Muslim groups, and IIS is candid that the early period remains less well understood than it deserves to be.

entries.title: The Abbasid revolution and Shia disappointment (749-750 CE)
questions: Who were the Abbasids?
How did the Abbasids come to power?
Why were Shia Muslims disappointed by the Abbasids?
Did the Abbasids persecute the Shia?
What was the Abbasid da'wa?
When did the Umayyads fall?
Why did the Abbasids claim descent from Abbas?
entries.answer:
The Abbasids were descendants of the Prophet's uncle Abbas. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes their rise as, in its origins, part of the broad pro-Alid and pro-Ahl al-Bayt current of the late Umayyad period.

They organised carefully. They set up secret headquarters at Kufa while concentrating their activity in eastern Iran and Central Asia, and preached their da'wa (mission) in the name of an unnamed member of the Prophet's family. The vagueness was deliberate: it allowed them to draw support from Shia of many different persuasions who wanted the Ahl al-Bayt in power. Pro-Alid risings, provoked by fierce Umayyad repression, had already helped undermine the dynasty.

In 749 CE the Abbasids defeated the Umayyads, and Abu'l-Abbas al-Saffah (r. 749-754 CE) was proclaimed caliph in the mosque of Kufa; IIS elsewhere dates the Umayyad collapse to around 750 CE.

For the Shia the victory was a bitter disappointment. Those who had expected a descendant of Imam Ali rather than an Abbasid to take the caliphate found their hopes betrayed. Once in power the Abbasids reversed course, persecuting many of their former Shia supporters and the Alids, and promoting a Sunni interpretation of Islam, in part from fear that the Shia might unseat them. The break with their Shia roots was completed when the third Abbasid caliph, Muhammad al-Mahdi (d. 785 CE), declared that the Prophet had in fact appointed his uncle Abbas, not Ali, as his successor.

The Shia who felt betrayed were therefore pushed back into opposition, where they remained. The Abbasids became the principal rivals of the Ismaili Imams and, later, of the Fatimid caliphate.

entries.title: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 765 CE)
questions: Who was Ja'far al-Sadiq?
Why is Ja'far al-Sadiq so respected?
What is the Ja'fari school of law?
Did Sunni Muslims respect Ja'far al-Sadiq?
What did Ja'far al-Sadiq teach about the Imamate?
When did Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq die?
Who studied with Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
What are nass and ilm as Ja'far al-Sadiq taught them?
entries.answer:
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 148 AH / 765 CE) is the figure around whom Shia thought decisively crystallised. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he acquired a wide reputation as a teacher and scholar, was a reporter of hadith cited in the chains of transmission (isnad) accepted by all Muslim schools of law, and taught jurisprudence. With his father al-Baqir he is credited with founding the Imami Shia school of religious law, which is named Ja'fari after him.

His standing went well beyond his own followers. IIS notes that he was accepted as a leading authority by many Sunni Muslims too, and that a circle of eminent jurists, traditionists and theologians gathered around him, among them Hisham ibn al-Hakam (d. 795 CE), the foremost representative of Imami scholastic theology (kalam) of the day. IIS also credits him with a significant influence on the development of the mystical interpretation of Islam.

During his Imamate the Shia developed distinct positions in theology and law and took part in the wider intellectual debates of the Muslim world. Out of his and his father's teaching the doctrine of the Imamate received its main outline. Two principles were central. The first was nass, the transfer of the Imamate by explicit designation, which located the office in a particular individual whether or not he held political power; this effectively separated the Imamate from the need for temporal rule. The second was that the Imamate rests on 'ilm, a divinely inspired religious knowledge transmitted through the nass of the preceding Imam, making the Imam of the time the source of knowledge and spiritual teaching for his followers.

Like his father and grandfather, he held no political office. When he died in 765 CE, a dispute over the succession divided the Shia.

entries.title: The succession after Ja'far al-Sadiq: Ismail and Musa al-Kazim
questions: What happened after Ja'far al-Sadiq died?
Who was Imam Ismail?
Why did the Shia split after 765?
Who was Musa al-Kazim?
How did Ismailis and Twelvers separate?
Was Ismail's designation revoked?
Did Ismail die before his father?
When did the Ismaili and Twelver branches form?
entries.answer:
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq died in 765 CE, and a conflict quickly arose over who should be Imam after him. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes this dispute as the point from which the two main Shia communities eventually took shape.

One body of his followers remained loyal to the line of his descendants through his son Ismail, whom they regarded as his designated heir. These became the Ismailis. Others held either that Ismail had already died or that his appointment as heir had been revoked, and turned instead to his brother Musa al-Kazim (d. 799 CE), whom they accepted as Imam. IIS notes that the majority of Ja'far's followers acknowledged Musa.

The group that followed Musa continued through five more Imams after him. They came to be known as the Ithna'ashariyya, the Twelvers, also called Imamis, because they believe their twelfth Imam went into hiding (ghayba) and will one day reappear to bring final salvation to his followers. Twelver accounts record that Musa was constrained by the Abbasid authorities and, according to his followers, poisoned while detained in Baghdad, and that several of the later Imams of this line lived under similar restriction.

The Ismailis instead followed the line through Ismail and his descendants. IIS describes them today as the second largest Shia community after the Twelvers. The third Shia branch, the Zaydis, had a separate history of its own.

IIS writers are careful to add that although this dispute is the point where the communities separated institutionally, Ismailis themselves see their tradition as an expression of attitudes reaching back to the Prophet's lifetime rather than as something founded in the eighth century.

entries.title: How the Ismailis got their name
questions: Why are Ismailis called Ismailis?
Who was Ismail ibn Ja'far?
What does the word Ismaili mean?
Did the Ismailis call themselves that?
Was Ismail the eldest son of Ja'far al-Sadiq?
What did early Ismailis call their movement?
Is the name Ismaili an outsider's label?
entries.answer:
The Ismailis take their name from Ismail, the son of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines Ismailis as adherents of the branch of Shia Islam that considers Ismail to be his father's successor, and describes him as the eponym of the community: those who remained faithful to Ja'far's line through Ismail 'came to be known as Ismailis'.

IIS adds an important qualification about the name. Early Ismaili writers, even under the Fatimids, often preferred terms such as al-da'wa al-hadiya, 'the rightly guided mission', to Isma'iliyya and its variants. The implication that the community originated in a dynastic dispute over one figure comes mostly from hostile, heresiographical writers such as Ibn Rizam, al-Nawbakhti, al-Qummi, al-Ash'ari and al-Baghdadi, whose aim was to place the Ismailis somewhere on a scale of predefined 'orthodoxy' and who therefore branded the movement a heresy.

From the community's own point of view, IIS explains, Ismailism embodies a set of attitudes to truth and to how society should be ordered that can be traced back to the lifetime of the Prophet and the period immediately after his death, centred on the figure of Imam Ali. On that view, looking for a founding date and a founder in the eighth century is a misunderstanding of what the tradition is.

So the name is best read as a historical label for the community that kept to one line of succession, not as the name of a movement that someone set out to establish.

sources.title: The Ismaili Imamat: a brief history

entries.notes: IIS pages are not fully consistent about Ismail's birth order: most describe him as Ja'far al-Sadiq's eldest son and designated heir, while one IIS-published article calls him the second eldest son. Nothing on the allowed sites resolves this.

entries.title: Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail
questions: Who was Muhammad ibn Ismail?
Who came after Imam Ismail?
Why is Muhammad ibn Ismail important to Ismailis?
Did early Ismailis expect Muhammad ibn Ismail to return?
What did early Ismailis believe about the Mahdi?
Who is the seventh Imam for Ismailis?
Why is there little known about Muhammad ibn Ismail?
entries.answer:
Muhammad ibn Ismail was the son of Imam Ismail and a grandson of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. The Institute of Ismaili Studies identifies the Ismailis as those who followed him after the dispute over Ja'far al-Sadiq's succession.

He belongs to the beginning of the long stretch that Ismaili sources call the dawr al-satr, the period of concealment. IIS records that the Imams who followed Ismail maintained anonymity, living in hazardous circumstances while organising the community, so relatively little detailed biography survives for any of them, including Muhammad ibn Ismail.

He also became the focus of a strand of early expectation. IIS explains that the Fatimid-era thinker Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani (d. after 971) used dawr al-satr for the age in which truth is concealed from the senses, an age beginning with Adam that he expected to end with the return of Muhammad ibn Ismail as the Mahdi. This reflects an older current in early Ismailism, described by IIS, in which prophets and Imams were reckoned in groups of seven and a qa'im, the 'seal' of the Imamate, was expected as the seventh Imam, who would disclose the inner meaning of religion once and for all and establish universal justice.

That expectation was later reinterpreted. By the Fatimid period, IIS notes, the notion had changed, so that each Imam was understood to discharge the function that had earlier been assigned to a single awaited qa'im, and each was seen as contributing his share towards the eventual reign of peace and justice.
entries.notes: The allowed sources give no dates or biographical narrative for Muhammad ibn Ismail, and do not name the Imams between him and al-Mahdi. Early groups that stopped the line with him are not discussed on these sites.

entries.title: The period of concealment (dawr al-satr)
questions: What is dawr al-satr?
Why were the Ismaili Imams hidden?
How long did the period of concealment last?
What does satr mean?
Is dawr al-satr the same as the Twelver occultation?
When did the concealment end?
What did the Imams do while in concealment?
Did the term dawr al-satr change meaning over time?
entries.answer:
Dawr al-satr means 'period of concealment'. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that the Fatimid jurist al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 974) used the term for the roughly 150 years during which the Ismaili Imams were hidden from public knowledge, a period that ended with the appearance of Abdallah (also called Ubaydallah) 'al-Mahdi'. In al-Nu'man's vocabulary, al-Mahdi's emergence opened the dawr al-kashf, the period of disclosure.

According to Ismaili sources summarised by IIS, the Imams who succeeded Imam Ismail used this time to organise the community, so that when they emerged publicly in the ninth century they did so with a well-developed body of doctrine and an effective political structure. Concealment therefore did not mean inactivity. One of its features was the use of pseudonyms, and the Imams are said to have settled at Salamiyya in Syria, with their identity and whereabouts known only to a few completely trusted disciples.

It is important not to confuse this with the Twelver doctrine of ghayba. In the Ismaili case the Imams were physically present and leading the community; what was hidden was their identity. In Twelver belief the twelfth Imam himself went into a state of absence.

The term also carried other senses. Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani (d. after 971) used it for the whole age in which truth is veiled from the senses, beginning with Adam. Much later, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (d. 1274) spoke of periods of concealment as times when the Imam's true spiritual reality is not manifested, even though he is physically available.

entries.title: Salamiyya and the early Ismaili mission
questions: What was Salamiyya?
Where were the hidden Ismaili Imams based?
How did the early Ismaili mission work?
When did the Ismaili da'wa begin to spread?
Who knew where the Imams were?
Why was Syria the base of the early Ismailis?
How did the Ismailis keep in touch with scattered communities?
entries.answer:
Salamiyya, a town in Syria, was the headquarters of the Ismaili Imams during the period of concealment. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that by the middle of the ninth century CE the descendants of Imam Ismail, who had been living in hazardous circumstances in various secret localities, had settled there. Their identity and whereabouts were known only to a small number of completely trusted disciples.

From Salamiyya the Imams built and directed a network of emissaries known as the da'wa, the 'summons' or mission. The scholars and local leaders who carried it out were called da'is, 'summoners'. They maintained contact with the Imams and organised themselves into a network bound together by shared commitment to the Imam and by shared intellectual values, which allowed a widely dispersed community to be consolidated and coordinated.

By the middle of the ninth century the da'wa had begun to appear across many regions of the Muslim world. Its message combined an anti-Abbasid campaign with the promise of justice under the rule of the Ismaili Imam, and da'is preached it successfully in Iraq, Yemen, Iran, Central Asia and elsewhere, appealing to people across different strata of society. IIS notes that this made the Ismailis the most politically active wing of Shia Islam in that period.

IIS is clear that the central direction for these widely separated activities came from the Imams, who for most of this period were resident at Salamiyya. When the community stepped into public view at the beginning of the tenth century, it was, as IIS puts it, remarkably well organised and cohesive.

entries.title: The da'wa and the da'is: how the mission was organised
questions: What was the Ismaili da'wa?
What is a da'i?
Were da'is missionaries?
What training did a da'i need?
Where did the early da'wa operate?
Who were Ibn Hawshab and Hamdan Qarmat?
What is a jazira in the da'wa system?
How did da'is teach ordinary people?
entries.answer:
The da'wa was the organised mission through which the Ismaili Imams reached scattered communities. The word is not exclusively Ismaili, but the Institute of Ismaili Studies argues that the skill of the organisation and the elaborate communications network built within it were distinctively so.

IIS insists that 'missionary' or 'propagandist' are poor translations of da'i. The ideal da'i, as Ismaili circles came to describe him, was expected to lead an ethically exemplary life and to command the highest intellectual sciences of the day: logic, rhetoric and jurisprudence, alongside diplomacy and a gift for dealing with people. The da'i Ahmad al-Naysaburi listed qualities including the expertise of a skilled lawyer, patience, intelligence, psychological insight, honesty, sound judgement, generosity, administrative ability, tact and tolerance. A da'i went out not only to summon people to the rightful Imam but to promote the social, moral and spiritual welfare of his followers.

Teaching was graded and adapted. Da'is chose their examples and arguments to suit their audience: speaking to a tailor about needle, thread and scissors, to a shepherd about his staff and flock. IIS relates this to a Qur'anic principle that the Prophet should address each person according to their capacity. Initiates took an oath and were led step by step into deeper understanding.

By the late ninth century a hierarchy was in place, with officials assigned to geographical regions called jaza'ir (singular jazira). Main areas of activity included Yemen, where the da'i Ibn Hawshab, helped by Ali ibn al-Fadl, had a secure base by 881 CE; Kufa, where Hamdan Qarmat founded a mission; Khurasan and Transoxiana; Sind, where Ibn Hawshab's nephew al-Haytham won over the local ruler; and North Africa.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide

entries.title: Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i and the Kutama Berbers
questions: Who was Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i?
How did the Fatimids come to power in North Africa?
Who were the Kutama Berbers?
What did Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i achieve?
How was the Imam rescued at Sijilmasa?
What was Raqqada?
Who were the Aghlabids?
entries.answer:
Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i (d. 911 CE) was the da'i whose work in North Africa made the Fatimid caliphate possible. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he won the support of the Kutama Berbers, and that the base he built among them anticipated the political and religious goal that the Fatimid dynasty later realised.

IIS presents Sind and North Africa as the two clearest illustrations of how a da'i could succeed. In Sind, al-Haytham and his supporters converted the ruler and established control, so that an Ismaili principality already existed there by the time the Fatimids came to power. In North Africa, Abu Abdallah's Kutama following gave the movement an army.

The decisive moment came at the beginning of the tenth century. The Imam Abd Allah, also called Ubayd Allah, had travelled from Syria and arrived at Sijilmasa, in the far west, where he was held by his opponents. The da'i's forces rescued him and brought him to Raqqada, which had already been taken from the ruling Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya, the medieval name for what is now Tunisia. Early in 910 CE, by the dating IIS uses in this account, the Imam was proclaimed amir al-mu'minin, 'commander of the believers', with the title al-Mahdi.

IIS elsewhere gives 297 AH / 909 CE as the founding date of the caliphate, and treats the proclamation as the opening of the Ismaili attempt to give concrete shape to their vision of an Islamic polity. A reading guide published by IIS lists Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, alongside al-Qadi al-Nu'man, as one of the two most important da'is of the period.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide

entries.notes: IIS materials date the proclamation of al-Mahdi both to 909 CE (297 AH) and, in one narrative account, to early 910 CE. The sources do not explain the difference; 909 is the date IIS uses for the founding of the caliphate.

entries.title: The Qarmatians (Carmatians)
questions: Who were the Qarmatians?
What does Qarmati mean?
Why did the Qarmatians break away?
Who was Hamdan Qarmat?
What happened at Mecca in 930?
Were the Qarmatians the same as the Fatimids?
Where was the Qarmatian state?
How did the Qarmatians affect the Ismaili reputation?
entries.answer:
Qaramita, singular Qarmati, is the name of a dissident branch of the Ismailis that took shape in the ninth century CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that Hamdan Qarmat established a mission at Kufa in southern Iraq and was later to split from the main da'wa, and that the Ismailis of that region became known after him.

By 899 CE the Ismaili Imams, who had until then led the movement in secret from various headquarters, emerged from their underground existence. Around the same time a faction of the community disagreed with the central leadership over certain doctrinal issues and seceded; this is the group later designated Qarmati.

The dissidents founded a powerful state of their own in Bahrayn, in eastern Arabia. IIS describes a long and damaging period of hostility that followed, directed both against Ismailis loyal to the Imams and against other Muslims, culminating in their attack on Mecca in 930 CE. IIS also describes the Qarmatians as a comparatively 'extreme' offshoot, greatly feared across the Muslim world, engaged in a long drawn out period of hostility against the Fatimids. Relations between the Fatimids and the Qarmatiyya of Bahrayn were still hostile a century later, under the imam-caliph al-Hakim.

IIS notes the long consequence: enemies of the Ismailis capitalised on the Qarmatians' violent reputation to discredit the entire Ismaili community. Distinguishing the Qarmatians from the Fatimid Ismailis is therefore an important correction in modern scholarship.

entries.title: The founding of the Fatimid caliphate (909 CE)
questions: When was the Fatimid caliphate founded?
Where did the Fatimid caliphate begin?
Why are they called Fatimids?
What was significant about 909 CE?
Was the Fatimid caliphate the first Shia state?
Who founded the Fatimid caliphate?
How long did the Fatimid caliphate last?
What did the Fatimids want to achieve?
entries.answer:
The Fatimid caliphate was established in 297 AH / 909 CE in Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia, and lasted until 1171 CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as the crowning success of the early Ismaili da'wa and as the first major Shia state.

The dynasty took the name al-Fatimiyyun, rendered in English as Fatimids, after Fatima, the Prophet's daughter and the wife of Imam Ali, from whom the Imams traced their descent. They were Ismaili Imams ruling as caliphs, which is why IIS and other Imamat institutions usually call them imam-caliphs.

What made 909 significant was the change in kind. Until then the Imams had led a clandestine movement from concealment; now the Ismaili Imam was also the head of a state, and the theological claim that the Imam should hold both religious and temporal authority took institutional form. The proclamation of Abd Allah al-Mahdi as the first Fatimid caliph marked, in the IIS formulation, the beginning of the Ismaili attempt to give concrete shape to their vision of Shia Islam.

It also set up a direct rivalry. The Fatimids challenged the legitimacy of the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, and the two dynasties competed across vast territories for the allegiance of Muslims generally. That competition shaped Fatimid policy, including their lavish patronage of scholars and scientists.

IIS highlights the pluralist character of the state. The Imamat's own account describes the Fatimid caliphate as notable for religious tolerance and intellectual achievement, and as one of the more successful attempts in Muslim history to avoid both despotism and anarchy.

entries.title: Imam-caliph Abd Allah al-Mahdi (r. 909-934 CE)
questions: Who was al-Mahdi, the first Fatimid caliph?
What does the title al-Mahdi mean?
When did al-Mahdi rule?
What city did al-Mahdi found?
How did al-Mahdi come to power?
Was al-Mahdi also called Ubayd Allah?
What did al-Mahdi do as ruler?
entries.answer:
Abd Allah al-Mahdi, also recorded as Ubayd Allah, was the Ismaili Imam who founded the Fatimid caliphate. The Institute of Ismaili Studies gives his reign as 297-322 AH / 909-934 CE and names him as the first Fatimid caliph.

His emergence closed the dawr al-satr. Al-Qadi al-Nu'man, who entered his service in 313 AH / 925 CE, described his appearance as the end of the period of concealment and the beginning of the period of disclosure. He had travelled from Syria to North Africa; after being rescued from custody at Sijilmasa by the forces of the da'i Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, he was brought to Raqqada and proclaimed amir al-mu'minin, commander of the believers, with the title al-Mahdi, 'the guided one', which IIS glosses as equivalent to 'the saviour'.

He founded a new capital on the Tunisian coast named al-Mahdiyya after himself. IIS quotes a medieval account describing how he travelled in person along the whole coast, visiting Tunis, Carthage and other places, looking for a site that would make him and his successors secure, and settled on the spot where al-Mahdiyya now stands. The city was a palace city, home to the royal family, the administration and a naval base. The mosque he built for himself still survives and was restored in the 1960s.

Under al-Mahdi and his successors the Fatimids built a powerful army and navy. Coins struck in his name and in that of his successor followed the style used by the Aghlabid rulers of Tunisia whom they had displaced, with a marginal inscription around a central field.

entries.title: Imam-caliphs al-Qa'im and al-Mansur, and the North African capitals
questions: Who was al-Qa'im bi-Amr Allah?
Who was al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah?
What was the revolt of Abu Yazid?
What was al-Mansuriyya?
Where was the Fatimid capital before Cairo?
When did al-Qa'im and al-Mansur rule?
What challenges did the early Fatimids face in North Africa?
entries.answer:
The second and third Fatimid imam-caliphs ruled from North Africa in a period of consolidation and serious danger.

Al-Qa'im bi-Amr Allah reigned 322-334 AH / 934-946 CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that coins struck in his name kept the older Aghlabid style; a gold dinar of 331 AH / 942-943 CE from the mint at al-Mahdiyya carries his regnal title alongside Qur'anic verses in the margins.

Al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah reigned 334-341 AH / 946-953 CE. His title, 'the victorious', reflects the crisis he inherited. The Berbers of North Africa resisted Fatimid authority, and under the Khariji leader Abu Yazid they mounted a long revolt. It was suppressed, and by the middle of the tenth century the Fatimids had re-established their dominion over the region.

IIS records that the early Fatimids faced pressure from several directions at once: the risk of splinter movements within the da'wa as it was centralised, the hostility of the Qarmatians of Bahrayn, the opposition of the Abbasids and of other dynasties, and Berber resistance.

Both rulers left cities behind them. Al-Mahdi had founded al-Mahdiyya on the Tunisian coast; in 335 AH / 946 CE al-Mansur ordered the construction of a new palace city half a mile southeast of Qayrawan, officially called al-Mansuriyya, 'the victorious city'. The capital moved there from al-Mahdiyya, and IIS notes that al-Mansuriyya later served as a model for Cairo. A gold dinar of 341 AH / 952-953 CE bearing the mint name al-Mansuriyya shows a more open design, with the inscription set within concentric circles.

The North African phase lasted 64 years, from 909 to 973 CE, spanning the reigns of al-Mahdi, al-Qa'im, al-Mansur and al-Mu'izz.

entries.title: Imam-caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah (r. 953-975 CE)
questions: Who was al-Mu'izz?
Which Fatimid caliph took Egypt?
What kind of ruler was al-Mu'izz?
When did al-Mu'izz reign?
Who was Jawhar?
What languages did al-Mu'izz know?
What did al-Mu'izz bring with him to Cairo?
entries.answer:
Al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, the fourth Fatimid imam-caliph, reigned 341-365 AH / 953-975 CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes his reign as the point at which Fatimid military, political and religious achievement reached its height.

The central event was the acquisition of Egypt. In 969 CE his general Jawhar took the country, which IIS materials describe as having been acquired peacefully; Jawhar then governed Egypt from 969 to 973 CE. The building of the new city of Cairo began at once, and in 970 CE the foundation of the al-Azhar mosque was laid. Around the same time Mecca and Medina came under Fatimid control. Al-Mu'izz himself arrived in Cairo in 973 CE, accompanied by his sons, brothers and uncles and by the other descendants of al-Mahdi, and bringing with him the coffins of his three predecessors, al-Mahdi, al-Qa'im and al-Mansur.

IIS describes him as an excellent planner, an efficient organiser and a statesman with a real gift for diplomacy. One older account quoted by IIS adds that he was highly educated: he wrote Arabic poetry and loved its literature, studied Greek, mastered Berber and Sudani dialects, and was said to have taught himself a Slavonic language as well; he was eloquent, generous and known for a love of justice.

His reign also shows in the coinage. A distinctive Fatimid style appears under him, abandoning the horizontal central field in favour of three concentric bands of calligraphy. A gold dinar of 358 AH / 969 CE, the first Fatimid coinage struck in Egypt, carries this design, with phrases of specifically Shia character in the middle circle.

It was al-Mu'izz who confirmed al-Qadi al-Nu'man as chief judge and authorised him to hold the 'sessions of wisdom'.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide
Documents of History, Symbols of Authority: The Coinage of the Fatimids

entries.notes: IIS materials vary slightly on the date of the Fatimid takeover of Egypt, giving 969 CE in most accounts and 973 CE in one; 973 is the year al-Mu'izz himself moved to Cairo.

entries.title: The founding of Cairo (969-973 CE)
questions: Who founded Cairo?
When was Cairo founded?
What does al-Qahira mean?
Why did the Fatimids build a new capital?
What was Cairo like under the Fatimids?
When did Cairo become the Fatimid capital?
What were the Fatimid palaces in Cairo like?
entries.answer:
Cairo, in Arabic al-Qahira, was founded by the Fatimids in 969 CE, and in 973 CE the imam-caliph al-Mu'izz transferred the capital there from North Africa. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that the building work began as soon as the general Jawhar took Egypt.

From then on Cairo was the centre of a far-flung empire. At its height Fatimid territory reached westward across North Africa to Sicily and other Mediterranean islands, and eastward to Palestine, Syria, Yemen and the Hijaz with Mecca and Medina. IIS notes that Fatimid strength rested significantly on naval power; Crete, Corsica, Malta and Sicily came under their control, giving them a measure of command over the Mediterranean, and ports such as al-Mahdiyya served a flourishing maritime trade. In 1058 CE the Fatimids briefly occupied Baghdad.

The city itself became a magnet. IIS describes Cairo drawing mathematicians, physicians and astronomers from across the Muslim world, and functioning as an inland port linking Mediterranean and Red Sea trade. The Persian traveller Nasir-i Khusraw, writing in the eleventh century, estimated that Cairo had no fewer than twenty thousand shops, stocked with goods from all over the world.

The scholar Oleg Grabar, in an essay published by IIS, argues that the Fatimids' most obvious legacy was the transformation of Egypt, at the time barely Islamicised and economically exploited by others, into a major centre of Islamic culture, and that instead of elevating some minor town into a temporary capital they coalesced Cairo into one of the great metropolises of the Muslim world for more than a millennium.

The completion of the city walls is commemorated on a rare gold dinar of 394 AH / 1003-1004 CE bearing the mint name al-Qahira al-Mahrusa, 'Cairo the Protected'.

sources.title: Documents of History, Symbols of Authority: The Coinage of the Fatimids

entries.title: Al-Azhar
questions: Who founded al-Azhar?
When was al-Azhar built?
Why is it called al-Azhar?
Was al-Azhar always Sunni?
What was taught at al-Azhar under the Fatimids?
Could women study at al-Azhar?
Is al-Azhar the oldest university?
What is the link between al-Azhar and Fatima?
entries.answer:
Al-Azhar in Cairo was founded by the Fatimid Ismaili dynasty. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that the Imam al-Mu'izz acquired Egypt in 969 CE, that the building of the new city of Cairo began under his general Jawhar, and that the foundation for the al-Azhar mosque was laid in 970 CE; the Imam himself arrived in Cairo in 973 CE.

IIS describes al-Azhar as the chief Cairo mosque, built by the Imam and Caliph al-Mu'izz and endowed by his successors, which became a great centre of learning and the primary centre of learning in Fatimid Cairo.

IIS notes an important distinction in what was taught there. Rather than being the centre for esoteric Ismaili da'wa teaching, as is sometimes assumed, al-Azhar was where the outward meaning of the law, the shari'a, was taught according to the Ismaili interpretation. These sessions were open to everyone, including women. The inner meaning of the law was taught separately, in the majalis al-hikma held in the Imam's palace, which were open only to initiates who had already pledged their allegiance to the Imam.

The mosque is also a monument of Fatimid architecture. In an essay published by IIS, Oleg Grabar lists it alongside the mosque of al-Hakim among the best known large Fatimid mosques of Egypt.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide

entries.notes: The allowed sources cover al-Azhar only in the Fatimid period. They do not explain its name, and they say nothing about its later history as a Sunni institution, so neither point is made here.

entries.title: Imam-caliph al-Aziz billah (r. 975-996 CE)
questions: Who was al-Aziz billah?
When did al-Aziz rule?
What happened under al-Aziz?
Who succeeded al-Mu'izz?
Who was al-Hakim's father?
What do we know about al-Aziz's coinage?
entries.answer:
Al-Aziz billah was the fifth Fatimid imam-caliph, reigning 365-386 AH / 975-996 CE. He succeeded al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, under whom the Fatimids had taken Egypt and founded Cairo, and he was the father of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies gives comparatively little narrative detail about his reign on its public pages. A reading guide published by IIS notes that his rule, together with that of al-Mu'izz, receives fair consideration in the scholarly literature on the Fatimids in Egypt, though attention has tended to concentrate on his son al-Hakim.

What IIS does record concretely comes from the coinage. Only one coinage type is known from his reign, with the inscriptions arranged in double concentric circles on both faces of the coin. From 386 AH / 996 CE onwards, that is, from the accession of al-Hakim, Fatimid coins began to carry the distinctively Shia legend attesting to the walaya of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib, in the phrase 'Ali wali Allah'.

IIS records his death in 996 CE, and that his son Abu Ali Mansur, then eleven years old, succeeded him on 28 Ramadan 386 / 14 October 996 with the caliphal title al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah. Al-Hakim had been proclaimed heir apparent (wali al-ahd) in 383 AH / 993 CE, on the death of his elder and only brother Muhammad.

This was the period in which Fatimid Egypt was consolidating the position it had won under al-Mu'izz, with Cairo established as the capital of a wide empire.

entries.title: Imam-caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (r. 996-1021 CE)
questions: Who was al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah?
Why is al-Hakim controversial?
What happened to al-Hakim?
When did al-Hakim rule?
Was al-Hakim a persecutor?
What did al-Hakim found?
How old was al-Hakim when he became caliph?
How did al-Hakim disappear?
entries.answer:
Abu Ali Mansur, who took the caliphal title al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, was the sixth Fatimid caliph and sixteenth Ismaili Imam, reigning 386-411 AH / 996-1021 CE. Born in 375 AH / 985 CE, he was the first Fatimid ruler born in Egypt, and he succeeded his father al-Aziz at the age of eleven.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies calls him arguably the most controversial member of the dynasty. His reign brought many difficulties: Ismaili communities in North Africa were massacred by Sunni mobs led by influential Maliki jurists, relations with the Qarmatians of Bahrayn stayed hostile, and rivalries between the Berber and Turkish factions of the army overshadowed everything else. His Syrian policy, by contrast, succeeded, extending Fatimid authority to the emirate of Aleppo. After removing his powerful intermediary Barjawan in 390 AH / 1000 CE he governed directly, limiting the authority and terms of his viziers, of whom there were more than fifteen in his remaining twenty years.

He took a close interest in the da'wa, which was systematically intensified outside Fatimid territory, especially in Iraq and Persia, where the theologian-philosopher Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani was the foremost da'i. He founded the Dar al-Ilm in 395 AH / 1005 CE, reorganised the 'sessions of wisdom', funded them himself and often attended, and completed the Friday mosque in Cairo that still bears his name.

IIS records that Christian and Sunni chroniclers painted a highly distorted picture of him as erratic and persecuting, but that modern scholarship, working from his own edicts (sijillat) and the circumstances of his reign, is producing a different account, in which he appears as a tactful leader popular with his subjects.

In his last years he turned increasingly to asceticism. On the night of 27 Shawwal 411 / 13 February 1021 he rode out to the Muqattam hills outside Cairo and never returned; only his donkey and bloodstained garments were found, and the mystery was never solved.

entries.title: Dar al-Ilm, the House of Knowledge (founded 1005 CE)
questions: What was Dar al-Ilm?
Who founded the House of Knowledge?
When was Dar al-Ilm founded?
What was taught at Dar al-Ilm?
Was Dar al-Ilm open to non-Muslims?
How big was the Dar al-Ilm library?
What happened to Dar al-Ilm?
What is Dar al-Hikma?
entries.answer:
Dar al-Ilm, the 'House of Knowledge', sometimes also called Dar al-Hikma, was founded in Cairo by the imam-caliph al-Hakim in 395 AH / 1005 CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as one of his most important contributions in education and learning, and as a leading institution of its age.

Its distinguishing feature was breadth. Its programme combined a wide range of disciplines, from the Qur'an and hadith to jurisprudence, philology and grammar, medicine, logic, mathematics and astronomy. IIS notes that this united religious and non-religious fields in a way that was unusual in Islamic intellectual history, treating knowledge as one interconnected enterprise rather than a set of separate specialisms.

It was equipped with a vast library, which IIS puts at over 400,000 manuscripts, and its facilities were open to the public and to followers of different religions. Lectures were given there by Qur'an readers, astronomers, grammarians, philologists and physicians. Many Fatimid da'is received at least part of their training there, and the institution served the da'wa until the fall of the dynasty.

IIS quotes the fifteenth-century Egyptian chronicler al-Maqrizi, whose Khitat remains a principal source for Fatimid history, on how its endowment was spent: sums for mats and household effects, for the copyist's paper, for the librarian, for water, for a servant, for paper, ink and writing reeds for the scholars, for repairing curtains and torn books, and for felt blankets and carpets in winter.

The institution's roots ran deep enough that struggles over its survival, and over the building of an observatory, continued even during the political and military disintegration of the Fatimid state.

entries.title: The sessions of wisdom (majalis al-hikma)
questions: What were the majalis al-hikma?
Where were the sessions of wisdom held?
Who could attend the sessions of wisdom?
What was taught in the majalis al-hikma?
Who gave the sessions of wisdom?
Did the Imam approve the lectures?
How did the sessions of wisdom differ from teaching at al-Azhar?
entries.answer:
The majalis al-hikma, 'sessions of wisdom', were the Fatimids' teaching sessions in the esoteric dimension of the faith. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them as held in the Imam's palace in Cairo and open only to initiates who had already pledged allegiance to the Imam.

This was the counterpart to the public teaching at al-Azhar. IIS draws the distinction carefully: at al-Azhar the outward meaning of the law, the shari'a, was taught according to the Ismaili interpretation, in sessions open to everyone, including women. The inner meaning belonged to the majalis al-hikma.

The content was the esoteric Ismaili sciences, known collectively as hikma, together with ta'wil, the esoteric interpretation of the Qur'an and of the commandments of the law. IIS records that all lectures delivered in the sessions were reviewed and approved by the Imam before being given, which kept the teaching consistent across a scattered empire. The sessions were not only instructional: they were also an occasion on which charitable dues were submitted.

The imam-caliph al-Mu'izz authorised al-Qadi al-Nu'man to hold the sessions every Friday in the royal palace, and much of the surviving literature comes from that tradition. Under al-Hakim the sessions were reorganised so as to be accessible to different categories of participants, with financial support and endowments provided; IIS records that al-Hakim often attended in person.

Together with al-Azhar and the Dar al-Ilm, the majalis al-hikma made up a layered educational system in which different levels of teaching were matched to different audiences.

entries.title: The 'Baghdad manifesto' and the question of Fatimid descent
questions: Were the Fatimids really descended from the Prophet?
What was the Baghdad manifesto?
Why did the Abbasids attack Fatimid ancestry?
Who disputed the Fatimids' lineage?
When was the Baghdad manifesto issued?
How did the Fatimids justify their claim to the caliphate?
Was the dispute about genealogy political?
entries.answer:
The Fatimids claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his daughter Fatima and Imam Ali, and took their dynastic name from her. This claim was the basis of their right to the caliphate, and it was fiercely contested by their rivals.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the sharpest episode. In the reign of al-Hakim, Fatimid da'is working in Iraq had won over local rulers: in 401 AH / 1010 CE the Shia Uqaylid ruler of Mosul, Kufa and other towns acknowledged al-Hakim's suzerainty, and the chief of the Banu Asad declared his loyalty in Hilla. Others followed. Alarmed at Ismailism spreading into the heart of his own realm, the Abbasid caliph al-Qadir retaliated. In 402 AH / 1011 CE he assembled Sunni and Twelver Imami Shia scholars at his court and directed them to sign a written declaration that al-Hakim and his predecessors lacked genuine Alid ancestry. This so-called 'Baghdad manifesto' was read out in Friday mosques across Abbasid territory. Al-Qadir also commissioned refutations of Ismaili doctrine.

IIS places this in a wider pattern. The Fatimid imam-caliphs had successfully challenged Abbasid legitimacy, and in doing so became ready targets for the polemical attacks of the Abbasids and of the scholars who legitimised them. In a period when two caliphates were competing across vast territories for the allegiance of Muslims, accusations of heresy and of false genealogy were weapons of statecraft.

Ismailis hold that the Imamat is a hereditary office descending in the Prophet's bloodline through Ali and Fatima, and the Fatimid Imams within that line. IIS treats the manifesto as a polemical document produced under political pressure rather than as a historical finding.

entries.title: The origins of the Druze movement in al-Hakim's time
questions: How did the Druze religion begin?
What is the connection between the Druze and al-Hakim?
Did al-Hakim claim to be divine?
Who were Hamza and Darzi?
How did the Ismaili leadership respond to the Druze movement?
When did the Druze movement start?
Are the Druze Ismailis?
entries.answer:
The Druze religion had its beginnings in the closing years of the imam-caliph al-Hakim's reign. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that from around 408 AH / 1017 CE a number of da'is who had come to Cairo from Persia and Central Asia, prominent among them Hasan Akram, Hamza ibn Ali and Muhammad Darzi (Darazi), began propagating new doctrines that attributed divinity to al-Hakim and proclaimed that the era of Islam had ended. The movement was later named after Darzi.

IIS is explicit on two points. First, contrary to the claims of later Sunni authors, there is no evidence that al-Hakim himself encouraged these teachings. Second, the leadership of the Fatimid da'wa opposed the movement categorically: the chief da'i Khatkin al-Dayf summoned Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, the most accomplished Ismaili theologian-philosopher of the Fatimid period, to Cairo to refute the new doctrines on theological grounds. Al-Kirmani wrote several works to that end, which succeeded in checking the spread of such ideas within the inner circles of the da'wa.

The movement nevertheless caused considerable unrest in al-Hakim's last years. Elsewhere IIS notes that immediately after his reign a group who preferred to remain faithful to his memory broke away from the Fatimid da'wa, and that this is the origin of what became the Druze community.

The Druze are therefore best described as a separate religious tradition that emerged out of the Fatimid Ismaili milieu and was rejected by the Ismaili da'wa at the time, rather than as a branch of Ismailism.

entries.title: Imam-caliphs al-Zahir and al-Mustansir (1021-1094 CE)
questions: Who was al-Zahir li-I'zaz Din Allah?
Who was al-Mustansir billah?
How long did al-Mustansir reign?
What was the great famine in Egypt?
When did the Fatimid empire reach its peak?
What problems did the later Fatimids face?
What did the Fatimids build in Jerusalem?
Why is al-Mustansir's death important?
entries.answer:
Al-Zahir li-I'zaz Din Allah reigned 411-427 AH / 1021-1036 CE, following the disappearance of his father al-Hakim. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records three coinage styles from his reign. His period also saw substantial Fatimid building in Jerusalem: an essay published by IIS notes that after the shortening of the city walls in his time, and devastating earthquakes early in the eleventh century, major reconstruction was needed, and that after the Umayyads the Fatimids were responsible for the most consistent building up of the Haram al-Sharif, including the celebrated mosaics of the Aqsa mosque.

His son al-Mustansir billah reigned 427-487 AH / 1036-1094 CE, one of the longest reigns in Islamic history. IIS describes the Fatimid caliphate as reaching the peak of its power during his long reign. Fatimid forces briefly occupied Baghdad in 1058 CE, and the da'wa made significant gains: the da'i Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi secured Yemen, da'is went to Gujarat and along the western coast of India, and Nasir-i Khusraw preached in the Upper Oxus region, writing works in Persian that became part of the heritage of the Ismailis of Badakhshan.

The same reign brought grave difficulties. A great famine caused widespread suffering. Sections of the army, made up of Berbers, Turks, Sudanese and Armenians, fought one another. Territories were lost: Mahmud of Ghazna's forces devastated Sind and massacred Ismailis there, and around mid-century Ifriqiya was lost to a local rebellion in favour of the Abbasids, again with massacres of Ismaili communities.

The crisis brought Badr al-Jamali to power, and al-Mustansir's death in 1094 CE produced the permanent split between Nizari and Musta'li Ismailis.

entries.title: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 974 CE)
questions: Who was al-Qadi al-Nu'man?
Who founded Fatimid Ismaili law?
What did al-Qadi al-Nu'man do?
Which Fatimid caliphs did al-Nu'man serve?
When did al-Qadi al-Nu'man die?
Was al-Nu'man a convert?
What was the mazalim?
Why is al-Nu'man important?
entries.answer:
Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad al-Tamimi, universally known as al-Qadi al-Nu'man, was the foremost Ismaili jurist and the founder of Fatimid Ismaili jurisprudence. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he was born around 290 AH / 903 CE into a learned family in Qayrawan, in North Africa, and that his father was apparently a convert to Ismaili Shi'ism from Maliki Sunnism, the prevailing Sunni school in Ifriqiya.

Educated as an Ismaili, he entered the service of Abd Allah al-Mahdi in 313 AH / 925 CE and went on to serve the first four Fatimid imam-caliphs. He was at various times keeper of the palace library and judge of Tripoli and of al-Mansuriyya, the new capital from 337 AH / 948 CE. In that same year the imam-caliph al-Mansur appointed him chief judge (qadi al-qudat) of the Fatimid state. Al-Mu'izz confirmed him in the post and in 343 AH / 954 CE also entrusted him with the mazalim, the grievance proceedings, throughout the caliphate.

He was equally central to teaching. Al-Mu'izz authorised him to hold the majalis al-hikma every Friday in the royal palace, instructing Ismaili audiences in the esoteric sciences and in ta'wil, the inner interpretation of the Qur'an and of the commandments of the law.

He accompanied al-Mu'izz to Egypt in 362 AH / 973 CE and died in Cairo on the last day of Jumada II 363 AH, 27 March 974 CE. The imam-caliph led his funeral prayer in person.

IIS also cites his historical vocabulary: he wrote of the iftitah al-da'wa, the opening phase of the mission, and the ibtida al-dawla, the inception of the state, terms that help modern historians reconstruct how the da'wa worked.

entries.title: The Da'a'im al-Islam and Fatimid Ismaili law
questions: What is the Da'a'im al-Islam?
How did Ismaili law differ from Sunni law?
What is walaya?
Whose hadith did Ismaili law rely on?
Did the Fatimids follow the shari'a?
What is the role of qiyas and ijma in Ismaili law?
Who wrote the Pillars of Islam?
How was Fatimid law applied in practice?
entries.answer:
The Da'a'im al-Islam, 'The Pillars of Islam', is al-Qadi al-Nu'man's great work of jurisprudence and the foundation of Fatimid Ismaili law. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as a systematic, logical treatment of the principles of jurisprudence that sets out a body of rules governing the life of the believer from birth to death.

IIS stresses a point often overlooked: the Ismailis recognised the law of Islam and urged scrupulous observance of it. The Fatimids insisted on careful adherence to Islamic practice, and fiqh was one of the major sciences to which Ismaili scholars devoted themselves. The outward dimension, the zahir, was understood as the letter of the law promulgated by the Prophet, and it formed the foundation of the faith even though the Ismailis gave a higher stature to the batin, the inner meaning, which they held to extend the zahir without contradicting it.

The Ismaili shari'a therefore shared much with the Sunni one, with two important differences. It rested on the principle of walaya, devotion to the Imams, which al-Nu'man treats as the foremost of the pillars. And its legal materials derive from traditions going back to the recognised Ismaili Imams rather than to the Prophet's companions in general. Principles important in Sunni fiqh, such as qiyas (analogical deduction) and ijma (communal consensus), are here subordinate to the authoritative guidance of the Imam.

The work also carries doctrine. In it al-Nu'man distinguishes islam (submission) from iman (faith) on the basis of Qur'an 49:14, arguing that one can be a Muslim without yet being a mu'min, since true faith involves belief in and devotion to the rightful Imam. He grounds the claim in Imam Ali's closeness to the Prophet and in the declaration at Ghadir Khumm.

entries.title: The da'wa beyond Fatimid territory
questions: Did Ismailism spread outside Egypt?
Why did Ismailism not take root in North Africa?
Where was the Fatimid da'wa most successful?
How did Ismailism survive after the Fatimids fell?
Who was Nasir-i Khusraw?
What happened to Ismailis in Sind and Yemen?
How did the da'wa work inside the Fatimid state?
entries.answer:
The Fatimid da'wa had a curious record: it was weakest where the state was strongest.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that inside the Fatimid state the da'wa enjoyed unbridled freedom to propagate the faith and develop its ideas, and its structure was continually refined and expanded. Yet the Fatimids' own policies of tolerance and religious freedom meant that Ismailism never rooted deeply in the North African population, and it remained a minority faith there for the whole of Fatimid rule.

Outside Fatimid territory the picture was different. The da'wa established substantial Ismaili communities across Asia and into the Indian subcontinent, and IIS argues that it is this stability, achieved beyond the frontiers of the state, that allowed Ismailism to survive and continue after Fatimid rule declined.

The records bear this out. The da'i Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi secured the allegiance of Yemen; from there efforts were made to re-establish a presence in Sind after the massacres carried out by Mahmud of Ghazna. Da'is also travelled to Gujarat and along the western coast of India. In the Upper Oxus region the eminent da'i Nasir-i Khusraw (d. after 1070 CE) preached with lasting results, and the Persian works he wrote during his stay at Yumgan became an integral part of the heritage of the Ismailis of Badakhshan. In Iran the da'wa persisted, though after the rise of the militantly Sunni Saljuq dynasty, one of whose declared aims was to exterminate Fatimid influence, it had to operate undercover.

Because the empire's parts were separated by vast distances, IIS notes, geographical disconnection had to be compensated for by ideological loyalty, which the da'is sustained.
