entries.title: Learning and science under the Fatimids
questions: Why were the Fatimids famous for learning?
What science was done in Fatimid Egypt?
Who was Ibn al-Haytham?
Which thinkers flourished under the Fatimids?
Did Fatimid learning reach Europe?
Why did the Fatimids patronise scholars?
What is the Ismaili attitude to reason and faith?
What did Fatimid writers contribute to Muslim thought?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies judges that it was in intellectual life that Fatimid achievement was most brilliant. The imam-caliphs were lavish patrons of learning, and their encouragement of scientific research drew mathematicians, physicians and astronomers to Cairo from across the Muslim world, regardless of religious persuasion, along with poets, historians and geographers such as Ibn Hani, Tamim ibn al-Mu'izz, al-Musabbihi and al-Muhallabi.

IIS gives several reasons for this. In Shia theology the Imam possesses a special 'ilm through which he interprets revelation, which gave a spiritual motive for valuing knowledge. The Fatimids had come to power through a movement with complex intellectual doctrines, and the close link between state and da'wa reinforced teaching. They were also competing with the Abbasids of Baghdad and the Umayyads of Spain for the leadership of Muslims, and patronising the best minds was part of that contest.

The outstanding scientific figure is Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra in 965 CE, a polymath invited to Cairo by al-Hakim to lead the construction of a dam across the Nile. The dam project came to nothing, but he wrote widely on physics, philosophy, astronomy, mathematics and medicine. In his Kitab al-manazir, on optics, he refuted the theory of Euclid and Ptolemy that the eye emits rays towards what it sees, arguing instead that the form of the object passes into the eye through a transparent body. European scientists confirmed this centuries later.

On the Ismaili side, thinkers such as Abu Hatim al-Razi, Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani, al-Nasafi, Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi and Nasir-i Khusraw used the philosophical tools of the age, including Neoplatonic ideas, to expound tawhid, prophecy and the Imamate. IIS notes one scholar's comparison of this flowering to eighteenth-century Europe, and that the influence of Cairo's academic institutions reached the West, contributing to optics, medicine and astronomy.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide

entries.title: Fatimid art and architecture
questions: What was Fatimid art like?
What did the Fatimids build?
What is muqarnas?
Why is Fatimid art considered original?
What materials did Fatimid artists work in?
Where can Fatimid art be seen?
What influences shaped Fatimid art?
What is the al-Aqmar mosque?
entries.answer:
The Fatimid period produced some of the finest work in the history of Muslim civilisation. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that over two hundred categories of artisan existed under Fatimid rule, and that surviving carved woodwork, textiles, ceramics, stone and ivory, glass, metalwork and jewellery give a glimpse of the magnificence that once surrounded the court. Oleg Grabar, whose essay IIS publishes, described Fatimid art as both a culmination of older traditions and a forerunner of later developments; Louis Massignon called the tenth century 'the Ismaili century of Islam'.

The best known Fatimid buildings are in Egypt: large mosques such as al-Azhar and the mosque of al-Hakim, small ones such as al-Aqmar, mausoleums in Cairo, Qus and Aswan, palaces, fortifications and ceremonial gates. Grabar argues that most of this architecture is conservative in its forms, but that several changes proved far-reaching. Small mosques reflected a shift of patronage from the state to private individuals, which spread across the Muslim world and expressed a plurality of pious ways rather than a single model. Large congregational mosques became settings for elaborate royal ceremonial, with formal entries, changes of vestments, incense, chanting and processions. Only one architectural function was genuinely new, the mausoleum, and only one new form, the muqarnas, the stalactite-like vaulting that became a standing feature of Islamic architecture thereafter. Composed façades with decorated central gates and corner minarets also developed in Fatimid Tunisia.

In representational art, Grabar points to an unusually high number of surviving images across all media, and to a striking mixture of sources: Iraqi Abbasid elements, local Egyptian traditions, Hellenistic and ancient Egyptian memories, and Byzantine devices. He suggests that under the Fatimids wider segments of society were able to express their own taste than anywhere else in the Muslim world at the time.

The Fatimids also built extensively at the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem.

The Art Lovers who founded Cairo

entries.title: The Fatimid economy, trade and coinage
questions: How rich were the Fatimids?
What did the Fatimids trade?
Why were Fatimid gold dinars famous?
What can coins tell us about Fatimid history?
Where were Fatimid coins minted?
How was the Fatimid state administered?
What did Nasir-i Khusraw say about Cairo's markets?
What is a diwan?
entries.answer:
Fatimid Egypt sat at the centre of a trading system reaching from Spain in the west to India in the east, and beyond the Muslim world as well. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that the Fatimids held strategic control over Mediterranean and Red Sea routes, that Cairo functioned as an inland port, and that Egypt traded vigorously with North Africa, Nubia, Europe, Byzantium, the Mediterranean islands and the Far East. Agriculture reached general self-sufficiency and industry received active state encouragement.

The Persian traveller Nasir-i Khusraw left a vivid picture of Cairo's markets, describing something like twenty thousand shops, rare goods from all over the world, tortoiseshell boxes and knife handles, very fine crystal, an abundance of fruit and vegetables, and porcelain so thin you could see your hand through it, and glass so pure it was sold by weight.

This prosperity produced elaborate administration, with a series of diwans or ministries including the diwan al-insha, the chancery, and the diwan al-amwal, the ministry of finance. IIS notes that the Imam stood at the apex of a highly centralised hierarchy, aided by the wazir, with the military and civil service organised on the same pattern.

Coins were both an economic instrument and a public statement. They were struck in state-run mints, whose supervision fell under the qadi, at sites including Cairo, Alexandria, Damascus, Aleppo, Jerusalem's region, Mecca, Medina, Qayrawan, al-Mahdiyya, al-Mansuriyya, Fez, Sijilmasa, Palermo, Tyre, Tripoli, Sanaa and Zabid. Their high gold content was maintained throughout the period, which testified to the wealth of the state and shaped how others viewed Fatimid power. Because most Fatimid coins are dated, they are valuable historical documents. From 386 AH / 996 CE they carried the Shia legend 'Ali wali Allah'. Quarter-dinars from Palermo show a distinctive 'stellate' or windmill design.

sources.title: Documents of History, Symbols of Authority: The Coinage of the Fatimids

entries.title: How the Fatimids treated Sunnis, Christians and Jews
questions: Were the Fatimids tolerant?
How did the Fatimids treat Christians and Jews?
Could Sunnis hold office under the Fatimids?
Did the Fatimids force people to become Ismaili?
What was Fatimid religious policy?
Did Copts and Armenians serve the Fatimid state?
What is the Ahl al-Kitab?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies presents religious pluralism as a defining feature of Fatimid rule.

Fatimid law, IIS writes, was formulated and applied with deference to a universalistic philosophy of religious tolerance and respect for difference. IIS quotes the spirit of one Fatimid edict as allowing each Muslim to seek his own solution within his religion. In the same spirit, the Fatimids encouraged private patronage of mosques and other pious endowments by Muslims of different legal schools, a policy that acknowledged a plurality of pious ways rather than imposing a single interpretation.

Appointments followed merit. In elevating a Sunni jurist to the office of chief qadi, the imam-caliph al-Hakim praised the man's sense of justice and intellectual calibre as the determining factors.

Christians and Jews were supported and encouraged within the state. IIS records that many Coptic and Armenian Christians, as well as Jews, attained important positions, and that both communities took an active part in the social, cultural, intellectual and economic life of the wider society. The Fatimids grounded this in the Qur'anic principle of respect for the Ahl al-Kitab, the People of the Book.

Patronage of learning worked the same way. Scholars and scientists were drawn to Cairo regardless of religious persuasion, and the facilities of the Dar al-Ilm were open to followers of different religions.

IIS observes a paradox in this. Precisely because the Fatimids did not press their faith on their subjects, Ismailism never took deep root in the North African population and remained the faith of a minority throughout their rule. The Imamat's own account presents the Fatimid state as one of the more successful attempts in Muslim history to avoid both despotism and anarchy.

entries.title: Badr al-Jamali and the rise of the military viziers
questions: Who was Badr al-Jamali?
How did Badr al-Jamali restore order in Egypt?
What were the viziers of the sword?
Who was al-Afdal?
Why did power shift from the Fatimid caliphs to viziers?
When did Badr al-Jamali die?
What crisis did the Fatimid state face in the 1070s?
entries.answer:
By the middle of al-Mustansir's long reign the Fatimid state was in serious trouble: famine, breakdown of law and order, and factional fighting among Berber, Turkish, Sudanese and Armenian troops.

The response was to hand extraordinary powers to a soldier. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that Badr al-Jamali, described in one IIS-published account as an Armenian general in Syria and in another as the head of the Syrian troops, was given wide authority in the belief that strong military action was needed. He succeeded in restoring order and peace.

The consequences outlasted the emergency. IIS notes that Badr al-Jamali and his successors, known as the 'viziers of the sword', came to wield increasing military and political power. His son al-Afdal became the powerful vizier of al-Mustansir after his father's death, and it was al-Afdal who, on al-Mustansir's death in 1094, moved swiftly to secure the allegiance of the Fatimid nobles and of the da'wa in Cairo for his own preferred candidate. By the later period, IIS writes, the vitality of the Fatimid regime had been sapped and effective power was exercised by the viziers rather than by the imam-caliphs.

This was also the Cairo into which Hasan-i Sabbah arrived: a capital that had passed through famine and disorder and in which real authority had shifted away from the caliphal palace.

IIS records that Badr al-Jamali died in 1094, the same year as al-Mustansir.

entries.title: The Nizari-Musta'li split (1094 CE)
questions: What happened when al-Mustansir died?
Who were Nizar and al-Musta'li?
Why did the Ismailis split in 1094?
Who are the Nizari Ismailis?
Who are the Musta'li Ismailis?
What role did al-Afdal play in the succession?
Who are the Tayyibi Ismailis?
How does the Aga Khan relate to Imam Nizar?
entries.answer:
The imam-caliph al-Mustansir billah died in 487 AH / 1094 CE, and the Ismaili community suffered a permanent schism over the succession.

According to Nizari sources summarised by the Institute of Ismaili Studies, al-Mustansir had designated his eldest son Nizar, born in 1054, to succeed him. But the powerful vizier al-Afdal, son of Badr al-Jamali, favoured a younger son, Abu'l-Qasim Ahmad, who took the title al-Musta'li and who was married to al-Afdal's sister. Al-Afdal moved quickly to obtain the allegiance of the Fatimid nobles and of the da'wa in Cairo, and al-Musta'li took the throne.

The community divided. In Iran and parts of Syria, Nizar was hailed as Imam; in Egypt, Yemen and Sind, al-Musta'li was recognised. IIS records Nizar's death in 488 AH / 1095 CE and al-Musta'li's reign as 487-495 AH / 1094-1101 CE. From this point the two groups followed divergent paths in both politics and religion.

The Musta'li line divided again. Al-Musta'li was succeeded by his son al-Amir, and when al-Amir died in 524 AH / 1130 CE the majority of his followers, chiefly in Yemen, accepted his infant son al-Tayyib as Imam, but believed that he went into concealment and that the Imams succeeding him remain hidden until the end of time. A Da'i al-Mutlaq, or chief da'i, was appointed to guide the community on the hidden Imam's behalf. Others, mainly in Egypt, supported al-Amir's cousin al-Hafiz.

The Nizari Imamate continued in Iran, where the seat moved to the fortress of Alamut. The Nizari Ismaili Imams of modern times, known by the hereditary title Aga Khan, trace their descent to Imam Nizar.

entries.title: The end of the Fatimid caliphate (1171 CE)
questions: When did the Fatimid caliphate end?
Who ended Fatimid rule?
Who was the last Fatimid caliph?
Why did the Fatimids decline?
What replaced the Fatimid caliphate?
How long did the Fatimids rule?
What happened to Ismailis after 1171?
Did Fatimid learning survive the dynasty?
entries.answer:
Fatimid rule ended in 567 AH / 1171 CE, when Salah al-Din, known in English as Saladin, took control of Egypt and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that the Cairo-based line was finally overthrown as the fourteenth and last Fatimid caliph, who had reigned 555-567 AH / 1160-1171 CE, lay dying in Cairo. The caliphate had lasted from 909 to 1171 CE.

The collapse was long prepared. IIS describes the later Fatimid period in Egypt as marked by grave internal disorders: the great famine of al-Mustansir's reign, feuding between the Berber, Turkish, Sudanese and Armenian sections of the army, loss of imperial territories, and the severe economic difficulties and popular disaffection that followed. After Badr al-Jamali, effective power passed to the military viziers, and by the twelfth century the vitality of the regime had been sapped, with the caliphs reduced to figureheads. The succession disputes of 1094 and 1130 divided the community that had sustained the state.

IIS is careful to distinguish the end of the dynasty from the end of the tradition. The Musta'li da'wa flourished in Yemen under its Da'i al-Mutlaq, and its headquarters were later transferred to Gujarat in India in 1567 CE. The Nizari Imamate continued in Iran, where a state centred on the fortress of Alamut had been founded in the 1090s and lasted until the Mongols took Alamut in 1256 CE.

The intellectual legacy also outlived the state. IIS notes that struggles over the survival of the Dar al-Ilm and over the construction of an observatory continued even during the political and military dissolution of the Fatimid regime, and that Nizari Ismaili history can be seen as an extension of groundwork laid in the Fatimid period.

entries.title: The Nizari-Musta'li split of 1094
questions: Why did the Ismailis divide in 1094?
What was the Nizari-Musta'li schism?
Who was Nizar?
Why are there Nizari and Musta'li Ismailis?
What happened when the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir died?
How did today's Ismaili communities come to be separate?
Who was al-Afdal and what did he do?
Where do the Bohras and the Khojas divide?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili community divided in 487 AH / 1094 CE, when the Fatimid Imam-caliph al-Mustansir died in Cairo after a reign of nearly sixty years. According to the Institute of Ismaili Studies, his eldest son Nizar was the designated heir, but the immensely powerful vizier al-Afdal installed Nizar's younger brother al-Musta'li on the Fatimid throne instead.

The result was a permanent division of a single community into two lines of Imams, both descended from al-Mustansir. The da'wa headquarters in Cairo and the Ismailis of Egypt, Yemen and western India accepted al-Musta'li; the Ismailis of Persia and the lands nearby upheld Nizar's right and recognised his Imamate. Nizar himself rose against al-Musta'li, was defeated, and died in 488 AH / 1095 CE.

The two branches then developed separately, each with its own literature, law and religious vocabulary. The Musta'li line later divided again on the death of al-Amir in 524 AH / 1130 CE into Hafizi and Tayyibi groups; Tayyibi Ismailism survives today, chiefly as the Bohra communities of Yemen and India, led by da'i mutlaqs in the absence of a manifest Imam. The Nizari line continued through a living, hereditary Imam and is the branch led today by the Aga Khan.

In Persia, the senior da'i Hasan-i Sabbah supported Nizar and broke off relations with Cairo, so the split also marks the beginning of an independent Nizari da'wa and, before long, of a Nizari state.

entries.title: Hasan-i Sabbah
questions: Who was Hasan-i Sabbah?
Who founded the Nizari state at Alamut?
Was Hasan-i Sabbah an Imam?
How did Hasan-i Sabbah take Alamut?
What did Hasan-i Sabbah teach?
When did Hasan-i Sabbah die?
Why did Hasan-i Sabbah break with Cairo?
Was Hasan-i Sabbah the Old Man of the Mountain?
entries.answer:
Hasan-i Sabbah (d. 518 AH / 1124 CE) was the Persian da'i who founded the Nizari Ismaili state. He was born in Qum in the 440s AH / 1050s CE into a Twelver Shi'i family and converted to Ismailism at Ray as a young man, giving his allegiance to the Fatimid Imam-caliph al-Mustansir. In 464 AH / 1072 CE he was recruited into the da'wa hierarchy by the chief da'i Abd al-Malik ibn Attash, and he later studied in Isfahan and in Fatimid Egypt.

Returning to Persia, he concentrated his work in the mountainous region of Daylam and in 483 AH / 1090 CE gained the fortress of Alamut, not by siege but by patient infiltration of its garrison. That date effectively marks the foundation of the Nizari state. When al-Mustansir died in 1094, Hasan supported Nizar and severed relations with Cairo, so establishing a Nizari da'wa independent of the Fatimid regime.

He was never himself claimed as Imam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes him as the hujja, the Imam's representative, during a period when the Nizari Imams were concealed. His doctrinal contribution, set out in a Persian work known as the Chahar fasl (Four Chapters), was the argument that unaided human reason cannot reach religious truth and that an authoritative teacher is necessary - the doctrine of ta'lim, which gave the Nizaris their common name of Ta'limiyya.

He is said never to have left Alamut in his thirty-four years there, writing, organising the da'wa, and building a library. He died on 26 Rabi' II 518 AH / 12 June 1124 CE, having designated Kiya Buzurg-Ummid as his successor.

entries.title: Alamut
questions: What was Alamut?
Where is Alamut?
What does the name Alamut mean?
Why was Alamut important to the Ismailis?
What happened to Alamut?
Was there really a library at Alamut?
Can you visit Alamut today?
Is Alamut a World Heritage Site?
entries.answer:
Alamut is a mountain fortress in the central Alborz range of northern Iran, roughly 45 km north-east of Qazvin. A Justanid ruler is said to have built it in the ninth century CE. A well-known story explains the name as 'the eagle's teaching' (in Arabic ta'lim al-uqab), from a legend that an eagle showed a Daylami ruler the site; Ismaili scholarship notes the coincidence that in the abjad system the name yields the number 483, the Hijri year in which Hasan-i Sabbah took it.

Hasan-i Sabbah gained Alamut in 483 AH / 1090 CE and made it the seat of the Nizari Ismaili state. He strengthened the defences, improved the irrigation and farmland of the valley, and assembled a library with manuscripts and scientific instruments. For 166 years Alamut was the centre of a network of strongholds reaching east to Quhistan and, by way of regular contact, to the Nizari castles of Syria.

The Mongols took Alamut in 654 AH / 1256 CE, dismantled much of it and burned the library. Under the Safavids the site was repaired and used as a prison into the seventeenth century, after which it was abandoned and decayed.

In July 2026 Alamut and six associated fortifications - Lamasar, Navizarshah, Shams Kalayih, Qustinlar, Shirkuh and Ilan - were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The Institute of Ismaili Studies welcomed the citation's description of Alamut as an intellectual centre, a side of the site long obscured by hostile and legendary writing.

entries.title: The doctrine of ta'lim
questions: What is ta'lim?
What did the Nizaris mean by authoritative teaching?
Why were Ismailis called the Ta'limiyya?
What was al-Ghazali's argument against the Ismailis?
Why do Ismailis need a living Imam?
What is the teaching of the Imam of the time?
What did Hasan-i Sabbah actually teach?
entries.answer:
Ta'lim means 'teaching' or 'authoritative instruction'. It is the doctrine most closely associated with Hasan-i Sabbah and with the Nizari Ismailis of the Alamut period, who became widely known as the Ta'limiyya or Ta'limis because of it.

The argument, as the Institute of Ismaili Studies presents it, runs roughly like this: people disagree about religious truth, and reason alone cannot settle the disagreement, because each reasoner begins from different premises and arrives at different conclusions. What is needed is a trustworthy teacher (mu'allim) whose guidance is divinely supported. Ismailis hold that this teacher is the Imam of the time, a living descendant of the Prophet through Ali and Fatima. Knowledge of God is not, on this view, reached by assembling theological categories from outside, but through the instruction of that teacher.

The doctrine was influential enough that al-Ghazali, writing his refutation of Ismailism for the Abbasid court, treated ta'lim as the Ismaili's central claim and attacked it directly. Nasir al-Din Tusi, who lived among the Nizaris in the thirteenth century, later described Ismaili philosophy as a rational ascent carried out under the guiding instruction of the Imam, rather than free and unfettered rational inquiry.

Ta'lim remained the backbone of Nizari thought through later doctrinal developments, including the qiyama of 1164 and the writings produced during the Anjudan revival, and the principle of guidance by a living hereditary Imam continues to define the Nizari Ismaili community today.

entries.title: The Nizari state in Persia
questions: What was the Nizari Ismaili state?
How big was the Ismaili state in Iran?
Where were the Ismaili strongholds in Persia?
Who ruled after Hasan-i Sabbah?
Did the Ismailis fight the Seljuks?
What was Quhistan?
How long did the Nizari state last?
What language did the Nizaris use?
entries.answer:
From 483 AH / 1090 CE until 654 AH / 1256 CE the Nizari Ismailis held a territorially scattered but durable state in Persia, governed from Alamut by eight successive lords.

It was never a contiguous kingdom. It consisted of clusters of mountain strongholds with their surrounding valleys: Rudbar and Daylam around Alamut in the north; Quhistan in south-eastern Khurasan, taken from 484 AH / 1091 CE under the da'i Husayn-i Qa'ini; and outposts in the Zagros, including Shahdiz overlooking the Saljuq capital Isfahan, seized around 1100 CE. Smaller forts, watchtowers and beacons linked the centres, and communication with the Syrian Nizaris was kept open.

Hasan-i Sabbah's armed revolt against Saljuq rule did not succeed, but the Saljuqs, for all their superior armies, could not destroy the fortress communities either, and a stalemate set in. Kiya Buzurg-Ummid (518-532 AH / 1124-1138 CE) consolidated the state and revived the Syrian mission; Muhammad b. Buzurg-Ummid (532-557 AH / 1138-1162 CE) extended activity as far as Georgia and Ghur in central Afghanistan.

One of the lasting choices of this period was linguistic. Hasan-i Sabbah adopted Persian rather than Arabic as the religious language of the community - the Institute of Ismaili Studies describes this as a first among Muslim communities - and the Nizari literature of the Alamut and post-Alamut periods is overwhelmingly Persian. Quhistan under its muhtashams also became a refuge for scholars fleeing the Mongol advance.

entries.title: How the Nizari fortresses worked
questions: What were the Ismaili castles like?
How did the Ismailis build their fortresses?
Why were the Ismaili castles so hard to capture?
How did Alamut get water?
What is Lamasar?
Were the Ismaili castles offensive or defensive?
What remains of the Ismaili castles?
entries.answer:
Nizari castle-building is one of the better documented sides of the Alamut period, and it shows a consistently defensive strategy rather than an offensive one.

Sites were chosen for natural strength and remoteness, so that a far more numerous Saljuq enemy would be discouraged from attacking. Castles were grouped so they could support one another and signal by beacon. A site needed timber and stone nearby for quick construction, and fertile ground and water close at hand. Approaches were kept as steep as possible, which removed the need for long outer walls and made it hard for besiegers to set up siege engines or to mine the walls.

Underground storerooms were dug to hold several years of food. The Mongol-era historian Juwayni, no friend of the community, complained about how hard Alamut was to demolish and was struck by the quantity and good condition of the stores he found there. Kiya Buzurg-Ummid (518-532 AH / 1124-1138 CE) seems to have been the military mind behind much of the building; he rebuilt Lamasar, the largest of the Persian castles, with an elaborate water system. Surveys in the 1970s estimated Lamasar's cisterns at around 400,000 litres, enough for roughly 500 men and 50 animals for three months.

The Syrian castles, except for Kahf and Masyaf, were smaller and more compact, since there was less room to expand, but they were well provisioned. Khawabi was never taken by the Crusaders and its ruins were reoccupied by local Syrian families in the early twentieth century.

entries.title: The Nizari Ismailis of Syria
questions: When did the Ismailis reach Syria?
What were the Syrian Ismaili castles?
What is Masyaf?
Did the Ismailis fight the Crusaders?
What happened to the Syrian Ismailis?
Who were the Ismailis of the Jabal Bahra?
Did Baybars conquer the Ismailis?
entries.answer:
A Nizari presence was established in Syria early in the twelfth century. A leader known as al-Hakim al-Munajjim gained a foothold in Aleppo around 1100 CE under the protection of the Saljuq ruler Ridwan; after Ridwan's death in 1113 CE hostility grew and many Ismailis left, and the community's effort shifted south towards Damascus and then west to the mountains.

Between about 1124 and 1141 CE the Syrian Nizaris acquired a network of castles in the Jabal Bahra (Jabal Ansariyya), the range between Hama and the coast: Qadmus around 1132-33 CE, Kahf shortly afterwards, and Masyaf about 1140-41 CE, which became their principal stronghold. The Crusader chronicler William of Tyre reckoned there were around ten castles and a large Ismaili population in the region by mid-century.

The community's most famous leader was Rashid al-Din Sinan (d. 1193 CE), sent from Alamut, who balanced the Crusader states, Saladin and the local Muslim rulers against one another to keep his community independent. Contacts with Latin rulers continued after him: Frederick II sent envoys in 1227 CE, and Louis IX exchanged gifts with Ismaili emissaries around 1250 CE.

The fall of Alamut in 1256 CE cut Syria off from its central leadership. Four fortresses including Masyaf submitted to the Mongols under Ket-Buqa by 1260 CE, and after the Mamluk victory at Ayn Jalut the sultan Baybars dismantled Ismaili independence fortress by fortress between 1271 and 1273 CE, ending with Kahf in July 1273 CE. The community kept several strongholds under Mamluk and later Ottoman supervision - Ibn Battuta saw them still in Ismaili hands in 1326 CE - and maintained its libraries and learning.

entries.title: The fida'is and the truth about political killings
questions: Did the Ismailis really assassinate people?
Who were the fida'is?
Were the Ismailis a cult of killers?
Did the Ismailis use drugs on their fighters?
Why did the Nizaris target rulers?
How many people did the Assassins kill?
Is the assassin reputation deserved?
entries.answer:
The Nizaris of the Alamut period did carry out targeted killings, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies does not deny it. Hasan-i Sabbah's strategy against the Saljuqs, who vastly outnumbered him, combined the holding of near-impregnable strongholds with the selective removal of particular adversaries - commanders and officials who were directing campaigns against the community - while avoiding attacks on ordinary people. Those who undertook these missions were called fida'is, 'devotees', and they frequently did not expect to survive.

This was neither unusual nor uniquely Ismaili in the period; what was unusual was the notoriety it acquired. Crusaders in Syria encountered stories of the fida'is under Rashid al-Din Sinan and found their willingness to die inexplicable. To explain it they invented a cause: that the young men were drugged with hashish, or shown a secret garden of paradise and promised its return. Marco Polo's version added the garden. IIS points out that hostile Muslim sources of the time, who had every reason to say so, offer no evidence of drugging.

The long-term effect was that a limited and calculated tactic of a small mountain state was inflated into the defining identity of an entire religious community, and then exported into European languages as a common noun for murder.

The allowed sources give the outline of the strategy and dismantle the legends around it, but they do not give a documented list of killings, numbers, or an internal Nizari account of how fida'is were chosen or trained.

entries.title: Where the word 'assassin' came from
questions: Where does the word assassin come from?
Does assassin come from hashish?
Did the Ismailis smoke hashish?
Why are Ismailis called Assassins?
What does hashishi mean?
Who was the Old Man of the Mountain?
Is the word assassin an insult?
entries.answer:
The word entered European languages from the Crusader states in twelfth-century Syria, where it was applied to the local Nizari Ismailis. It goes back to Arabic forms such as hashishi, plural hashishiyya. The Institute of Ismaili Studies is explicit that this was a term of abuse used by other Muslims, meaning something like low-class rabble or people of no standing, and that it carried no actual reference to the use of cannabis.

Europeans picked the insult up locally without understanding it. Once its original sense was lost, the word survived in Europe purely as a label for the people it had been thrown at, and then as a common noun meaning a murderer - which is how 'assassin' reached modern English, French and Italian.

The figure attached to the word was Rashid al-Din Sinan (d. 1193 CE), leader of the Syrian Nizaris, who became for Crusader writers the 'Old Man of the Mountain'.

The modern etymological link between 'Assassin' and hashish was worked out in 1818 by the French orientalist Antoine Isaac Silvestre de Sacy (1758-1838). IIS credits him with solving the linguistic puzzle while noting that he, like his contemporaries, still took the legendary narratives themselves at face value. Recovering the correct history of the word therefore meant two separate corrections: tracing where it came from, and then establishing that its literal meaning was a slur rather than a description.

entries.title: Why the Assassin legends are myth
questions: Are the Assassin legends true?
Did Marco Polo make up the garden of paradise?
Who invented the Assassin stories?
What is the black legend about the Ismailis?
How do we know the legends are false?
Why did Western writers believe these stories?
Who was Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall?
How did scholars correct the record?
entries.answer:
The legends about the Nizaris grew out of two separate bodies of hostile writing, which eventually reinforced each other.

The first was Muslim polemic. From the ninth century onward anti-Ismaili writers produced a 'black legend' portraying Ismailism as a heresy and a conspiracy, and this material circulated widely from Transoxania to North Africa and shaped later Islamic scholarship.

The second was Crusader storytelling. Westerners in Syria from 1096 onward met the Nizaris without any real knowledge of Islam and filled the gap with invention - the drugging of the fida'is, the promise of a paradise garden. The Institute of Ismaili Studies, following Farhad Daftary, calls these accounts the imaginative constructions of uninformed observers. The best-known version is the one attached to Marco Polo in the thirteenth century, which added the secret garden used as a training ground; by the fourteenth century the story was standard in Europe.

These tales then passed into modern scholarship. Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1774-1856) accepted them, and his 1818 history of the Assassins remained the standard reference into the 1930s. The problem was not bad faith so much as sources: no one outside the community had access to Ismaili texts, so scholars worked from Crusader reports and hostile Muslim chronicles.

What changed was the recovery and study of genuine Ismaili manuscripts from the early twentieth century, much of it through the work of Wladimir Ivanow and the communities of Badakhshan and India who had preserved the texts. IIS's position is that it is this material, not a defensive reinterpretation, that now allows legend to be separated from history.

entries.title: Rashid al-Din Sinan
questions: Who was Rashid al-Din Sinan?
Who was the Old Man of the Mountain?
What did Sinan do in Syria?
Did Sinan negotiate with Saladin?
Why is Sinan famous in Europe?
When did Sinan die?
Was Sinan an Imam?
entries.answer:
Rashid al-Din Sinan (d. 589 AH / 1193 CE) led the Nizari Ismailis of Syria for about thirty years and brought them to the height of their power. He was born in Basra and was sent to Syria by the Imam Hasan II around 1162 CE. He was a da'i and a governor, not an Imam.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes him as an outstanding organiser and statesman. He reorganised a community that had been repeatedly displaced, strengthened the castles of the Jabal Bahra, and kept Nizari independence alive by playing the region's competing powers against one another. He negotiated with Amalric I of Jerusalem around 1173 CE, though Templar interference broke off the arrangement. After Saladin invaded Ismaili territory and besieged Masyaf in 1175 CE, mediation by a local governor produced a truce and, afterwards, a workable coexistence.

Relations with Alamut were not always smooth. There is evidence of tension between Sinan and the Imam Nur al-Din Muhammad II, though an open break was avoided.

To the Crusaders, Sinan was the original 'Old Man of the Mountain', and it is largely around him that the European legend of the Assassins formed. He died at the castle of Kahf, which had served as his headquarters and which was the last Syrian Ismaili stronghold to fall to the Mamluks eighty years later.

entries.title: The Qiyama of 1164
questions: What was the qiyama?
What happened at Alamut in 1164?
Did the Ismailis abolish the shari'a?
What does the Resurrection mean in Ismaili thought?
Why is 1164 important?
Was the qiyama permanent?
What is the Great Resurrection?
entries.answer:
On 17 Ramadan 559 AH / 8 August 1164 CE, the Imam Hasan II made a solemn proclamation before the assembled community at Alamut announcing the qiyama - the Resurrection. A second ceremony followed on 28 Dhu'l-qi'da 559 AH / 18 October 1164 CE at the castle of Mu'min-Abad in Quhistan.

In Nizari understanding this was not a claim that the physical world was ending. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the qiyama as the manifestation of unveiled truth in the person of the Imam: the inner reality (batin) which religious law had until then carried in concealed form was now disclosed. Those who recognised the Imam and lived in this awareness were spoken of as ahl-i wahdat, the people of unity. Because the truth was now open, the outward observance of the shari'a as a set of obligations was declared no longer binding in the way it had been.

The declaration reoriented Nizari identity and marked the end of the long period of satr, the concealment of the Imams that had begun after Nizar's death. Hasan II's son Nur al-Din Muhammad II spent a forty-four-year reign systematically expounding the doctrine, with the living Imam's independent teaching authority at its centre. Nasir al-Din Tusi later explained the qiyama of 1164 as falling in the middle of the millennium of the Prophet Muhammad's era and setting the pattern for the final qiyama at its end.

The condition did not prove permanent: Jalal al-Din Hasan III restored shari'a observance in 1210 CE, and Tusi accounted for that as a return to satr.

entries.title: Imam Hasan II, 'ala dhikrihi al-salam
questions: Who was Hasan II of Alamut?
Who declared the qiyama?
What does 'ala dhikrihi al-salam mean?
How did Hasan II die?
Was Hasan II descended from Nizar?
When did the Nizari Imams come out of hiding?
entries.answer:
Hasan II, known in the tradition by the honorific 'ala dhikrihi al-salam ('on his mention be peace'), was born in 520 AH / 1126 CE and led the Nizari community and state from 557 to 561 AH / 1162 to 1166 CE, succeeding Muhammad b. Buzurg-Ummid. He was known for his learning in Ismaili doctrine and esoteric interpretation.

His proclamation of the qiyama at Alamut in 559 AH / 1164 CE is the defining event of his short reign, and with it the Nizari Imamate emerged openly after decades of concealment. In the proclamation and in his epistles he claimed the Imamate itself, presenting himself as God's khalifa on earth in the manner of the Fatimid Imam al-Mustansir, and indicating descent from Imam Nizar b. al-Mustansir - although he had until then been regarded publicly as the son of Muhammad b. Buzurg-Ummid, the third lord of Alamut.

He was stabbed to death on 6 Rabi' I 561 AH / 9 January 1166 CE at the castle of Lammasar by his brother-in-law Hasan b. Namavar, who opposed his changes. His son Nur al-Din Muhammad II succeeded him and defended and elaborated his father's teaching for the next forty-four years.

sources.title: The Mediaeval Ismailis of the Iranian Lands

entries.notes: The question of Hasan II's descent - whether the Imams of Alamut were the hidden line of Nizar - is a matter of Nizari religious tradition rather than of independent documentation, and IIS presents it as the community's own account.

entries.title: Nur al-Din Muhammad II
questions: Who was Nur al-Din Muhammad II?
Who explained the qiyama doctrine?
Who ruled Alamut longest?
What happened after Hasan II died?
Did Muhammad II quarrel with Sinan?
When did Muhammad II die?
entries.answer:
Nur al-Din Muhammad II (542-607 AH / 1148-1210 CE) was the fifth lord of Alamut and the Nizari Imam. Born in March 1148 CE, he succeeded on the murder of his father Hasan II on 6 Rabi' al-Awwal 561 AH / 9 January 1166 CE and reigned for roughly forty-four years, longer than any other lord of Alamut.

His rule in Persia was comparatively peaceful, with little military conflict, and he devoted himself to administration and to writing. His principal contribution was doctrinal: he took the qiyama his father had proclaimed in 559 AH / 1164 CE and set it out as a worked-through system. At its centre he placed the autonomous teaching authority of the Imam of the time - a development of the older doctrine of ta'lim now framed within the disclosure of the qiyama.

Relations with Rashid al-Din Sinan, who led the Syrian Nizaris until his death in 589 AH / 1193 CE, appear to have been strained during this period, though the sources suggest a full break was avoided.

He died on 10 Rabi' al-Awwal 607 AH / 1 September 1210 CE, possibly by poison. His son Jalal al-Din Hasan III succeeded him and almost immediately reversed his religious policy, reintroducing observance of the shari'a.

entries.title: Jalal al-Din Hasan III and the return to the shari'a
questions: Who was Jalal al-Din Hasan?
Why did the Ismailis go back to Sunni law?
What was the New Preaching reversal?
Did an Ismaili Imam become Sunni?
How did the Abbasid caliph recognise the Nizaris?
Was this taqiyya?
What happened to Nizari lands under Jalal al-Din Hasan?
entries.answer:
Jalal al-Din Hasan III led the Nizari community and state from 607 to 618 AH / 1210 to 1221 CE, and made one of the most striking policy reversals in Ismaili history. Within a short time of his accession he instructed his followers to observe Sunni shari'a, invited Sunni jurists into Nizari territory, and publicly repudiated the practice of his predecessors.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies presents this as a form of taqiyya - precautionary dissimulation - in which outward conformity protected the community while its esoteric Ismaili beliefs were maintained. The policy worked in political terms. The Abbasid caliph al-Nasir (575-622 AH / 1180-1225 CE) formally recognised Jalal al-Din Hasan's rights over Nizari territories, and the community gained a standing it had not had since Hasan-i Sabbah's revolt. When the Mongol invasions began, Sunni scholars fleeing Khurasan took refuge in Nizari Quhistan.

Nasir al-Din Tusi, writing a generation later, gave the reversal a doctrinal explanation: the reimposition of the shari'a was a return to satr, a time when truth is hidden beneath the shell of the law, in contrast to the qiyama when it stands unveiled. In this framework satr and qiyama could alternate within the era of the Prophet Muhammad, according to the decision of each Imam, since every Imam is potentially the qa'im.

Jalal al-Din Hasan's son Ala al-Din Muhammad III, the Imam during Tusi's years in Quhistan, again relaxed the application of the shari'a without formally abolishing it.

entries.title: Satr and taqiyya: concealment in Ismaili history
questions: What does satr mean?
What is taqiyya?
Why did the Ismaili Imams hide?
Is taqiyya lying about your faith?
What is dawr al-satr?
When were the Nizari Imams concealed?
How did the doctrine of satr change?
entries.answer:
Satr means 'concealment'. Ismailis have used it in several related senses, and it is central to understanding how the community survived long periods of persecution.

In early Ismaili history dawr al-satr was a period stretching from soon after the death of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in 148 AH / 765 CE to the founding of the Fatimid state in 297 AH / 909 CE, during which the Imam was out of public view (mastur) and was represented by hujjas, his full representatives.

After the Nizari-Musta'li schism of 487 AH / 1094 CE the early Nizaris entered a second period of satr. The Imams, descendants of Nizar b. al-Mustansir (d. 488 AH / 1095 CE), remained concealed for several decades and were again represented by hujjas - beginning with Hasan-i Sabbah, who also governed the Nizari state from Alamut. This period ended in 559 AH / 1164 CE with the open emergence of the Imamate at the qiyama.

The term then took on a new meaning. As Nasir al-Din Tusi explains it, satr in the late Alamut period no longer referred to the physical hiding of the Imam but to a time when spiritual truths (haqa'iq) are veiled within the batin of religion, so that taqiyya - prudent concealment of one's faith - is required of the community.

Satr also belongs to the Ismaili view of sacred history as a series of eras, all but the last being eras of concealment, to be completed by a final age of manifestation (dawr al-kashf) in which the distinction between the outward and inner dimensions of religion falls away.

entries.title: Nasir al-Din Tusi among the Nizaris
questions: Who was Nasir al-Din Tusi?
Was Tusi an Ismaili?
What did Tusi write at Alamut?
What is the Akhlaq-i Nasiri?
What is the Rawdat al-taslim?
Why did Tusi later disown his Ismaili writings?
Did Tusi help the Mongols?
entries.answer:
Nasir al-Din Tusi (597-672 AH / 1201-1274 CE) was among the foremost philosophers, mathematicians and astronomers of the medieval Muslim world, and he spent roughly three decades in Nizari Ismaili service.

He entered the household of the muhtasham of Quhistan, Nasir al-Din Abd al-Rahim b. Abi Mansur, around 624 AH / 1227 CE, and later spent long periods at Alamut, where the library and its instruments supported work in logic, philosophy, mathematics and astronomy. Around 633 AH / 1235 CE he completed the Akhlaq-i Nasiri (Nasirean Ethics), the most admired Persian book on ethics, named for his patron and opened with a dedication invoking blessings on the Imam of the time, Ala al-Din Muhammad III.

He also produced, or is credited with, the Rawdat al-taslim, described by IIS as the most comprehensive surviving treatise on Nizari Ismaili teaching. It is the main source for how the community explained the sequence of qiyama and satr, and for the doctrine of the Imam as the necessary teacher.

After the Mongol conquest and the surrender of Rukn al-Din Khurshah in 654 AH / 1256 CE, Tusi entered Mongol service. He replaced the dedication of the Akhlaq-i Nasiri with a Sunni preamble and stated that his stay among the Ismailis had been involuntary and his praise of their leaders a matter of self-preservation.

How sincere either phase was has been debated ever since. What is not in doubt is that a great deal of what survives of late Alamut Nizari thought survives in his writing.

entries.notes: Whether Tusi was a convinced Ismaili, a hostage, or something in between is genuinely disputed; the IIS sources record both his Ismaili-period dedications and his later retraction without settling the question.

entries.title: Alamut as a centre of learning
questions: Was Alamut a place of scholarship?
What was in the library at Alamut?
Which scholars worked at Alamut?
Did the Ismailis do science?
What happened to the Alamut library?
Why is Alamut's intellectual side forgotten?
entries.answer:
Alongside its military reputation, Alamut was a working centre of scholarship. Hasan-i Sabbah founded a library there with manuscripts and scientific instruments and, according to the tradition, spent his thirty-four years in the fortress reading and committing the teachings of the da'wa to writing.

The Nizaris were also, unusually, a community that produced chronicles. A historiographical tradition began with the Sargudhasht-i Sayyidna, an account of Hasan-i Sabbah's life and reign whose first part may have been autobiographical, continued with the Kitab-i Buzurg-Ummid for his successor, and was carried on by later Nizari chroniclers down to the Mongol conquest. These works were held in the libraries of Alamut and the Quhistan castles.

Nasir al-Din Tusi worked at Alamut for a long stretch of the thirteenth century, producing writing on logic, philosophy, mathematics and astronomy as well as the Nizari doctrinal works associated with his name.

Almost all of it was lost. The Mongols burned the library in 654 AH / 1256 CE, and the Nizari chronicles are believed to have perished then or soon after. They survive only at second hand: the Ilkhanid historians Juwayni (d. 681 AH / 1283 CE), Rashid al-Din (d. 718 AH / 1318 CE) and Abu'l-Qasim Kashani (d. c. 736 AH / 1335 CE) read and used them, and their hostile histories remain the main primary sources for the Nizari state.

When UNESCO inscribed Alamut in July 2026, the Institute of Ismaili Studies drew particular attention to the citation's description of the site as an intellectual centre.

entries.title: The Mongol destruction of 1256
questions: What happened to the Ismailis in 1256?
Why did the Mongols attack the Ismailis?
Who was Hulegu?
When did Alamut fall?
Did the Mongols wipe out the Ismailis?
What did Juwayni write about the Ismailis?
How did the Nizari state end?
entries.answer:
The Nizari state in Persia was destroyed by the Mongols in 654 AH / 1256 CE. Mongol pressure on the region had begun a generation earlier under Chinggis Khan, who took Samarqand in 617 AH / 1220 CE and overran Khurasan by 619 AH / 1222 CE. The Great Khan Mongke resolved to end the Nizari state and assigned the task to his brother Hulegu.

The Imam at the start of the invasion was Ala al-Din Muhammad III (618-653 AH / 1221-1256 CE). His son Rukn al-Din Khurshah, the last lord of Alamut, negotiated and then surrendered on 29 Shawwal 654 AH / 19 November 1256 CE. Alamut itself was taken about a month later, partially dismantled, and its library burned. Girdkuh held out far longer, into 669 AH / 1270 CE. Khurshah was sent east and killed by his Mongol guards in 655 AH / 1257 CE.

The campaign mattered enormously to Mongol propaganda. The historian Juwayni, who served Hulegu and who saw the Alamut library before it burned, gives the destruction of this small Ismaili enclave the final third of his History of the World Conqueror - more prominence than the fall of Baghdad and the Abbasid caliphate.

That emphasis had consequences. Juwayni insisted the extermination was total, later Persian historians followed him, and Western scholarship long accepted it. As a matter of history it was not true: the community survived, dispersed and leaderless for a time, but continuous.

entries.title: Girdkuh and the last resistance
questions: What was Girdkuh?
Which Ismaili fortress held out longest?
Where is Girdkuh?
How long did Girdkuh resist the Mongols?
How did the Ismailis get Girdkuh?
Who was Ra'is Muzaffar?
Did any Ismaili castle survive the Mongols?
entries.answer:
Girdkuh is a fortress near Damghan, on the road between Rayy and Khurasan, and it was one of the most important Nizari strongholds outside the Alamut valley.

Its origins are unknown and it may be a pre-Islamic site. The earliest reference connects it to the early Ismaili movement in the Jibal in the fourth AH / tenth CE century, when it is said to have been the residence of the da'i Abd al-Malik Kawkabi. By the fifth AH / eleventh CE century it was in the hands of local Saljuq amirs of Damghan.

It came to the Nizaris by infiltration rather than assault. Ra'is Muzaffar b. Ahmad, a secret Ismaili convert serving the Saljuqs, persuaded his superior, the amir Habashi, to obtain Girdkuh from Sultan Barkiyaruq in 489 AH / 1096 CE; Habashi then appointed Muzaffar to hold it, and around 493 AH / 1100 CE Muzaffar placed it at Hasan-i Sabbah's disposal. From then until the middle of the seventh AH / thirteenth CE century its history runs with that of the Nizari state.

Girdkuh's greatest distinction is how long it lasted. Alamut fell in 654 AH / 1256 CE, but Girdkuh's garrison - reduced, according to one contemporary, to a hundred or two hundred men by 658 AH / 1260 CE - held out until 669 AH / 1270 CE, some fourteen years after the supposed extinction of the community.

entries.title: Ismaili activity at Alamut after the Mongols
questions: Did the Ismailis recapture Alamut?
What happened at Alamut after 1256?
Were the Ismailis really wiped out by the Mongols?
Who was Naw Dawlat?
Did Ismailis remain in Daylam and Gilan?
Why did historians say the Ismailis were destroyed?
entries.answer:
The claim that the Mongols exterminated the Ismailis comes mainly from Juwayni, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies has published research arguing that it is false in a much stronger sense than was previously realised.

Shafique Virani's study of the south Caspian region assembles the evidence. Within a few years of the fall of Girdkuh, a group of Ismailis led by a son of Imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah, titled Naw Dawlat or Abu Dawlat, retook Alamut itself, in 674 AH / 1275 CE - in alliance with a descendant of the Khwarazmshahs. The community's weakened state meant the fortress was soon lost again, but the Mongols did not keep a strong presence there, and Ismailis seem to have lived in the area largely undisturbed until Uljaytu Khan entered Gilan in 706 AH / 1307 CE. That campaign too was brief.

After the death of the last powerful Ilkhan, Abu Sa'id, in 735 AH / 1335 CE, there was no strong central authority in the region at all, and the mountainous districts between Persian Iraq and Gilan reverted to semi-independence. Ismailis are attested at Qazvin and around Taliqan in the fourteenth century, and a figure known as Khudawand Muhammad was politically significant enough in Daylam for a local ruler to court his support. Timur's forces later massacred Ismailis in Mazandaran and then at Anjudan.

Virani's reading of why Juwayni overstated the destruction is straightforward: anything short of total annihilation would have looked like failure on the part of his Mongol patron.

entries.title: Survival after Alamut
questions: How did the Ismailis survive after 1256?
What is the post-Alamut period?
Did the Ismailis hide as Sufis?
Why did Ismailis pretend to be Sunni?
Where did the Nizaris go after Alamut?
How long were the Imams hidden?
Did the community stay in contact with the Imam?
entries.answer:
The two centuries after 1256 CE are the least documented stretch of Nizari history, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies says so plainly: the history of the Imamate for most of this period remains almost entirely obscure.

What is clear is the shape of the survival. Without a state, a capital or an accessible Imam, the scattered communities of Persia, Syria, Central Asia and India developed largely independently of one another, often ignorant of each other's existence and of their own history. Literary activity nearly ceased. Protection came through disguise: Nizaris in Persia adopted the outward forms of Sufism, with the Imams treated by outsiders as Sufi pirs and the community as a dervish following; elsewhere they took on Sunni or Twelver Shi'i appearances. IIS describes this as taqiyya, protective dissimulation, and notes that the Sufi vocabulary of pir and murid was absorbed deeply enough that it remained in Nizari usage long afterwards.

Meanwhile the Ismailis had not in fact vanished from their old heartlands. Communities persisted in Daylam, Gilan and Mazandaran, in Quhistan, in the Syrian castles under Mamluk supervision, and in the mountains of Badakhshan, where Persian Ismaili manuscripts of the Alamut period were copied and preserved - which is a large part of why those texts exist today.

In India, meanwhile, the Nizari da'wa was expanding rather than contracting, through the pirs of the Satpanth tradition.

The period of deepest concealment ended in the second half of the fifteenth century, when the Imams re-emerged at Anjudan in central Persia.

entries.title: Imam Shams al-Din Muhammad
questions: Who was Shams al-Din Muhammad?
Who was the Imam after Rukn al-Din Khurshah?
Where did the Imams live after Alamut fell?
Was Shams al-Din Muhammad the same as Shams of Tabriz?
Why do we know so little about him?
Which Imams followed Shams al-Din?
entries.answer:
Shams al-Din Muhammad is the Imam who carried the Nizari Imamate through the catastrophe of 1256. He was a son of Rukn al-Din Khurshah, the last lord of Alamut, who was murdered by his Mongol guards in 655 AH / 1257 CE.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies names him as the first of a sequence of concealed Imams in the post-Alamut period, followed by Qasim Shah, Islam Shah and Muhammad b. Islam Shah. Beyond that the record thins out almost to nothing. IIS states directly that little is known of the Imamate in these generations beyond the barest outlines: the Imams lived in hiding, without a state, and the community's own chroniclers had ceased writing.

What is attested is that a dispute over the succession to Shams al-Din Muhammad divided the Nizaris into two lines - the Qasim-Shahi, which became and remained the main body, and the Muhammad-Shahi.

He is a figure around whom a good deal of later tradition has gathered, including an identification with Shams of Tabriz, the companion of Rumi. The permitted sources do not support that identification and do not discuss it, so this entry leaves it aside rather than repeating it.

For a newcomer the useful point is structural rather than biographical: Nizari Ismailis hold that the line of hereditary Imams was never broken, even when the Imam was unknown to most of his own followers, and Shams al-Din Muhammad stands at the hinge of that claim.

entries.title: The Qasim-Shahi and Muhammad-Shahi lines
questions: Why did the Nizaris split after Alamut?
What is the Qasim-Shahi line?
What is the Muhammad-Shahi line?
Which Ismaili line survives today?
What happened to the Muhammad-Shahi Ismailis?
When did the Nizaris divide again?
entries.answer:
Some time after the death of Imam Shams al-Din Muhammad, the Nizaris divided over the succession into two lines: the followers of Qasim Shah and the followers of Muhammad Shah.

The evidence for this split was first set out by Wladimir Ivanow in an article of 1938, and further Muhammad-Shahi material was later published by the Syrian scholar Arif Tamir. Scholarship generally places the division in the fourteenth century, and has cautiously identified the Daylami figure known as Khudawand Muhammad with Muhammad Shah b. Mu'min Shah (d. 807 AH / 1404 CE) of that line - though newer evidence associated with the Qasim-Shahi Imam Islam Shah may point to a different identification.

The Qasim-Shahi line became, and remains, the main body of Nizari Ismailism. It is the line that re-emerged at Anjudan in the fifteenth century, that continued through the Safavid and Qajar periods in Persia, and whose Imams are the Aga Khans.

The Muhammad-Shahi line, sometimes called Mu'mini, had its own following in Persia, Syria, Central Asia and India. Its most celebrated figure was Shah Tahir al-Husayni, who carried the line to the Deccan in the sixteenth century. The line eventually lapsed: its Imams became untraceable and the branch dissolved, the Institute of Ismaili Studies indicating the late eighteenth century. A small Muhammad-Shahi community persisted in Syria.

The practical upshot is that when modern writing says 'Nizari Ismaili' without qualification, it means the Qasim-Shahi line.

When did Shah Tahir die?
entries.answer:
Shah Tahir al-Husayni (d. 956 AH / 1549 CE) was the most prominent Imam of the Muhammad-Shahi branch of Nizari Ismailism, and one of the most accomplished figures the community produced in the early modern period - the Institute of Ismaili Studies describes him as a learned theologian, poet, stylist and skilled diplomat.

He was born in the late ninth AH / fifteenth CE century in the village of Khund near Qazvin in northern Persia, into the Khundi Sayyids, a family established there since the fourteenth century. He inherited the Imamate from his father Shah Radi al-Din, who was killed in 915 AH / 1509 CE by a Timurid ruler then persecuting Ismailis in Badakhshan.

From early in his life Shah Tahir practised taqiyya by presenting himself as a Twelver Shi'i, and he wrote commentaries on Twelver theological works. He also moved in Sufi circles and composed a commentary on Mahmud Shabistari's celebrated poem Gulshan-i raz.

He left Persia for India and became a figure of real political weight in the Deccan, serving as a courtier of Burhan Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar (r. 1508-1554 CE). His influence there is usually credited with the Nizam Shahi state's adoption of Shi'ism - though what he professed publicly was Twelver Shi'ism, not Ismailism.

He is the clearest single illustration of how the post-Alamut Imams survived: outward conformity, genuine scholarship in the idiom of the host society, and the quiet continuation of the da'wa behind it.

entries.title: The Anjudan revival
questions: What was the Anjudan revival?
Where is Anjudan?
When did the Ismaili Imams come out of hiding?
How did the Imams rebuild the community?
Why were the Imams taken for Sufi pirs?
What is at Anjudan today?
How long did the Anjudan period last?
entries.answer:
Anjudan is a village about 37 km east of Arak, in Markazi province in central Iran. In medieval times it was a sizeable and prosperous market town, and it gives its name to the revival of Nizari Ismaili life after the Alamut catastrophe.

Following the Mongol destruction of the Nizari state in 654 AH / 1256 CE the Persian Nizaris survived for a long time under the outward forms of Sufism. In the second half of the ninth AH / fifteenth CE century the Imams re-emerged at Anjudan. Taken by outsiders for Sufi pirs, and helped by the rise of the Safavids from 907 AH / 1501 CE and their patronage of certain Shi'i dervish organisations, they were able to operate more openly than before.

What followed over roughly two centuries was a reconstruction of the community: the Imams re-established their authority over outlying Nizari populations in Persia, India and Central Asia, reorganised the da'wa with pirs and da'is reporting to the Imam, resumed the collection of tithes, and set off a genuine literary renaissance in Persian. The Nizari da'wa was particularly successful in Central Asia and in India, where Hindu converts became the Khojas.

Two mausoleums survive at Anjudan holding the tombs of several Imams, dated 885 AH / 1480 CE and 904 AH / 1498 CE and known locally as Shah Qalandar and Shah Gharib. An inscription of 1036 AH / 1627 CE records tax exemptions granted to the Imam Shah Khalil Allah by Shah Abbas I.

In the later eleventh AH / seventeenth CE century the Imams moved to nearby Kahak and Anjudan declined, especially after the Afghan invasion of 1135 AH / 1722 CE.

entries.title: Nizari writing in the Anjudan period
questions: What did Ismailis write after Alamut?
Who was Abu Ishaq Quhistani?
What is the Haft bab?
Who was Khayrkhah Harati?
What is the Kalam-i Pir?
How was Ismaili literature preserved?
Did the Nizaris write in Persian?
entries.answer:
One of the clearest signs that the Anjudan revival was real is that the Nizaris started writing books again, in Persian, for the first time since Alamut.

Abu Ishaq Quhistani (d. after 904 AH / 1498 CE) is the earliest major figure. Born at Mu'minabad east of Birjand in Quhistan, he came from a non-Ismaili family, converted as a young man, and was appointed into the regional da'wa by its chief da'i. His one surviving work, the Haft bab ('Seven Chapters'), opens with an autobiographical chapter and then sets out the Nizari teaching of the time. It is probably the first substantial Nizari doctrinal treatise of the post-Alamut period, and it was preserved by the Nizaris of Central Asia.

Khayrkhah Harati (d. after 960 AH / 1553 CE) is second only to him. Born near Herat in what is now western Afghanistan, he was the son of a da'i who was murdered by brigands while travelling to see the Imam at Anjudan. The Imam - probably Mustansir bi'llah II, known by the Sufi name Shah Gharib - appointed the nineteen-year-old Khayrkhah as chief da'i, or pir, of Khurasan and Badakhshan. His Risala preserves unique detail on how the Imam ran the da'wa from his concealed headquarters, and on the standing of the pir in the Nizari hierarchy.

A recension of Quhistani's Haft bab later circulated as the Kalam-i Pir, attributed to Nasir Khusraw to increase its authority among the Nizaris of Afghanistan and Central Asia. Almost all of this literature survives because families in Badakhshan kept and copied it.

entries.title: The Imams under the Safavids
questions: How did the Ismailis fare under the Safavids?
Did the Safavids persecute Ismailis?
Which Imam was executed by the Safavids?
Did the Imams pretend to be Twelver Shi'i?
What was life like for Persian Ismailis in the 1600s?
Who was Khaki Khurasani?
Did relations with the Safavids improve?
entries.answer:
The Safavid adoption of Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion in 907 AH / 1501 CE was not, as one might assume, a relief for the Nizaris. For the first time the Ismaili Imamate found itself inside a Shi'i-majority state, and Safavid rulers were largely hostile to it, seeing in a living Shi'i Imam a rival to their own claim to inherit the authority of the twelve Imams.

The consequences were real. The Imam Murad Mirza (d. 981 AH / 1574 CE) was executed by the Safavids on a charge of spreading heresy; other Imams were forced into hiding or exile. The Nizari poet Abu'l-Qasim Muhammad Amri Shirazi (d. 999 AH / 1590 CE) was blinded and killed.

The pressure eased somewhat from the late tenth AH / sixteenth CE century, under Shah Abbas I (r. 1587-1629 CE), and there is evidence that the Imams adopted Twelver Shi'ism during his reign as a form of taqiyya. An inscription of 1036 AH / 1627 CE records Shah Abbas granting tax exemptions to the Imam Shah Khalil Allah at Anjudan.

The career of the poet and preacher Khaki Khurasani (d. after 1056 AH / 1646 CE) of Dizbad, between Mashhad and Nishapur, shows both sides. A visit by the Imam Murad Mirza set the course of his life; he was later arrested and tortured, probably under Shah Abbas I; but around 1640 CE relations had improved far enough that the Imam Nur al-Din accompanied Shah Abbas II to Mashhad, and Khaki was likely released and returned home.

Only after the Safavid collapse in the early eighteenth century did the Imams cease to practise taqiyya.

entries.title: Kahak and the move towards Kirman
questions: Where did the Ismaili Imams live after Anjudan?
What is Kahak?
Did Khojas travel from India to see the Imam?
Where is Shah Nizar buried?
When did the Imams move to Kirman?
Where was Aga Khan I born?
entries.answer:
Kahak is a village roughly 35 km north-east of Anjudan, north-west of Mahallat in central Iran. It became the seat of the Qasim-Shahi Nizari Imamate at the end of the Anjudan period.

Khalil Allah II, the thirty-ninth Qasim-Shahi Imam, was the last of his line to live at Anjudan; he died in 1680 CE and was buried there. His son and successor Shah Nizar moved his residence and the headquarters of the da'wa to Kahak in the early decades of his Imamate, and Anjudan was permanently abandoned by the Imams. Shah Nizar died in September 1722 CE, shortly before the Afghan invasion reached Kahak, and was buried in a chamber of the building that had been his residence. His son Sayyid Ali (d. 1754 CE) also lived and was buried there.

The Kahak compound and its garden contain several tombstones inscribed in Khojki Sindhi characters - evidence of Khoja Ismailis who made the long and dangerous journey from India to see their Imam. Kahak is named in several ginans as the Imam's place of residence. A stone platform in the garden, on which the Imam sat to receive his followers, was recorded by Wladimir Ivanow in 1937 but had gone by 1976.

By the middle of the eighteenth century the Imams had moved their headquarters to Shahr-i Babak and Kirman, probably to be closer to the pilgrimage route from India, while keeping their roots at Kahak. Shah Khalil Allah III re-established himself there after 1792 CE, and his son Hasan Ali Shah, the future Aga Khan I and forty-sixth Imam, was born at Kahak in 1804 CE.

entries.title: Nasir Khusraw and Badakhshan
questions: Who was Nasir Khusraw?
Why do Badakhshani Ismailis revere Nasir Khusraw?
What is the Safarnama?
Where did Nasir Khusraw die?
Was Nasir Khusraw a Nizari?
What is Yumgan?
Why is Nasir Khusraw important to Central Asian Ismailis?
entries.answer:
Nasir Khusraw (b. 394 AH / 1004 CE, d. after 462 AH / 1070 CE) belongs to the Fatimid period rather than the Nizari one, but no account of the Ismailis of Central Asia can begin anywhere else.

He was born at Qubadiyan, near Marv in Khurasan, into a family of government officials, and worked in administration until a religious turning point around the age of forty. He then travelled for seven years to Egypt, Arabia and the Mediterranean, recording it in the Safarnama, a travelogue still read for its detail. In Cairo he studied Ismaili doctrine and law, and he returned to Khurasan as hujjat - the Fatimid da'wa's regional head - for his home province.

His success as a missionary made him dangerous to the authorities, and he had to flee. He spent his last fifteen years or so in exile in Yumgan, in the mountains of Badakhshan north of the Hindu Kush, under the protection of the local Ismaili ruler Ali b. Asad, writing poetry and philosophy in Persian.

That exile had consequences far beyond his lifetime. The Ismailis of Badakhshan - today divided between Tajikistan and Afghanistan - built a distinctive literary and devotional tradition around his teaching, and it was largely in their private libraries that Persian Ismaili manuscripts of both the Fatimid and Alamut periods survived. Later writers borrowed his name to give authority to their work: the Anjudan-period Kalam-i Pir was attributed to him for precisely that reason. In parts of Central Asia people still claim descent from him.

entries.title: The Ismailis of Central Asia
questions: Where do Ismailis live in Central Asia?
Who are the Badakhshani Ismailis?
Are there Ismailis in Tajikistan and Afghanistan?
Are there Ismailis in China?
Why did Ismailis move to the mountains?
What is the Pamir Ismaili community?
How did Ismailis survive in Central Asia?
entries.answer:
Central Asia holds some of the oldest and largest concentrations of Ismailis anywhere. The core of the community lives in Badakhshan, the mountain valleys on both sides of the Panj river, which today divides Tajikistan from Afghanistan, with related communities in central Afghanistan, the northern areas of Pakistan and the Tashkurghan district of Xinjiang in China.

The Ismaili da'wa reached Transoxania early, and da'is carried it as far as the Samanid court under Nasr II b. Ahmad (914-943 CE). Under the Ghaznavids and then the Saljuqs, Ismailis and other communities faced persecution, and many moved out of the cities and valleys of Khurasan and Transoxania into remote mountain districts such as Badakhshan. It was into that refuge that Nasir Khusraw came in the eleventh century, and his teaching became the foundation of the regional tradition.

After the Mongol period, under the Timurids, Shaybanids and the Safavid state next door, Ismaili influence in the region was marginalised. Geographical isolation and the institution of the da'wa - with pirs and khalifas serving local jamats - carried religious life forward alongside the Sufi tariqas of the region, and Badakhshani families preserved the Persian Ismaili manuscript tradition that modern scholarship depends on.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies is careful to say that Central Asian Ismailis are not a single homogeneous group: allegiance to a living Imam and shared Islamic principles unite them, but their languages, customs and histories differ considerably. The period between the Timurids and the nineteenth century remains, by IIS's own account, relatively unexamined.

entries.title: The Syrian Ismailis after the Mamluk conquest
questions: What happened to the Syrian Ismailis?
Do Ismailis still live in Syria?
Did the Syrian Ismailis keep their castles?
What did Ibn Battuta see in Syria?
Were the Syrian Ismailis cut off from the Imam?
What is Salamiyya?
entries.answer:
After Baybars reduced their fortresses between 1271 and 1273 CE, the Syrian Nizaris lost political independence but not their communities or their homes.

Under Mamluk suzerainty they kept around eight strongholds, now held on the sultan's terms rather than their own. Ibn Battuta, travelling in 1326 CE, found Maniqa, Ullayqa, Qadmus, Kahf and Masyaf still in Ismaili hands under close Mamluk supervision. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them in this period as loyal subjects first of the Mamluks and then of the Ottoman authorities in Syria. Despite the political constraints, they maintained intellectual life, kept libraries and continued a scholarly tradition.

The fall of Alamut in 1256 CE had severed them from central leadership, and in the long post-Alamut concealment the Syrian community, like others, developed largely on its own. Part of it adhered to the Muhammad-Shahi line, and Muhammad-Shahi material later reached modern scholarship through Syrian sources - the twentieth-century scholar Arif Tamir published from them.

The community's later situation was hard: a massacre of Syrian Nizaris by the Nusayris in 1809 is recorded by the French consul Jean-Baptiste Rousseau, whose reports were among the first accounts to reach European scholars that the Ismailis had not been exterminated at all.

Ismailis still live in Syria today, and the country is regularly listed among those with established Nizari communities. Salamiyya in central Syria, which had served as the secret headquarters of the early Ismaili da'wa long before, is again a centre of Ismaili life.

entries.title: Satpanth, the true path
questions: What is Satpanth?
What does Satpanth mean?
How did Ismailism reach India?
What is the Satpanth tradition?
Why does Ismaili tradition in India look Indian?
Who are the Satpanthis?
Were Satpanthis Hindu or Muslim?
entries.answer:
Satpanth means 'the true path'. It is the vernacular rendering of the Qur'anic phrase sirat al-mustaqim, and it is the name for the distinctive form Nizari Ismaili tradition took in the Indian subcontinent.

Ismaili preaching in Sind goes back to 883 CE, and a Fatimid-linked principality existed at Multan around 958-1005 CE, so there were Ismailis in the region long before the Nizari mission. From around the thirteenth century Nizari da'is - called pirs in South Asia - began working in Sind, where Ismailism had persisted quietly since Fatimid times. The main centre became Ucch, south of Multan, and from there the mission spread into Punjab, Gujarat, Kutch and Rajasthan.

What developed was a tradition expressed in local languages and local religious idiom rather than in Arabic or Persian. The pirs presented Ismaili teaching through the imagery and narrative forms already familiar to their audiences, and conversion in western India worked through persuasion and discourse rather than conquest, and did not require abandoning established life-cycle customs. Research published by the Institute of Ismaili Studies situates Satpanth alongside the bhakti and Sant movements and the Sufi vernacular literatures of Gujarat and Sind, and suggests Ismailis may have played a larger part in South Asian religious and literary history than has been recognised.

The living expression of Satpanth is the ginans. Its main community became the Khojas. In the next two or three centuries Ismailism re-emerged in the subcontinent in forms sharing much with Sufism - the pirs of Ucch, for instance, had Suhrawardi connections - and the exact nature of that relationship is still being worked out.

entries.title: The pirs of South Asia
questions: Who were the pirs?
Who was Pir Shams?
Who was Pir Sadr al-Din?
Who was Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din?
Where are the pirs buried?
Were the pirs the same as da'is?
Who are the Imam-Shahis?
entries.answer:
In South Asia the Nizari da'i was called a pir, and the pirs are the figures around whom the whole Satpanth tradition is organised.

Pir Shams al-Din is the earliest named figure associated with the start of Nizari activity in Sind; tradition has him travelling in Sind and Punjab and carrying the message as far as Kashmir and Bengal. Another early name is Satgur Nur. After Pir Shams, the mission continued secretly in Sind through his descendants, and by the time of his great-grandson Pir Sadr al-Din the pirs had become a hereditary line, in sporadic contact with the Imams, who were still in Persia.

Pir Sadr al-Din is the consolidating figure. He organised Nizari activity in South Asia, strengthened the community, converted many from the Lohana trading caste and gave them the title Khoja. His shrine is near Ucch, south of Multan.

His son Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din settled at Ucch, which became the seat of Nizari Ismailism in the subcontinent. He is reported to have been affiliated with the Suhrawardi Sufi order, then prominent in western and northern India - Multan and Ucch were also headquarters of the Suhrawardi and Qadiri orders, which gives some sense of the religious environment the pirs worked in.

After Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din's death a section of the community broke away and established itself in Gujarat, becoming known as the Imam-Shahis. The majority continued to give allegiance to the Nizari Imams.

entries.title: The Khojas
questions: Who are the Khojas?
What does Khoja mean?
Where did the Khojas come from?
Are all Khojas Ismaili?
Why did some Khojas become Twelver or Sunni?
How did Khojas reach East Africa?
Is Khoja an ethnic or religious term?
entries.answer:
'Khoja' comes from the Persian khwajah, meaning lord or master. It is the title given to those in the Indian subcontinent who joined the Nizari Ismaili tradition from roughly the thirteenth century onwards, and it is associated particularly with Pir Sadr al-Din's conversion of families from the Lohana trading caste.

The Khojas were concentrated in Gujarat, Kutch and Sind. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them as keeping strong Indian ethnic roots and caste customs while maintaining a Muslim religious identity under continual threat of persecution. Their Imams lived far away in Persia, and Khoja pilgrims made the long journey to Anjudan and later Kahak to see them; tombstones at Kahak inscribed in Khojki Sindhi characters record those visits, and Kahak is named in the ginans as the Imam's residence.

When the Imamate itself moved to India in the nineteenth century - Aga Khan I emigrated from Iran in the 1840s and settled in Bombay - the community was reorganised, and that process produced divisions. Most Khojas remained Ismaili; some became Twelver (Ithna ashari) Shi'i and others Sunni, and those communities exist to this day.

Under Aga Khan III the ethnic sense of 'Khoja' faded in favour of the broader identity 'Ismaili Muslim'. Khojas were among the earliest Asian communities to settle in East Africa in the nineteenth century, and from the 1970s many moved on to Europe and North America. Today they form one part - alongside Central Asian, Persian and Arab heritages - of a Nizari community spread across more than twenty-five countries.
