entries.title: The ginans
questions: What are ginans?
What does ginan mean?
Who wrote the ginans?
What languages are the ginans in?
Are ginans scripture?
How old are the ginans?
Why are ginans sung?
What is Khojki?
entries.answer:
Ginan comes from the Sanskrit jnana, meaning contemplative or reflective knowledge. Among Ismailis of the Indian subcontinent the word refers to the body of devotional poetry whose authorship is attributed to the pirs who preached and converted in South Asia.

The ginans exist in the languages of the regions they came from - Sind, Punjab and Gujarat - and were long transmitted in the Khojki script. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that they arose in a setting where oral and written transmission both flourished, and that because their primary role was in ritual and religious life, their performative and recited character is more pronounced than in, for example, Sufi poetry. They are sung, and they are learned by heart.

They are not historical chronicles, and IIS is careful about this. The narratives about the pirs preserved in the ginans rarely aim at objective record; their value, the Institute suggests, is twofold - they show the continuing influence of the early pirs in the community's collective memory, and they reveal what the community believed and understood at different stages of its history. The earliest surviving manuscripts date from the eighteenth century, although the material plainly refers to earlier events.

Ginans are also a historical source in a more literal way: Kahak, where the Imams lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, is named in several of them.

They remain in active devotional use in Nizari Ismaili communities of South Asian heritage today, and are an ongoing subject of scholarly work.

entries.title: How we know: sources for Nizari history
questions: How do we know about Ismaili history?
Why were Ismaili books lost?
Who was Wladimir Ivanow?
Why do we rely on hostile sources?
Where did Ismaili manuscripts survive?
When did Ismaili studies begin?
Can we trust Juwayni?
entries.answer:
Ismaili communities did not, on the whole, write history. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains why: the da'is who were also the community's scholars usually worked in hostile territory under conditions of taqiyya, and they were trained as theologians rather than chroniclers. The surviving Ismaili literature is overwhelmingly doctrinal and concerned with esoteric interpretation (ta'wil).

There were two exceptions, both in periods when Ismailis held states: the Fatimid era and the Alamut era. The Nizari chronicles began with the Sargudhasht-i Sayyidna on Hasan-i Sabbah's life, continued through works on his successors, and were kept in the libraries of Alamut and the Quhistan castles. They are all believed to have perished in or shortly after the Mongol invasion.

What survives of them is second-hand. Three Ilkhanid historians - Juwayni (d. 681 AH / 1283 CE), Rashid al-Din (d. 718 AH / 1318 CE) and Abu'l-Qasim Kashani (d. c. 736 AH / 1335 CE) - read the Nizari material and used it extensively, and their accounts remain the principal primary sources for the Nizari state despite being written by opponents.

For centuries, therefore, outsiders wrote Ismaili history from hostile chronicles and Crusader legend. That changed in the twentieth century with the recovery and study of genuine Ismaili manuscripts, much of it through the work of Wladimir Ivanow and through the private libraries of Badakhshan and the Khoja communities of India, which had preserved texts the Persian heartland had lost.

This entry, and the others in this collection, rest on that recovered scholarship as published by the Ismaili community's own institutions.

Who became Imam after Aga Khan IV?
entries.answer:
"Hazir" (also written Hazar) means present. When Ismailis speak of the Hazir Imam, or Mawlana Hazar Imam, they mean the Imam who is alive and present in the world now, as distinct from an Imam of the past or one awaited in the future.

Since 4 February 2025 that Imam has been His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, the 50th hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims. He succeeded his father, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, who died in Lisbon on 4 February 2025 at the age of 88 after an Imamat of 67 years.

The Imamat's own institutions describe the line as unbroken: Ismailis believe the Imam is a direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his progeny) through the Prophet's daughter Hazrat Bibi Fatima and his cousin and son-in-law Hazrat Ali, whom Shia Muslims regard as the first Imam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the Ismailis are today the only Shia community led by a living, hereditary Imam in direct descent from the Prophet.

The Imamat states that the Ismailis live in over 35 countries and number roughly 12 to 15 million people. Because the Imam is living and present, Ismailis look to him for guidance on the faith in current circumstances rather than only to past rulings, and the Imamat describes his mandate as covering both the interpretation of the faith and the quality of life of the community and the societies around it.

entries.title: What the Ismaili Imamat is
questions: What is the Ismaili Imamat?
Is the Imamat a country or a government?
What authority does the Ismaili Imam have?
Is the Imamat political?
What is the difference between the Imam and the Imamat?
Why do governments sign agreements with the Imamat?
Does the Imam rule any land?
How old is the institution of the Imamat?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Imamat describes itself as a supra-national entity: a hereditary religious office running in succession from Hazrat Ali, and an institution with a history of more than 1,400 years. The word distinguishes the office from the person who holds it, much as "the papacy" differs from a particular pope.

Its own description of the role is careful. The Imam's authority is that of religious interpretation; it is not a political role, and in the modern era the Imams govern no territory. The Imamat calls itself strictly non-political and says Ismailis are expected to be loyal, law-abiding citizens of the countries where they live.

At the same time, the Imamat holds that in Islam the spiritual and the material are inseparable, so the office carries responsibility for improving quality of life as well as for interpreting faith. In practice that has meant building institutions: councils and boards for the community's social governance, and the agencies of the Aga Khan Development Network for wider society.

Because it has legal personality but no territory, the Imamat enters formal agreements with states. It lists Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brazil, Canada, France, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mali, Pakistan, Portugal, Syria and Tajikistan, the European Commission and the East African Community among those with which it has formal relationships. A scholar writing for The Institute of Ismaili Studies has described this arrangement as authority exercised without territory, resting on spiritual legitimacy and institutional frameworks rather than on political control.

entries.title: Nass: how one Imam designates the next
questions: What is nass?
How is the next Ismaili Imam chosen?
Is the Imam elected?
Can the Imam's successor be a brother or nephew?
Why do Ismailis say the line is unbroken?
What does Ghadir Khumm have to do with succession?
Does the community vote on the next Imam?
When does a designated successor actually become Imam?
entries.answer:
Ismailis believe the Imamat passes by nass, an explicit designation made by the Imam of the Time, not by election or by seniority. The Institute of Ismaili Studies and the community's own explanations trace the doctrine to the early decades of Shia Islam, when rival claims to leadership arose, and associate its articulation with the Imams Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq: that an Imam can only be designated by the preceding Imam, informed by divine support or inspiration (ta'yid), and that the designation must be explicit and made before witnesses.

The model for this, in Shia belief, is the Prophet Muhammad's own designation of Hazrat Ali at the oasis of Ghadir Khumm on the return from his last pilgrimage, when he is recorded in both Shia and Sunni hadith collections as raising Ali's hand and declaring that whoever's master he was, Ali was his master too.

The Preamble to the Ismaili Constitution ordained in 1986 puts the rule plainly: succession is by nass, and it is the absolute prerogative of the Imam of the Time to appoint his successor from among any of his male descendants, whether sons or more distant male issue.

Designation happens during the Imam's lifetime, but takes effect at his death. Aga Khan IV explained this in a 1985 television interview: the next Imam is appointed in the sense that the current Imam alone knows who he will be, but he becomes Imam when the current Imam dies. Ismailis also believe that light and divinely inspired knowledge pass to the successor at that moment, so the Jamat is never without an Imam.

sources.title: How does the Ismaili Imam designate his successor?

entries.notes: The wording of the Constitution's Preamble is quoted by The Ismaili; the full text of the Constitution is not published openly on these sites.

entries.title: How the Jamat learns who the next Imam is
questions: How is a new Ismaili Imam announced?
Where is the designation written down?
What happened after Aga Khan IV died?
Who reads the Imam's will?
Is there a gap between one Imam and the next?
How quickly was the 50th Imam named?
Who was present when the will was read?
entries.answer:
The designation made by nass is recorded in the Imam's will, and the will is read after his death in the presence of the Imam's family, the executors, and senior international leaders of the Jamat. Only then is the community told who the new Imam is.

The 2025 transition shows the sequence clearly. Aga Khan IV died in Lisbon on 4 February 2025. On the same day the community was informed that his successor as 50th Imam had already been designated in conformity with the tradition and practice of nass, and that the designation was recorded in his will, which was still to be read.

The following day, 5 February 2025, the will was unsealed in Lisbon and Prince Rahim al-Hussaini was named the 50th hereditary Imam, taking the title Aga Khan V. Both the Imamat and The Ismaili described the Nur of Imamat as vested in him in unbroken hereditary succession from Hazrat Mawlana Ali.

In answering questions at the time, The Ismaili emphasised the belief that the Jamat is never without an Imam even in the interval before the announcement: as soon as one Imam leaves the physical world his spiritual light passes to his designated successor. The public naming, on this understanding, informs the community of something that has already taken effect rather than creating it.

sources.title: 50th Imam Declared: Mawlana Hazar Imam Shah Rahim al-Hussaini Aga Khan V
Prince Rahim Aga Khan V Named 50th Hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims
What to expect in the next few days

entries.title: The line and numbering of the Ismaili Imams
questions: How many Ismaili Imams have there been?
Why is the Aga Khan called the 50th Imam?
Who was the first Ismaili Imam?
Why are Ismailis called Ismailis?
How do Ismailis count their Imams?
What is the Nizari line?
Is the numbering the same as for other Shia Muslims?
Where can I read about each Imam?
entries.answer:
Ismailis count Hazrat Ali as the first Imam and number the line forward from him. Prince Rahim Aga Khan V is the 50th. His father Aga Khan IV was the 49th, Aga Khan III the 48th, Aga Khan II the 47th and Aga Khan I the 46th.

The branch point that gives the community its name comes early. The Imamat's own account is that after the fifth Imam, Jafar as-Sadiq, the Shia subdivided, and the Ismailis take their name from upholding his eldest son Ismail as the rightful successor. Note that this counting is internal to the Ismaili tradition; other Shia communities number the early Imams differently, so the same historical figure may carry a different number elsewhere.

A second division came in 1094, when the community split over the succession to the Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mustansir. The branch that leads to the present Imams is the Nizari line, named for his son Nizar, and it is this line that later produced the Imams known as the Aga Khans.

The Ismaili is publishing a series called Stories of the Ismaili Imams, drawing on materials from The Institute of Ismaili Studies, with a short biography for each Imam from Mawlana Ali to the present day. Entries released so far run from the first Imam through the Fatimid period and include the modern Imams, and each gives dates, place of burial and a note on the Imam's contribution.

sources.title: The Ismaili Imamat: a brief history

entries.notes: These sources give the branch points and the modern numbers but do not publish a single continuous numbered list of all fifty Imams in one place; the numbering above is assembled from the individual Imam biographies on The Ismaili.

entries.title: Where the title "Aga Khan" comes from
questions: What does Aga Khan mean?
Where does the title Aga Khan come from?
Who gave the Imam the title Aga Khan?
Is Aga Khan a family name?
Is the title hereditary?
Which Imam was the first Aga Khan?
Is Aga Khan a religious title?
How is it different from His Highness?
entries.answer:
"Aga Khan" is not a religious office. It is an honorific granted by the ruler of Persia in the early nineteenth century, which then became hereditary in the family of the Imams.

The Ismaili's biography of the 46th Imam, Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, says he received the hereditary title of Aga Khan from Fath Ali Shah Qajar, the ruler of Persia, and also married the Shah's daughter, Sarv-i Jahan Khanum. The Ismaili's tribute to the 49th Imam dates the grant to 1817. The Institute of Ismaili Studies likewise records that he was the first Imam to bear the title of Aga Khan, bestowed by the Persian emperor Fath Ali Shah.

Because it is hereditary, each successive Imam in this line has carried it: Hasan Ali Shah as Aga Khan I, his eldest son Aqa Ali Shah as Aga Khan II, Sultan Mahomed Shah as Aga Khan III, Shah Karim al-Hussaini as Aga Khan IV, and Prince Rahim al-Hussaini, named the 50th hereditary Imam on 5 February 2025, as Aga Khan V. The numbering of the Aga Khans therefore runs separately from, and is much shorter than, the numbering of the Imams.

The style "His Highness" is different again. IIS records that it was a courtesy granted by the British government, first to Aga Khan I and then to his successor Aga Khan II. The Ismaili records that Aga Khan IV was designated "His Highness" by Queen Elizabeth II early in his Imamat, which began in 1957.

sources.title: Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, our 46th Imam
Mawlana Shah Karim: Our Beloved 49th Imam
The Ismaili Imamat: a brief history

entries.notes: The 1817 date comes from The Ismaili; the allowed sources that name Fath Ali Shah Qajar as the grantor do not all give a year. On 'His Highness' the sources describe two distinct grants: IIS treats it as a British courtesy first held by Aga Khan I, while The Ismaili records Queen Elizabeth II designating Aga Khan IV early in his Imamat.

entries.title: Aga Khan I: Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, 46th Imam
questions: Who was the first Aga Khan?
Why did the Imam leave Persia?
When did the Imams move to India?
How long was Aga Khan I the Imam?
Where is Aga Khan I buried?
What is Hasanabad?
Did the first Aga Khan write anything?
When did the seat of the Imamat leave Persia?
entries.answer:
Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, the 46th Imam, was born in 1804 at Kahak in Persia and succeeded to the Imamat in 1817, aged only thirteen. He is the first Imam to bear the title Aga Khan, which The Institute of Ismaili Studies records was bestowed by the Persian emperor Fath Ali Shah.

He held office under the Qajar dynasty, serving as governor of Qum and later, from 1835, as governor of Kirman. Political intrigue at the court of Muhammad Shah Qajar and an armed confrontation with Qajar forces led to his departure from Persia in 1841. The Ismaili notes that this ended seven centuries of the Imamat's residence in Persia. He recorded the confrontation and his journey in a memoir, the Ibrat-afza.

He settled in Mumbai in 1848 and turned to organising the community in India. IIS describes the move as having an uplifting effect on the community in India and on the religious and communal life of the whole Ismaili world, helping the community gain a greater sense of confidence and identity as a Shia Muslim community and laying the foundations for its social progress; it also began an era of more regular contact between the Imam and his widely dispersed followers, whose deputations travelled to Mumbai from as far as Kashgar, Bokhara, Iran, the Middle East and the African coast.

A dispute with a small group who rejected his rights over communal property came before the Bombay High Court in 1866 as the Aga Khan Case; The Ismaili records that the judge formally recognised him as the Ismaili Imam and confirmed that the community were historically Shia Ismaili Muslims, establishing the legal authority of the Imamat in modern times.

He died in April 1881 after an Imamat of 64 years, the third longest in the line, and his mausoleum is at Hasanabad in Mumbai. A short passage attributed to him and quoted by The Ismaili gives a sense of his teaching on God: that God is neither matter nor material, has neither direction nor place, and cannot be seen except through spiritual sight.

sources.title: Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, our 46th Imam
The Ismaili Imamat: a brief history

entries.notes: The Ismaili cites a translation of the Ibrat-afza (Beben and Mohammad Poor, 'The First Aga Khan') but the allowed sources do not state who published it, so the publisher is not named here.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Case of 1866
questions: What was the Aga Khan Case?
Why did the Imam go to court in Bombay?
How was the Imam's authority recognised legally?
What did the 1866 ruling decide?
Who challenged the Imam's authority in India?
Why does the Aga Khan Case matter?
When was the community legally identified as Ismaili?
entries.answer:
After Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah settled in Mumbai in 1848, a small group within the community rejected his rights over communal properties. The dispute reached the Bombay High Court in 1866 in what became known as the Aga Khan Case.

The ruling went in the Imam's favour. A British judge formally recognised Hasan Ali Shah as the Ismaili Imam and confirmed that the community before the court were, historically, Shia Ismaili Muslims. The judgment granted him full authority over the community's affairs and institutions, which he then set about reorganising.

The Ismaili describes the case as important because it firmly established the legal authority of the Imamat in modern times. In practical terms it settled, within the legal system of British India, both who the Imam was and what the community's religious identity was, and so made possible the constitutions, councils and endowments that his successors built during the following century.

This entry rests on a single account published by The Ismaili. The allowed sources do not set out the pleadings, the judgment's reasoning or the arguments of those who brought the challenge, so the summary here is limited to the outcome and its significance as the community's own institutions describe it.

sources.title: Mawlana Hasan Ali Shah, our 46th Imam

entries.notes: Only one allowed source covers this case, and it gives the outcome rather than the detail of the proceedings.

entries.title: Aga Khan II: Mawlana Aga Ali Shah, 47th Imam
questions: Who was Aga Khan II?
How long was Aga Khan II the Imam?
Where is Aga Khan II buried?
What did Aga Khan II do for education?
Who was the Muhammadan National Association?
Was Aga Khan II involved in Indian public life?
Who was Aga Khan III's father?
entries.answer:
Mawlana Aga Ali Shah, known as Aga Khan II, was born in 1830 at Mahallat in central Persia and succeeded to the Imamat in 1881. He married a Qajar princess, Shams al-Muluk, a granddaughter of the same Fath Ali Shah Qajar who had bestowed the hereditary title of Aga Khan on his father.

His was the shortest of the modern Imamats, just four years. He died in 1885 and is buried in a family mausoleum at Najaf, alongside his grandfather Mawlana Khalil Allah Ali II and other relatives.

Despite its brevity, The Ismaili credits him with contributions well beyond the Ismaili community. He was appointed to the Bombay Legislative Council and was elected President of the Muhammadan National Association, through which he promoted educational and philanthropic projects intended to benefit Muslims across British India.

Within the community he concentrated on raising educational standards for children and on strengthening contact with Ismailis in places where the Imamat had long had little direct reach, particularly Central Asia, Burma and East Africa. The Ismaili's assessment is that these four years laid the foundations for the very large institutional growth that followed under his son and grandson. His son Sultan Mahomed Shah succeeded him in 1885 as Aga Khan III.

sources.title: Mawlana Aga Ali Shah, our 47th Imam
Aga Khan III: A Statesman and a Champion for Education and Social Reform

entries.title: Aga Khan III: Sir Sultan Mahomed Shah, 48th Imam
questions: Who was Aga Khan III?
How long was Aga Khan III the Imam?
When was Sultan Mahomed Shah born?
How old was Aga Khan III when he became Imam?
What is Aga Khan III known for?
Where is Aga Khan III buried?
Was Aga Khan III involved in Indian politics?
When did the seat of the Imamat move to Europe?
entries.answer:
Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, Aga Khan III, was born in Karachi on 2 November 1877, the son of Aga Khan II and Nawab A'lia Shamsul-Muluk. He succeeded to the Imamat on 17 August 1885, aged seven, and held it until his death on 11 July 1957 in Geneva. At 72 years it is the longest Imamat in the recorded line.

He is remembered by the community's institutions on several fronts at once. Within the Ismaili community he modernised its institutions, establishing written constitutions and a system of councils, and building hundreds of schools across Asia and Africa with a particular insistence on educating girls.

In the wider public life of British India he was a prominent Muslim leader. He presided over the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1902; when it reconvened in 1906 it resolved to create the All-India Muslim League, and he was chosen as its first President. He supported the development of Aligarh Muslim University, which he later called his greatest service to Islam, and pressed repeatedly for modern and scientific education as the route to social and economic progress.

On the world stage his career culminated in his election in 1937 as President of the Assembly of the League of Nations, the forerunner of the United Nations. He eventually transferred the seat of the Imamat to Europe. His mausoleum stands at Aswan in Egypt.

sources.title: Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, our 48th Imam
Aga Khan III: A Statesman and a Champion for Education and Social Reform
A Golden Prince of History: Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah and his Contributions to Pakistan
Aga Khan III: A Study in Humanism

entries.title: Aga Khan III and the League of Nations
questions: Was the Aga Khan president of the League of Nations?
When was Aga Khan III elected at the League of Nations?
What international role did Aga Khan III play?
Did an Ismaili Imam lead an international body?
How did Aga Khan III represent India abroad?
What is the link between the Imamat and international diplomacy?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan III was active in international affairs for decades, and his public career abroad culminated in 1937 when he was elected President of the Assembly of the League of Nations, the body that preceded the United Nations.

The Ismaili's biography of the 48th Imam records the 1937 election plainly and treats it as the high point of his work on the global stage. A background paper on the Ismaili community published by the community's own institutions goes further and describes him as twice President of the League of Nations; it also argues that through this work he gave a contemporary articulation to the public international role of the Imamat.

That framing matters for understanding the Imamat today. The same paper states that the Imamat under his successors has continued his tradition of strict political neutrality, while maintaining formal relationships with governments and international organisations. The modern pattern of protocols and agreements between states and the Ismaili Imamat is presented as a continuation of what Aga Khan III began, rather than as a new departure.

The allowed sources do not set out the substance of his work at Geneva, the issues he handled, or the 1930s political context in any detail, so this entry stays with what those institutions state.

sources.title: Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, our 48th Imam

entries.notes: The allowed sources differ: The Ismaili's biography of the 48th Imam gives a single election in 1937, while the community's background paper says he was twice President of the League of Nations. Neither explains the discrepancy.

entries.title: Aga Khan III and the first Ismaili constitutions and councils
questions: When was the first Ismaili constitution written?
Who created the Ismaili councils?
What did the 1905 constitution cover?
How was the Ismaili community governed before 1986?
Why did the Imam give the community a constitution?
Were there different constitutions in different regions?
What is personal law in the Ismaili constitutions?
entries.answer:
The practice of the Imam giving the community written rules of conduct is an old one, but the first Ismaili constitution of the modern period was ordained by Aga Khan III in 1905 for the Ismailis of East Africa.

That constitution gave the community a form of administration built on a hierarchy of governance structures at local, national and regional levels. It set out rules of personal law governing matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance, and it laid down guidelines for mutual cooperation and support within the community and for its dealings with other communities.

Similar constitutions were then promulgated in South Asia under the Imam's instructions, and all of them were revised periodically as circumstances changed. The Imamat presents this as the modern system of social governance that Aga Khan III pioneered during the colonial era.

The importance of the 1905 framework is that it is the direct ancestor of the arrangements Ismailis live under now. When Aga Khan IV succeeded in 1957, his task as the Imamat describes it was to adapt this colonial-era system to a world of nation states; the global Ismaili Constitution he ordained in 1986 brought the separate regional constitutions under one common aegis for the first time. The councils that Ismailis elect and serve on today are the continuation of the structure Aga Khan III created.

sources.title: Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, our 48th Imam

entries.title: Aga Khan III on education, science and the education of girls
questions: What did Aga Khan III say about educating girls?
Why did the Imam say to educate the daughter first?
What did Aga Khan III think about science?
How many schools did Aga Khan III found?
What was Aga Khan III's view of women's education?
Did Aga Khan III support Aligarh?
When did the Imam speak about educating girls?
entries.answer:
Education was the centre of Aga Khan III's programme of reform, and the education of girls was the part of it he pressed hardest.

The Ismaili records his best-known guidance: that if financial constraints forced a family to choose, the education of daughters should be given priority over that of sons, in order to redress a balance that had long favoured men. His reasoning had a practical side, that an educated woman could support herself and her children without depending on a husband, and that mothers shape the next generation. But The Ismaili is careful to note that he did not rest the argument there. Speaking in 1918, he held that a woman's own happiness and welfare were reason enough for her to seek learning, and he saw educated partnership between women and men, resting on mutual respect for each other's intelligence, as the goal.

Alongside this he argued repeatedly for modern and scientific education. In his inaugural address to the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference in Delhi on 4 December 1911 he told his audience that if their people took to science in the right spirit, the industrial and economic future of the community would no longer be in doubt. He regarded the study of nature as a religious obligation and reminded Muslim audiences of the periods when Islamic civilisation had led the sciences.

He founded hundreds of schools across Asia and Africa, including the Diamond Jubilee Schools funded from his 1946 jubilee, and supported Aligarh Muslim University, which he called his greatest service to Islam.

sources.title: Empowering women: A legacy of the Ismaili Imamat
A Golden Prince of History: Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah and his Contributions to Pakistan
Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, our 48th Imam

entries.title: The jubilees of Aga Khan III and the weighing ceremonies
questions: What were the Aga Khan's weighing ceremonies?
Why was the Imam weighed against gold and diamonds?
What is a jubilee in the Ismaili tradition?
When were Aga Khan III's jubilees?
What happened to the gold and diamonds?
What is a nazrana?
What institutions came out of the jubilees?
What is Diamond Trust Bank?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan III marked three jubilees: Golden in 1935-36 for fifty years of his Imamat, Diamond for sixty years (due in August 1945 but deferred to 1946, since the immediate post-war period seemed an unsuitable moment), and Platinum for seventy years, observed in Karachi in 1954 and Cairo in 1955.

At these occasions he was weighed against gold, diamonds and platinum. The Imamat explains that such ceremonies were common among rulers and faith leaders in South Asia at the time and served to generate resources for social and economic development. The gifts were offered by the community as an unconditional gift, or nazrana, and in each case the Imam returned the proceeds to be used for the community's own advancement. The Ismaili notes that despite sensationalised press coverage, the ceremonies were not displays of the Imam's wealth.

The institutions created are still visible. The Golden Jubilee funded overseas scholarships, secondary schools, child welfare centres and nursing homes, and established the Jubilee Insurance Company; it also prompted the East African Muslim Welfare Society, which over the following decades built schools, mosques, clinics and a polytechnic for the region's indigenous Muslims. The Diamond Jubilee created education and welfare trusts, funded Diamond Jubilee Schools in places such as Hunza and Chitral, and set up the Diamond Jubilee Investment Trust, which continues today as Diamond Trust Bank. The Platinum Jubilee funded the Platinum Jubilee Finance and Investment Corporation, building societies, schools and housing, and the Platinum Jubilee Hospital in Nairobi, now the Aga Khan University Hospital.

sources.title: Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah, our 48th Imam

entries.title: Why Aga Khan III chose his grandson in 1957
questions: Why did Aga Khan III skip his son?
Why was Prince Karim chosen instead of Prince Aly Khan?
What did Aga Khan III's will say?
How old was Aga Khan IV when he became Imam?
When did Aga Khan IV succeed?
Can an Imam designate a grandson?
What reasons did the will give?
entries.answer:
When Aga Khan III died on 11 July 1957, the Imamat passed not to his son but to his grandson, Prince Karim, then a twenty-year-old student of Islamic history at Harvard.

Under the rule of nass this was entirely within the Imam's prerogative: he may designate any of his male descendants, whether a son or a more distant male issue. The Constitution's Preamble states this explicitly, so the choice of a grandson required no special justification in principle.

The reasoning the will itself gave is quoted by The Ismaili. Aga Khan III referred to the fundamentally altered conditions in the world, which had provoked many changes, and expressed the view that the office should now pass to a young man who brings a new outlook on life to his office. The community's account frames the transition in those terms: from the full and eventful life of an eighty-year-old Imam to a young man facing a rapidly changing post-war world.

Aga Khan IV himself later described the qualities he thought the office needed, in a 1985 interview: a thorough and deep understanding of the faith he must interpret and lead, an understanding of the issues facing the Ismaili community and the countries where they live, and the equipment to handle a leadership office.

In his first address as Imam he paid tribute to his grandfather, saying that he would always be his ideal and example, and pledged his life to the progress of Ismailis worldwide.

sources.title: Mawlana Shah Karim: Our Beloved 49th Imam
How does the Ismaili Imam designate his successor?

entries.notes: The allowed sources quote the will's stated reasoning but do not publish its full text, and they do not discuss Prince Aly Khan's position directly.

entries.title: Aga Khan IV: Mawlana Shah Karim al-Hussaini, 49th Imam
questions: Who was Aga Khan IV?
When was Prince Karim born?
How long was Aga Khan IV the Imam?
What did Aga Khan IV achieve?
When did Aga Khan IV found the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
What is the Global Centre for Pluralism?
Where did Aga Khan IV work from?
What was Aiglemont?
entries.answer:
Mawlana Shah Karim al-Hussaini, Aga Khan IV, was born in Geneva on 13 December 1936, the son of Prince Aly Khan and Princess Tajuddawlah, and spent his early childhood in Nairobi. He succeeded his grandfather on 11 July 1957 at the age of twenty and led the community for 67 years, the second longest Imamat in the recorded line, until his death in Lisbon on 4 February 2025 at the age of 88.

AKDN describes his understanding of the office as twofold: to interpret the faith for the Ismaili community, and to take a lead in improving their quality of life and the quality of life of the people among whom they live.

The institutions he built follow from that. He established the Aga Khan Development Network; he founded The Institute of Ismaili Studies in 1977 to promote scholarship about Islam and the intellectual heritage of the Ismailis, and chaired it thereafter; he ordained the first global Ismaili Constitution in 1986; and he founded the Global Centre for Pluralism with the Government of Canada.

He worked for decades from his private secretariat at Aiglemont in France before establishing a formal Seat of the Ismaili Imamat in Lisbon in 2015. He returned to Harvard after his first year as Imam to finish his degree, and later said that much of what he achieved was anchored in the education he received there.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Development Network
questions: What is the AKDN?
Who founded the Aga Khan Development Network?
Is AKDN a religious organisation?
What does AKDN do?
How big is the AKDN?
Does AKDN only help Ismailis?
What is Aga Khan University?
Who leads AKDN now?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Development Network is the cluster of agencies through which the Imamat pursues what it calls the material dimension of its mandate. The Imamat describes AKDN as a group of private, international, non-denominational agencies working to improve living conditions and opportunities in some of the poorest parts of the developing world, across Central Asia, South Asia, Africa and the Middle East.

Its mandates cover education from pre-school to university and research, health from primary to tertiary care, culture, rural development, human habitat, crisis response, microfinance, economic development and the strengthening of civil society. Its institutions include Aga Khan University, founded in 1983 as Pakistan's first private international university; the University of Central Asia, founded in 2000 for high mountain societies; the Aga Khan Award for Architecture, established in 1977; the Aga Khan Music Programme; the Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme; and the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto, which opened in 2014.

At the time of Aga Khan IV's death, AKDN reported operating more than 200 schools with over 85,000 students and more than 700 health facilities, employing around 96,000 people, mostly from Asia and Africa, and spending roughly one billion US dollars a year on non-profit activity.

The key point for newcomers is that AKDN is non-denominational. It serves whole populations, not Ismailis specifically. His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V now chairs it, as his father did before him.

entries.title: The jubilees of Aga Khan IV: Silver, Golden and Diamond
questions: When was the Aga Khan's Golden Jubilee?
What was the Diamond Jubilee of Aga Khan IV?
What did the Silver Jubilee fund?
What is a jubilee visit?
When did the Diamond Jubilee begin?
What projects came out of the Golden Jubilee?
Did Aga Khan IV have weighing ceremonies?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan IV marked three jubilees. The Silver Jubilee of 1982-83 celebrated twenty-five years of his Imamat, the Golden Jubilee of 2007-08 fifty years, and the Diamond Jubilee sixty years, opening on 11 July 2017 and closing in July 2018.

As in his grandfather's time, the community presented an unconditional gift, which the Imam allocated to projects chosen in consultation with community leaders. The Silver Jubilee funded, among other things, Aga Khan University in Karachi, the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme in Gujarat, the Aga Khan Hospital in Dar es Salaam, medical centres in Kisumu and Singal, immunisation clinics in Dacca, and the Ismaili Centres in London and Burnaby.

During the Golden Jubilee he travelled to more than twenty countries and initiated twenty-two community and development projects, including the opening of the Ismaili Centre in Dubai, the inauguration of the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat in Ottawa, foundation ceremonies for an Aga Khan Academy in Dhaka and a hydropower project at Bujagali in Uganda, and the restoration of historic sites in Aleppo.

The Diamond Jubilee took a different shape: he accepted invitations from heads of state for formal visits to countries with longstanding ties to the Imamat, combining meetings with Ismaili communities and engagements around Imamat and AKDN projects. He concluded the jubilee year in Portugal, where on 11 July 2018 he designated the Seat of the Ismaili Imamat in Lisbon.

entries.title: The honours and titles of Aga Khan IV
questions: Why is the Aga Khan called His Highness?
Who gave the Aga Khan the title His Highness?
What honours did Aga Khan IV receive?
Did Aga Khan IV have honorary degrees?
Was the Aga Khan an honorary Canadian citizen?
What awards did the Aga Khan win?
Are these titles religious?
entries.answer:
The style "His Highness" is a civil honour, not a religious one. It was conferred on Aga Khan IV by Queen Elizabeth II in 1957, early in his Imamat. "Aga Khan" itself is likewise a civil title, hereditary in the family since the early nineteenth century.

Over his 67 years he accumulated a very large number of state decorations, honorary degrees and prizes. AKDN's tribute counts 44 international awards and 24 honorary degrees. The Imamat's own listing records decorations from, among others, Portugal, Iran, Pakistan, Italy, Senegal, Morocco, France, Spain, Bahrain, the United Kingdom, Canada, Kenya, Mali, the Kyrgyz Republic and Uganda, including Nishan-e-Pakistan in 1983, a Knight Commander of the British Empire in 2004, Honorary Companion of the Order of Canada in 2005 and the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour in 2018.

Honorary degrees came from institutions including McGill, London, Wales, Brown, Toronto, the American University of Beirut, the American University in Cairo, Harvard, Cambridge, Ottawa and Lisbon. Other recognitions included the Andrew Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2005, honorary Canadian citizenship in 2009, India's Padma Vibhushan in 2015 and the Adrienne Clarkson Prize for Global Citizenship in 2016.

Most of these were given for his development and architectural work rather than for his religious office, which is part of why the community's own sources present them as recognition of the Imamat's engagement with the material world.

sources.title: His Highness Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, 1936-2025
Mawlana Shah Karim: Our Beloved 49th Imam

entries.notes: The honours list on ismaili.imamat now sits beneath a biography of Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, but its entries run from 1960 to 2019 and are those of Aga Khan IV; the page appears not to have been fully reorganised after the 2025 transition.

entries.title: The Seat of the Ismaili Imamat in Lisbon
questions: Where is the headquarters of the Ismaili Imamat?
Why is the Imamat based in Portugal?
What is the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat?
When was the agreement with Portugal signed?
What is the Henrique de Mendonca Palace?
Is the Imamat recognised in international law?
What is the 2010 Faith Agreement with Portugal?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Imamat's global headquarters, its Seat, is in Lisbon. This is the first time in the modern history of the Imamat that it has had a formal Seat at all.

The relationship with Portugal was built in stages. In 2010 the Portuguese parliament unanimously ratified a Faith Agreement with the Ismaili Imamat, recognising it as an international legal entity with the capacity to enter national and international treaties, and giving formal recognition to the community's constitutional bodies. In 2015 the Ismaili Imamat and the Republic of Portugal signed the landmark agreement that enabled the establishment of the Seat, which the Imamat describes as strengthening its institutional capacity and giving it a global headquarters for all dimensions of its work: the affairs of the Ismaili community, its international engagement, and its commitment to quality of life.

On 11 July 2018, marking the conclusion of his Diamond Jubilee year, Aga Khan IV formally designated the Henrique de Mendonca Palace on Rua Marques de Fronteira in Lisbon as the Seat, and declared that it should be known as the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat.

Lisbon is consequently where the events of February 2025 took place: Aga Khan IV died there, his will was read there, his funeral was held at the Ismaili Centre Lisbon, and the Takht-nishini of the 50th Imam was held at the Diwan.

sources.title: Mawlana Hazar Imam accepts pledges of allegiance from Global Jamat

entries.notes: The two Imamat sites date the Seat agreement differently: ismaili.imamat gives 3 June 2015, while The Ismaili's page gives November 2015.

entries.title: The death and funeral of Aga Khan IV, February 2025
questions: When did the Aga Khan die?
Where did Aga Khan IV die?
How old was the Aga Khan when he died?
Where was the Aga Khan's funeral?
Who attended the funeral?
Could ordinary Ismailis attend?
What happened at the funeral ceremony?
What is a janaza?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan IV died peacefully in Lisbon on 4 February 2025, aged 88, surrounded by his family, after 67 years as the 49th hereditary Imam.

His funeral was held at the Ismaili Centre Lisbon at 11:00 GMT on Saturday 8 February 2025. It was an intimate ceremony open to invited guests: his family, the newly declared 50th Imam, world leaders including the President of Portugal and the Prime Minister of Canada, the 22 National Council presidents representing Jamats worldwide, and past and present senior leaders of Imamat institutions. Members of the community were asked not to seek to attend in person unless specifically invited, but the ceremony was broadcast live on The Ismaili TV and screened in Jamatkhanas so that the global Jamat could take part in the prayers.

The Ismaili's account describes the janaza, the casket, being carried into the hall by Ismaili Volunteers to the sound of the salawat, draped in white cloth bearing the late Imam's personal standard embroidered in gold. Selected verses of the Qur'an were recited, those present filed past to pay their respects, and after the recitation of the Fatiha members of the family, led by the new Imam, carried the janaza out to a hearse as the shahada was proclaimed.

In keeping with Muslim practice, the body did not lie in state and the funeral was held as soon as arrangements allowed. Special prayers were offered in Jamatkhanas worldwide, and again on the fortieth day after the death.

entries.title: The burial of Aga Khan IV at Aswan
questions: Where is the Aga Khan buried?
Why was the Aga Khan buried in Egypt?
What is at Aswan?
Who else is buried at Aswan?
Will there be a new mausoleum?
What is the connection between the Imamat and Egypt?
When was the burial?
Who is Mata Salamat?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan IV was laid to rest on Sunday 9 February 2025 at a private burial ceremony in Aswan, in southern Egypt. The new Imam and his family were present, together with senior leaders of the Jamat.

The Governor of Aswan facilitated and joined a procession through the city to the banks of the Nile, and the casket was carried by boat in a ceremonial crossing to the mausoleum of the late Imam's grandfather, Mawlana Sultan Mahomed Shah. The janaza was carried by hand up to the hilltop mausoleum, where the body was interred. Afterwards the Governor presented the new Imam with a symbolic key to the city. A new mausoleum is to be built for Aga Khan IV on land adjacent to the existing structure, as his final resting place.

The choice of Aswan reflects two long connections. Egypt was the centre of the Fatimid Caliphate, governed by Ismaili Imam-Caliphs in the tenth and eleventh centuries, who founded Cairo as a centre of learning and culture. And Aswan is where Sultan Mahomed Shah and his wife, known as Mata Salamat, are buried; both had warm relations with the people of the city, a relationship Aga Khan IV sustained through the development work of the Om Habibeh Foundation and later the Aga Khan Foundation. AKDN's best-known Egyptian project, Al-Azhar Park in Cairo, opened in 2005 after twenty years of work.

sources.title: Mawlana Shah Karim laid to rest

entries.title: Aga Khan V: Prince Rahim declared 50th Imam
questions: Who is Aga Khan V?
When was Prince Rahim named Imam?
Where was the 50th Imam declared?
What is Prince Rahim's full name?
How was the succession announced?
Is Prince Rahim the eldest son?
What does 50th Imam mean?
entries.answer:
On 5 February 2025, in Lisbon, Prince Rahim al-Hussaini was named the 50th hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims, taking the title Aga Khan V. The announcement followed the unsealing and reading of the will of his father, Aga Khan IV, who had died the previous day.

The declaration was made in the presence of the Imam's family and senior Jamati leaders. Both the Imamat and The Ismaili framed it in the language of the tradition: the designation had been made by Mawlana Shah Karim in accordance with the historical Shia Imami Ismaili practice of nass, and the Nur of Imamat, in unbroken hereditary succession from Hazrat Mawlana Ali, is vested in the 50th Imam.

The Imamat's announcement also described him as a direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad through the Prophet's daughter Hazrat Bibi Fatima and his cousin and son-in-law Hazrat Ali, and noted that throughout their 1,400-year history the Ismailis have been led by a living, hereditary Imam, living today in over 35 countries and numbering approximately 12 to 15 million.

He is styled Mawlana Hazar Imam by the community, and Mawlana Shah Rahim al-Hussaini in formal usage. His accession took effect on 4 February 2025, the day of his father's death, which is why that date, rather than 5 February, is the one the community now observes as Imamat Day.

sources.title: 50th Imam Declared: Mawlana Hazar Imam Shah Rahim al-Hussaini Aga Khan V
Prince Rahim Aga Khan V Named 50th Hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims

entries.title: Aga Khan V: background before the Imamat
questions: What is Prince Rahim's background?
When was Prince Rahim born?
Where did Prince Rahim study?
Does the Imam have children?
What did Prince Rahim do before becoming Imam?
What is Prince Rahim's work on climate?
Who is Princess Salimah?
How old was Prince Rahim when he became Imam?
entries.answer:
Prince Rahim Aga Khan V was born on 12 October 1971, the eldest son of Prince Karim Aga Khan IV and his first wife, Princess Salimah. The Ismaili gives his birthplace as Geneva. He was 53 when he succeeded to the Imamat.

He was educated at Phillips Academy Andover and graduated from Brown University in 1995 with a Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Literature. He has two sons from his former wife, Princess Salwa: Prince Irfan, born 2015, and Prince Sinan, born 2017.

AKDN describes him as having worked closely with his father for more than thirty years. He served on the boards of many AKDN agencies, and followed closely the work of The Institute of Ismaili Studies and of the Ismaili community's social governance institutions, so he came to the office already familiar with the machinery he now leads.

Two concerns are singled out in the institutions' accounts of his work before 2025. The first is the environment and climate: he chaired AKDN's Environment and Climate Committee and represented the Network at international climate meetings, including COP28 and COP29. The second is poverty: sustained attention to the needs of those living in the greatest poverty and to improving their livelihoods through education, training and enterprise.

He also represented his father on formal occasions, and met regularly with leaders of government, international organisations and civil society.

entries.title: Takht-nishini: the enthronement of the 50th Imam
questions: What is Takht-nishini?
What happened on 11 February 2025?
What is the homage ceremony?
What objects are presented to the new Imam?
What is a khilat?
How did Ismailis take part in the ceremony?
What is the Nashid al-Imamah?
Did the new Imam change the Constitution?
entries.answer:
Takht-nishini is a Persian term meaning to ascend the throne, from takht, throne, and nishastan, to sit ceremonially. In the Shia Ismaili tradition it is the ceremony in which the Imam formally assumes his office.

The Takht-nishini of Mawlana Shah Rahim al-Hussaini took place on Tuesday 11 February 2025 at the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat in Lisbon. It had first been announced as a Homage Ceremony; the Imam then declared that it would be his Takht-nishini.

Leaders of the Jamat presented him with the khilat of the preceding Imam, together with his chain and signet ring, symbolising the transfer of the office. A rendition of the Nashid al-Imamah was played, and the ceremonial symbols of authority were presented: the Holy Qur'an, the Ismaili Constitution, a ceremonial sword, an intricate parasol and an inkwell. Verses of the Qur'an were recited, including the Light Verse (24:35), followed by qasidas in Arabic, Persian and Dari and a South Asian munajat first composed in 1885 for the enthronement of Sultan Mahomed Shah, its verses updated for the new transition.

The Chair of the Ismaili Leaders' International Forum offered a loyalty address on behalf of the global Jamat, and each Ismaili Council President submitted bay'ah, the oath of allegiance, for their jurisdiction. The Imam signed a constitutional instrument confirming that the Ismaili Constitution, updated to reflect developments since 1998, remains in force worldwide, and blessed the Jamat with Farman Mubarak. For the first time, Ismailis everywhere watched by live stream in Jamatkhanas.

sources.title: The Takht-nishini of Mawlana Shah Rahim

entries.title: The first year of Aga Khan V's Imamat
questions: What has Aga Khan V done since becoming Imam?
Which countries has the new Imam visited?
What did the Imam promise at his Takht-nishini?
Has the new Imam met his community?
What is a didar?
What has Aga Khan V said publicly?
What institutions does the new Imam lead?
What happened on the first Imamat Day?
entries.answer:
In his Takht-nishini Farman of 11 February 2025, Aga Khan V pledged to dedicate his life to the spiritual and material well-being of the Ismaili Jamat. He assumed leadership of the institutions founded by his father, including AKDN, The Institute of Ismaili Studies and the community's social governance institutions.

The Ismaili reports that meeting as many of his Jamats as possible was among his highest early priorities. During 2025 he made official visits to France, Kenya, Uganda, the United States and Portugal, granting didar, the occasion of being in the Imam's presence, to the Jamats of those jurisdictions; a visit to the United Kingdom and Ireland was announced for early February 2026. By the time of his first Salgirah in October 2025 the institutions listed travel to Portugal, Qatar, Mozambique, France, Kenya, the United Arab Emirates, Uganda, the Kyrgyz Republic and Egypt.

Alongside this he met heads of state and international leaders, including the President of France, the President of Kenya, the President of the United Arab Emirates, the President of Egypt and the President of the World Bank, and he received Uganda's highest civilian honour while opening a new Aga Khan University campus in Kampala. In May 2025 he conferred the title of Diwan on Vazir Shafik Sachedina, explaining in a Talika Mubarak that it is among the highest recognitions an Imam can give a murid. In a video message to the Global Encounters Festival in July 2025 he spoke of the unity that has carried the community through every challenge.

His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V

entries.title: The Ismaili Constitution
questions: What is the Ismaili Constitution?
When was the Ismaili Constitution ordained?
Who writes the Ismaili Constitution?
Is the Ismaili Constitution published?
What does the Constitution cover?
Was the Constitution changed in 2025?
What does the Preamble say about succession?
Can Ismailis amend the Constitution?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Constitution is the written framework the Imam gives the community for its social governance. It is ordained by the Imam of the Time rather than adopted by a vote, which distinguishes it from a civil constitution.

Written constitutions of this kind go back to 1905, when Aga Khan III ordained one for the Ismailis of East Africa, with similar instruments following in South Asia. In 1986 Aga Khan IV ordained a single Ismaili Constitution that for the first time brought the social governance of the worldwide community under one common aegis, with flexibility for the different circumstances of different regions. Its stated aims are to secure the community's peace and unity, its spiritual and social welfare, to foster collaboration among different peoples, to make good use of resources, and to enable Ismailis to contribute to the societies in which they live as responsible citizens. It was revised again, most recently before 2025, in 1998.

The Preamble sets out the rule of succession: succession to Imamat is by way of nass, the absolute prerogative of the Imam of the Time to appoint his successor from among any of his male descendants.

The Constitution is one of the ceremonial symbols presented to a new Imam at his Takht-nishini. At his own Takht-nishini on 11 February 2025, Aga Khan V signed a constitutional instrument in his name as Imam of the Time, confirming that the current Constitution, with updates reflecting developments since 1998, remains in force for the Jamat worldwide.

sources.title: The Takht-nishini of Mawlana Shah Rahim

entries.notes: The full text of the Constitution is not published on these sites; the institutions quote the Preamble and summarise its structure.

entries.title: Councils, boards and institutions under the Constitution
questions: How is the Ismaili community organised?
What is a National Council?
What do Ismaili councils do?
What are the Religious Education Boards?
What are Conciliation and Arbitration Boards?
Who runs Ismaili institutions locally?
Do non-Ismailis use Ismaili arbitration?
What is the Leaders' International Forum?
keywords: Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
entries.answer:
Within the framework of the Ismaili Constitution, National, Regional and Local Councils carry responsibility for the community's overall social governance. Alongside them, Central Institutions provide services in education, health, social welfare, housing, economic welfare, cultural and women's activities, and youth and sports development.

The Constitution also incorporates Religious Education Boards, responsible for religious education at every level of the community, for the human resource development that requires, and for research and publication. In practice these are the bodies through which any change to the community's religious practice, which is at the sole discretion of the Imam of the Time, is communicated in Jamatkhanas.

A third strand is dispute resolution. National and International Conciliation and Arbitration Boards exist to encourage amicable resolution of conflict through impartial conciliation and arbitration. The Imamat notes that in some countries this service is increasingly used by non-Ismailis as well.

At the top of the structure sits the Ismaili Leaders' International Forum. Its Chair offered the loyalty address on behalf of the global Jamat at the Takht-nishini in February 2025, and each Ismaili Council President then submitted the oath of allegiance for their own jurisdiction. There were 22 National Council presidents representing Jamats worldwide at the 2025 ceremonies, which gives a sense of the scale of the structure.

entries.title: Imamat Day
questions: What is Imamat Day?
When is Imamat Day?
Why did Imamat Day change date?
Was Imamat Day on 11 July?
What do Ismailis do on Imamat Day?
Is Imamat Day a religious festival?
What does Imamat Day celebrate?
Why is 4 February important to Ismailis?
entries.answer:
Imamat Day marks the anniversary of the present Imam's accession to the Imamat. It is not a fixed calendar feast in the way Eid is; the date moves with each succession.

For 68 years it fell on 11 July, the day Aga Khan IV succeeded his grandfather in 1957. Since Aga Khan V succeeded his father on 4 February 2025, the community now observes 4 February. The Ismaili marked the first anniversary in February 2026.

The Ismaili describes it as an occasion to reaffirm allegiance and gratitude to the Imam for his guidance, to renew commitment to the ethics of the faith, and to give thanks to God for the continuity of the Imamat itself, which it presents as a light through good times and difficult ones. In its explanation of the day, it restates the underlying belief: that Ismailis have been led throughout history by a living, hereditary Imam descended from the Prophet Muhammad through Hazrat Ali and Hazrat Bibi Fatima, that the Prophet designated Hazrat Ali at Ghadir Khumm, and that the line has continued by nass ever since.

In practice the day is observed in Jamatkhanas and with community celebrations, often described as Khushiali, meaning rejoicing. Aga Khan IV's jubilees were all anchored to this date: the Diamond Jubilee began on 11 July 2017 and closed on 11 July 2018, the day he designated the Seat of the Imamat in Lisbon.

entries.title: Salgirah: the Imam's birthday
questions: What is Salgirah?
When is Salgirah now?
Why do Ismailis celebrate the Imam's birthday?
What does Salgirah mean?
What is Salgirah Khushiali?
Was Salgirah on 13 December?
How do Ismailis celebrate Salgirah?
How old is the current Imam?
entries.answer:
Salgirah is the celebration of the birthday of the Imam of the Time. Like Imamat Day, the date changes with each Imam: it was 13 December, the birthday of Aga Khan IV, and is now 12 October, the birthday of Aga Khan V, who was born in 1971 and marked his 54th birthday on 12 October 2025.

The Ismaili explains the reasoning simply. Birthdays are generally a time to celebrate and be thankful for those we care about, and in that spirit Ismailis celebrate the birthday of the living Imam as a way of expressing love, devotion and gratitude to him. Because Ismailis pledge bay'ah, allegiance, to the Imam of the Time, and understand this as the acceptance of a permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and each murid, or follower, the day is also an occasion for reflecting on that bond.

Celebrations are held in Jamatkhanas and in community gatherings worldwide, often called Salgirah Khushiali, and the greeting exchanged is Salgirah Mubarak. The Ismaili publishes explainer videos and articles around the date as part of its What Ismailis Believe series.

One point worth noting for newcomers: the celebration is of the office as much as the person. The community's own explanation ties it to the Imam's guidance and leadership, and to what he does for the community and for the wider world, rather than treating it as a personal birthday party.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis celebrate their Imam's birthday?

entries.title: The Imam's dual role: spiritual and material
questions: Why does the Imam run hospitals and universities?
What is din and dunya?
Is the Imam a religious or a worldly leader?
Why is the Aga Khan involved in development?
What does quality of life mean to the Imamat?
How does faith connect to worldly work in Ismaili thought?
Is the Imam's role political?
What is the Imam's mandate?
entries.answer:
The question newcomers most often ask is why a religious leader runs universities, hospitals, banks and architecture prizes. The Imamat's own answer is that the division the question assumes does not exist in Islam as it understands it.

The Imamat states that the role of the Ismaili Imam is a spiritual one, his authority that of religious interpretation, and that it is not a political role and involves governing no land. But it holds that Islam believes fundamentally that the spiritual and material worlds are inextricably connected, so faith does not remove Muslims or their Imams from daily practical matters in family life, in business or in community affairs.

Aga Khan IV put this in terms of din and dunya, faith and world: his institutional responsibilities for interpreting the faith were accompanied by engagement with quality of life, not only for the Ismaili community but for those among whom they live. Speaking at Harvard in 2015, he said that leadership in the spiritual realm for any imam, Sunni or Shia, implies responsibility in worldly affairs and a calling to improve the quality of human life.

The Imamat also stretches the meaning of quality of life. It says the phrase covers the entire ethical and social context in which people live, not only material well-being, and so includes investing in people, in pluralism, in intellectual pursuits and in the search for useful knowledge. This holistic vision is the stated rationale for AKDN.

entries.title: Bay'ah and didar: allegiance and the Imam's presence
questions: What is bay'ah?
What is didar?
What is a mulaqat?
What is the bond between the Imam and a murid?
How do Ismailis pledge allegiance?
Can anyone meet the Imam?
What is spiritual didar?
What is a Farman?
entries.answer:
Two words come up constantly in Ismaili life and are worth learning early.

Bay'ah is the pledge of allegiance to the Imam of the Time. The Ismaili describes it as the acceptance of the permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and each murid, or follower. It is offered individually, and also formally on behalf of the whole community: at the Takht-nishini in February 2025, each Ismaili Council President submitted bay'ah to the new Imam on behalf of their jurisdiction's Jamats.

Didar means sight or vision, and the community's teaching distinguishes two senses. Physical didar refers to the occasions when Ismailis are granted the opportunity to see and be in the presence of the Imam of the Time; these occasions, often called mulaqat, are usually tied to an official visit to a country and are organised through the councils. Spiritual didar refers to an inner experience in which, through the Imam's guidance, one experiences the presence of God's light.

During 2025 Aga Khan V granted didar to the Jamats of France, Kenya, Uganda, the United States and Portugal, and The Ismaili published practical guidance for members preparing to attend.

A related term is Farman, the Imam's guidance addressed to the Jamat, delivered in person; a Talika is a written message. Aga Khan V's Takht-nishini Farman of 11 February 2025, in which he pledged his life to the Jamat's spiritual and material well-being, is the one most often referred to in the institutions' reporting.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis celebrate their Imam's birthday?
Mawlana Hazar Imam accepts pledges of allegiance from Global Jamat

entries.title: What Ismailis call the Imam
questions: Why do Ismailis say Mawlana Hazar Imam?
What does Khudavind mean?
What does murshid mean?
Why is the Imam called pir?
Is Khudavind a name for God?
What does Mawla mean?
What are the different names for the Aga Khan?
How should I refer to the Imam?
entries.answer:
Newcomers meet several names for the same person, and they carry different registers.

Mawlana Hazar Imam is the most common usage in the community: mawlana means our master or our lord, and hazar means present, so the phrase means roughly our lord, the Imam who is present. Imam-of-the-Time carries the same sense.

Khudavind, or khudawand, is Persian for a king, prince, lord, master or person of great authority. The Ismaili explains that many Persian and Central Asian empires used the term for people of high standing, and that the community adopted it for the Imam during the centuries when the Imams lived in Persia, from the twelfth to the nineteenth. Its sense is close to the Arabic mawla. The Ismaili is explicit that khudavind used on its own should not be confused with a name for God: more specific expressions such as khudawand-i alam, lord of the world, are used for God, and Ismailis, like all Muslims, affirm the oneness of God in the shahada.

Pir and murshid both mean spiritual guide; the community's writing describes the Imam as the pir and murshid of his followers, who are called murids, and sometimes as their spiritual father and mother.

His Highness and Aga Khan are civil titles, not religious ones, and are the forms most often used in the press and in official settings.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis call their Imam Khudavind?
Mawlana Shah Karim's funeral held in Lisbon

entries.title: Tawhid: the oneness of God
questions: What do Ismailis believe about God?
What is tawhid?
Do Ismailis believe in the same God as other Muslims?
Is tawhid different for Ismailis?
What does 'there is no god but God' mean?
How do Ismailis describe God's unity?
Is God knowable in Ismaili thought?
What is tanzih?
entries.answer:
Tawhid, the oneness and uniqueness of God, is the first article of faith for all Muslims, and Ismailis share it fully. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the Qur'an as thoroughly theocentric: God is the Creator and Sustainer of everything, and the declaration of faith begins with the words that there is no god but God.

What distinguishes classical Ismaili thought is how far it pushes God's transcendence. Writers such as Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani (d. after 361 AH/971 CE) and Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani (d. shortly after 411 AH/1020 CE) argued that two errors have to be avoided at once: tashbih, likening God to created things, and ta'til, stripping God of all description so completely that one has simply relocated Him among spiritual beings. Their solution was a double negation. First you deny that God can be described, located or limited; then you negate that denial too. God is therefore neither within the sensible world nor within the world of intellect and spirit, and language cannot finally hold Him.

Madelung notes that Ismaili theology did not try to prove God's existence by reason, since a rational proof of what lies beyond reason would be futile. Instead, knowledge of God is held to come through revelation and through guidance. Ismailis understand affirming God's unity in this careful way as itself an act of worship.

entries.title: Prophethood and the Prophet Muhammad
questions: What do Ismailis believe about the Prophet Muhammad?
Do Ismailis believe Muhammad was the last prophet?
What is nubuwwa?
Do Ismailis accept earlier prophets?
How is revelation understood in Ismaili belief?
What is tanzil?
Why is there still a need for guidance after the Prophet?
How does prophethood relate to the Imamat?
entries.answer:
Ismailis affirm, with all Muslims, that God sends guidance through chosen messengers and that Prophet Muhammad was the last of them. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the Qur'anic view of revelation as a descent, tanzil, by which divine guidance enters human time; the Qur'an names a long line of earlier prophets including Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and Jews and Christians are addressed as People of the Book who share that lineage of revelation.

Revelation came to the Prophet over roughly twenty-two years (610-632 CE), responding to the situation of the young Muslim community as it grew. During his lifetime the Prophet was both the recipient of revelation and its expounder.

From the Shia point of view, his death ended prophecy but did not end the need for interpretation. IIS puts it this way: the function of prophethood, to convey God's message, was complete, but the need for affirmation, interpretation, stewardship and spiritual leadership remained. That is the role Ismailis assign to the Imamat, which they hold complements prophethood rather than competing with it. Classical Ismaili writers also placed Muhammad within a larger pattern of prophetic cycles, in which each messenger brings a revealed law and is followed by someone charged with unfolding its inner meaning.

entries.title: The Qur'an in Ismaili belief
questions: What do Ismailis believe about the Qur'an?
Do Ismailis have their own Qur'an?
How do Ismailis read the Qur'an?
What is the 'speaking Qur'an'?
Who interprets the Qur'an for Ismailis?
Is the Qur'an recited in jamatkhana?
How was the Qur'an compiled?
Does the Qur'an have more than one level of meaning?
entries.answer:
Ismailis hold the same Qur'an as all other Muslims. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as the foundational text of Islam, the word of God entering human time and history, revealed to Prophet Muhammad and recited aloud by him. Recitation was how the revelations were preserved and taught, and it remains central to Muslim religious life. The written text was compiled after the Prophet's death, and Shia accounts give Imam Ali a leading role in that work.

What is distinctive is the Ismaili understanding of who carries its meaning forward. All Muslims agree that the Qur'an must be rightly interpreted; they differ over who holds that authority. In the Sunni view, IIS explains, that role came to rest with the ulama. In the Shia view it belongs to the Imam from the family of the Prophet, designated by nass and possessing divinely inspired knowledge, ilm.

An early Fatimid da'i, Ja'far b. Mansur al-Yaman, expressed this by calling the Imams the speaking Qur'an and the written text, after the Prophet's death, the silent Qur'an. Ismailis therefore read the Qur'an as having both an apparent sense and an inner one, each intertwined with the other like body and soul, and believe the Imam of the time continues to provide its interpretation and teaching for each age.

entries.title: Zahir and batin: outer and inner
questions: What do zahir and batin mean?
What is the inner meaning of scripture in Ismaili thought?
Do Ismailis reject the outward law?
Why are Ismailis called esotericists?
How do the outer and inner relate to each other?
What are the haqa'iq?
Is the literal meaning of the Qur'an denied?
What is the difference between shari'a and haqiqa?
entries.answer:
Ismaili thought works with a paired distinction: zahir, the apparent or outward aspect of a text, ritual or commandment, and batin, its inner or hidden meaning. The Institute of Ismaili Studies is explicit that the validity of the literal is not denied. The zahir is one real aspect of an overall meaning that also has an inner dimension, and the two are described as complementary and intertwined, like body and soul.

In the classical formulation, the outward law brought by each messenger-prophet changes from era to era, while the inner truths, the haqa'iq, are held to be eternal and unchanging. The Fatimid jurist al-Qadi al-Nu'man wrote in both registers: the Da'a'im al-Islam sets out the sphere of ritual action, and his Ta'wil al-da'a'im sets out the inner meaning of that same action.

Because of this emphasis, hostile writers labelled Ismailis batiniyya, mere esotericists. IIS treats that as a polemical caricature. Azim Nanji notes that Ismaili thought shows no tendency to reject the material world: without action in it, the spiritual quest is considered unworthy. The point of the pairing is that outward practice and inner understanding perfect one another, so that ritual performed outwardly is at the same time an exercise of the intellectual and spiritual faculties.

entries.title: Ta'wil: drawing out inner meaning
questions: What is ta'wil?
How is ta'wil different from tafsir?
What does ta'wil do in Ismaili thought?
Who is qualified to perform ta'wil?
Can you give an example of ta'wil?
Is ta'wil the same as allegory?
What did Nasir Khusraw say about ta'wil?
How does ta'wil relate to prayer?
entries.answer:
Ta'wil is the practice of leading a text or a rite back to its original or root meaning. The Institute of Ismaili Studies pairs it with tanzil, the descent of revelation: tanzil gives the letter, ta'wil works back through the letter to what it carries. Its goal is described as enabling a believer to move past the literal surface and reach a settled sense of what a passage ultimately means.

The method is applied to doctrine and to ritual alike. Al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi (d. 470 AH/1078 CE) read the Qur'anic 'six days' of creation not as solar days, since there was no sun before creation, but as six cycles of prophecy. Al-Qadi al-Nu'man read the daily prayer as symbolising the summons to the Prophet's message and its continuing affirmation, and the prayer times as standing for the great epochs of revealed law. Nasir Khusraw read the stages within the prayer itself as stages in the soul's journey, and described the esoteric sense of prayer as turning towards the qibla of the spirit.

IIS stresses that ta'wil in this tradition is not free-floating allegory. It assumes an exegetical basis rooted in the community and its tradition, and Ismailis hold that its authoritative exercise belongs to the Imam of the time.

entries.title: The Imamat: the central Ismaili doctrine
questions: What is the Imamat?
Why is the Imam so central for Ismailis?
What does the Imam actually do?
Is the Imam a political leader?
Who is the present Ismaili Imam?
How is the Imam chosen?
Do Ismailis worship the Imam?
How does the Imamat differ from other Shia views?
entries.answer:
The Imamat is the doctrine at the centre of Ismaili belief. Ismailis hold that the Imamat is a divinely sanctioned and guided institution through which Muslims are able to place the practice of their faith in its own time and to grasp both the outward and the inner dimensions of the Qur'an. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as existing to complement prophethood, so that the divine purpose continues to be served in every place and age.

Succession runs by heredity in the Prophet's progeny through Imam Ali and Bibi Fatima, and passes by nass, explicit designation by the Imam of the time from among his male progeny. Two principles shape the office: nass, which locates the Imamat in a named individual whether or not he holds political power, and ilm, the divinely inspired knowledge that makes him the reference point for teaching and interpretation.

The Imamat's official site states that the Imam's role is spiritual and his authority is that of religious interpretation, not a political one. Ismailis are the Shia community with a living hereditary Imam, and the guidance they follow covers both faith and the quality of daily life. Prince Rahim Aga Khan was named the 50th hereditary Imam on 5 February 2025, following the death of his father, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV.

Seeking the Imam's intercession is not understood as equating him with God; Ismailis affirm tawhid.

entries.title: Why the Shia hold that the Prophet designated a successor
questions: Why do Shia Muslims believe Ali was the successor?
What happened at Ghadir Khumm?
What is the Ahl al-Bayt?
What is the hadith of the two weighty things?
What is the main difference between Sunni and Shia Muslims?
What is nass?
Where does the Qur'an support the Imamat according to Shia?
Do Sunnis and Shia share these traditions?
entries.answer:
Sunni and Shia Muslims share the central beliefs of Islam, including tawhid and the finality of Prophet Muhammad's message. The Ismaili community's own account says the main difference turns on whether the Prophet explicitly designated a successor. Sunnis hold that he did not, and look to the caliphs, and later to the consensus of scholars, for religious authority. The Shia hold that he did.

The best-known instance cited is the Prophet's address at the oasis of Ghadir Khumm on the return from his final pilgrimage, recorded in both Sunni and Shia hadith collections, where he raised Imam Ali's hand and said that whoever's mawla he was, Ali was his mawla. The word mawla can mean friend, client or master; the Shia read it as master, and as designation to lead after him.

Shia sources also point to Qur'anic verses on the purification of the Ahl al-Bayt, the people of the Prophet's household, and to the hadith of the two weighty matters, in which the Prophet is reported to have left behind the Book of God and his kindred. Al-Qadi al-Nu'man argued further that designating a successor, a wasi, was the practice of earlier prophets too. On this basis the Shia hold that authority passes by nass, explicit designation, within the Prophet's family.
