entries.title: Nur: the Light of Imamat
questions: What is the Light of Imamat?
What does nur mean?
Why is the Imam associated with light?
Is the light passed from Imam to Imam?
What is the Qur'anic verse of light?
How do aql, nur and nafs relate?
Is nur a literal light?
What does the image of light mean in Ismaili poetry?
entries.answer:
Nur is the Arabic word for light, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies glossary lists it as a Qur'anic term used of God. Azim Nanji identifies the Qur'anic image of divine radiant light (Qur'an 24:35) as the symbol that best expresses the act of knowing and being illumined in Ismaili spirituality, and notes the related image of a pillar of light by whose power the ranks of the hierarchy of faith are drawn upward.

In Shia belief the light associated with the Prophet is held to continue in the hereditary Imams descended from him. The Ismaili community's own material describes Hazrat Ali as bearing the same nur as the Prophet, and Ismailis understand the Imam-of-the-Time as carrying that light forward in each age.

The community teaches this alongside two other terms. Nur, the light or guidance of the Imam, and aql, human intellect, are described as the two principal factors that allow the soul, nafs, to flourish. Ismailis therefore do not treat the light of the Imam as replacing human reasoning but as working with it.

The fuller devotional and doctrinal content associated with the Light of Imamat is taught within the community, through its religious education institutions and jamatkhana practice, and is not elaborated in public sources.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis seek help from Hazrat Ali and the Imams?

entries.notes: The public institutional sources treat nur mainly through Qur'anic symbolism and the aql/nur/nafs formulation. The detailed teaching on the Light of Imamat is a community-internal matter taught through ITREB and jamatkhana, so it is deliberately left unelaborated here.

entries.title: Walaya: devotion and allegiance to the Imam
questions: What is walaya?
What is the difference between wilaya and walaya?
Why is walaya called the first pillar?
What is the difference between islam and iman for Ismailis?
Does walaya mean obedience?
Who wrote about walaya in Ismaili law?
Is walaya political or spiritual?
How does walaya relate to bayah?
entries.answer:
Walaya is loving devotion and allegiance to the Imam and the Prophet's family. In Fatimid Ismaili law it is the first and highest of the seven pillars, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies calls it the cornerstone of Ismaili faith. The Da'a'im al-Islam of al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 363 AH/974 CE) was the first juristic text to give walaya legal status, making it the condition on which the other acts of worship are acceptable. This is one of the points that distinguishes Ismaili jurisprudence from Twelver Shia jurisprudence.

Al-Nu'man builds the idea on a distinction drawn from Qur'an 49:14 between islam, submission, and iman, faith. One may be a Muslim, a member of the religion of Islam, without yet being a mu'min; belief in and devotion to the rightful Imam is what constitutes true faith in this scheme. He grounds the claim historically in Imam Ali's closeness to the Prophet and in the declaration at Ghadir Khumm.

IIS notes that in al-Nu'man's scheme walaya matters because the Imam deserves the love and allegiance of the community whether or not the Imamat is, at any given moment, a political office. For the Fatimids it was also the basis of their claim to lead the Muslim community. Today it is expressed above all through the pledge of allegiance, bay'a.

entries.title: The seven pillars in the Fatimid formulation
questions: What are the seven pillars of Ismaili Islam?
Why do Ismailis have seven pillars instead of five?
What is the Da'a'im al-Islam?
Is walaya really a pillar?
What is tahara?
Did Fatimid law use analogy and personal opinion?
Who wrote Ismaili law?
Do Ismailis still follow Fatimid law?
entries.answer:
Ismaili jurisprudence emerged as a distinct system after the Fatimid state was founded in North Africa in 909 CE. Before that, the Institute of Ismaili Studies notes, the Ismailis emphasised the batini or esoteric sciences over the zahiri or exoteric ones, and law had little practical use until they had obtained political power.

The Da'a'im al-Islam, composed by al-Qadi al-Nu'man at the commission of the fourth Fatimid Imam-caliph al-Mu'izz, was officially promulgated as the Fatimid code. Reporting on the authority of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, it sets out seven pillars: walaya, devotion to the Imam; tahara, ritual purity; salat, prayer; zakat, charitable giving; sawm, fasting in Ramadan; hajj, pilgrimage to Mecca; and jihad. IIS describes walaya as the cornerstone of Ismaili faith and the highest and noblest of the seven, without which acts of devotion are not acceptable to God, and notes that the Da'a'im was the first juristic text to give walaya a legal status. Tahara, the familiar requirement of purity for valid prayer, was raised by al-Nu'man to the status of an independent pillar.

His method set aside ra'y, personal opinion, and qiyas, analogical reasoning, and worked instead from the Qur'an, the sunna of the Prophet, and the teachings of the Imams, referring unresolved questions to the Imam of the time. IIS records that this followed a decree of al-Mu'izz instructing him on the roots of jurisprudence, that the Da'a'im was closely supervised by al-Mu'izz himself, and that in the day-to-day running of the state ultimate authority lay with the ruling Imam.

After al-Nu'man, IIS describes no significant further development in Ismaili law; later work in India took the form of glosses, collections of questions and answers, and restatements.

entries.title: How Nizari Ismailis understand practice today
questions: How do Ismailis practise Islam today?
Do Ismailis still follow the seven pillars?
What happens in a jamatkhana?
Why are jamatkhana prayers only for Ismailis?
Who decides Ismaili practice?
What is a tariqa?
Do Ismailis pray five times a day?
What prayers do Ismailis say?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili community's own website describes jamatkhanas as private tariqa spaces. Tariqa means path; a tariqa is a community of Muslims following a path of interpretation and practice under a spiritual leader, in this case the hereditary Imam. Ismailis understand their practices as expressions of the bond between the Imam-of-the-Time and his followers, conveyed in the pledge of allegiance, bay'a.

The practices named publicly include forms of prayer recommended in the Qur'an: du'a, supplication; tasbih, glorification; dhikr, remembrance; and salawat, seeking blessings on the Prophet and his progeny. They also include recitation of Qur'anic verses, affirming the shahada, devotional poetry such as qasidas, nashids and ginans, and the reading of farmans. Special prayers mark festivals, times of difficulty and rites of passage. Voluntary service and freewill offerings are treated as forms of devotion as well.

The community states plainly that jamatkhana practices are the sole prerogative of the Imam-of-the-Time and are specific to the Ismaili community, and that the Imam alone determines them at any time. Their detail is taught within the community and is not set out publicly, which is why jamatkhana prayers are attended by Ismailis. The Fatimid seven-pillar code remains part of the historical heritage; what Ismailis observe now follows the guidance of the Imam of the time.

entries.title: Bay'a: the pledge of allegiance
questions: What is bayah?
What does it mean to give bayah to the Imam?
Is bayah a one-time act?
Where does bayah come from in Islam?
Is bayah political?
What is a murid?
How often do Ismailis renew their allegiance?
Do other Muslims practise bayah?
entries.answer:
Bay'a comes from an Arabic root meaning to sell or to clasp hands. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glossary describes it as an oath of allegiance, an act by which people individually or collectively recognise someone's authority. It has deep roots in Arab practice and in the Prophet's own time, and is referred to in the Qur'an; historically it was how caliphs were recognised.

Many Muslim traditions also read bay'a spiritually, as the offering of oneself to a spiritual master, a pir, murshid or shaykh, in return for spiritual knowledge and guidance.

In the Shia Ismaili context, IIS defines bay'a as the acceptance of the permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and the murid, the follower, uniting Ismailis worldwide in loyalty, devotion and obedience to the Imam within the Islamic idea of universal brotherhood.

The community describes bay'a as reaffirmed daily rather than sworn once: the pledge to the Imam-of-the-Time is renewed in various prayers and jamatkhana practices. Azim Nanji notes that in Nasir Khusraw's account of his own conversion, the decisive moment of transformation is the taking of the oath of allegiance to the Imam, an image the poet links to Qur'an 48:18.

entries.title: Farmans and the guidance of the Imam
questions: What is a farman?
Are farmans written down?
What is a farman book?
Are farmans binding on Ismailis?
Where does the word farman come from?
Do farmans change over time?
Are farmans published publicly?
How do Ismailis receive the Imam's guidance?
entries.answer:
Farman is a Persian word meaning command, authority, will or permission. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glossary notes its Ottoman use for any order of the sultan, and, from the fifteenth century CE, for a written document opening with a prayer to God and addressed to officials or dependent rulers. In the Shi'i Ismaili tradition, the glossary gives the meaning directly: an address by the Imam to his community.

In practice, farmans are the living form of the Imam's guidance. The community's own account of jamatkhana practice lists the reading of farmans, described as guidance from the Imam, among the observances in jamatkhana alongside prayer and devotional recitation. Collections of farmans are periodically authorised by the Imam and made available to the Jamat as farman books, distributed through jamatkhanas; the community's announcements record sets covering particular periods of an Imam's addresses.

Farmans respond to circumstances, so guidance is understood as addressed to a time and place as well as to the community as a whole. Because they are authorised for the Jamat and read in jamatkhana, farmans are a community-internal matter; their contents are not published for a general readership, and this entry does not summarise them.

entries.title: Ta'lim: authoritative teaching
questions: What is talim?
Why do Ismailis need a teacher?
Who was Hasan-i Sabbah?
What is the doctrine of the true teacher?
What were the Four Chapters?
Why were Nizaris called Talimiyya?
Does talim deny the use of reason?
What is the da'wa jadida?
entries.answer:
Ta'lim means education or authoritative instruction. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as an early Shia doctrine that Hasan-i Sabbah (d. 518 AH/1124 CE), founder of the Nizari state at Alamut, restated with new force in a Persian treatise known as the Chahar fasl, the Four Chapters. The original is lost and survives mainly in quotations by al-Shahrastani (d. 548 AH/1153 CE).

The argument runs that human reason on its own cannot arrive at knowledge of God, so an authoritative teacher, a mu'allim-i sadiq or true teacher, is needed, and that teacher is the Ismaili Imam of the age. Hasan-i Sabbah pressed the point to the heart of theology, speaking of the failure of reason with respect to knowing God and of the need for prophecy for a true confession of unity.

Outsiders called this the new preaching, da'wa jadida, and the Persian Nizaris became known as the Talimiyya. IIS is careful that this was a reformulation of established Shia doctrine rather than an innovation.

Ta'lim is not a rejection of thinking. IIS notes that accepting the Imam's authority was understood as an act of human reasoning that recognises its own limits in spiritual matters. Nasir al-Din Tusi later described his own search for such a teacher in these terms.

entries.title: Intellect (aql) and faith
questions: How do Ismailis view reason?
Is faith opposed to the intellect in Ismaili thought?
What does aql mean?
Why is knowledge so important to Ismailis?
Does following the Imam mean blind obedience?
What is the dialectic of reason and authority?
What is Rahat al-aql?
How are the two kinds of knowledge related?
entries.answer:
Ismaili thought treats intellect and faith as working together rather than against each other. Azim Nanji writes that in Ismailism true understanding came to be defined as the fullest unfolding of human reason, aql, under the guidance of the Imam. Accepting the Imam's authority is described by the Institute of Ismaili Studies not as blind obedience but as an act of reasoning that recognises reason's own limits in spiritual matters, and IIS calls this dialectic of reason and spiritual authority the underlying thread of Ismaili intellectual history.

The Fatimid curriculum illustrates the point. A student began with the practical sciences needed to grasp the shari'a, called al-ibadat al-amaliyya or practical worship, and only then moved to al-ibadat al-ilmiyya, intellectual worship, the sciences that interpret the levels of meaning within those same practices.

Al-Kirmani's summary work is titled Rahat al-aql, the repose or balm of the intellect, and Nanji reads the title itself as signalling the aim: a settling of the mind through its proper engagement with revelation, not a victory of reason over it.

The Imamat's own statements put the same idea plainly: knowledge is twofold, what is revealed through the Prophet and what human beings discover by their own intellect, and these involve no contradiction so long as one remembers that the mind is itself created by God.

entries.title: God beyond being and the double negation
questions: What is the double negation?
Why do Ismailis say God is beyond being?
What are tashbih and ta'til?
Did Ismaili thinkers try to prove God exists?
How is this different from the Mu'tazila?
What is the via negationis?
Can God be described at all?
Who developed this idea?
entries.answer:
Classical Ismaili theology refuses to place God anywhere on the map of being. Wilferd Madelung describes it as following the via negationis: all attributes and names are removed from God, who is said to transcend both being and non-being. God is not the Universal Intellect, and is not to be described as Intellect at all, as the Aristotelian tradition would have it.

Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani pressed the argument further than the rationalist Mu'tazila, who were already accused of stripping God bare. In his view their ta'til, denuding God of attributes, was itself a hidden tashbih, a likening: to deny only that God resembles the physical world is to assimilate Him to the spiritual beings. So the negation must itself be negated. As Azim Nanji sets it out, the first negation frees the idea of God from all association with the material, and the second removes Him from association with the non-material, leaving God neither within the sensible world nor within the extra-sensible.

Both writers held that the point was not to prove God rationally, since proving what lies beyond reason would be futile, but to understand God as He deserves to be understood and so to worship rightly. Madelung notes al-Sijistani's claim that God is more certain than everything certain, a certainty that becomes evident to the mind only through revelation.

sources.title: Aspects of Ismaili Theology: The Prophetic Chain and the God Beyond Being

entries.title: Creation as origination: ibda, amr, Intellect and Soul
questions: How do Ismaili thinkers explain creation?
What is ibda?
What is the divine Command in Ismaili cosmology?
What is the Universal Intellect?
Is Ismaili cosmology the same as Neoplatonism?
What is inbi'ath?
Why is God not called the first cause?
What is the Pen and the Throne in this system?
entries.answer:
Early Ismaili writers took over Neoplatonic vocabulary but reworked it so that creation stays a free act of God. In the Neoplatonic scheme the One emanates the Universal Intellect. In the Ismaili version, Madelung explains, the Intellect is not emanated from God but brought forth through His Command, amr, or Word, kalima, in a timeless act of origination called ibda. God is the Originator, al-Mubdi, drawing on the Qur'anic description of God as badi of the heavens and the earth (Qur'an 2:117), and the Command is identified with the creative imperative kun, 'Be'.

Paul Walker distinguishes three levels in al-Sijistani's account. In the sensible world things come to be out of other things through time. In the intelligible world, Soul, nafs, springs forth from Intellect by a special process called inbi'ath, distinguished from ordinary emanation. Above both is ibda, the coming-to-be of being from what is not being, which happens all at once, dafatan wahidatan.

Against the philosophers, Ismaili theology denied that God is the first cause; the first cause is His Command, united in existence with the Intellect. The Universal Intellect was also identified with Qur'anic terms such as the Pen, qalam, the Throne, arsh, and the Decree, qada. Nanji notes that this spiritual hierarchy was mirrored on earth by the hierarchy of faith.

questions: What is al-Kirmani's cosmology?
What are the ten intellects?
How did al-Kirmani change earlier Ismaili cosmology?
How do Ismailis read the story of Adam's fall?
Do Ismailis believe in original sin?
What is spiritual Adam?
Who was Iblis in this reading?
How does the cosmos relate to the hierarchy of faith?
entries.answer:
Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani (d. shortly after 411 AH/1020 CE) marks what the Institute of Ismaili Studies calls a third stage in Ismaili cosmology. Where his Iranian predecessors worked with a pair of principles in the spiritual world, Intellect and Soul, al-Kirmani replaced that dyad with a series of ten separate intellects, adapting in part the Aristotelian cosmic scheme of al-Farabi. He also tended, unlike earlier writers, to identify the divine Command with the First Intellect rather than setting it above. His summary work, Rahat al-aql, was composed in 411 AH/1020 CE.

This scheme gave Ismaili writers a way to read the Qur'anic story of Adam. In the account developed by al-Hamidi (d. 595 AH/1199 CE) and others, the drama takes place on a cosmic plane in the non-material world of origination. Spiritual Adam, Adam ruhani, originally holds the rank of the third intellect; the forbidden tree is the rank of the first; and Iblis represents Adam's own refusal to accept the station given him. His fall to the tenth rank is a loss of standing, not an inheritance of original sin, and through repentance he seeks to ascend again.

Azim Nanji notes the point of the story: the hierarchy of faith on earth mirrors the hierarchy of intellects, and its task is to show the path of return.

entries.title: Cycles of prophecy: natiq, wasi and Imam
questions: What are the cycles of prophecy?
Who are the six speaking prophets?
What is a natiq?
What is a wasi or asas?
What does samit mean?
Why is the number seven important to Ismailis?
How is sacred history understood by Ismailis?
How is this drawn from the Qur'an?
entries.answer:
Classical Ismaili thought reads history as a patterned, purposeful sequence rather than a random one. Wilferd Madelung sets out the scheme: human religious history unfolds in seven eras, each opened by a messenger-prophet or enunciator, natiq. In the first six eras these are Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad. Each brings a scripture whose outward aspect, zahir, contains a religious law.

Each natiq is followed by a legatee, wasi, also called the asas or the Silent One, samit, whose task is to disclose the inner truths concealed in that scripture to those able to receive them. The legatee is in turn followed by a series of Imams who guard the meaning of the scripture in both its outward and inner aspects.

Al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi reached the same scheme by ta'wil of the Qur'anic six days of creation (Qur'an 7:54), arguing that days measured by a sun that did not yet exist cannot be literal, and that the six days signify six cycles of prophecy. Nasir Khusraw mapped the three stages of the ritual prayer onto natiq, asas and the qa'im.

This emphasis on sevens is why hostile heresiographers called Ismailis sab'iyya, 'seveners'. IIS treats that as an outsiders' label rather than a self-description.

sources.title: Aspects of Ismaili Theology: The Prophetic Chain and the God Beyond Being

entries.title: The qa'im and the resurrection
questions: What is the qaim?
What is qiyama in Ismaili thought?
Is the qaim the same as the Mahdi?
What happened at Alamut in 1164?
Did Ismailis abolish the law?
What does spiritual resurrection mean?
What is the seventh era?
How did the doctrine of qiyama develop?
entries.answer:
In the classical scheme the seventh and final era belongs to the expected qa'im, sometimes identified with the Mahdi. Madelung explains that his role differs from the six messengers before him: he is not to bring a new law but to make fully public the inner truths that had until then been disclosed only in part, to a few, under conditions of secrecy. He would thus open an era of pure spiritual knowledge before the end of the world. In the wider Ismaili reading of sacred history, the whole movement returns to its source and culminates in the Qur'anic qiyama, a resurrection of souls.

The Nizaris gave this a particular turn. On 8 August 1164 CE at Alamut, Imam Hasan II (r. 1162-1166 CE) proclaimed the qiyama. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes this as announcing the Last Day in the sense of unveiling the spiritual truth concealed beneath outward religious law; the Imam, as qa'im al-qiyama, held supreme spiritual authority, and those who recognised him were held to have paradise actualised for them in this world. IIS also records the reported abrogation of literal adherence to the law, a marked break with his predecessors' practice.

His son Nur al-Din Muhammad devoted a long reign to working the announcement into systematic doctrine. Later Nizari writing described the setting aside of ritual law as applying to those who had reached a high stage of spiritual perfection, and the conditions for that were strict.

entries.title: Satr and kashf: concealment and disclosure
questions: What is satr?
What is the period of concealment?
Why were the Ismaili Imams hidden?
What is dawr al-kashf?
Did different thinkers understand satr differently?
What is taqiyya?
Does satr mean the Imam is absent?
How does satr relate to the cycles?
entries.answer:
Satr means concealment. The Institute of Ismaili Studies uses the term for a period of public quiescence and concealment in early Ismaili history: the Imams between Imam Isma'il and the Imam-caliph al-Mahdi are regarded as belonging to it, as they sought to escape persecution. It ended with the public proclamation in 297 AH/909 CE of the Imamat of 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi, the first Fatimid caliph.

IIS describes the conditions of that period. The descendants of Imam Isma'il lived in hazardous circumstances in various secret localities, and by the middle of the ninth century CE had settled at Salamiyya in Syria, concealing their identity from the public while they consolidated and organised a widely dispersed community. Scholars and local leaders known as da'is maintained contact with the Imams and organised themselves into a da'wa, so that when the community emerged into public view at the beginning of the tenth century it was remarkably well organised and cohesive.

The related practice of taqiyya is the precautionary dissimulation of one's true religious belief and practice, to protect the Imams and their followers under adverse circumstances. IIS attributes its introduction to Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (d. 731 CE).

IIS presents Ismaili history more broadly as unfolding in two alternating patterns: periods of quiescence and interiorisation, when circumstances limit a broader engagement with the world, and more enabling times when it is possible to engage intellectually and institutionally.

entries.title: The da'wa and the hierarchy of faith
questions: What is the da'wa?
What is a da'i?
What is a hujja?
How was the Fatimid da'wa organised?
What is hudud al-din?
What qualities did a da'i need?
What was the majalis al-hikma?
Did Ismailis try to convert people in large numbers?
entries.answer:
Da'wa means summons or invitation. Farhad Daftary describes the Ismaili da'wa as a network of representatives, each called a da'i, responsible for teaching Ismaili doctrine and winning followers for the Imam. Azim Nanji notes that the term is rooted in the Qur'an and that what made the Ismaili da'wa distinctive was the quality of its organisation, communications and scholarship.

The Fatimid organisation, known as hudud al-din, the ranks of religion, was fully developed by the time al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi was chief da'i in Cairo. Below the Imam stood the chief da'i, called bab or bab al-abwab in Ismaili sources and da'i al-du'at elsewhere, who appointed provincial da'is. The wider world was divided into twelve jaziras, 'islands', each headed by a chief da'i called a hujja. The ranks mirrored an ideal order and were not always filled.

Daftary records that Ismailis never aimed at mass proselytisation. A da'i needed the Imam's permission, had to know the initiate personally, and was expected to be familiar with other religions and with the language and customs of his region. Teaching was tiered: at al-Azhar the outward sense of the law was taught openly, including to women, while the inner sense was taught in the majalis al-hikma, sessions of wisdom, held in the Imam's palace and open only to those who had already pledged allegiance, with lectures reviewed and approved by the Imam.

entries.title: Faith as action: iman and the meaning of ritual
questions: What is iman?
Is faith belief or action in Ismaili thought?
What did Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq say about faith?
Do rituals have inner meaning?
Can faith be incomplete?
How is prayer understood symbolically?
What is the relationship between the material and spiritual?
Do Ismailis reject the material world?
entries.answer:
The Da'a'im al-Islam preserves a definition of faith attributed to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), answering whether faith is profession with action or without it. The answer given is that faith consists entirely in action and that profession is itself part of action, and that faith has stages, grades and stations, so that it may be complete or incomplete.

Azim Nanji treats this as the basis for the Ismaili approach to ritual. Because action is integral to spiritual development, outward practice and inner meaning, zahir and batin, are read together. Al-Qadi al-Nu'man wrote one work on the sphere of ritual action and another, Ta'wil al-da'a'im, on its inner meaning.

The daily prayer is the standard illustration. Al-Nu'man read the prayer as symbolising the summons to the Prophet's message and its continuing affirmation by the Imam of the time, and the prayer times as the epochs of revealed law. Nasir Khusraw read its successive steps as stages in the soul's search for the inner realities of faith.

Nanji draws a conclusion for how Ismailis regard the world: there is no tendency here to reject material life. The zahir is the arena in which a spiritual life is shaped, and without action in it the spiritual quest is considered unworthy.

entries.title: Intercession and devotion to the Prophet's family
questions: Why do Ismailis ask the Imam for help?
What is intercession in Islam?
Do Ismailis worship the Aga Khan?
Is asking the Imam for help shirk?
What is mushkil asan?
Do Sunnis believe in intercession too?
Why do Ismailis recite salawat?
What did Aga Khan III and IV say about being called divine?
entries.answer:
Many religious communities, including both Sunni and Shia Muslims, hold that those close to God may intercede on a believer's behalf. The Ismaili community's own material grounds this in the Qur'anic passage in which those who have wronged themselves are told to come to the Prophet and seek God's forgiveness, so that the Messenger might ask forgiveness for them (Qur'an 4:64), and in a hadith in which the Prophet teaches a blind man to turn to God through him.

The Shia extend the Prophet's role as intercessor to the Imams descended from him through Hazrat Ali and Bibi Fatima. Ismailis therefore invoke the names of Allah, the Prophet, Hazrat Ali and the Imams in prayer, and sometimes address prayers for the easing of difficulties, mushkil asan, to the Prophet or the Imams. The understanding stated is that all help comes from God, but that grace is often channelled through others.

The community is explicit that this does not equate the Prophet or the Imams with God, and that Ismailis affirm tawhid. Asked in a 1985 interview whether he was regarded as a living god, Aga Khan IV answered that this is not true and would be blasphemous, noting that Islam prohibits all forms of idolatry.

Freewill offerings to the Imam are described in the same devotional frame, on the model of offerings made to the Prophet (Qur'an 9:103).

entries.title: The Ikhwan al-Safa and their Epistles
questions: Who were the Ikhwan al-Safa?
What are the Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa?
Were the Brethren of Purity Ismailis?
What subjects did the Epistles cover?
When and where did they write?
Why are the Epistles important?
Did they draw on non-Muslim sources?
Is IIS publishing the Epistles?
entries.answer:
The Ikhwan al-Safa, the Brethren of Purity, were members of an esoteric circle based in Basra and Baghdad around the last quarter of the tenth century CE. They produced the Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa, the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity, an encyclopaedia of fifty-two treatises covering mathematics, music, logic, astronomy and the physical and natural sciences, together with the nature of the soul, ethics, revelation and spirituality. A dense summary, al-Risala al-jami'a, and a further condensation accompany it.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the authorship and dating remain unsettled among scholars. Their writings have been linked at various times to Sufi, Sunni and Mu'tazili currents, but it is more generally accepted that they belong to a Shi'i legacy with strong connections to the Ismaili tradition; some attribute them to early Fatimid circles, while others read the authors as free thinkers who crossed sectarian lines.

They drew on the Qur'an and on Jewish and Christian scripture, and were inspired by Greek thinkers including Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle and Plotinus, alongside Indian and Persian material. They found truth in every religion, treated knowledge as nourishment for the soul, and worked with the analogy of the human being as microcosm and the universe as macrocosm. IIS is publishing the complete text in bilingual volumes with Oxford University Press.

entries.title: Muhammad al-Nasafi
questions: Who was al-Nasafi?
What did al-Nasafi write?
Who introduced Neoplatonism into Ismaili thought?
What is the Kitab al-mahsul?
Where did al-Nasafi work?
What happened to al-Nasafi?
Was al-Nasafi a Qarmati?
How did later thinkers respond to him?
entries.answer:
Muhammad b. Ahmad al-Nasafi (d. 332 AH/943 CE) came from Nakhshab in Central Asia and moved the seat of the da'wa to Transoxania, where he won converts among dignitaries of the Samanid court. He was executed at Bukhara during a Samanid persecution of Ismailis.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies credits him with introducing Neoplatonic philosophy into Ismaili thought, setting out a new emanational cosmology in his Kitab al-mahsul, the Book of the Yield. The work itself has not survived, but it circulated widely and is described as helping to unify Qarmati circles around a shared philosophical framework. Azim Nanji names al-Nasafi as the first to elaborate in detail the cosmological system that al-Sijistani, al-Kirmani and Nasir Khusraw would later refine.

He was also among the da'is of the Iranian lands who first committed the Ismaili cyclical view of sacred history to writing. In his system, as in al-Sijistani's, the divine Command was treated as distinct from and higher than the Intellect, a position al-Kirmani would later modify.

His work drew criticism from Abu Hatim al-Razi, and al-Sijistani wrote in his defence. IIS records that al-Nasafi, like Abu Hatim, evidently belonged to the dissident Qarmati branch and did not recognise the imamate of Abd Allah al-Mahdi.

entries.title: Abu Hatim al-Razi
questions: Who was Abu Hatim al-Razi?
What is the Kitab al-islah?
Where did Abu Hatim al-Razi work?
Why did he criticise al-Nasafi?
What did he think about the Mahdi?
Was Abu Hatim a Qarmati?
How did the da'wa spread to Daylam?
What is his place in Ismaili thought?
entries.answer:
Abu Hatim al-Razi (d. 322 AH/934 CE) was a native of Rayy in northern Persia who served as chief da'i there between roughly 300 and 310 AH/912 and 923 CE. He extended the da'wa into Adharbayjan and Daylam and converted local rulers, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that his success in Daylam brought the mission into the Rudbar of Alamut, the region where the Nizari state would later be founded.

He is described as among the foremost early Ismaili theologians and as providing important doctrinal links between the pre-Fatimid Ismailis and the Fatimids. Like al-Nasafi he adopted Neoplatonism, and his Kitab al-islah, the Book of the Correction, was written to correct positions in al-Nasafi's Kitab al-mahsul. That exchange continued when al-Sijistani defended al-Nasafi, and al-Kirmani later acted as an arbiter in his Kitab al-riyad, the Book of Meadows.

His ideas on Ismaili sacred history are expounded mainly in the Kitab al-islah.

IIS records that Abu Hatim, like al-Nasafi, evidently belonged to the dissident Qarmati branch and did not recognise the imamate of Abd Allah al-Mahdi; he expected the Mahdi to appear in 316 AH/928 CE and corresponded with the Qarmati leadership in Bahrayn.

entries.title: Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani
questions: Who was Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani?
What did al-Sijistani write?
What is the Kitab al-yanabi?
Why is al-Sijistani important?
Was al-Sijistani a philosopher?
How did he die?
Did he join the Fatimids?
What is his view of God?
entries.answer:
Abu Ya'qub Ishaq b. Ahmad al-Sijistani led the Ismaili da'wa in Khurasan and in Sistan, his original base, in succession to al-Nasafi and al-Nasafi's son, and may also have headed the da'wa in the Jibal and in Iraq. The Institute of Ismaili Studies calls him perhaps the foremost Shi'i Neoplatonist of his time, and Paul Walker, writing for IIS, judges him the most influential and perhaps most important of the Fatimid-Ismaili theologians. A contemporary of the Imam-caliph al-Mu'izz, he was executed as a heretic on the order of the Saffarid ruler of Sistan, Khalaf b. Ahmad, not long after 361 AH/971 CE.

He wrote the Kitab al-nusra, the Book of the Defence, upholding al-Nasafi against Abu Hatim al-Razi's criticisms; the Kitab al-yanabi, the Book of Springs; and the Kitab al-maqalid, the Book of Keys. IIS notes that he belonged to the dissident Qarmati camp and was won over to the Fatimid da'wa by al-Mu'izz, the communities under his leadership switching their allegiance with him and recognising al-Mu'izz as the rightful Imam of the time.

His contribution is above all to how God and creation are spoken about. IIS records his argument that denying God any similarity to creatures is not enough, since it still likens Him to the intelligible beings of the spiritual world, so that the negation must itself be negated; in this paradoxical double negation he reaffirmed the suprarational nature of Ismaili belief. He distinguished creation by origination, ibda, from emanation and from the subsequent procession of Soul from Intellect.

sources.title: The Mediaeval Ismailis of the Iranian Lands
Aspects of Ismaili Theology: The Prophetic Chain and the God Beyond Being

entries.notes: The allowed sources describe al-Sijistani as a da'i, theologian and philosopher. They do not record how he would have described himself, so the earlier remark that he would not have called himself a philosopher has been removed.

entries.title: Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani
questions: Who was al-Kirmani?
What is Rahat al-aql?
Why was al-Kirmani called to Cairo?
What was his role in the da'wa?
What did he think about the Imam and justice?
How did he settle the dispute among earlier da'is?
What is the Kitab al-riyad?
Why is he called the summit of Ismaili philosophy?
entries.answer:
Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani (d. shortly after 411 AH/1020 CE) is described by the Institute of Ismaili Studies as the most eminent Ismaili theologian of the Fatimid period and the most accomplished Ismaili philosopher of that era. Probably born in the province of Kirman, he served as chief da'i in Iraq with the title hujjat al-Iraqayn, and was summoned to Cairo in 405 AH/1014 CE, during the reign of the Imam-caliph al-Hakim, to refute the doctrines that became the Druze movement. His summary work, Rahat al-aql, the repose of the intellect, was completed in 411 AH/1020 CE.

He acted as arbiter in the long dispute among al-Nasafi, Abu Hatim al-Razi and al-Sijistani in his Kitab al-riyad, the Book of Meadows. His own system replaced the earlier pair of Intellect and Soul with ten separate intellects, adapting al-Farabi, and tended to identify the divine Command with the First Intellect.

Azim Nanji draws out his account of the Imamat. For al-Kirmani, governing means ordering human beings, with all their differing opinions, into a divinely ordered pattern; the Imam interprets revelation so that each element finds its place in the whole, and individuals and society find equilibrium in material and spiritual matters alike. Justice, adl, is conceived as that state of equilibrium, and the Imam's guidance keeps a balance between din and dunya.

entries.title: Al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi
questions: Who was al-Mu'ayyad al-Shirazi?
What are the Majalis al-Mu'ayyadiyya?
What was the Sirat al-Mu'ayyad?
What did al-Mu'ayyad teach about the six days of creation?
Was al-Mu'ayyad a poet?
What is the da'i al-du'at?
Who did al-Mu'ayyad train?
When did he live?
entries.answer:
Al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi (d. 470 AH/1078 CE) was an Ismaili scholar of Persian origin who, the Institute of Ismaili Studies records, excelled as a da'i, statesman and poet. He tried to win Buyid rulers to the Fatimid cause, moved to Cairo, and carried out diplomatic missions in Syria and Iraq. Towards the end of his life, under the Fatimid Imam-caliph al-Mustansir, he became head of the da'wa as chief da'i.

His memoirs, the Sirat al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din, are described by IIS as a rich source on how the Ismaili mission was organised and how it functioned, and as a window onto the political struggles of the fifth AH/eleventh century CE.

In his teaching role he composed lectures for the majalis al-hikma, the sessions of wisdom, which under the Fatimids were held for those who had already pledged allegiance to the Imam and whose content was approved by the Imam beforehand.

Azim Nanji singles out his ta'wil of the Qur'anic verse that God created the heavens and the earth in six days (Qur'an 7:54). Since there was no sun before creation, he argued, the days cannot be solar days; read rightly, the six days signify the six cycles of prophecy, each an event of cosmic significance. He is also named as one of the teachers who trained Nasir Khusraw in Cairo.

entries.title: Nasir Khusraw
questions: Who was Nasir Khusraw?
What did Nasir Khusraw write?
What is Jami al-hikmatayn?
Why is Nasir Khusraw revered in Badakhshan?
What was his conversion story?
What did he teach about the intellect and the soul?
Did he write in Persian?
What is the Safarnama?
entries.answer:
Nasir Khusraw (394 AH/1004 CE - after 465 AH/1072 CE) was born near Balkh in Khurasan and held administrative posts at Marw before a spiritual upheaval at the age of forty-two, which the Institute of Ismaili Studies links to his conversion to Ismailism. He resigned his post in 437 AH/1045 CE and set out on a long journey, arriving at the Fatimid capital in 439 AH/1047 CE. He stayed three years in Cairo, received intensive training as a da'i, saw the Imam-caliph al-Mustansir, and formed close relations with al-Mu'ayyad al-Shirazi, who remained his mentor. He returned east in 444 AH/1052 CE as hujja, the chief da'i of Khurasan.

By 452 AH/1060 CE the hostility of Sunni scholars, who denounced him as a heretic and destroyed his house, had driven him to the valley of Yumgan in Badakhshan. He extended the da'wa throughout Badakhshan, and Ismailis there and in the Hindukush regard him as the founder of their communities and still revere him as Pir or Shah Sayyid Nasir.

His works include the Safarnama, the travelogue of his journey; Zad al-musafirin, written in 453 AH/1061 CE; and Jami al-hikmatayn, his last known work, completed in 462 AH/1070 CE, in which he sought to harmonise the esoteric understanding of Islam with the wisdom of the ancients and which he called the synthesis of the two wisdoms. IIS describes him as the last major proponent of philosophical Ismailism in the Iranian lands, as much influenced by al-Sijistani, and as the only Fatimid-era writer who wrote in Persian.

He is also the clearest exponent of the Ismaili approach to scripture, distinguishing tanzil, the revelation as it came down, from ta'wil, the interpretation that leads back to its original meaning. In the cosmology he shares with that tradition, God creates not by emanation but by a timeless and transcendent command, and the Universal Intellect and Universal Soul are the first and second originated beings.

sources.title: The Mediaeval Ismailis of the Iranian Lands

entries.notes: The allowed sources do not contain the argument that God would not send a message without a guide to interpret it, so that formulation has been removed and replaced with the tanzil/ta'wil distinction that they do set out.

entries.title: Nasir al-Din Tusi
questions: Who was Nasir al-Din Tusi?
Was Tusi an Ismaili?
What is the Rawda-yi taslim?
What is Sayr wa suluk?
What is the Akhlaq-i Nasiri?
Why did Tusi say a teacher was necessary?
Did Tusi leave the Ismailis?
What did Tusi contribute to Ismaili thought?
entries.answer:
Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 672 AH/1274 CE) was a polymath who joined the Nizari Ismaili community and spent years under Ismaili patronage, first with the governor of Quhistan and later at Alamut, before the Mongol conquest, after which he served the Mongols. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he produced over 150 works across theology, philosophy, mathematics and astronomy.

In his spiritual autobiography, Sayr wa suluk, Contemplation and Action, he describes realising that the human intellect can move from potentiality to actuality only under the influence of another, perfect intellect and a divinely guided teacher, a mu'allim, and says he hoped to find that teacher among the Ismailis. Madelung links this to the influence of al-Shahrastani. Tusi also held that if the speaker of truth appears in different forms or institutes the divine law differently in different ages, this reflects changing worldly circumstances, not any change in his truthfulness.

The Rawda-yi taslim, Paradise of Submission, gathers lectures he gave at sessions of wisdom, compiled by his associate Hasan-i Mahmud-i Katib; IIS calls it the single most important Ismaili text of the Alamut period, and credits his work with deepening Nizari treatment of tawhid, imamat, qiyamat and ta'lim. His Akhlaq-i Nasiri, the Nasirean Ethics, was completed around 633 AH/1235 CE in Ismaili service.

Tusi later left Ismaili allegiance; IIS presents his intellectual path as moving between philosophy, Shi'ism and Sufism.

entries.notes: Tusi's degree of personal commitment to Ismailism, as against prudent accommodation, is treated differently by different scholars; IIS presents his trajectory as genuinely mobile between traditions.

entries.title: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man
questions: Who was al-Qadi al-Nu'man?
What is the Da'a'im al-Islam?
What is Ta'wil al-da'a'im?
What was his role under the Fatimids?
Did he hold the sessions of wisdom?
How did he approach legal reasoning?
When did he live?
Why is he called the founder of Ismaili law?
entries.answer:
Al-Qadi al-Nu'man, an Ismaili Shi'i from Qayrawan in North Africa, entered the service of the Fatimid dynasty at an early age and served its first four Imam-caliphs consecutively for over half a century, from 312 AH/924 CE until his death in 363 AH/974 CE.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes a distinct Ismaili system of jurisprudence as having been founded after the establishment of the Fatimid dynasty, and regards al-Nu'man as the one who propounded Ismaili law. Commissioned by the fourth Imam-caliph al-Mu'izz, he composed the Da'a'im al-Islam, his magnum opus, which was officially promulgated as the Fatimid code and, according to a later Tayyibi historian, was closely supervised by al-Mu'izz himself. Reporting on the authority of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, it sets out the seven pillars with walaya, devotion to the Imam, first and highest.

He set aside ra'y, personal opinion, and qiyas, analogical reasoning, in favour of the Qur'an, the sunna of the Prophet and the teachings of the Imams of the Prophet's family, referring what remained doubtful to the Imam of the time; IIS records a decree of al-Mu'izz instructing him in exactly these terms.

His other legal works include the voluminous Kitab al-izah, an attempt to collect and classify the legal traditions transmitted from the Prophet's family, several abridgements of it, and refutations of the Sunni schools of jurisprudence and their founders. IIS notes that the Da'a'im remains a source of supreme authority in legal matters for the Musta'li-Tayyibi Ismailis. Nanji records that the Da'a'im defines the sphere of ritual action, the sharia, and that al-Nu'man went on to write the Ta'wil al-da'a'im on the inner meaning of those same acts.

sources.title: Ismaili Jurisprudence
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 195-197

entries.notes: The allowed sources do not give al-Nu'man's date or place of birth, his court appointments such as chief judge, or the account of al-Mu'izz leading his funeral prayer. They also do not cover his conduct of the majalis al-hikma, so that is not described. CORRECTED 2026-09-22: an earlier note claimed the allowed sources do not cover his Ta'wil al-da'a'im either. They do — Nanji's 'Isma'ilism' (IIS) states that the Da'a'im defines the sphere of ritual action and that al-Nu'man went on to write the Ta'wil al-da'a'im. entries.title: Ethics: din and dunya
questions: What are Ismaili ethics?
What do din and dunya mean?
Are the spiritual and material worlds separate?
What is the Muslim idea of stewardship?
What does khalifa mean in the Qur'an?
Do Ismailis believe in original sin?
How do faith and daily life connect?
Why does the Imam engage in development work?
entries.answer:
Ismaili ethics begin from the idea that faith and worldly life are not two separate compartments. The Aga Khan Development Network states that the ethics of Islam bridge the realm of faith and the realm of practical life, what the tradition calls din and dunya, and that the Imam's responsibility for interpreting the faith is accompanied by engagement with the quality of life and wellbeing.

Azim Nanji grounds this in the Qur'anic account of the human being. Adam is shaped from clay, given divine spirit and endowed with the capacity to name things, so that material, spiritual and intellectual orientations are combined in one creature. He is called khalifa, vicegerent, entrusted with the earth. That standing carries accountability for the choices made, and Nanji notes that the Qur'anic story of Adam's lapse and recovery carries no doctrine of original sin; it describes an ongoing struggle to find equilibrium.

Muslim writing on ethics, on this account, did not split human action in two but sought an integrated vision in which being Muslim means engaging both the material and the spiritual and holding them in balance.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes AKDN as a contemporary effort of the Ismaili Imamat to realise the social conscience of Islam through institutional action, aimed at enabling each person to live up to the status of vicegerent of God on earth.

sources.title: Divine Law / Divine Command: The Ground of Ethics in the Western Tradition - Muslim Perspectives
Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN): An Ethical Framework

entries.title: Pluralism
questions: Why do Ismailis emphasise pluralism?
Is pluralism an Islamic value?
What does the Qur'an say about diversity?
How did the Fatimids treat other communities?
Do Ismaili institutions serve non-Ismailis?
What is the Global Centre for Pluralism?
How do Ismailis view other Muslim interpretations?
What is the People of the Book?
entries.answer:
Pluralism is presented by Ismaili institutions as growing out of Islamic sources rather than being imported into them. Azim Nanji cites the Qur'anic verse that God granted each community a path and a way of life, and could have made humanity a single community but chose otherwise (Qur'an 5:48), reading it as a call to strive in virtue rather than to enforce uniformity. The Qur'anic category of Ahl al-Kitab, People of the Book, frames Jews and Christians as sharing a lineage of revelation.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies points to Fatimid practice as a historical instance. Fatimid policy encouraged private patronage of mosques by Muslims of different legal schools, appointed on merit including Sunni jurists to senior judicial office, and gave Christians and Jews positions and active participation in the life of the state. The Dar al-Ilm founded in Cairo in 1005 CE, with a library of over 400,000 manuscripts, was open to followers of different religions. IIS also records a Fatimid edict to the effect that each Muslim might seek his own solution within his religion.

In the present, AKDN names pluralism as a central pillar of its ethical framework and states that its institutions and programmes work without regard to the faith, origin, race or gender of the people they serve.

sources.title: Divine Law / Divine Command: The Ground of Ethics in the Western Tradition - Muslim Perspectives

entries.title: Knowledge and learning
questions: Why do Ismailis value education so highly?
What is ilm?
What was Dar al-Ilm?
What was al-Azhar under the Fatimids?
Were Fatimid institutions open to everyone?
Is science part of faith for Ismailis?
What subjects did the Fatimids study?
How is knowledge connected to the Imam?
entries.answer:
Shia thought places great weight on knowledge, and the Institute of Ismaili Studies traces the Fatimid commitment to learning partly to this: the Imam is held to possess a special ilm through which he interprets revelation, and that link between knowledge and religious authority gave a spiritual motive for supporting scholarship.

The institutions reflect it. Al-Azhar, built under the Imam-caliph al-Mu'izz, became the principal centre of learning in Fatimid Cairo, where sessions on the outward meaning of the law were open to everyone, women included. The Dar al-Ilm, House of Knowledge, founded by the Imam-caliph al-Hakim in 1005 CE, was unusual in uniting religious and non-religious disciplines under one roof: Qur'an readers, astronomers, grammarians, philologists and physicians all lectured there, and the facilities were open to all. Its library held over 400,000 manuscripts and served people of different religions. Ibn al-Haytham (b. 965 CE), invited to Cairo by al-Hakim, wrote his Kitab al-manazir there, correcting Greek theories of vision.

IIS presents this as a balanced approach to reason and faith rather than a subordination of one to the other, and notes that Fatimid thinkers engaged the most advanced forms of thought available to them. The Imamat has expressed the same idea by describing knowledge as twofold, revealed and discovered, with no contradiction between them.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide
The Ismaili Imamat: a brief history

entries.title: Service, giving and the common good
questions: Why do Ismailis volunteer so much?
What is voluntary service in the Ismaili community?
Is charity only about money?
What does service to God mean in Islam?
Do Ismaili institutions help non-Ismailis?
What values guide Ismaili service?
What is the social conscience of Islam?
How does service relate to faith?
entries.answer:
Service is treated in Ismaili institutional teaching as an expression of faith rather than an optional extra. AKDN states that in Islam service to God is not only worship but also service to humanity, and abiding by a duty of trust towards the rest of creation. The ethical principles it names are consultation, solidarity with those less fortunate, self-reliance and human dignity, with compassion exercised in a way that does not compromise the dignity of the person helped.

Charity in this framing is not only material. AKDN notes that it can take the form of gifts of time, knowledge, expertise and skills.

Within the community, the Ismaili's own account of jamatkhana life describes voluntary service as a form of offering. Community institutions, jamatkhanas included, are largely run by volunteers giving time and knowledge out of love and devotion to the Imam and the community, and jamatkhanas are described as places where Islamic values such as humility, generosity, kindness, compassion and service to others are put into practice.

Outward-facing institutions work on the same basis. The community's own literature records that under the Imam's guidance Ismailis have established schools, hospitals, health centres, housing societies and development institutions for the common good of all citizens regardless of race or religion, and AKDN works in some of the poorest regions of Asia and Africa without regard to faith or origin.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN): An Ethical Framework

entries.title: The spiritual quest and the seeker
questions: What does the spiritual path look like in Ismaili thought?
What is the Kitab al-alim wa'l-ghulam?
How did Nasir Khusraw describe his conversion?
What are the ginans about?
What is the role of poetry in Ismaili devotion?
Is there an initiation in Ismaili tradition?
What does the soul seek?
How is Ismaili spirituality related to Sufism?
entries.answer:
Azim Nanji identifies a recurring narrative shape in Ismaili literature: a quest that leads to transformation. The seeker is awakened out of ignorance, is taught to read symbols and use ta'wil, comes to desire knowledge of the one who holds the keys to inner meaning, and is finally changed.

Three examples carry the pattern. Nasir Khusraw's autobiographical ode turns a dream into an awakening, a journey, and an oath of allegiance taken beneath an exalted tree; he describes himself as having been stone and becoming a ruby. The Kitab al-alim wa'l-ghulam, the Book of the Master and the Disciple, unfolds as a series of dialogues in which a disciple's questioning is aroused, then deepened, and finally sealed in a ceremony whose content the text does not disclose. In the ginans of South Asia the pirs arrive unknown, win disciples, face rejection, and eventually depart, with images such as bride and bridegroom marking the passage from search to union.

Nanji notes that later Ismaili writing has features analogous in some respects to Sufi theosophy, arising from shared contexts and mutual influence, and that poetry rather than prose best carries these moments. He also observes that what is communicated at the point of transformation is withheld from the text; it is passed personally. Contemporary practice follows the same reticence.

sources.title: Intellectual Life in Fatimid Times: A Reading Guide
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The content of initiation, in the medieval texts and in present-day practice alike, is deliberately not recorded in the sources and is not reconstructed here.

entries.title: Justice, equilibrium and the shape of history
questions: What do Ismailis mean by justice?
What is adl?
How does the Imam relate to justice?
Why do Ismailis describe history in cycles of quiet and engagement?
Is the Imam's role political?
How do din and dunya stay in balance?
What does equilibrium mean here?
Does the Imamat need a state?
entries.answer:
Justice in Ismaili thought is described less as a set of rules than as a state of balance. Azim Nanji draws this from al-Kirmani, for whom the essence of governing is organising human beings, with all their differing opinions, into a divinely ordered pattern; the Imam interprets revelation so that each element takes its proper place, and individuals and society find equilibrium in both material and spiritual matters. Justice, adl, is conceived as that equilibrium, at the personal and the social level alike, and it depends on the intellectual, spiritual and social maturity of people in society.

Din, religion, and dunya, the world, are both elements in the proper ordering of society, and the Imam's guidance is understood to sustain the balance between them.

Nanji also describes two recurring patterns in Ismaili history: periods of quiescence and interiorisation, when circumstances limit engagement with the world, and more enabling periods when intellectual and institutional engagement is possible. Through both, justice remains the constant goal, and the function of the Imamat is to give that goal personal meaning and institutional expression in changing conditions.

The wider Shia tradition supplies the moral charge: the defence of social justice is evoked above all through Imam Husayn's stand at Karbala in 61 AH/680 CE.

entries.title: What is a Jamatkhana?
questions: What is a jamatkhana?
What does the word jamatkhana mean?
Is a jamatkhana the same as a mosque?
What happens inside a jamatkhana?
Where do Ismailis pray?
Why is it called a house of the community?
What is a JK?
entries.answer:
Jamatkhana means "house of the community". The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that the word joins the Arabic jama'a, meaning group or congregation, with the Persian khana, meaning house. It describes a place where certain Sunni and Shia Muslim communities come together for prayer and communal gathering, and it is used for the Shia Ismaili spaces of worship and gathering.

The Ismaili, the community's official site, describes the jamatkhana as a designated space where Shia Ismaili Muslims gather to perform tariqah practices. These include supplicatory prayer (du'a), meditative sessions of remembrance (dhikr or zikr), and the recitation of devotional poetry such as ginans and qasidas.

The community describes jamatkhanas as places of prayer and contemplation, of hope, humility and spiritual enlightenment, and as a space where members strengthen their personal bond with the Imam-of-the-Time. Beyond prayer, jamatkhanas function as hubs of social life where the community gathers, learns, and marks important life events including birth, marriage and death.

A jamatkhana is not a mosque, though it sits among the many kinds of Muslim spaces of gathering. The community places it alongside the ribat, zawiyya and khanaqa as one of several historic institutional forms that have co-existed with the masjid.

sources.title: The Grace and Blessings of Jamatkhanas in our Lives
The History of Jamatkhanas and Their Significance

entries.title: Who may attend a Jamatkhana?
questions: Can non-Ismailis go into a jamatkhana?
Why are jamatkhana prayers only for Ismailis?
Can I visit a jamatkhana as a guest?
Is the jamatkhana open to the public?
Can my Ismaili friend bring me to prayers?
Why is the jamatkhana private?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili explains that participation in formal prayers in jamatkhanas is restricted to those who have pledged bay'a, the oath of allegiance, to the Ismaili Imam-of-the-Time. Ismaili jamatkhanas are described as private tariqa spaces, and the practices observed in them are said to be the sole prerogative of the Imam-of-the-Time.

The community frames this the way many religious communities draw a line between public and private. Just as households keep family life private, communities that understand themselves as an extended family may reserve certain spaces and rituals for those formally initiated into them. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses bay'a as, in the Shia Ismaili tradition, the acceptance of a permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and the murid, or follower.

This does not make the buildings closed. Outside formal prayer times, many jamatkhanas — and particularly the Ismaili Centres — welcome multi-faith family members and the wider public to educational, cultural and social programmes. The Ismaili presents this as a deliberate effort to build bridges with the societies in which Ismailis live. Community reports of festivals such as Salgirah describe multi-faith families being invited to celebrate alongside the Jamat, with a separate programme running during prayer time.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.title: The Jamatkhana among Muslim spaces of gathering
questions: How does a jamatkhana relate to a mosque?
What other Muslim spaces are like a jamatkhana?
What is a khanaqa or a zawiyya?
Where did jamatkhanas come from historically?
Do other Muslim communities use jamatkhanas?
Is the jamatkhana an Ismaili invention?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili situates the jamatkhana within a long history of varied Muslim spaces. It notes that the earliest Muslim community in Mecca had no special building and that arrangements for communal worship were informal, citing a well-known saying of the Prophet that the whole world is a masjid. After the migration to Medina, dedicated spaces emerged, beginning with the courtyard beside the Prophet's house, which served as a place of worship but also as a social, educational, political and ambassadorial centre.

As different communities of interpretation developed — Shia and Sunni branches, and many Sufi tariqahs — they developed their own distinctive gathering spaces alongside the masjid, retaining their own names and characteristics: ribat, zawiyya, khanaqa and jamatkhana among them.

The community is explicit that the jamatkhana is not exclusively Ismaili. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes it is primarily associated with the activities of Sufi groups and also refers to Shia Ismaili spaces of worship and gathering. Speaking at the foundation ceremony of the Ismaili Centre, Dubai, in 2003, the late Aga Khan described the congregational space within an Ismaili Centre as belonging to the historic category of jamatkhana, an institutional category that also serves a number of sister Sunni and Shia communities, while being reserved there for practices specific to the Shia Ismaili tariqah.

sources.title: Situating Jamatkhanas within Diverse Muslim Spaces of Gathering and Piety
The History of Jamatkhanas and Their Significance

entries.title: The Jamatkhana in everyday community life
questions: What does a jamatkhana do besides prayer?
Is there a library or offices in a jamatkhana?
What is a Darkhana?
How important is the jamatkhana to Ismaili identity?
What role did jamatkhanas play in migration?
Do jamatkhanas host cultural events?
entries.answer:
Beyond prayer, jamatkhanas have long carried the everyday weight of community life. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the historic Town Jamatkhana in Nairobi as housing spaces for prayer and contemplation alongside social events, learning and administration, including a well-stocked library where members read newspapers and offices for the Ismaili Council. Designated a heritage monument in 2001, it now also hosts cultural events and exhibitions that bring together officials, diplomats and partners.

A principal jamatkhana serving a jurisdiction is known as a Darkhana. The Institute records that in 1944 the young Prince Karim recited the Eid al-Fitr namaz at what was then the Darkhana in Nairobi.

The Institute's publication Experiences of the Jamatkhana presents jamatkhanas as sacred spaces of piety, practice and social gathering, and as pillars of the community that offered strength and solace through periods of upheaval — including the expulsion from Uganda and departures from Tanzania — as Ismailis migrated and resettled. The community's own account adds that jamatkhanas are where important life events, from birth through marriage to death, are marked.

sources.title: The Grace and Blessings of Jamatkhanas in our Lives

entries.title: The Ismaili Centres
questions: What is an Ismaili Centre?
Where are the Ismaili Centres?
Can anyone visit an Ismaili Centre?
How is an Ismaili Centre different from a jamatkhana?
Why are they called ambassadorial buildings?
What goes on inside an Ismaili Centre?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Centres are purpose-built buildings that the community describes as ambassadorial. The Ismaili presents them as symbolic markers of the community's permanent presence in the regions where they stand, developed as the Jamat settled in new countries. The Centres listed by the community include London, Lisbon, Dubai, Dushanbe, Vancouver, Toronto and Houston.

Each Centre contains a congregational space belonging to the historic category of jamatkhana, together with a range of other, non-religious spaces. The community describes these as places for social and cultural gathering, intellectual engagement and reflection, where Ismailis can extend a hand of friendship to the wider society around them. The stated purpose is to encourage exchange and understanding between diverse peoples, communities and faiths, and to support cultural, educational and social programmes from a broad, non-denominational perspective within an Islamic ethical framework.

Speaking at the opening of the Ismaili Centre, Toronto, in 2014, the late Aga Khan described the building as focused around its jamatkhana but also including many secular spaces, with a crystalline dome above through which light from the prayer hall would act as a beacon. At the opening of the Centre in Dushanbe he framed the aim as demonstrating that spiritual insight and worldly knowledge nourish one another rather than oppose each other.

sources.title: The Ambassadorial Role of the Ismaili Centres
The History of Jamatkhanas and Their Significance
Situating Jamatkhanas within Diverse Muslim Spaces of Gathering and Piety

entries.title: What are Ismaili tariqah practices?
questions: What is tariqa in Islam?
What are Ismaili tariqah practices?
What prayers do Ismailis say in jamatkhana?
Who decides what Ismailis practise?
What is the Ismaili path?
Are Ismaili practices in the Qur'an?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses tariqa as way or path — the path followed by mystical schools of interpretation in Islam. The Ismaili explains that tariqas are communities of Muslims following a path guided by a spiritual leader, such as a Shia Imam or a Sufi murshid, who shapes the community's interpretation and practice as part of an inward search for spiritual enlightenment.

The community states that Ismaili jamatkhana practices express the spiritual bond between the Imam-of-the-Time and his followers, conveyed in the bay'a each Ismaili offers, and that the Imam-of-the-Time has sole authority to determine those practices at any time.

The Ismaili lists the forms of prayer involved as du'a (supplication), tasbih (glorification), dhikr (remembrance) and salawat (seeking blessings on the Prophet and his progeny). Practices also include recitation of verses of the Qur'an, affirming the shahada, reciting devotional poetry such as qasidas, nashids and ginans, and the reading of farmans, which is guidance from the Imam. Special prayers may be observed at festivals, in times of difficulty, and at rites of passage, particularly deaths.

Ismailis understand these practices as reaffirming belief in the oneness of God, in the Prophet Muhammad as His Messenger, and in those in authority (uli'l-amr), the hereditary Imams.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.title: The Dua and daily prayer
questions: What is the Ismaili Dua?
How many times a day do Ismailis pray?
Do Ismailis pray namaz?
What is du'a in Islam?
What does the Ismaili daily prayer contain?
Is the Dua different from salat?
entries.answer:
Du'a is the prayer of supplication. The Ismaili lists it first among the forms of prayer that make up Ismaili tariqah practice in jamatkhana, alongside tasbih, dhikr and salawat, and describes these as prayers recommended in the Qur'an. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses the related Qur'anic term salat as prayer in general, which later came to be used more specifically for the daily ritual prayer.

The community's published material describes the Dua as recited in jamatkhana and states that the bay'a, the pledge of allegiance to the Imam-of-the-Time, is reaffirmed daily in various prayers and jamatkhana practices. Reporting on the Eid al-Fitr of 1944, the community records that the future Aga Khan, then aged seven, recited the Eid namaz at Nairobi's Town Jamatkhana, indicating that namaz is also part of the community's vocabulary for prayer.

Beyond this, the wording of the Dua, the number and timing of daily prayers, and the order of the jamatkhana ceremony are not published on the community's own institutional sites. These are matters internal to the community, determined by the Imam-of-the-Time, and this entry does not attempt to describe them. Anyone wanting detail on how the Dua is recited should approach the community directly.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The text and structure of the Dua, and the daily prayer timetable, are internal to the community and are not published by the Ismaili institutions in the allowed source set. Deliberately not described here.

entries.title: Salawat: blessings on the Prophet and his family
questions: What is salawat?
Why do Ismailis recite salawat?
What does Allahumma salli ala Muhammad mean?
Do Sunnis also recite salawat?
Why include the Prophet's family in the blessing?
What is durud sharif?
entries.answer:
Salawat is the plural of salat, meaning prayer, and refers to invoking God's blessings on the Prophet Muhammad. The Ismaili explains that all Muslims recite salawat in their daily prayers, and that various forms developed on the basis of Qur'anic guidance. The community cites Surah 33, verse 56, which calls on believers to invoke blessings on the Prophet and greet him with peace.

According to a hadith the community recounts, when this verse was revealed the Prophet's companions asked how they should recite the blessing; he is said to have answered with a form invoking blessings on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as God had blessed Ibrahim and his family. A common form is therefore Allahumma salli ala Muhammad wa-aali Muhammad — O God, send Your blessings on Muhammad and his family.

Salawat is also known as tasliya or durud-i sharif. After naming the Prophet, many Muslims add "salla Allahu alayhi wa-sallam"; Shia Muslims and some Sunnis extend this to include his family. Ismailis understand salawat as a source of grace and blessing and as a prayer of intercession — a means of drawing near to the Prophet and seeking his intercession with God. The community notes that salawat appears widely in Muslim artistic expression, in calligraphy beside the Prophet's name and in poetry and music across many cultures.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis recite salawat for the family of the Prophet (pbuh)?
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Dhikr: the remembrance of God
questions: What is dhikr?
What is zikr in the Ismaili tradition?
How do Ismailis practise remembrance of God?
Is dhikr silent or spoken aloud?
What phrases are used in dhikr?
Why is remembrance important in Islam?
entries.answer:
Dhikr means the act of reminding, or remembrance. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes the Qur'anic exhortation to remember God with much remembrance, and describes dhikr as a form of prayer consisting in the constant repetition of a name or a formula, performed either alone or collectively. The Institute records that mystical writers treated dhikr as a discipline giving access to higher spiritual states, and that manuals were written on how to perform it.

The Ismaili describes dhikr as one of the most frequent forms of Muslim prayer and lists a broad range of meanings: recollection, invocation, repetition, recitation and glorification. It notes that dhikr may be performed aloud (jali) or silently (khafi), in solitude or in a group.

The community's own account gives examples of phrases used, such as Allahu Akbar (God is Greater) and Subhan Allah (Glory be to God), and of remembrance through God's names, including Ya Allah, Ya Rahman, Ya Rahim and Ya Ali. It grounds this in the Qur'anic verse that the most beautiful names belong to God and that He should be called by them. Through dhikr, the community writes, believers seek nearness to God, ask forgiveness, and give thanks; it cites the verse asking whether hearts are not at peace in the remembrance of God.

sources.title: Losing and Finding Ourselves in Dhikr
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Tasbih: glorification of God
questions: What is tasbih?
What is a zikr tasbih?
How is tasbih different from dhikr?
Do Ismailis use prayer beads?
What does glorification mean in prayer?
Is tasbih part of jamatkhana practice?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili lists tasbih, glossed as glorification, as one of the forms of prayer that make up Ismaili tariqah practice in jamatkhana, alongside du'a, dhikr and salawat. The community presents all four as forms of prayer recommended in the Qur'an, through which Ismailis seek God's grace and mercy.

Tasbih and dhikr are closely related and overlap in practice. Community material announcing a devotional audio series describes its contents as Qur'anic recitations, zikr tasbihs, ginans, Arabic and Persian qasidas and manqabats — putting zikr tasbihs among the recognised devotional forms, and indicating that they are recited rather than read silently.

The allowed Ismaili institutional sources do not publish the specific tasbih formulae recited in jamatkhana, nor a dedicated explainer on tasbih comparable to those they have published on salawat and dhikr. Related material on dhikr does describe repeated phrases of praise such as Subhan Allah, meaning Glory be to God, and remembrance through the names of God. Beyond that, the detail of how tasbih is performed in jamatkhana is internal to the community and is not described here.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
Losing and Finding Ourselves in Dhikr

entries.notes: The community's institutions name tasbih as a practice but do not publish a dedicated explanation of it or the formulae used. Treated here as partly internal.

entries.title: Baitul Khayal
questions: What is Baitul Khayal?
Do Ismailis meditate?
What is the Ismaili meditation practice?
When does Baitul Khayal happen?
Why can't I find information about Baitul Khayal?
Is Ismaili meditation secret?
entries.answer:
Baitul Khayal is a practice of contemplation observed within the Ismaili community. It is an internal tariqah practice, and the Ismaili community's own institutions do not publish an account of it. This entry therefore does not describe how it is performed, when it takes place, or what it involves.

What the community does publish is the wider frame. The Ismaili describes the jamatkhana as a place of contemplation and of meditative sessions of remembrance, and states plainly that Ismaili tariqah practices are the sole prerogative of the Imam-of-the-Time and are specific to the Ismaili community. The Institute of Ismaili Studies, writing about dhikr more generally in Muslim traditions, notes that remembrance may be performed silently (khafi) as well as aloud, and that it has long been understood as a discipline for living in God's presence.

Readers should treat the absence of published detail as deliberate rather than as a gap in the record. Practices that a community reserves for its members are not usually documented for outside readers, and the right place to ask about Baitul Khayal is the community itself.

entries.title: Ginans
questions: What is a ginan?
What language are ginans in?
Who composed the ginans?
What is Khojki script?
What are ginans about?
Are ginans sung or read?
How many ginans are there?
entries.answer:
Ginans are devotional poems of the South Asian Nizari Ismaili communities, historically known as Khojas. The Institute of Ismaili Studies traces the word to the Sanskrit jnan, meaning knowledge — more fully, contemplative or reflective knowledge — and describes ginans as compositions in an Indian language ascribed to the Pirs who led the Khoja community between roughly the thirteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The languages involved reflect the communities that produced them: Sindhi, Punjabi, Gujarati, Hindi and Multani, with the community's own account also noting Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian vocabulary. The Institute characterises ginans as having elements of both didactic and mystical poetry, and legendary in nature. They were transmitted orally before being committed to writing in Khojki, a script the Institute describes as developed among the Khojas of the subcontinent to record their literature.

The Ismaili reports that several hundred ginans are thought to have been composed, ranging from as few as four verses to several hundred. Their subjects range widely: religious stories, moral teaching, references to festivals and ceremonies, and themes of divine love and longing. The community gives as an example a ginan attributed to Pir Shams expressing the desire for the didar, the sight, of the Lord. Ginans are recited in jamatkhana as part of tariqah practice, and the Institute has developed an interdisciplinary research programme treating them as literary, devotional and intellectual texts.

sources.title: Ginans
