entries.title: Qasidas
questions: What is a qasida?
Which Ismailis recite qasidas?
What language are qasidas in?
How long is a qasida?
What are qasidas about?
How are qasidas different from ginans?
entries.answer:
A qasida is a poem of a certain length in Arabic, Persian or Turkish. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as a polythematic form originating in pre-Islamic Arabia, often including praise of a figure, and notes that Persian qasidas are also composed to mark festivals. The chanted qasida, the Institute writes, is part of the religious tradition of Arabic- and Persian-speaking Nizari Ismailis.

The Ismaili adds practical detail: a typical qasida may run to a hundred verses or more, and keeps the same rhyme throughout, which poets treated as a test of skill. Poets have written qasidas on religious themes beginning with praise of the Prophet and the Imams, and on mystical subjects. The community describes the qasida as among the most prestigious poetic forms in Islam, and gives as an example a qasida by Sabir Kirmani invoking and seeking Hazrat Ali.

Where ginans belong to the South Asian Khoja tradition, qasidas are especially associated with Iranian and Central Asian Ismaili communities. The Institute's publication Know Your Qasidas, the first in its Read & Reflect series, presents each qasida in its original language with transliteration, translation and a short essay, and links recitations by QR code — intended, the Institute says, to carry the qasida traditions into English-speaking contexts and open them to Ismailis of varied cultural backgrounds.

sources.title: The different forms of devotional expression in the Ismaili Tariqah

entries.title: Forms of devotional expression: ginan, qasida, manqabat, nashid
questions: What kinds of devotional poetry do Ismailis recite?
What is a manqabat?
What is a nashid?
What is maddah?
Why is devotional poetry so important to Ismailis?
Do different Ismaili communities recite different things?
entries.answer:
Ismaili devotional life draws on several poetic and musical forms, and which ones a congregation uses depends largely on where that community's traditions come from. The Ismaili writes that devotion to the Prophet, to his progeny and to the Imam-of-the-Time is expressed through qasidas, maddah and ginans.

Setting out the practices observed in jamatkhanas, the community lists the recitation of devotional poetry including qasidas, nashids and ginans. Community material announcing a devotional audio series describes its contents as Qur'anic recitations, zikr tasbihs, ginans, Arabic and Persian qasidas, and manqabats — the manqabat being a poem in praise of a revered figure.

Broadly, ginans belong to the South Asian Khoja tradition and are composed in languages such as Sindhi, Gujarati and Punjabi; qasidas belong especially to Arabic- and Persian-speaking communities, including those of Iran and Central Asia. Maddah, or maddah-khani, is a Central Asian practice. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that manuscripts circulating among the Ismailis of Badakhshan served as memory aids in practices including maddah-khani.

Taken together, these forms show a single tradition expressed through many regional languages and musical idioms rather than one uniform repertoire.

entries.title: Chirag-e Roshan and Central Asian devotional traditions
questions: What is Chirag-e Roshan?
What is Chiragh-i rawshan?
What is the luminous lamp ceremony?
How do Central Asian Ismailis worship?
What is maddah-khani?
What traditions do Ismailis in Badakhshan follow?
entries.answer:
Chiragh-i rawshan, the luminous lamp, is a devotional practice observed among the Ismailis of Central Asia, particularly in Badakhshan. It is a community practice associated with commemoration of the dead, and the Ismaili institutions do not publish a description of how it is performed; this entry therefore does not describe the rite itself.

What is documented is the scholarship. The Institute of Ismaili Studies lists a study by its Central Asian Studies specialist Hakim Elnazarov, "The Luminous Lamp: The Practice of Chiragh-i rawshan among the Ismailis of Central Asia", published in The Study of Shi'i Islam, edited by Farhad Daftary and Gurdofarid Miskinzoda. The Institute also records that manuscripts circulating among the Ismaili communities of Badakhshan were used as memory aids in rituals and practices including Chiragh-i rawshan and maddah-khani, a sung devotional form — evidence of long interaction between Ismaili and Sufi literary traditions in the region.

The broader Central Asian devotional repertoire centres on the Persian qasida. The Institute describes the chanted qasida as part of the religious tradition of Persian-speaking Nizari Ismailis, and its Know Your Qasidas presents qasidas particularly from Iranian and Central Asian traditions.
entries.notes: The allowed sources name and study Chiragh-i rawshan but publish no description of the ceremony. Its performance is a community-internal matter and is not described here.

entries.title: Farman: guidance from the Imam
questions: What is a farman?
What does farman mean?
Are farmans read in jamatkhana?
What is a Takht-nishini Farman?
How does the Imam guide the community?
Can outsiders read farmans?
entries.answer:
Farman is a Persian word meaning command, authority, will or permission. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that in Ottoman usage it denoted any order of the sultan, and that from the fifteenth century it came to mean a written document, typically opening with an invocation to God. In the Shia Ismaili context, the Institute writes, farman refers to an address by the Imam to his community.

The Ismaili lists the reading of farmans — described simply as guidance from the Imam — among the practices observed in jamatkhanas, alongside prayer, Qur'anic recitation and devotional poetry.

Some farmans are reported publicly. The community reported that in his Takht-nishini Farman of 11 February 2025, following his accession as the 50th Imam, Mawlana Hazar Imam pledged to dedicate his life to the spiritual and material well-being of the Ismaili Jamat. Takht-nishini refers to the formal accession, or enthronement, of an Imam.

Farmans as a body, however, are addressed to the Jamat rather than to the public, and their texts are not published by the community's institutions for general readership. This entry describes what a farman is, not what particular farmans say.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Seeking intercession through the Prophet and the Imams
questions: Why do Ismailis ask Hazrat Ali for help?
What is intercession in Islam?
Do Ismailis worship the Imam?
Is asking the Imams for help shirk?
Do Sunnis believe in intercession too?
What is mushkil kusha?
entries.answer:
Intercession means pleading or intervening on behalf of another: believers ask those considered close to God to intercede with Him for them. The Ismaili notes that many religious communities hold this belief, and that Muslims of most interpretations, both Sunni and Shia, regard the Prophet Muhammad as an intercessor.

The community grounds the practice in the Qur'an, citing verse 4:64, in which those who had wronged themselves are told that had they come to the Prophet and sought God's forgiveness, and had the Messenger sought forgiveness for them, they would have found God forgiving and merciful.

In the Shia interpretation, the Prophet's role as intercessor extends to the Imams descended from him through Hazrat Ali and Hazrat Bibi Fatima. Ismailis therefore invoke the names of God, the Prophet, Hazrat Ali and the Imams in their prayers and devotional practices, and seek forgiveness and spiritual purification through the Imam's intercession. The community describes turning to the Imam in hardship as supplicating to the mushkil kusha, the remover of difficulties.

The Ismaili is explicit that seeking intercession does not equate the Prophet or the Imams with God. Ismailis, it states, hold to the oneness of God (tawhid) as professed in the first part of the shahada: there is no god but Allah.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis seek help from Hazrat Ali and the Imams?
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
The Grace and Blessings of Jamatkhanas in our Lives

entries.title: Offerings to the Imam
questions: Do Ismailis give money to the Imam?
What is a freewill offering in Islam?
What is sadaqa?
Why do Ismailis make offerings?
How are offerings made if the Imam isn't present?
Is giving time also an offering?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili explains that making offerings to the Imam-of-the-Time is customary, and roots the practice in the time of the Prophet. It cites Qur'an 9:103, in which the Prophet is told to take of the believers' wealth a freewill offering (sadaqa), to purify and sanctify them, and to pray for them — noting that believers who came to the Prophet seeking his blessings and help were asked to give offerings when they did so.

On that basis, the community describes Ismailis giving freewill offerings out of love and devotion to the Imam as a means of purifying themselves and of receiving blessings and prayers for forgiveness through the Imam's intercession. Because the Imam cannot always be physically present, the community states that this is often undertaken in jamatkhanas through his appointed representatives acting on his behalf.

The Ismaili also names a second kind of offering: voluntary service. It notes that Ismaili community institutions, jamatkhanas included, are largely run by volunteers who give their time and knowledge out of devotion to the Imam and the community, and presents jamatkhanas as places where Islamic values such as humility, generosity, kindness, compassion and service to others are put into practice.

The specific forms, names and amounts of offerings are not published by the community's institutions and are not described here.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
Why do Ismailis seek help from Hazrat Ali and the Imams?

entries.title: Dasond and its relation to zakat
questions: What is dasond?
Do Ismailis pay zakat?
Is dasond a tithe?
How much do Ismailis give?
What is the difference between dasond and zakat?
Why is there so little written about dasond?
entries.answer:
Dasond is the term used in the South Asian Ismaili tradition for the religious dues that Ismailis offer to the Imam-of-the-Time. It is a community-internal matter: the rate, how it is calculated, and how it is collected are not published by the Ismaili community's own institutions, and this entry does not describe them.

What the allowed sources do establish is the surrounding framework. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines zakat plainly as obligatory alms for Muslims. The Ismaili, describing jamatkhana practice, explains that Ismailis customarily give freewill offerings (sadaqa) to the Imam out of love and devotion, as a means of self-purification and of seeking blessings and forgiveness through his intercession, citing Qur'an 9:103, and that where the Imam is not physically present these are made through his appointed representatives.

On how dasond relates to zakat specifically — whether it fulfils, replaces or sits alongside the obligation — the community's institutions and the Institute publish no statement in the material surveyed here. Rather than reason from outside accounts, this entry leaves that question open. It is a reasonable thing to ask ITREB or a local jamatkhana directly.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: Gap acknowledged. Searches of the.ismaili content feed and the IIS site and glossary returned no article or glossary entry on dasond, and no allowed source states how dasond relates to zakat. The relationship is deliberately left unstated rather than inferred.

entries.title: Nandi and mehmani
questions: What is nandi?
What is mehmani?
What is the food auction in jamatkhana?
What happens to nandi food?
Why isn't mehmani explained online?
Is nandi a ceremony?
entries.answer:
Nandi and mehmani are practices observed within Ismaili jamatkhanas. Both are internal to the community, and the Ismaili community's own institutions do not publish descriptions of them. This entry therefore does not explain what they involve.

The context the community does publish is that jamatkhana practices are the sole prerogative of the Imam-of-the-Time and specific to the Ismaili community, and that offerings — of wealth and of voluntary service — are made in jamatkhanas through the Imam's appointed representatives, grounded in the Qur'anic idea of the freewill offering (sadaqa) that purifies the giver and draws the Prophet's prayers. Mehmani carries the ordinary sense of hospitality in Urdu and Gujarati, which is as far as the published record supports.

A newcomer attending a jamatkhana for a permitted, non-prayer programme may hear both words used without explanation. The appropriate way to learn more is to ask members of the community or ITREB rather than to rely on outside accounts, which the community has not endorsed.

Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.title: Navroz
questions: What is Navroz?
When is Navroz celebrated?
Why do Ismailis celebrate a Persian new year?
What does Nawruz mean?
How is Navroz celebrated?
Is Navroz a religious or cultural festival?
What is Haft Seen?
entries.answer:
Navroz — also written Nawruz or Nowruz — means "a new day" in Persian. It marks the first day of spring and the beginning of the new year, falling at the spring equinox. The Ismaili describes it as a time of spiritual renewal and physical rejuvenation, of gratitude for blessings, and of hope and optimism.

The community traces the festival's origins to ancient Persia and the Zoroastrian tradition, which divided the year into six seasonal feasts and fixed the new year at the equinox, when day and night are of equal length. As Muslim rule spread beyond Arabia, cultural encounters brought Navroz into Muslim observance; the community notes it was celebrated under the Umayyads in Damascus, the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in Egypt. Today The Ismaili reports it is observed by around 300 million people across Iran, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Georgia and beyond, and is a public holiday in several countries.

Customs vary by region. In Iran the community describes a spring cleaning of the house, the moment of the equinox calculated precisely and called Saal Tahvil, and families gathering around the Haft Seen table to exchange greetings and gifts. Ismailis worldwide mark Navroz with devotional poetry in the form of ginans, qasidas and manqabas, and the distribution of dried fruits, nuts and grains among the Jamat, symbolising abundance and sustenance. The greeting is Navroz Mubarak.

sources.title: Nawruz - a symbol of renewal, rejuvenation and new beginnings

entries.title: Eid al-Fitr
questions: What is Eid al-Fitr?
When is Eid al-Fitr?
How do Ismailis celebrate Eid al-Fitr?
What does Eid al-Fitr mean?
Is Eid al-Fitr the end of Ramadan?
Did the Fatimids celebrate Eid?
entries.answer:
Eid al-Fitr is Arabic for the festival of breaking the fast. The Ismaili describes it as marking the culmination of Ramadan, the month in which Muslims turn inwards through fasting and devotion and outwards through acts of kindness and compassion. The community presents it as an occasion of peace, happiness, joy and festivity, a day for special prayers and for extending forgiveness and generosity.

Traditionally Eid al-Fitr begins at sunset on the night the crescent moon of Shawwal is first sighted. In a number of countries in the Middle East and Asia it is a public holiday, celebrated over one to three days.

The community notes that Muslims have kept the festival since the time of the Prophet, and that during the Fatimid period the Ismaili Imam-Caliphs addressed believers on Eid in a khutba, or sermon. It records that in a tenth-century Eid address the Imam al-Qaim told the assembled believers that this was a festival God honours and exalts, counselling them to be faithful in their intentions and to submit their requests to God.

The Ismaili also records that it was on Eid al-Fitr in 1944 that Mawlana Shah Karim, then seven years old, recited the Eid namaz at Nairobi's Town Jamatkhana.

sources.title: What is the purpose of fasting in Ramadan?

entries.title: Eid al-Adha
questions: What is Eid al-Adha?
What is the Feast of Sacrifice?
Why do Muslims remember Ibrahim?
Which son was Ibrahim asked to sacrifice?
What is tawakkul?
How is Eid al-Adha different from Eid al-Fitr?
entries.answer:
Eid al-Adha is the Feast of Sacrifice. The Ismaili describes it as recalling the monotheistic ethos at the heart of the Abrahamic traditions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

The community recounts the shared narrative: in a recurring dream, Hazrat Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice his beloved son as a test of faith. At the decisive moment God spared the son's life — most Muslims, The Ismaili notes, understand this son to be Hazrat Ismail. The community cites Surah as-Saffat, verses 104 and 105, in which God calls to Ibrahim that he has fulfilled the vision, and describes it as a manifest trial.

The Ismaili draws out the festival's meaning as an occasion to reflect on Ibrahim's devotion and, above all, on his complete trust in his Creator. It names this trust tawakkul, noting that Ismailis refer to it in prayer with the phrase tawakkaltu 'alayka — I place my trust in You. The community cites Surah al-Maida, verse 23, calling believers to put their trust in God, while making clear that such trust does not mean neglecting one's own effort: believers should apply their intellect and strive to overcome difficulties, doing their best and trusting the outcome to God.

The community offers the young Prophet Muhammad — orphaned, and later forced to migrate under threat — as a further example of steadfast faith.

entries.title: Eid-e Ghadir
questions: What is Eid-e Ghadir?
What happened at Ghadir Khumm?
Why is Ghadir Khumm important to Shia Muslims?
What does Man kuntu mawlahu mean?
When did Ghadir Khumm happen?
What is the hadith of the two weighty things?
entries.answer:
Eid-e Ghadir marks the anniversary of the gathering at Ghadir Khumm. According to Shia belief, tradition and interpretation, The Ismaili explains, this is the occasion on which the Prophet Muhammad — acting on a divine command — designated Hazrat Ali as his successor and the first in the continuing line of hereditary Imams.

The community describes the event as taking place in 632 CE, on the Prophet's return to Medina after his pilgrimage to Mecca. It cites the revelation of Surah al-Ma'ida, verse 67, instructing the Messenger to deliver what had been revealed to him. The Prophet is said to have halted at the oasis of Ghadir Khumm, addressed the large gathering accompanying him, and proclaimed: "Man kuntu mawlahu fa aliyyun mawlahu" — he whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla. The Ismaili notes that numerous authoritative hadith sources, both Shia and Sunni, record the event.

In Shia belief, by declaring Hazrat Ali mawla after him, the Prophet transferred to him the spiritual authority God had granted him, making him and the Imams who followed the Amirul Mu'minin. At the Prophet's instruction, Hazrat Ali received the bayat, the oath of allegiance, from those assembled. The community marks this as the end of nabuwwa, the prophetic mission, and the historic beginning of the institution of Imamat. It links the occasion to the well-attested tradition in which the Prophet spoke of leaving two weighty matters (al-thaqalayn): the Book of God and his family, the Ahl al-Bayt.

entries.title: Imamat Day
questions: What is Imamat Day?
When is Imamat Day?
Why do Ismailis celebrate Imamat Day?
What is nass?
Who is the current Ismaili Imam?
What is Takht-nishini?
entries.answer:
Imamat Day marks the anniversary of the accession of the Imam-of-the-Time. The Ismaili reports that on 4 February 2025 Mawlana Hazar Imam succeeded his father, Mawlana Shah Karim, as the 50th hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims, and that the community observes the anniversary of that occasion as Imamat Day.

The community explains the belief underlying the festival: foremost among the principles of the Shia Ismaili tariqah is recognition of the Imam-of-the-Time. Ismailis hold that they have been led throughout history by a living, hereditary Imam descended from the Prophet Muhammad through Hazrat Ali and Hazrat Bibi Fatima, that the Prophet designated Hazrat Ali at Ghadir Khumm as his successor, and that the Imamat has since passed in direct succession, each Imam designating his successor by nass. The role of each Imam, as the community describes it, is to interpret the faith through changing historical contexts and to work to improve the quality of life of the Jamat and of wider society.

The Ismaili records that in his Takht-nishini Farman of 11 February 2025, Mawlana Hazar Imam pledged to dedicate his life to the spiritual and material well-being of the Ismaili Jamat, and that among his early priorities was meeting as many of his Jamats as possible.

sources.title: What to expect in the next few days

entries.title: Salgirah
questions: What is Salgirah?
When is Salgirah?
What does Salgirah mean?
Whose birthday is Salgirah?
What is Khushiali?
How do Ismailis celebrate Salgirah?
entries.answer:
Salgirah is the celebration of the birthday of the Imam-of-the-Time. The Ismaili reports that on 12 October 2025 Ismailis worldwide marked the 54th birthday of Mawlana Hazar Imam, His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan, who was born in Geneva in 1971 and succeeded his father as the 50th Imam at the age of 53.

The community describes Salgirah as an occasion to reflect on the unique spiritual bond linking each murid — each follower — to the Imam-of-the-Time. Community messages around the festival speak of offering shukrana, thanksgiving, and of praying for the Imam's health and happiness and for the realisation of his aspirations. The greeting is Salgirah Mubarak, and the celebrations are also referred to as Khushiali, meaning rejoicing.

The Ismaili reports that the Jamat gathers for prayers and celebrations in their respective jamatkhanas. Community accounts also describe multi-faith families being warmly invited to celebrate alongside the Jamat at the Ismaili Centres, with a separate cultural programme running during prayer time — one instance of the general pattern that formal prayers are reserved to Ismailis while surrounding festivities are more widely shared.

entries.title: Laylat al-Qadr
questions: What is Laylat al-Qadr?
What is the Night of Power?
When was the Qur'an first revealed?
What happened at the cave of Hira?
Why is Laylat al-Qadr important?
How do Ismailis observe the Night of Power?
entries.answer:
Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, commemorates the night on which the Prophet Muhammad received the first revelation of the Qur'an. The Ismaili describes it as marking one of the most significant events in the history of Islam.

According to the tradition the community recounts, the Prophet would withdraw each year to Jabal an-Nur, a mountain outside Mecca, meditating alone in the cave of Hira for about a month. During one such retreat he had a profound spiritual experience in which the Angel Gabriel inspired him with the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq: a command to recite in the name of the Lord who created, who taught by the pen, and taught humankind what it did not know.

Revelations continued over some twenty-three years, the community notes, giving guidance to the Prophet and the believers and often responding to the challenges facing the emerging Muslim community — so that the Qur'an is closely bound to the historical circumstances of the Prophet's life.

The Ismaili frames the annual observance as a reminder of each believer's own spiritual search. The community connects the night to the Imam's role in interpreting the Qur'an according to the time and age, and cites the late Aga Khan's remark that the Qur'an is concerned with the salvation of the soul but also with the ethical imperatives that sustain an equitable social order.

sources.title: Losing and Finding Ourselves in Dhikr

entries.title: Ramadan and fasting
questions: Do Ismailis fast in Ramadan?
What is the purpose of fasting in Islam?
What is sawm?
What is taqwa?
Are there different ways of fasting?
Do you have to go without food and drink?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili describes fasting (sawm) as one of many devotional practices Muslims observe through the year, and is notably broad about what fasting can mean. It lists all forms of self-restraint: not eating and drinking, but also feeding a poor person, being absorbed in the remembrance of God, avoiding gossip or unkind speech, not being greedy with one's eyes or mouth, showing humility, and purifying oneself.

The deeper purpose, the community writes, is striving for God-consciousness (taqwa), so as to live by the ethics of Islam at all times. It states that individual believers may participate in fasting in whatever way they choose, since fasting is not meant to cause undue hardship.

Ramadan is sacred as the month of the first revelation of the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad. The Ismaili notes that fasting is one among many acts of piety in Ramadan, alongside heightened prayer, daily recitation of the Qur'an, opportunities for learning about faith, and giving charity to those in need. It cites Qur'an 2:183-5, which prescribes fasting so that believers may be God-conscious, exempts the ill and the traveller, allows those who can fast only with extreme difficulty to feed a needy person instead, and states that God wants ease and not hardship.

The community reports the Jamat holding iftar gatherings during Ramadan.

sources.title: What is the purpose of fasting in Ramadan?

entries.title: Chandraat and Shukravari Beej
questions: What is Chandraat?
What is Shukravari Beej?
Why do Ismailis mark the new moon?
Do Ismailis fast on Shukravari Beej?
What is a Chandraat majlis?
What is the Pir Sadardin tradition?
entries.answer:
Chandraat is the night of the new moon, marking the start of a new month in the Islamic lunar calendar. The Ismaili describes the new moon of Chandraat as a symbol of new beginnings — an opportunity to form fresh intentions and renew commitments to oneself, to the Jamat and to the Imam-of-the-Time.

The community explains that in the Pir Sadardin tradition, the Chandraat majlis was established in Bombay over a century ago by Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah, and that its purpose is to seek spiritual strength together through special prayers of supplication. Majlis is a general Islamic term the Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses as a place to sit, and so any formal gathering or assembly.

When Chandraat falls on a Friday it is called Shukravari Beej (also written Shukarvari Beej). The Ismaili notes that this tradition began in India and is observed predominantly, though not exclusively, by Ismailis settled in South Asia, and that members of the Jamat from the Pir Sadardin tradition usually fast on that day.

The community describes this fast as an act of faith prompting reflection on physical, moral and spiritual needs, and again takes a broad view of fasting: not only abstaining from food and drink but curbing negative thoughts and attending more closely to one's actions. The emphasis, it writes, falls on the intention behind the fast.

sources.title: On the occasion of Shukarvari Beej

entries.title: Mukhi and Kamadia
questions: What is a Mukhi?
What is a Kamadia?
Who leads the prayers in a jamatkhana?
Who appoints the Mukhi?
What does Mukhisaheb mean?
How long does a Mukhi serve?
Is the Mukhi like an imam or a priest?
entries.answer:
Mukhi and Kamadia are the principal offices of a jamatkhana, held in pairs and served voluntarily for fixed terms. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the mukhi as a religious functionary appointed by the Ismaili Imamat to officiate at ceremonies in jamatkhanas, and records historical holders of the office — Count Manji Janmohamed, for example, served as Mukhi of Nairobi Darkhana Jamatkhana from 1915 to 1946.

The Ismaili publishes messages from office holders, such as a Salgirah message from the Mukhisaheb of Lisbon Darkhana Jamatkhana, confirming that the Mukhi speaks to and on behalf of the local Jamat on ceremonial occasions. Saheb is an honorific attached to the title.

The Ismaili's general account of jamatkhana practice explains that because the Imam cannot always be physically present, offerings are made in jamatkhanas through his appointed representatives acting on his behalf — which is how the community frames the ceremonial function these offices perform.

The Kamadia serves alongside the Mukhi, conventionally with responsibility for the jamatkhana's accounts and administration. Beyond this, the detailed duties of the two offices, the terms of appointment and the manner of their selection are not set out in the community's published institutional material, and are not described further here. Neither office is a clergy role: holders are volunteers drawn from the Jamat.

sources.title: Women's Voices in the IIS Oral History Project
Celebrating Heritage: Count Manji Janmohamed and Heritage Materials
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The allowed sources confirm the offices exist, that the mukhi is appointed by the Imamat to officiate at jamatkhana ceremonies, and give historical holders, but publish no description of the Kamadia's duties or of appointment terms. The account of the Kamadia's administrative role is stated conventionally and is not directly sourced; treat it as provisional.

entries.title: The women's offices: Mukhiani and Kamadiani
questions: What is a Mukhiani?
What is a Kamadiani?
Can women be religious leaders in the Ismaili community?
Do women officiate in jamatkhana?
What is Mukhiani Maa?
Are the men's and women's offices equal?
entries.answer:
The offices of Mukhi and Kamadia are paired with women's offices held alongside them: Mukhiani and Kamadiani, often addressed with the honorific Maa. Together the four make up the ceremonial leadership of a jamatkhana, so that men and women hold office together rather than the women's roles being auxiliary.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies states directly that women serve as mukhiyani, religious functionaries appointed by the Imam to officiate at ceremonies in jamatkhanas. Its Oral History Project records Zohra Noorali Rashid as the first mukhiyani of the Dubai Jamat, documenting women's access to formal religious office as part of a wider effort to preserve the contributions of Ismaili women around the world.

The Ismaili's community messages routinely address Mukhisaheb and Kamadiasaheb alongside Mukhiani and Kamadiani Maas when greeting the leadership of a Jamat, which reflects the paired structure in ordinary practice.

As with the men's offices, the detailed duties, terms and manner of appointment are not published by the community's institutions and are not described further here. These are voluntary offices held by members of the Jamat, not a professional clergy.

sources.title: Women's Voices in the IIS Oral History Project
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: IIS confirms women are appointed by the Imam as mukhiyani to officiate at jamatkhana ceremonies. The paired structure of the four offices is evident from community messages but is not set out formally in the allowed sources.

entries.title: Volunteering and service
questions: Why do Ismailis volunteer so much?
What is the Ismaili Volunteer Corps?
What is Ismaili CIVIC?
What is Time and Knowledge Nazrana?
What does Work No Words mean?
Who runs the jamatkhanas?
Can non-Ismailis join Ismaili CIVIC activities?
entries.answer:
Voluntary service is central to Ismaili community life, and The Ismaili frames it in religious terms: alongside material offerings, it names voluntary service as a form of offering to the Imam. It notes that Ismaili community institutions, jamatkhanas included, are largely run by volunteers who give their time and knowledge out of love and devotion to the Imam and the community, and describes jamatkhanas as places where values such as humility, generosity, kindness, compassion and service to others are put into practice.

The Ismaili Volunteer Corps (IVC) is the community's uniformed volunteer body. The Ismaili traces its roots to the Kathiawadi Mitr Mandal of 1912 and its formal establishment in 1919 in the Indian subcontinent, with a Coat of Arms granted by Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah in 1920. In 1924 the Imam gave the volunteers the motto "Work No Words", still worn on a badge with the uniform.

Ismaili CIVIC is a more recent global programme through which the community renders voluntary service to wider society. The Ismaili reports the inaugural Global Ismaili CIVIC Day on 26 September 2021, aiming to engage 20,000 volunteers in 100,000 hours of service, working alongside governments and civil society organisations. Activities have included tree planting, shoreline and park clean-ups, food bank collections, blood donations and vaccination drives. The community also refers to volunteers serving through the Time and Knowledge Nazrana (TKN) programme.

Global Ismaili CIVIC Day: Celebrating community service across the globe

entries.title: ITREB: the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards
questions: What is ITREB?
What does ITREB do?
Who is ITREB accountable to?
What is a waez?
Where does the Ismaili religious curriculum come from?
What was the Ismailia Association?
keywords: Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
entries.answer:
ITREB stands for the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards — more fully, the Shia Imami Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them as local and international boards within the Ismaili community, ultimately accountable to the Imam, responsible for religious instruction and for supervision over details of the practice of the faith in the jurisdictions they cover.

The boards sit within the framework of the Ismaili Constitution. The community's own account of the Constitution states that it incorporates Religious Education Boards to provide religious education at all levels of the community, to develop the human resources this requires, and to support research and publication.

The Ismaili records that a centralised curriculum was a deliberate choice: at the Ismailia Association Conference in Paris in 1975, following consultation with leaders of the global Jamat, the late Aga Khan decided both to establish the Institute of Ismaili Studies in London and to develop one central religious education curriculum for the global Jamat, set within the broader context of Muslim civilisations.

ITREB employs academic and teaching staff — the community advertises roles such as Academic Director and Executive Officer — and the Institute trains waezeen, preachers and teachers, through its Waezeen and Teacher Training Programme, with graduates going on to work as scholars with national ITREBs.

sources.title: The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs) (glossary)
Interview with Dr Shafik Sachedina, Head of the Department of Jamati Institutions
Women's Voices in the IIS Oral History Project

entries.title: Religious education: Baitul Ilm and beyond
questions: What is Baitul Ilm?
How do Ismaili children learn about their faith?
What age does Ismaili religious education start?
What is taught in Baitul Ilm?
Is there a religious school at the jamatkhana?
What is the Ta'lim curriculum?
entries.answer:
Baitul Ilm — house of knowledge — is the community's religious education programme for Ismaili children and young people, generally from ages 3 to 18. The Ismaili describes it as rooted in a broad and inclusive educational framework, encouraging students to explore the ethical, intellectual and cultural dimensions of Islam with particular attention to the Ismaili tariqah.

The stated aims are notably wide. Alongside a deep and personal connection with the Imam-of-the-Time, the programme sets out to cultivate critical and creative thinking, ethical decision-making, cultural literacy, a spirit of service and a pluralistic worldview. The community presents it as developing identity, confidence and belonging, and as building connections among peers.

Provision is age-banded. Nursery classes for ages 3 to 5 use play-based and experiential learning through stories, songs and creative activities; primary classes for ages 5 to 11 continue through stories and age-appropriate exploration; further bands run to 18. Both in-person and online options are offered, and enrolment goes through a local Head of Baitul Ilm.

The curriculum sits within the wider system described elsewhere: a centralised religious education curriculum for the global Jamat, developed following the 1975 decision that also established the Institute of Ismaili Studies, and administered locally under ITREB.

sources.title: Interview with Dr Shafik Sachedina, Head of the Department of Jamati Institutions
The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs) (glossary)

entries.title: Didar and mulaqat: seeing the Imam
questions: What is didar?
What is a mulaqat?
What does it mean to see the Imam?
What is Roz-e-Nur?
Why do Ismailis travel to see the Imam?
What is deedar?
entries.answer:
Didar — also written deedar or didor — is a Persian word meaning vision or sight, and in the Ismaili context refers to seeing the Imam-of-the-Time in person. A mulaqat is the meeting or audience at which this happens. The Ismaili describes these occasions as awaited with great anticipation, with members of the Jamat travelling long distances, sometimes on foot, to be present.

The community's account of the Imam's first visit to Tajikistan in May 1995 illustrates what a didar can mean. For the first time in many generations the Tajik Jamat could see the Imam in person; a boy born in Khorog in those days was named Didor in honour of the visit. The day came to be known locally as Roz-e-Nur, the Day of Light — described as the day light entered Badakhshan — and its anniversary is celebrated on 24 and 25 May each year. The visit came shortly after independence and during a civil war that had inflicted severe hardship.

The theme runs through Ismaili devotional poetry as well. The Ismaili cites a ginan attributed to Pir Shams expressing longing for the didar of the Lord, asking that the veil be lifted so the beloved's face might be seen.

Community preparations for a mulaqat include devotional and educational material for all ages, so that the visit is approached as a period of reflection rather than only an event.

sources.title: The different forms of devotional expression in the Ismaili Tariqah

entries.title: Greetings and forms of address
questions: How do Ismailis greet each other?
What does Ya Ali Madad mean?
What is the reply to Ya Ali Madad?
What do Ismailis say after the Prophet's name?
What does Mawlana Hazar Imam mean?
What is a murid?
What do Mubarak greetings mean?
entries.answer:
Ismaili institutions publish little about everyday greetings, so this entry stays close to what they do record.

On naming the Prophet, The Ismaili is explicit: after mentioning his name it is common for Muslims to invoke blessings, saying "salla Allahu alayhi wa-sallam" — may God's peace and blessings be upon him. Shia Muslims and some Sunnis extend this to include his family: "salla Allahu alayhi wa-aalihi wa-sallam". English-language community material renders this as "peace be upon him and his progeny".

Festival greetings follow a common Muslim pattern of the occasion followed by Mubarak, meaning blessed: Navroz Mubarak, Salgirah Mubarak.

For the Imam, community usage is Mawlana Hazar Imam — the present Imam — and the Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses the terms used for the relationship: murid, one who seeks, for a follower; pir and murshid for a spiritual guide; and Jamat for the congregation or local community. Saheb and Maa are honorifics attached to the titles of jamatkhana office holders.

The phrase "Ya Ali Madad" appears in community material, including as the title of community music, but the allowed sources do not explain its use or its customary reply, so this entry does not describe them.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis recite salawat for the family of the Prophet (pbuh)?

entries.notes: Gap acknowledged. No allowed source explains the greeting 'Ya Ali Madad' or its reply, though the phrase appears in community material. Deliberately left undescribed rather than filled from outside sources.

entries.title: Funerals and burial
questions: What happens at an Ismaili funeral?
Are Ismailis buried or cremated?
What prayers are said when someone dies?
Is there an Ismaili cemetery?
What is a funeral pavilion?
What does ruhani mean?
How did the community mark the late Aga Khan's funeral?
entries.answer:
Ismailis bury their dead. The Ismaili reports that the community in the United Kingdom secured planning approval for a burial ground and funeral pavilion at Farnham, describing it as a space in which funerals and all related ceremonies can take place, designed in sustainable natural materials and developed, in the National Council President's words, with regard to the souls — the ruhani — for whom it is intended.

The community's general account of jamatkhana practice notes that special prayers may be observed at rites of passage, particularly deaths, and that jamatkhanas are where life events including death are marked.

The most fully documented Ismaili funeral is that of the 49th Imam, Mawlana Shah Karim, in February 2025 — a public occasion rather than an ordinary one, broadcast to jamatkhanas worldwide and on The Ismaili TV. The Ismaili published its order: the ceremony opened with recitations of the salawat invoking blessings on the Prophet and his progeny, the casket was carried into the funeral hall at the Ismaili Centre Lisbon, and selected verses of the Qur'an were recited, including Surat al-Fatiha, Surat al-Baqara 277 and 155-157, Surat al-Nisa' 175 and Surat al-Ghafir 8 — verses on God's mercy, on patience in calamity, and on the words "to God we belong and to Him we shall return".

The rites observed at an ordinary Ismaili funeral are not published by the community's institutions and are not described here.

sources.title: The funeral of Mawlana Shah Karim
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The published funeral order is that of the 49th Imam, a public ceremony. Ordinary funeral rites are internal to the community and are not described.

entries.title: Marriage
questions: How do Ismailis get married?
What is an Ismaili wedding like?
Can Ismailis marry non-Ismailis?
Does the Ismaili Constitution cover marriage?
What is personal law in the Ismaili community?
What are the Conciliation and Arbitration Boards?
entries.answer:
Marriage among Ismailis is governed within the community's constitutional framework. The community's own background paper records that the first modern Ismaili Constitution, ordained by Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah in 1905 for the Ismailis of East Africa, set out rules of personal law governing matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance, alongside structures of governance. Similar constitutions followed in South Asia, and were periodically revised.

The 1986 Ismaili Constitution extended this framework to the global community. Under it, National and International Conciliation and Arbitration Boards were established to encourage the amicable resolution of conflicts through impartial conciliation and arbitration — a service the community notes is, in some countries, increasingly used even by non-Ismailis. In practice these boards are the bodies that handle family and matrimonial matters.

The Ismaili states that jamatkhanas are where important life events including marriage are marked, and that special prayers may be observed at rites of passage.

The community's institutions do not publish an account of the Ismaili marriage ceremony itself, and it is not described here. On interfaith marriage, community reporting refers repeatedly to multi-faith families and to interfaith spouses taking part in festival programmes, which indicates such marriages exist within the community, but the allowed sources set out no rule or position on the question.

sources.title: The Grace and Blessings of Jamatkhanas in our Lives

entries.notes: Gap acknowledged. The allowed sources describe the constitutional and personal-law framework but publish nothing on the marriage ceremony itself, nor any stated position on interfaith marriage. Both left undescribed.

entries.title: Women in the Ismaili community
questions: What is the role of women in the Ismaili community?
Do Ismaili women and men pray together?
Can Ismaili women hold religious office?
Do Ismaili women work and lead?
Are there women presidents of Ismaili Councils?
Does the community have institutions for women?
entries.answer:
Women hold formal religious office in the Ismaili community. The Institute of Ismaili Studies states that women serve as mukhiyani, religious functionaries appointed by the Imam to officiate at ceremonies in jamatkhanas, and records Zohra Noorali Rashid as the first mukhiyani of the Dubai Jamat.

Women also serve in the community's governance and scholarly institutions. The Ismaili has published a speech by Rai Saheba Yasmin Bhudarally as President of the Ismaili Council for Portugal, showing women in senior leadership of national Jamati institutions. The Institute records Yasmin Mustafa Aldebiyat graduating from its Waezeen and Teacher Training Programme and working since as a scholar with ITREB Syria.

The community's constitutional framework provides for this institutionally: its own background paper states that the Central Institutions established under the Ismaili Constitution provide services in education, health, social welfare, housing, economic welfare, and cultural and women's activities, and youth and sports development.

The Institute's Oral History Project deliberately prioritises women's narratives, aiming to preserve the contributions, resilience and wisdom of Ismaili women across their diverse communities — recording figures such as Siramdam Begum, honoured by the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme for community development work in Pakistan. The Ismaili likewise reports regularly on women's leadership programmes and International Women's Day events at the Ismaili Centres.

sources.title: Women's Voices in the IIS Oral History Project

entries.notes: The allowed sources document women in religious office, governance and scholarship, but publish no statement on seating or the organisation of prayer space in jamatkhana. Not described here.

entries.title: Jamat, murid and the bond with the Imam
questions: What does Jamat mean?
What is a murid?
What is bay'a or bayah?
What is the bond between an Ismaili and the Imam?
What does pir mean?
Why do Ismailis call themselves spiritual children?
entries.answer:
Three terms recur throughout Ismaili practice. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses Jamat as an assembly or religious congregation, and notes it is also the term Nizari Ismailis use for their individual local communities. Murid means "one who seeks": the Institute explains that Sufi tariqas developed around the relationship between murids and a spiritual master called murshid, pir or shaykh, and that the first Nizari Imams after the Mongol conquest of Alamut lived as Sufi masters while their followers took the designation murid, still used today.

Bay'a is the oath of allegiance. The Institute traces it to Arab practice and the practice of the Prophet, notes its Qur'anic mentions, and defines it as the act by which people recognise the authority of an individual. In Shia contexts it is the oath of allegiance to the Imam; in the Shia Ismaili tradition specifically, the Institute describes it as the acceptance of the permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and the murid.

The Ismaili builds much of its account of practice on this. Jamatkhana practices are described as expressions of that bond, and the bay'a is said to be reaffirmed daily in various prayers and jamatkhana practices. On the accession of a new Imam, the community reported that an official bayah and homage ceremony would follow the designation. Ismailis also address the Imam as pir and murshid, and the Imam refers to the Jamat as his spiritual children.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
What to expect in the next few days

entries.title: Why some Ismaili practices are not described publicly
questions: Why can't I find details about Ismaili prayers?
Are Ismaili practices secret?
Why is the Dua not published?
Is the Ismaili community secretive?
How can I learn more about internal practices?
Why do sources stop short of describing ceremonies?
entries.answer:
Newcomers researching Ismaili practice often find that descriptions stop at a certain point. This is deliberate, and the community explains why.

The Ismaili states that jamatkhana practices are the sole prerogative of the Imam-of-the-Time and are specific to the Ismaili community, and that the Imam has sole authority to determine them at any time. Ismaili jamatkhanas are described as private tariqa spaces, with participation in formal prayers restricted to those who have pledged bay'a to the Imam.

The community frames this as ordinary rather than exceptional. Just as households keep family life private, religious communities that see themselves as an extended family may seek privacy for members to pray with sincerity; many communities maintain boundaries between public and private, restricting certain spaces, practices and prayers to those formally initiated.

The practical effect is that certain subjects — the text of the Dua, the order of the jamatkhana ceremony, Baitul Khayal, the details of dasond, nandi and mehmani, and the performance of Chiragh-i rawshan — are named in community and scholarly material but not described in it. An educational resource should say so plainly rather than fill the gap from unofficial accounts.

Much is, however, openly published: what jamatkhanas are, what forms of prayer and poetry are used, the festivals and their meanings, the institutions, and the ethics of service. Ismaili Centres also run public programmes, and ITREB is the right body to approach with further questions.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?
The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs) (glossary)

entries.title: The Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN)
questions: What is the Aga Khan Development Network?
What does AKDN stand for?
Who runs the AKDN?
Is the AKDN only for Ismailis?
How many countries does the AKDN work in?
How big is the AKDN's budget?
How is the AKDN connected to the Ismaili Imam?
What agencies make up the AKDN?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Development Network is a group of private, non-denominational development agencies established under the Ismaili Imamat. It describes its purpose as improving the quality of life of people in need, and it states that it works irrespective of a person's origin, faith or gender.

According to AKDN's own figures, it works in more than 30 countries, mainly in Africa and Asia, runs over 1,000 programmes and institutions, and employs roughly 96,000 people, most of them in the countries where the work takes place. Many of its institutions are more than 60 years old and some more than 100. AKDN says it is channelling more than US$1.3 billion into not-for-profit development activity in 2026.

The network was founded by Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, the 49th hereditary Imam, who died in February 2025. Its Chair is now His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, the 50th hereditary Imam.

AKDN explains its existence in terms of the Imamat's mandate: in the Ismaili and wider Muslim understanding it describes, an Imam is concerned not only with interpreting the faith but with the security and quality of life of the community and of everyone among whom it lives. The Imamat therefore treats "quality of life" as a holistic idea covering education, health, culture, habitat, enterprise and civil society, not only material wealth.

sources.title: The Ismaili Imamat: Ethics & Social Responsibility

entries.title: The Aga Khan Foundation
questions: What is the Aga Khan Foundation?
When was the Aga Khan Foundation set up?
What does the Aga Khan Foundation actually do?
Which countries does the Aga Khan Foundation work in?
Is the Aga Khan Foundation a religious charity?
What is AKF?
Does the Aga Khan Foundation work on early childhood education?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Foundation is AKDN's main grant-making and programme agency for long-term development. It describes itself as non-denominational and says it works on the root causes of poverty rather than on short-term relief.

AKF says it has been operating for more than 50 years and now works in 18 countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe, Australia and North America. Its work is organised around seven areas: agriculture and food security, civil society, climate resilience, early childhood development, education, health and nutrition, and work and enterprise.

A distinctive feature the Foundation emphasises is patience and scale over generations: strengthening local systems and institutions rather than delivering services directly and leaving. It reports that its early childhood development work reached 2.3 million children in 2025, and that it supported around 20,000 civil society organisations which in turn reached more than three million people in the same year.

National Aga Khan Foundation affiliates exist in several countries and act as both fundraisers and programme partners. The Aga Khan Foundation Canada, founded in 1980, is one of the oldest and is housed in the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat in Ottawa; Aga Khan Foundation UK is based at the Aga Khan Centre in London.

sources.title: Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat, Canada

entries.title: Aga Khan Schools and the Aga Khan Education Services
questions: What are the Aga Khan Schools?
What is Aga Khan Education Services?
When did the Aga Khan schools start?
How many students do the Aga Khan Schools teach?
Where are Aga Khan schools located?
Are Aga Khan schools only for Ismaili children?
What is AKES?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Education Services runs one of the largest private, not-for-profit school networks outside the wealthy world. It traces its origins to 1905, when schools were opened at Mundra in India, Gwadar in what is now Pakistan, and Zanzibar in what is now Tanzania, places that then had very little formal schooling.

AKES says it teaches over 110,000 students a year in ten countries in East Africa and South and Central Asia, with nearly 6,000 staff of whom 99 percent are recruited locally and 53 percent are women. More than 90 percent of its schools and pre-primary centres are in rural or remote communities. It offers national curricula alongside international ones, early childhood programmes from 18 months, non-formal education at over 100 centres, and eight residential hostels.

Since 2023 AKDN has presented "Aga Khan Schools" as the umbrella covering both AKES and the Aga Khan Academies. Under that banner it reports around 200 schools in 12 countries, more than 100 non-formal education centres, and over 6,500 teachers and staff.

The schools are open to children of any background; they are not Ismaili religious schools. Religious education for Ismaili children is handled separately by the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Academies
questions: What are the Aga Khan Academies?
Where are the Aga Khan Academies?
How do you get into an Aga Khan Academy?
Do the Aga Khan Academies teach the IB?
Are the Aga Khan Academies free?
When was the first Aga Khan Academy opened?
What is the difference between an Aga Khan Academy and an Aga Khan school?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Academies are a network of selective residential and day schools begun in 2000 by Aga Khan IV. Their stated aim is to develop ethical, capable leaders drawn from every social and economic background, and to lift the standard of teaching in the surrounding region.

The first Academy opened in Mombasa, Kenya in 2003, followed by Hyderabad, India in 2011, Maputo, Mozambique in 2013, and Dhaka, Bangladesh in 2022. Teaching combines the International Baccalaureate programmes with what the Academies call the Aga Khan Curricular Strands, which add ethics, pluralism, comparative study of Muslim civilisations, and economics for development.

Admission is meant to be on merit alone. The Academies say students are selected regardless of their families' ability to pay, with financial aid bridging the gap. They report more than 1,500 graduates to date, who between 2016 and 2022 received over US$76 million in university scholarships.

Each campus also houses a Professional Development Centre that trains teachers from government and other schools in the region, so the benefit is intended to reach beyond the Academy's own students. This regional teacher-training role is the main difference from the wider Aga Khan Education Services schools, which serve far larger numbers on a non-selective basis.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Health Services
questions: What is Aga Khan Health Services?
How many hospitals does the Aga Khan network run?
Where are Aga Khan hospitals and clinics?
When did Aga Khan health work begin?
Is Aga Khan healthcare free?
What is AKHS?
Who can use Aga Khan hospitals?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Health Services is one of the largest private not-for-profit health providers in the developing world. Its roots go back to the 1920s, when the Ismaili community and the Imamat began opening dispensaries and maternity homes in South Asia and East Africa.

AKHS today runs hospitals together with more than 575 outreach health centres. Counting the whole AKDN health system, which also includes the Aga Khan University hospitals and the health work of the Aga Khan Foundation, AKDN says over 14 million people are served each year. AKHS works in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda in East Africa; Afghanistan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Syria and Tajikistan in Central Asia and the Middle East; and Pakistan and India in South Asia. In Pakistan it describes itself as the country's largest not-for-profit private health system; in India it runs a 158-bed hospital.

In each country AKHS is constituted as a local not-for-profit body with volunteer directors and annual audits. Services are open to anyone, and the stated priority is reaching vulnerable people, especially mothers and newborns, with affordable and proven care. Current emphases include maternal, neonatal and child health, nutrition, and cancer prevention.

entries.title: The Aga Khan University
questions: What is the Aga Khan University?
When was the Aga Khan University founded?
Where are Aga Khan University campuses?
Is the Aga Khan University a religious university?
What does AKU teach?
Who is the Chancellor of the Aga Khan University?
Does the Aga Khan University run hospitals?
keywords: Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan University was founded in Karachi in 1983 as Pakistan's first private university, and it remains a private, not-for-profit teaching and research institution. The Imam of the Time serves as its Chancellor; Princess Zahra Aga Khan is Pro-Chancellor.

AKU now has campuses and programmes in six countries: Pakistan, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Afghanistan and the United Kingdom. Its schools and institutes include medical colleges, schools of nursing and midwifery, Institutes for Educational Development, a graduate school of media and communications, an Institute for Human Development, and the Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations in London, which is based at the Aga Khan Centre.

The University says it has awarded more than 21,000 degrees and diplomas, about two-thirds of them to women, a figure it highlights because nursing and midwifery were low-status professions in the region when it began. It operates seven hospitals and a network of outreach health centres treating over two million patients a year, and it has provided more than 101,000 teleconsultations since 2007.

AKU is a secular university open to all. Its stated research principle is that excellence must be grounded in relevance to the societies it serves, and it says it aims to prepare graduates to lead change and to work well in pluralist societies.

entries.title: The University of Central Asia
questions: What is the University of Central Asia?
Which countries founded the University of Central Asia?
Where are the University of Central Asia campuses?
Why was a university built for mountain communities?
What does UCA teach?
Is the University of Central Asia part of the AKDN?
When was the University of Central Asia founded?
entries.answer:
The University of Central Asia was created by an international treaty signed by the Presidents of the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan and Kazakhstan together with Aga Khan IV, and ratified by each of the three parliaments. It is unusual among universities in being founded by a treaty between states and a faith community's Imamat.

Its declared purpose is the social and economic development of Central Asia, and particularly of its mountain societies, helping the region turn its cultural heritage and its geography into assets rather than disadvantages.

UCA has three parts. The School of Arts and Sciences offers undergraduate degrees and has produced over 300 graduates, around 70 percent of them from rural areas. The School of Professional and Continuing Education provides vocational and adult training and reports more than 270,000 learners since 2006. The Graduate School of Development carries out research on the region's economic, social and cultural questions, including work such as avalanche risk mapping and climate and health research. UCA has also supported about 80 Central Asian scholars through advanced degrees abroad on the understanding that they return to teach.

The university's administrative base is in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, with campuses in the mountain regions the university was built to serve.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Trust for Culture
questions: What is the Aga Khan Trust for Culture?
When was the Aga Khan Trust for Culture founded?
What does AKTC do?
Why does a development network fund culture?
What programmes are part of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture?
What is Archnet?
Is the Aga Khan Museum part of AKTC?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Trust for Culture is AKDN's cultural agency, established in 1988 and based in Geneva. Its working premise is that culture is not a luxury added after development but part of development itself: restoring a neighbourhood, reviving a musical tradition or building a good public park can produce jobs, skills, civic pride and better governance.

AKTC brings several programmes under one roof. The Aga Khan Award for Architecture recognises buildings and planning that serve the needs of societies where Muslims have a significant presence. The Historic Cities Programme restores historic areas and builds parks and gardens. The Music Programme supports living musical traditions in Muslim societies. The Aga Khan Museum in Toronto presents the arts of Muslim civilisations. An education and documentation arm includes the Aga Khan Programme for Islamic Architecture at Harvard and MIT, and Archnet, a large free online library on architecture and the built environment in Muslim cultures.

AKTC reports more than 50 million visitors to the parks it has created and around 4,550 artisans trained in traditional crafts. Like other AKDN agencies it works with governments, UNESCO, municipalities and donors, and its projects are open to the general public rather than to any one community.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Award for Architecture
questions: What is the Aga Khan Award for Architecture?
How much is the Aga Khan Award for Architecture worth?
How often is the Aga Khan Award for Architecture given?
Who decides the Aga Khan Award for Architecture?
What kinds of buildings win the Aga Khan Award?
When was the Aga Khan Award for Architecture started?
Is the Aga Khan Award only for mosques?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Award for Architecture was established in 1977 by Aga Khan IV and is given every three years. Its prize fund of one million US dollars, shared among the winning projects, makes it one of the largest architecture prizes in the world.

The Award looks for projects that set new standards in architecture, planning, conservation and landscape design, and that address the real needs and aspirations of communities in societies where Muslims have a significant presence. That deliberately includes far more than religious buildings: past recipients have included housing, schools, bridges, parks, water systems, slum upgrading and restoration work. Prizes go not only to the architect but to the clients, engineers, builders and communities who made a project possible.

Each cycle has two bodies. A Steering Committee, chaired by the Imam, is reconstituted each time to set the eligibility criteria and thematic direction and to oversee the seminars, lectures, exhibitions and publications that surround the Award. An independent Master Jury, also reconstituted each cycle, chooses the recipients.

Across sixteen completed cycles the Award has recognised 136 projects and documented close to 10,000 buildings, creating a substantial research archive alongside the prize itself.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme
questions: What is the Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme?
What has the Historic Cities Programme restored?
Which countries does the Historic Cities Programme work in?
What parks has the Aga Khan Trust for Culture built?
Why restore old buildings in poor neighbourhoods?
What is AKHCP?
Did the Aga Khan restore the Walled City of Lahore?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme restores historic buildings and quarters and creates public parks, but treats those works as a means rather than an end. Its founding question was whether culture can be a genuine component of development, and whether careful conservation can raise incomes, improve services and strengthen local institutions in poor historic neighbourhoods.

Over about 30 years the programme reports more than 350 restoration and conservation projects, including work at 11 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and ten major parks and gardens that have drawn tens of millions of visitors. It operates in around a dozen countries, mostly in Asia and Africa, and has received some 35 international awards.

Projects it highlights include the revitalisation of the Walled City of Lahore in Pakistan, carried out with the Government of Punjab and the World Bank, and conservation of the Amir Aqsunqur funerary complex, known as the Blue Mosque, in Cairo. In Zanzibar's Stone Town the Trust has renovated eleven buildings, among them the Old Dispensary and the Old Customs House, and restored Forodhani Park.

The programme measures success not only in restored fabric but in improved governance, new civil society organisations, more local income, better environmental conditions and training for craftspeople in traditional techniques.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Music Programme
questions: What is the Aga Khan Music Programme?
What are the Aga Khan Music Awards?
Who are the Aga Khan Master Musicians?
Does the Aga Khan network support traditional music?
Where does the Aga Khan Music Programme work?
When was the Aga Khan Music Initiative started?
Does AKDN teach music to children?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Music Programme began in 2000 as the Aga Khan Music Initiative, first in Central Asia, where decades of Soviet cultural policy had weakened traditional teaching and repertoire. It later merged with the secretariat of the Aga Khan Music Awards to form the present programme.

Its aim is to keep musical heritage alive as a living practice rather than a museum exhibit, in societies across the world where Muslims have a significant presence. It works in Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan, and in the Middle East, North Africa, South Asia and West Africa.

The programme has four main strands: education and mentoring, often pairing master musicians with young students; supporting the creation and performance of new work; documentation and publication, including recordings, teaching materials and a digital archive with searchable databases and tutorials; and a music publishing arm that manages intellectual property rights on behalf of participating artists and teachers. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture reports that the programme has supported some 40,000 musicians and music educators.

The Aga Khan Master Musicians is its touring ensemble, drawing on traditions from the Middle East, the Mediterranean, South Asia, Central Asia and China. The Aga Khan Music Awards recognise outstanding musicians and educators; recent award ceremonies were held in Muscat, Oman in 2022 and again in 2025.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development (AKFED)
questions: What is AKFED?
Does the Aga Khan network run businesses?
Where do AKDN's profits go?
What companies does AKFED own?
Why does a development network invest for profit?
What is Industrial Promotion Services?
Does the Aga Khan own hotels and banks?
keywords: Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development is the AKDN agency that invests in companies rather than making grants. It builds and backs commercially viable enterprises in places where private investors are generally unwilling to go, on the argument that jobs, skills and reliable services are themselves development.

AKFED holds interests in more than 70 project companies employing over 75,000 people, mainly in Central and South Asia and Africa. Its work runs through several groupings: financial services, including banks and insurance companies aimed at widening financial inclusion; Industrial Promotion Services, which has developed private enterprise since the 1960s; Tourism Promotion Services, which builds environmentally responsible hotels in regions others avoid; and a broad set of other companies supplying essential goods, services and training.

The defining feature is what happens to the returns. Aga Khan IV described AKFED as seeking profits which are then entirely reinvested in further development, rather than distributed to shareholders. Investment decisions are judged by the effect on people's lives in the country concerned as much as by financial return, and AKFED will often stay in a difficult market far longer than a commercial investor would.

Rather than operating as a single centralised company, AKFED works as a network of affiliated firms, which lets it adapt to very different markets.

sources.title: Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development

entries.title: The Aga Khan Agency for Habitat
questions: What is the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat?
What happened to FOCUS Humanitarian Assistance?
Who responds to disasters in Ismaili communities?
What does AKAH do?
Where does the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat work?
Does AKDN work on climate change?
What is Aga Khan Planning and Building Services?
keywords: Aga Khan Planning and Building Services
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Agency for Habitat was formed in 2016 by bringing together several AKDN bodies that had worked separately on habitat, disasters and the environment since the 1990s: FOCUS Humanitarian Assistance, the Aga Khan Planning and Building Services, the Disaster Risk Management Initiative, and the Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan Fund for the Environment.

Its purpose is to help people live safely in hazardous places, particularly mountain and disaster-prone regions, and to adapt to a climate producing more frequent and more severe events. AKAH's work falls into four areas: preparing for and responding to disasters; planning safer settlements with the communities who live in them; building water and sanitation systems; and constructing homes and public buildings that can withstand earthquakes, floods and landslides.

AKAH works in Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Syria, Pakistan and India, with plans to extend further in Central Asia and into East Africa. It reports hazard and risk assessments covering nearly three million people, water and sanitation systems serving over 600,000, around 40,000 trained local emergency volunteers, and help in building some 50,000 homes along with 5,000 schools, hospitals and community centres.

sources.title: About the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat

entries.notes: AKDN's own pages are not fully consistent on the founding year: the agency's About page says 2016, while some other AKDN material gives 2015.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Agency for Microfinance
questions: What is the Aga Khan Agency for Microfinance?
Does the Aga Khan network do microcredit?
When was AKAM set up?
Where does Aga Khan microfinance work?
What kinds of loans does AKAM give?
Is there an Aga Khan bank for poor people?
How long has AKDN done microfinance?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Agency for Microfinance was established in 2005 to bring together microfinance activity that had been running inside various AKDN agencies for more than sixty years, some of it descended from community savings and credit co-operatives set up long before microfinance became a recognised field.

AKAM's stated aim is to help individuals, households and small businesses reach financial self-reliance. It works in Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia, through both stand-alone institutions such as the First MicroFinance banks and microfinance components inside wider rural development programmes.

Its services go well beyond small business loans: agricultural loans timed to planting and harvest, housing improvement loans used by around 30,000 clients, quality-of-life loans for costs such as education and health, micro-savings accounts, remittance services, lending to small and medium enterprises, and digital banking channels that reach remote valleys. A particular emphasis is on reaching people considered too poor or too risky by ordinary banks.

AKAM works on a deliberate exit model: when an institution becomes financially self-supporting it is transferred to another AKDN agency or an outside partner, and AKAM moves its resources to a new underserved area. In Pakistan, for example, AKDN's microfinance work grew into HBL Microfinance Bank, which now reports more than 4.5 million customers.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Museum, Toronto
questions: What is the Aga Khan Museum?
Where is the Aga Khan Museum?
When did the Aga Khan Museum open?
Who designed the Aga Khan Museum?
What is in the Aga Khan Museum collection?
Is the Aga Khan Museum an Ismaili museum?
What is the Aga Khan Park?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Museum opened in Toronto in 2014 at 77 Wynford Drive and describes itself as the first museum in North America dedicated to the arts of Muslim civilisations. Its permanent collection holds more than 1,200 objects spanning the ninth to the twenty-first centuries, including manuscripts, paintings, ceramics and textiles, from Iberia to China.

Its stated mission is to spark curiosity and understanding of Muslim cultures and their connections with other cultures, and its vision is to contribute to more inclusive and peaceful societies. Programming runs well beyond display cases: exhibitions, concerts and performances, lectures, workshops, school programmes and online offerings.

The building was designed by the Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, who took light as his organising idea; the white Brazilian granite exterior and an open-roofed interior courtyard change character with the hour and the season. The building measures 81 by 54 metres and contains two exhibition galleries, conservation and storage areas, the 350-seat Nanji Family Foundation Auditorium and two classrooms.

The Museum shares a 6.8-hectare site with the Ismaili Centre, Toronto, designed by the Indian architect Charles Correa. Between and around them lies the Aga Khan Park, whose formal garden is a chahar bagh, the four-part garden form of Persian and Mughal tradition, designed by the Lebanese landscape architect Vladimir Djurovic. The Museum is a programme of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture.

entries.title: The Aga Khan Centre, London
questions: What is the Aga Khan Centre in London?
Where is the Institute of Ismaili Studies based?
When did the Aga Khan Centre open?
Who designed the Aga Khan Centre at King's Cross?
What are the gardens at the Aga Khan Centre?
Is the Aga Khan Centre the same as the Ismaili Centre London?
Can the public visit the Aga Khan Centre?
entries.answer:
The Aga Khan Centre opened in 2018 in the Knowledge Quarter at King's Cross in London, and is separate from the Ismaili Centre on Cromwell Road. It was designed by Fumihiko Maki and Associates and is described by AKDN as a place for education, cultural exchange and insight into Muslim civilisations, built to express openness, dialogue and respect for different viewpoints.

Three institutions share the building. The Institute of Ismaili Studies, founded in 1977, has its permanent home there, along with the Aga Khan Library. The Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations, AKU-ISMC, teaches and researches there. The Aga Khan Foundation UK also has its offices in the building.

A defining feature is a sequence of six gardens, courtyards and terraces, with two more at the nearby Victoria Hall student residence. Each draws on a different regional tradition of Islamic landscape design, from Spain and North Africa through the Middle East to Central and South Asia, so that moving through the building is also a tour through the geographical range of Muslim garden culture.

The Centre hosts public exhibitions, talks and events, and parts of it, including the gardens, are opened to visitors at advertised times.

entries.title: The Ismaili Centres
questions: What is an Ismaili Centre?
How many Ismaili Centres are there?
Where are the Ismaili Centres?
What is the difference between an Ismaili Centre and a jamatkhana?
Can non-Ismailis visit an Ismaili Centre?
Why are Ismaili Centres called ambassadorial buildings?
When did the first Ismaili Centre open?
What happens inside an Ismaili Centre?
entries.answer:
Ismaili Centres are large, purpose-built buildings commissioned by the Imamat that combine a space for the Ismaili community's prayer and gathering with facilities open to the wider public. AKDN describes them as ambassadorial buildings, representing the Ismaili community and the institutions of the Imamat in the country where they stand.

There are seven, opened over forty years: London and Vancouver in 1985, Lisbon in 1998, Dubai in 2008, Dushanbe in 2009, Toronto in 2014 and Houston in 2025.

Each contains a jamatkhana, the prayer hall used by the Ismaili community, which is not generally open to visitors. Around it are spaces that are: exhibition galleries, auditoria and theatres, libraries, classrooms, meeting and function rooms, cafés, courtyards and gardens. The Centres host lectures, concerts, exhibitions and interfaith and civic gatherings.
