The design briefs have consistently asked architects for a synthesis rather than a copy: buildings that draw on the traditions of Islamic architecture, including geometry, courtyards, water and the handling of light, while using contemporary materials and meeting the needs of a modern city. Each Centre has been given to a different architect, so the results look markedly different from one another, from Charles Correa's building in Toronto to Farshid Moussavi's in Houston.

sources.title: His Highness the Aga Khan and Houston Mayor John Whitmire open Ismaili Center, Houston

entries.title: The Ismaili Center, Houston
questions: When did the Ismaili Center in Houston open?
Where is the Ismaili Center Houston?
Who designed the Ismaili Center Houston?
Is there an Ismaili Centre in the United States?
What is inside the Ismaili Center Houston?
Who opened the Ismaili Center Houston?
How big is the Ismaili Center Houston?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Center, Houston opened on 6 November 2025, the first Ismaili Center in the United States and the seventh worldwide. It was formally opened by the Mayor of Houston, John Whitmire, in the presence of His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, with civic and cultural figures from Houston and beyond in attendance.

The intention to build it was announced in March 2018, and a year later Farshid Moussavi was chosen as building architect and Thomas Woltz of Nelson Byrd Woltz Landscape Architects as landscape architect, working with AKT II and DLR Group.

The Center occupies an eleven-acre site overlooking Buffalo Bayou Park, at the intersection of Allen Parkway and Montrose Boulevard. The main building runs to about 150,000 square feet over five storeys and contains a prayer hall, or jamatkhana, a black box theatre seating around 150, an exhibition gallery, function and banquet rooms, classrooms, a café and administrative offices, set among gardens and courtyards.

The Ismaili describes the design as contemporary but rooted in a long architectural heritage, combining modern building technology with traditional Persian forms and ornament, including ceramic mosaics and mashrabiya screens. Its stated role is as a civic and cultural complex dedicated to dialogue, culture and shared human values, as well as a home for the Ismaili community in the United States.

sources.title: His Highness the Aga Khan and Houston Mayor John Whitmire open Ismaili Center, Houston

entries.title: The Ismaili Centre, London
questions: Where is the Ismaili Centre in London?
When did the Ismaili Centre London open?
What was there before the Ismaili Centre London?
Is the Ismaili Centre London opposite the V&A?
Can I visit the Ismaili Centre in London?
What is the address of the Ismaili Centre London?
Which was the first Ismaili Centre?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Centre, London stands on Cromwell Road in South Kensington, across the road from the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Natural History Museum and the Science Museum. It opened in 1985, the first of the Ismaili Centres, and was opened by the then British Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher.

It had predecessors. In 1951 the Ismaili community established a religious, cultural and social centre at Kensington Court, and in 1957 this moved to Palace Gate in the Borough of Kensington. As the community grew, much of it settling in or near London, those premises became too small, and a site on Cromwell Road was acquired for a purpose-built centre.

The building holds a jamatkhana for the community's prayer and gathering, together with a council chamber, exhibition and social spaces, and a well-known roof garden. It serves as the representative building of the Ismaili community and the institutions of the Imamat in the United Kingdom, and hosts lectures, exhibitions, concerts and civic and interfaith events that are open to the public.

The Centre should not be confused with the Aga Khan Centre at King's Cross, a separate and much later building that houses the Institute of Ismaili Studies, AKU-ISMC and Aga Khan Foundation UK.

sources.title: His Highness the Aga Khan and Houston Mayor John Whitmire open Ismaili Center, Houston

entries.title: The Ismaili Centre, Toronto
questions: Where is the Ismaili Centre in Toronto?
Who designed the Ismaili Centre Toronto?
When did the Ismaili Centre Toronto open?
Is the Ismaili Centre next to the Aga Khan Museum?
What is in the Ismaili Centre Toronto?
Who designed the Aga Khan Park in Toronto?
Which Ismaili Centre is in Canada?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Centre, Toronto opened in 2014 as the sixth Ismaili Centre worldwide, and Canada's second after Vancouver. It sits on a 6.8-hectare landscaped site on Wynford Drive that it shares with the Aga Khan Museum, forming a single public complex.

The project brought together three noted architects. The Indian architect Charles Correa designed the Ismaili Centre; the Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki designed the Museum; and the Lebanese landscape architect Vladimir Djurovic designed the park, whose formal garden takes the chahar bagh, or four-part garden, form. The Canadian firm Moriyama and Teshima acted as architects for the whole project and integrated its parts.

The Ismaili describes the Centre as a complex of varied spaces for contemplative, cultural, educational and recreational use. It contains a jamatkhana under a translucent crystalline dome, along with social and meeting halls, classrooms and a council chamber. Correa's stated aim was a building that responds to the traditions of Islamic architecture through contemporary design and modern materials rather than by imitation.

The surrounding Aga Khan Park, opened after the buildings, covers about seventeen acres of gardens, reflecting pools and lawns and is free and open to the public daily.

entries.title: The Ismaili Centre, Lisbon
questions: Where is the Ismaili Centre in Lisbon?
When did the Ismaili Centre Lisbon open?
How did Ismailis come to Portugal?
Is there an Ismaili Centre in Portugal?
What does the Ismaili Centre Lisbon do?
Is the Ismaili Centre Lisbon the Seat of the Imamat?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Centre, Lisbon opened in 1998, the third of the Ismaili Centres after London and Vancouver.

It grew out of the community's arrival in Portugal. The Ismaili records that from the 1970s Portuguese Ismailis, many with roots in Mozambique and other Portuguese-speaking territories, created places of gathering for cultural and social purposes in the major cities and towns where they settled, and found office space for the philanthropic organisations they sponsored. As those organisations grew, they drew in more institutional partners and engaged increasingly with the wider Portuguese public, and a permanent Centre followed.

The Centre houses a jamatkhana together with social, educational and cultural spaces, and hosts public and civic events. It is a significant landmark for the community in Portugal and has been the setting for major national and international occasions.

The Ismaili Centre should not be confused with the Seat of the Ismaili Imamat, which is a separate institution established later. The Seat, designated in 2018, is at the Henrique de Mendonça Palace on Rua Marquês de Fronteira in Lisbon and is known as the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat.

sources.title: His Highness the Aga Khan and Houston Mayor John Whitmire open Ismaili Center, Houston

entries.title: The Ismaili Centres in Burnaby, Dubai and Dushanbe
questions: Where is the Ismaili Centre in Vancouver?
When did the Ismaili Centre Burnaby open?
Is there an Ismaili Centre in Dubai?
Who gave the land for the Ismaili Centre Dubai?
Is there an Ismaili Centre in Tajikistan?
When did the Ismaili Centre Dushanbe open?
Which was the first Ismaili Centre in the Middle East?
What was Canada's first Ismaili Centre?
keywords: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum
entries.answer:
Three of the seven Ismaili Centres are less widely known than those in London, Toronto and Houston: Burnaby near Vancouver, opened in 1985, Dubai in 2008 and Dushanbe in 2009.

The Burnaby Centre in British Columbia was Canada's first purpose-designed Ismaili Centre, opening the same year as London's. It followed the community's arrival in Canada during the 1970s. The Ismaili records that in those years Ismailis across Canada established religious, cultural and social centres largely in rented premises, and that school halls often served as places of prayer in the evenings and at weekends. The architect, Bruno Freschi, was given what The Ismaili calls an unusual brief: a synthesis of Islamic architecture and contemporary design, drawing on principles rooted in the traditions of the faith while meeting the requirements of modern Canadian life.

The Dubai Centre was the first in the Middle East. Its site was a gift from the Ruling Family of Dubai, presented by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the United Arab Emirates and Ruler of Dubai, to Aga Khan IV on the occasion of the Silver Jubilee of his accession in 1982. Its design brief called for a sequential, experiential and integrated use of space, with emphasis on order and harmony and on fostering mutual respect within the Muslim ummah and across society.

The Dushanbe Centre serves a long-established Ismaili population in Central Asia, concentrated in the Pamir mountains of Gorno-Badakhshan. Its brief asked for a synthesis of the ethics, values and traditions of faith with the requirements of contemporary society, encouraging indigenous materials, patterns, colours, textures and shapes.

sources.title: His Highness the Aga Khan and Houston Mayor John Whitmire open Ismaili Center, Houston

entries.notes: The opening dates for all three come from AKDN's list of the seven Ismaili Centres; the pages on the individual Centres give background and design intent rather than dates.

entries.title: The Global Centre for Pluralism
questions: What is the Global Centre for Pluralism?
Where is the Global Centre for Pluralism?
Who founded the Global Centre for Pluralism?
What is the Global Pluralism Award?
Why did the Aga Khan and Canada set up a pluralism centre?
What does pluralism mean in the Aga Khan's institutions?
When was the Global Centre for Pluralism created?
entries.answer:
The Global Centre for Pluralism is an independent charitable organisation founded jointly by Aga Khan IV and the Government of Canada, established in 2006. It grew out of the view that Canada's experience of building a society from difference was a resource worth studying and sharing.

Its headquarters is in Ottawa at 330 Sussex Drive, in a restored heritage building that served as Canada's Public Archives from 1905 to 1967 and then as the War Museum from 1967 to 2005.

The Centre's stated purpose is to influence perspectives, inform policies and inspire pathways that advance pluralism, working from the belief that societies thrive when differences are valued. It draws a careful distinction: diversity is simply a fact of nearly every society, while pluralism is a deliberate and positive response to that fact, grounded in respect for human dignity and in tackling systemic inequality.

Its work includes global analysis, which develops research and measurement tools for how societies treat difference; Educating for Pluralism, which supports teachers and education systems; and work applying pluralist approaches to peace and conflict processes. Every two years it presents the Global Pluralism Award, which recognises people and organisations around the world building more peaceful and inclusive societies.
entries.notes: The Centre's own site, pluralism.ca, would not load for this research, so this entry relies on AKDN's description of it.

entries.title: The Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat, Ottawa
questions: What is the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat?
Where is the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat?
Does the Ismaili Imamat have diplomatic status in Canada?
When did the Delegation in Ottawa open?
Who designed the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat?
What happens at the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat?
Is the Delegation an embassy?
entries.answer:
The Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat opened in Ottawa in December 2008. AKDN describes it as a centre for building relationships and enabling quiet diplomacy, a secular and open facility where the Imamat's development agencies can work with government, diplomats and civil society.

It is not an embassy in the ordinary sense, since the Imamat governs no territory, but it functions in a comparable way. A Protocol of Understanding signed between the Ismaili Imamat and the Government of Canada in February 2014 grants diplomatic courtesies to the Delegation and provides for the exchange of diplomatic representatives between Canada and the Ismaili Imamat.

The building houses AKDN's Diplomatic Office in Canada, which coordinates the network's activities in the country and its relations with the Canadian government and diplomatic community, and it is the headquarters of the Aga Khan Foundation Canada, the development agency established in 1980.

It was designed by the Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, who also designed the Aga Khan Museum and the Aga Khan Centre. He took the natural luminosity and many-faceted shape of rock crystal as his starting point, aiming at a building that reads as open and transparent, with light shifting across its glass and translucent surfaces. It received the Governor General's Medal in Architecture in 2012, and in 2010 the Ontario Association of Architects' Celebration of Excellence Award and People's Choice Award.

entries.title: The Seat of the Ismaili Imamat in Lisbon
questions: Where is the headquarters of the Ismaili Imamat?
What is the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat?
Why is the Ismaili Imamat based in Portugal?
What is the agreement between Portugal and the Ismaili Imamat?
When was the Seat of the Imamat established?
What is the Henrique de Mendonça Palace?
Is the Ismaili Imamat recognised as a legal entity?
entries.answer:
The global headquarters of the Ismaili Imamat is in Lisbon. This is the first formal Seat in the modern history of the Imamat, and it followed a long relationship with Portugal.

In 2010 the Portuguese parliament unanimously ratified a Faith Agreement with the Ismaili Imamat. That agreement recognised the Imamat as an international legal entity with the capacity to enter into national and international agreements, and gave formal recognition to the Ismaili community's constitutional bodies as established by the Imam. It set out shared commitments to human dignity, pluralism, peace and stability and to improving the quality of life of vulnerable people in Portugal and elsewhere.

On 3 June 2015 the Imamat and the Portuguese Republic signed the agreement that enabled the establishment of a formal Seat of the Ismaili Imamat in Portugal. Then, on 11 July 2018, at the ceremony marking the conclusion of his Diamond Jubilee year, Aga Khan IV designated the Henrique de Mendonça Palace on Rua Marquês de Fronteira in Lisbon as the Seat of the Ismaili Imamat, and declared that it should be known as the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat.

The Seat brings together all dimensions of the Imamat's work in one place: the affairs of the Ismaili community, the Imamat's international engagement, and its development commitments.
entries.notes: The Imamat's own site dates the Seat agreement to 3 June 2015; the.ismaili's page on the Imamat gives November 2015 for the signing. The 2018 designation of the Palace is consistent across both.

entries.title: The Ismaili Imamat's relations with states
questions: Does the Ismaili Imamat have diplomatic relations?
Which countries have agreements with the Ismaili Imamat?
Is the Ismaili Imam a political leader?
Why does a religious leader sign treaties?
What is a Protocol of Understanding with the Imamat?
Is the Ismaili Imamat a state?
Does the Aga Khan have diplomatic status?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Imamat describes itself as a supra-national entity representing the succession of Imams since the time of the Prophet Muhammad. It is emphatic that the Imam's role is spiritual and that his authority is one of religious interpretation: in the contemporary era the Imams govern no land, and the Imamat presents itself as strictly non-political. Ismailis are expected to be loyal, law-abiding citizens of the countries where they live.

At the same time, the Imamat holds that faith and worldly life cannot be separated, so it engages formally with governments to enable its development work. Governments, regional bodies and international agencies extend diplomatic courtesies and privileges to the Imamat to make that collaboration possible, and protocols of co-operation have been agreed either directly or through AKDN institutions.

The Imamat lists among those who have entered into formal relationships with it: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brazil, Canada, the European Commission, the East African Community, France, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mali, Pakistan, Portugal, Syria and Tajikistan, together with the American states of California, Illinois and Texas.

This pattern is not new. Aga Khan III, the 48th Imam, was twice President of the League of Nations Assembly, and the Imamat describes his work as an earlier articulation of the same public international role.

entries.title: The Ismaili Constitution
questions: What is the Ismaili Constitution?
When was the Ismaili Constitution ordained?
Who wrote the Ismaili Constitution?
Was there an Ismaili constitution before 1986?
What does the Ismaili Constitution cover?
Does the Ismaili Constitution replace national law?
Why does a religious community have a constitution?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Constitution is the written framework for the Ismaili community's social governance, ordained by the Imam of the Time. The community's institutions describe it as a continuation of a long practice in which Imams have given rules of conduct and constitutions suited to the needs of their age.

The first modern Ismaili constitution was ordained in 1905 by Aga Khan III, the 48th Imam, for the Ismailis of East Africa. It set up a hierarchy of governance structures at local, national and regional level, laid down rules of personal law on matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance, and gave guidelines for mutual support within the community and for its relations with others. Similar constitutions were promulgated in South Asia, and all were periodically revised.

In 1986 Aga Khan IV, the 49th Imam, ordained a single Ismaili Constitution which for the first time brought the social governance of the worldwide community under one framework. Its stated purposes are to secure the community's peace, unity, spiritual and social welfare, to foster collaboration among different peoples, to make better use of resources, and to enable Ismailis wherever they live to contribute to the quality of life of their societies as responsible citizens.

It does not displace the law of any country. Ismailis are expected to be loyal and law-abiding citizens, and the Constitution governs the community's own internal institutions and processes.

entries.title: The Jamati institutions
questions: What are the Jamati institutions?
How is the Ismaili community organised?
Who runs the Ismaili community day to day?
Are Ismaili leaders paid?
What are the Central Institutions?
What is the difference between Jamati institutions and the AKDN?
How are Ismaili community leaders chosen?
What does 'jamat' mean?
entries.answer:
"Jamat" is the term Ismailis use for the community, and the Jamati institutions are the bodies that serve it under the Ismaili Constitution. They are distinct from the AKDN agencies, which are non-denominational and serve whole societies, though the two work closely together.

The Constitution creates three kinds of body. National, Regional and Local Councils carry overall responsibility for social governance. Central Institutions provide services to the community in education, health, social welfare, housing, economic welfare, cultural and women's activities, and youth and sports development; in most countries these take the form of boards such as the Aga Khan Education Board, the Aga Khan Health Board, the Aga Khan Economic Planning Board and the Aga Khan Social Welfare Board. Religious Education Boards, known as ITREBs, look after religious education, the training of teachers, research and publication. Conciliation and Arbitration Boards handle dispute resolution.

Office-holders are appointed under the Constitution, normally for fixed terms of about three years, and serve voluntarily and unpaid. The community presents this as a form of service, and service of time and professional skill is treated as a religious value in its own right.

A National Council coordinates and maintains liaison across the institutions in its country, so that education, health, economic and religious education work is not carried out in isolation.
entries.notes: The exact set of boards and their names varies between countries; the community's own published material describes the framework rather than a uniform list.

entries.title: National, Regional and Local Councils
questions: What is an Ismaili National Council?
What does a Local Council do?
Who is the President of an Ismaili Council?
How are Ismaili Councils organised?
What is a Regional Council?
Do the Councils run jamatkhanas?
Are Ismaili Council members elected?
entries.answer:
Under the Ismaili Constitution, Councils carry overall responsibility for the community's social governance. They exist at three levels: National Councils for a country or group of countries, Regional Councils within larger territories, and Local Councils serving individual towns or jamatkhana communities.

A National Council, headed by a President, is the senior Jamati institution in its territory. It coordinates the community's affairs, maintains liaison with the Central Institutions such as the education, health and economic planning boards, with the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board and with the Conciliation and Arbitration Board, and represents the community in its dealings with government and with other communities. Regional and Local Councils carry the same functions closer to the ground and are the bodies most members of the community deal with in practice.

Council members are appointed under the Constitution rather than elected in a public ballot, normally for fixed terms, and they serve without pay. Separately from the Councils, each jamatkhana has its own appointed officers, the Mukhi and Kamadia, who lead the congregation's religious and social life.

The Councils' work is social governance rather than religious interpretation, which remains the Imam's prerogative, and religious education, which is the responsibility of the ITREBs.
entries.notes: The allowed sources describe the Councils' role in general terms. They do not publish detail on appointment procedures or on the office of Mukhi and Kamadia, so specifics of how members are chosen are left out here.

entries.title: ITREB: the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
questions: What is ITREB?
Who teaches Ismaili religious education?
What does the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board do?
Who trains Ismaili religious education teachers?
What is a waez or waezeen?
How does ITREB relate to the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
Where do Ismaili children learn about their faith?
keywords: Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Constitution provides for Religious Education Boards, known in most countries as the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board, or ITREB. There is normally one for each country or region.

ITREB is responsible for religious education at all levels of the community, from young children to adults; for the training of religious education teachers and of waezeen, those who deliver religious discourses; for research and publication relevant to Islam and the Ismaili tariqah; and for serving as a point of reference for community leaders on matters of religious rites and practices. Its stated mission is to foster a unified, knowledgeable and engaged jamat, anchored in the ethics of the faith.

Its teaching work is closely tied to The Institute of Ismaili Studies in London. The IIS Department of Education plans and develops the Ta'lim curriculum, the international programme of religious, moral and cultural education for Ismaili children from pre-school to secondary level, and the ITREBs deliver it in their own countries, in local languages. Teachers of the secondary curriculum are typically graduates of the IIS Secondary Teacher Education Programme.

ITREB is distinct from the Councils, which handle social governance, and from the AKDN agencies, whose work is non-denominational.

entries.title: The Conciliation and Arbitration Boards
questions: What is the Conciliation and Arbitration Board?
How do Ismailis resolve disputes?
What is CAB in the Ismaili community?
When were the Conciliation and Arbitration Boards set up?
Can non-Ismailis use the Conciliation and Arbitration Boards?
Is CAB a court?
What is the International Conciliation and Arbitration Board?
entries.answer:
The Conciliation and Arbitration Boards are the Ismaili community's dispute resolution institutions. The community describes a long tradition of settling differences through voluntary mediation, conciliation and arbitration rather than litigation, and in 1986 Aga Khan IV gave that tradition a global institutional framework as part of the Ismaili Constitution.

CABs exist at national level, with an International Conciliation and Arbitration Board above them. They offer forms of alternative dispute resolution, chiefly mediation and conciliation, in which a trained and impartial third party helps the parties reach their own agreement, with arbitration also available. Typical matters include family and matrimonial disputes, inheritance questions and commercial disagreements.

Board members and mediators serve voluntarily and are trained; the International CAB maintains a faculty of certified trainers drawn from professional mediators, lawyers, academics, former judges and others, and has run mediation skills training in many languages for members around the world.

The Boards are not courts and cannot override national legal systems; they operate alongside them, and use of them is voluntary. The Imamat notes that although the Constitution serves primarily the Ismaili community, the conciliation and arbitration provisions are increasingly used in some countries by people who are not Ismaili.

entries.title: The Institute of Ismaili Studies
questions: What is the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
When was the Institute of Ismaili Studies founded?
Where is the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
What does the IIS publish?
Does the IIS have a manuscript collection?
Is the IIS a university?
Who founded the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
What is the Aga Khan Library?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies is a higher education, research and teaching institution devoted to scholarship on Islam and Muslim societies, with particular attention to Shi'i and Ismaili thought and history. It was established in London in 1977 at the direction of Aga Khan IV, at a time when Ismaili history was largely known through the writings of the community's opponents.

Its work rests on three activities: producing new scholarship, preserving manuscripts and other heritage materials, and disseminating knowledge through teaching, publishing and public programmes. It has published more than 170 books in English across eight academic series, on subjects including Ismaili history and thought, Shi'i and Qur'anic studies and Muslim heritage, alongside material for general readers, and many titles are translated into other languages.

Its collections, held in the Aga Khan Library, include over 3,000 manuscripts and rare books in Arabic, Persian, Gujarati and other languages, together with photographs and Fatimid coins. Research areas include Central Asian Studies, Ismaili heritage, South Asian Studies, Qur'anic Studies and the study of contemporary Ismaili communities.

Since 2018 the IIS has been based at the Aga Khan Centre in King's Cross, London. It is governed by a Board of Trustees and a Board of Governors, and is registered in England and Wales as a company limited by guarantee and as a charity.

entries.title: Study programmes at the Institute of Ismaili Studies
questions: What is GPISH?
What is STEP at the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
Can I study at the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
Does the IIS offer scholarships?
How do you become an Ismaili religious education teacher?
Does the IIS fund PhD students?
What courses does the Institute of Ismaili Studies teach?
keywords: Graduate Programme in Islamic Studies and Humanities
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies teaches as well as researches, and it funds the students it admits. Its two main graduate programmes are fully funded scholarship programmes.

The Graduate Programme in Islamic Studies and Humanities, GPISH, is a three-year programme that trains students in the intellectual methods of the humanities and social sciences and introduces a social, cultural and civilisational approach to the study of Islam, with attention to Shi'i and Ismaili material that has received comparatively little scholarly attention. It prepares graduates either for doctoral research or for a range of careers, and it covers tuition and a living allowance.

The Secondary Teacher Education Programme, STEP, is a master's-level programme combining academic study of Islam with practice-based teacher training. Its graduates are qualified to teach the IIS secondary curriculum and go on to teach in Ismaili communities around the world through the ITREBs.

The IIS also runs short courses offering an introduction to the study of Islam and Muslim societies, preparatory programmes in various parts of the world, and support for advanced research. This includes doctoral scholarships such as the Farhad Daftary and Mohammed Arkoun schemes and a dissertation writing scholarship, along with fellowships including the Post Graduate Research Fellowship for GPISH graduates and the Zahid Ali and Annemarie Schimmel fellowships.

entries.title: The Ta'lim curriculum
questions: What is the Ta'lim curriculum?
What do Ismaili children learn in religious education class?
Who writes the Ismaili religious education curriculum?
How many languages is the Ta'lim curriculum in?
What ages is the Ta'lim curriculum for?
What is the Ismaili secondary curriculum?
Where is the Ta'lim curriculum taught?
entries.answer:
Ta'lim, meaning teaching or instruction, is the international programme of religious, moral and cultural education developed by The Institute of Ismaili Studies for Ismaili children from pre-school through to secondary level. Its stated aim is to educate children in the faith and ethics of Islam and in the history and cultures of Muslims, including Ismaili Muslims.

The curriculum approaches Islam as both a faith and a civilisation, in world history and in the present, from humanistic, civilisational and normative perspectives. It uses modern educational principles and is designed to bridge religious and secular education rather than treat them as separate worlds. Materials include student readers and textbooks, teachers' and parents' guides, activity books, posters and picture cards.

The secondary curriculum, intended mainly for ages 12 to 16 and extendable to 17 and 18, consists of eight modules with student textbooks and teachers' guides, covering areas such as the Qur'an and its interpretations, faith and practice in Islamic traditions, Muslim societies and civilisations, Muslim devotional and ethical literature, and ethical pathways to human development. It is taught by professionally qualified teachers trained through the IIS Secondary Teacher Education Programme.

The IIS Department of Education plans and develops the curriculum; the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards deliver it. Materials are produced in ten or more languages and used by teachers and students in over 25 countries.

entries.title: Ismaili CIVIC
questions: What is Ismaili CIVIC?
What is Global Ismaili CIVIC Day?
Do Ismailis volunteer outside their own community?
What kind of volunteering does Ismaili CIVIC do?
When did Ismaili CIVIC start?
How many volunteers does Ismaili CIVIC have?
Can non-Ismailis join Ismaili CIVIC activities?
entries.answer:
Ismaili CIVIC is the community's global civic service programme. The Ismaili describes it as uniting the worldwide Ismaili community around a centuries-old tradition of serving humanity, through voluntary service that improves the quality of life of the communities in which Ismailis live, regardless of faith, gender or background. It is presented as an expression of Islam's values of service, peace, compassion and care for the vulnerable, and of good citizenship.

Its declared goals include conserving and creating a more sustainable environment, reducing human suffering caused by poverty, and improving health outcomes for people who lack access to basic services, including support during health emergencies. Activities are usually carried out in partnership with local organisations: food banks, clean-ups, blood drives, tree planting, shelter support and disaster relief.

Global Ismaili CIVIC Day brings these efforts together on a single day each year. It began in 2021, and the fifth edition was held on 28 September 2025 under a theme of environmental stewardship and community resilience. Since 2021 the programme reports more than 250,000 volunteers taking part in over 5,500 activities worldwide, working with close to 1,500 external partners, planting over 4.5 million trees and collecting more than 213,000 kilograms of waste.

Activities are generally open, and much of the work is done jointly with non-Ismaili partner organisations and volunteers.

entries.title: The Ismaili Volunteers and the ethic of service
questions: Who are the Ismaili Volunteers in uniform?
What does khidma mean?
Why do Ismailis volunteer so much?
What do volunteers do at jamatkhana?
Is volunteering part of Ismaili practice?
How long have there been Ismaili volunteers?
What is seva or service in the Ismaili community?
entries.answer:
Service is treated in the Ismaili tradition as a religious value rather than an optional extra, and the most visible expression of it is the corps of uniformed Ismaili Volunteers.

The Ismaili records that uniformed volunteers have been central to the community's wellbeing and progress for over a century, and that in every Jamati geography and culture volunteers serve in a wide range of situations, both inside and outside the jamatkhana. Their motto is khidma, an Arabic word meaning service, which The Ismaili describes as expressing the idea of unconditional service.

In practice volunteers manage the flow of people at gatherings, provide first aid, help elderly and disabled members, assist at funerals and community events, support large ceremonial occasions and turn out during emergencies. Volunteers are unpaid, and the role is regarded as an honour rather than a chore.

The wider ethic extends well beyond the uniformed corps: the Jamati institutions themselves are staffed almost entirely by volunteers serving fixed terms, Ismaili CIVIC organises service to the wider society, and the Time and Knowledge Nazrana channels professional expertise into the community's and the Imamat's work. The community's institutions describe this as an ethos of self-reliance and of sharing time, talent and material resources for the improvement of the societies in which Ismailis live.

entries.title: The Time and Knowledge Nazrana (TKN)
questions: What is the Time and Knowledge Nazrana?
What does TKN stand for?
What is a nazrana?
Can professionals volunteer their skills to Ismaili institutions?
How do Ismailis give time instead of money?
When did the Time and Knowledge Nazrana start?
How does TKN work?
entries.answer:
The Time and Knowledge Nazrana is a programme through which Ismailis offer professional time and expertise to the institutions of the Imamat and the community.

The Ismaili explains it as a combination of two long-standing traditions. The first is the nazrana, an unconditional gift presented to the Imam of the Time to mark significant occasions, offered as a gesture of love and homage. The second is the offering of one's intellectual capacity to assist the Imamat's efforts for the progress of the jamat and of the communities among whom the jamat lives.

In practice, TKN allows professionals to register their skills and be matched with defined assignments: lawyers, accountants, doctors, engineers, teachers, architects, IT specialists, project managers and many others give hours or months of work to Jamati institutions, AKDN agencies and Imamat bodies. Assignments may be local or international, short-term or sustained, and are undertaken without payment.

The programme is significant because it puts time and knowledge on the same footing as money as a form of giving, and because it lets a geographically dispersed community pool professional capacity that would be very expensive to buy. It is one of the ways the community's largely volunteer institutional structure is able to operate at the scale it does.
entries.notes: The Ismaili's public page on TKN gives the concept and its two traditions but little operational detail; the description of how assignments work here stays close to what that page states.

entries.title: Jubilees and the founding of institutions
questions: What is an Ismaili jubilee?
Why were Aga Khans weighed against gold and diamonds?
What came out of the Golden Jubilee of Aga Khan III?
What is Jubilee Insurance?
Where did Diamond Trust Bank come from?
What were the Diamond Jubilee Schools?
What did the Diamond Jubilee of Aga Khan IV mark?
Which institutions were founded at jubilees?
entries.answer:
Jubilees mark anniversaries of an Imam's accession, and in the Ismaili tradition they have been occasions both to express affection for the Imam and to found lasting institutions.

The pattern was set under Aga Khan III. At his Golden Jubilee in 1935-36 the community presented an unconditional gift of gold, which he returned for their own advancement: overseas scholarships, resettlement from congested districts, infant welfare, secondary schools and nursing homes, and the founding of the Jubilee Insurance Company. The East African Muslim Welfare Society was also formed, and over the following two decades built schools, mosques, clinics and a polytechnic for the region's indigenous Muslims.

At the Diamond Jubilee of 1945-46, marked by a weighing ceremony against diamonds, the proceeds funded a trust that created Diamond Jubilee Schools in rural and urban settings including Hunza and Chitral in present-day Pakistan, and in Dar es Salaam the Diamond Jubilee Investment Trust, which continues today as Diamond Trust Bank. The Platinum Jubilee of 1954-57 produced investment corporations and trusts, and the Platinum Jubilee Hospital in Nairobi, which is now the Aga Khan University Hospital there.

Under Aga Khan IV, the Silver Jubilee of 1982-83 saw the founding of the Aga Khan University in Karachi, the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme in Gujarat, hospitals in Tanzania, Kenya and Pakistan, and the Ismaili Centres in London and Burnaby. The Golden Jubilee of 2007-08 brought 22 projects in more than 20 countries, including the Ismaili Centre in Dubai and the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat in Ottawa. The Diamond Jubilee began on 11 July 2017.

entries.title: Where Ismailis live today
questions: How many Ismailis are there in the world?
Which countries do Ismailis live in?
Where is the largest Ismaili population?
Are Ismailis an ethnic group?
What languages do Ismailis speak?
Is the Ismaili community diverse?
How is a scattered community held together?
entries.answer:
The Ismailis are a transnational community with no single homeland. The Ismaili Imamat states that Ismailis live in over 35 countries and number approximately 12 to 15 million. The Ismaili's own community page puts the spread at more than 70 countries, mainly in Central, East and South Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, North America, Australia and New Zealand, and The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes settled communities in over 25 countries. These figures are published estimates by the community's own institutions and differ from one another; there is no census.

The community is not an ethnic group. The IIS describes four broad ethnographic traditions among Ismailis, Arab, Persian, Central Asian and South Asian, each with its own languages, customs and forms of devotional expression. Communities in Africa are largely of South Asian origin, descended from Khoja families who migrated from Gujarat in the nineteenth century, while populations in the Pamirs of Tajikistan and Afghanistan, in northern Pakistan, in Syria and in Iran have long continuous local histories. Populations in Europe, North America and Australia draw on all of these.

What holds the community together, according to its institutions, is allegiance to a living hereditary Imam and a shared institutional framework, rather than a common language, nationality or ethnicity. The IIS characterises the resulting ethos as self-reliance, a commitment to unity in diversity, and a strong emphasis on learning.
entries.notes: Population and country figures differ across the community's own publications: the Imamat gives 12-15 million in over 35 countries, the.ismaili says more than 70 countries, IIS says over 25 countries, and an older background paper on the.ismaili gives about 20 million in over 25 countries. No source explains the differences, so they are reported here rather than resolved.

entries.title: The Ismaili community in East Africa
questions: How did Ismailis come to East Africa?
What is the Khoja community?
Why is Zanzibar important in Ismaili history?
What did Aga Khan III build in East Africa?
When did Aga Khan schools start in Kenya and Tanzania?
Are there still Ismailis in East Africa?
What institutions did Ismailis found in Kenya and Tanzania?
entries.answer:
Ismailis reached East Africa mainly as part of nineteenth-century merchant migration from Gujarat. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that by the time of the first Aga Khan, who died in 1881, Nizari Ismaili communities were spread across Iran, Syria, Central Asia, China and India, with early communities already moving to East Africa, and that Zanzibar was an important point of entry for the Khojas, the Ismailis of the Indian subcontinent. From Zanzibar and Mombasa families moved inland into what are now mainland Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda.

Institution-building followed quickly. AKDN dates its schooling work in the region to 1905, when one of the first Aga Khan schools opened in Zanzibar, and says it has run hospitals and clinics in Tanzania for over fifty years and worked in Kenya for over a century. Several institutions that still exist began as jubilee projects of Aga Khan III: the Jubilee Insurance Company and the East African Muslim Welfare Society from the Golden Jubilee of 1935-36; the Diamond Jubilee Investment Trust of 1945-46, which continues today as Diamond Trust Bank; and the Platinum Jubilee Hospital in Nairobi, now the Aga Khan University Hospital.

The community's numbers in the region were reduced sharply by the expulsions and political upheavals of the 1970s, but communities and institutions remain. AKDN reports formal cooperation agreements with Tanzania in 1991 and Kenya in 1996, and substantial ongoing work in health, education and enterprise across all three countries.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.notes: The allowed sources give the broad outline of Khoja migration and institutional history but little detail on community size in East Africa at any period.

entries.title: The 1972 expulsion from Uganda
questions: What happened to Ismailis in Uganda in 1972?
Why were Asians expelled from Uganda?
Where did Ugandan Ismailis go?
How did Canada help Ismaili refugees?
What was Idi Amin's expulsion order?
How did the Uganda expulsion change the Ismaili community?
What is Canada's Private Sponsorship of Refugees Program?
entries.answer:
In 1972 the President of Uganda, Idi Amin, ordered the expulsion of the country's Asian population, regardless of faith, citizenship or standing. Many thousands of people left within days; AKDN's account notes that most carried away little more than their skills and the languages they spoke.

A large part of Uganda's Ismaili community was among them. Aga Khan IV appealed to governments on their behalf, and Canada agreed to take in thousands, through a combination of government resettlement and private sponsorship. Most Ugandan Ismailis went to Canada; a minority who had retained British citizenship at Ugandan independence went elsewhere, chiefly to the United Kingdom. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the Uganda crisis drove migration of Ismailis to Europe and North America in significantly larger numbers, mainly among Nizari Ismailis from the subcontinent.

AKDN describes the aftermath as an argument for pluralism: the community integrated rapidly and contributed to Canada's economy, civic life and multicultural fabric, and the experience helped shape Canada's Private Sponsorship of Refugees Program, which has since been taken up internationally as a model.

The expulsion is one of the decisive events in the modern history of the community. It created the large Ismaili populations of Canada, the United Kingdom and later the United States, and it underlies the close relationship between the Imamat and Canada.

sources.title: Why pluralism is more important than ever
Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.notes: AKDN's page on its work in Uganda does not mention the 1972 expulsion at all. The account here draws on AKDN's separate story on pluralism and on IIS; the community's own sites publish little detail on the expulsion itself.

entries.title: The Ismaili community and institutions in Canada
questions: How many Ismaili institutions are in Canada?
Why is Canada important to the Ismaili community?
When did Ismailis come to Canada?
What Aga Khan buildings are in Canada?
What is the Aga Khan Foundation Canada?
What is FOCUS Canada?
Why did the Aga Khan receive honorary Canadian citizenship?
entries.answer:
Canada holds more institutions of the Ismaili Imamat than any country outside Portugal, a direct consequence of its decision to resettle Ismailis and other Asians expelled from Uganda in 1972.

AKDN describes a partnership with Canada spanning more than five decades. The Aga Khan Foundation Canada was established in 1980 and works with communities across Africa and Asia. FOCUS Humanitarian Assistance was founded in Canada by the Ismaili community in 1994 and supports emergency preparedness and the integration of refugees within Canada.

The visible landmarks came later. The Ismaili Centre at Burnaby near Vancouver opened in 1985. The Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat opened in Ottawa in December 2008, and a Protocol of Understanding signed in February 2014 grants it diplomatic courtesies and allows the exchange of representatives between Canada and the Imamat. The Global Centre for Pluralism, founded jointly with the Government of Canada in 2006, occupies the former Public Archives building on Sussex Drive in Ottawa. In 2014 the Aga Khan Museum and the Ismaili Centre, Toronto opened together on a shared site, later completed by the Aga Khan Park. AKDN also notes two Islamic-inspired gardens given to Canadian cities.

Aga Khan IV was made an honorary Companion of the Order of Canada in 2005 and received honorary Canadian citizenship in 2009, one of very few people to be granted it.

entries.title: The Ismaili community and institutions in Portugal
questions: How did Ismailis come to Portugal?
Why is the Ismaili Imamat based in Portugal?
What does AKDN do in Portugal?
What is the Faith Agreement with Portugal?
When did the Aga Khan Foundation start in Portugal?
Is there an Ismaili community in Lisbon?
What is the relationship between Portugal and the Ismaili Imamat?
entries.answer:
Portugal now holds the global headquarters of the Ismaili Imamat, and the relationship that led there developed over several decades.

The community itself arrived largely in the 1970s, many families having roots in Mozambique and other Portuguese-speaking territories. The Ismaili records that Portuguese Ismailis created places of gathering for cultural and social purposes in the cities and towns where they settled, and found premises for the philanthropic organisations they sponsored; as these grew they drew in Portuguese institutional partners and the wider public. The Ismaili Centre, Lisbon opened in 1998.

AKDN has worked in Portugal since 1983, principally through the Aga Khan Foundation, with cooperation protocols signed in 2005, 2008 and 2009. Its work in the country focuses on migrant inclusion and underserved communities, spanning civil society support, early childhood development, education, employment skills and culture, and it extends to Portuguese-speaking countries including Mozambique.

The legal turning point came in 2010, when the Portuguese parliament unanimously ratified a Faith Agreement recognising the Ismaili Imamat as an international legal entity able to enter into agreements, and giving formal recognition to the community's constitutional bodies. In 2015 an agreement enabled the establishment of a formal Seat of the Imamat in Portugal, and in July 2018 Aga Khan IV designated the Henrique de Mendonça Palace in Lisbon as that Seat, the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat. Aga Khan IV died in Lisbon in February 2025, and it was there that Prince Rahim Aga Khan V was named 50th Imam.

entries.title: The Ismaili community and institutions in Central Asia
questions: Are there Ismailis in Tajikistan?
Where do Ismailis live in Central Asia?
What is Gorno-Badakhshan?
What does AKDN do in Tajikistan and Afghanistan?
What is Pamir Energy?
When did the Aga Khan network start work in Central Asia?
Are there Ismailis in Afghanistan?
Why is the University of Central Asia in the mountains?
entries.answer:
Central Asia holds some of the oldest continuously settled Ismaili populations, concentrated in the high mountains of Badakhshan, which straddles the border between Tajikistan and Afghanistan, and extending into northern Pakistan and parts of the Kyrgyz Republic and Xinjiang. These communities were isolated for much of the twentieth century by Soviet and Afghan borders.

AKDN's engagement began as the Soviet Union dissolved. It signed an agreement with the Government of Tajikistan in 1995, during and after that country's civil war, and committed over one billion dollars in development investment between 1995 and 2018; it now has more than 3,500 employees there and reports around 500,000 beneficiaries a year. Work spans agriculture and food security, health, education, microfinance, disaster preparedness and habitat. Pamir Energy, a public-private partnership, supplies electricity to about 99 percent of the population of Gorno-Badakhshan, an autonomous region that had suffered severe power shortages.

In Afghanistan, AKDN began in 1996 with emergency food distribution during the civil war and has invested over a billion dollars since 2002, reaching more than four million people in 20 provinces by 2025, in health, education, cultural restoration, microfinance and disaster response.

The University of Central Asia, created by treaty with the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan and Kazakhstan, was deliberately built to serve mountain societies. The Ismaili Centre, Dushanbe opened in 2009.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.notes: AKDN's country pages describe development work rather than the Ismaili population itself, and give no figures for how many Ismailis live in the region.

entries.title: The Ismaili community and institutions in Pakistan
questions: Are there Ismailis in Pakistan?
Where do Ismailis live in Pakistan?
What is Gilgit-Baltistan?
What does AKDN do in Pakistan?
When did the Aga Khan network start work in Pakistan?
What are the Diamond Jubilee Schools?
Is the Aga Khan University in Karachi?
What is the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme?
entries.answer:
Pakistan has one of the largest Ismaili populations and the densest concentration of Imamat institutions. Communities are found in Karachi and other cities and, in long-settled mountain populations, in Gilgit-Baltistan, including Hunza, and in Chitral.

AKDN dates its work in the territory to 1905, the year one of the first Aga Khan schools opened in Gwadar. The Diamond Jubilee of Aga Khan III in 1945-46 funded Diamond Jubilee Schools in rural and urban areas including Hunza and Chitral, which brought formal and in many cases girls' education to valleys that had none.

The Aga Khan University was founded in Karachi in 1983 and AKDN describes it as the country's leading medical institution. The Aga Khan Health Services runs 114 facilities serving around 932,000 people a year and describes itself as Pakistan's largest not-for-profit private health system. HBL Microfinance Bank, which grew out of AKDN's microfinance work, reports over 4.5 million customers. The Aga Khan Rural Support Programme, founded in 1982, pioneered village-level organisation in the northern areas. Habitat work has brought safe water and sanitation to over 500,000 people in the north, and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture's conservation projects, including the Walled City of Lahore, have earned 15 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards.
entries.notes: AKDN's Pakistan page does not discuss the Ismaili community's own presence or numbers; the locations given here come from the Imamat's account of the Diamond Jubilee schools and AKDN's description of where it concentrates its work.

entries.title: The branches of Ismailism: an overview
questions: What are the different branches of Ismailism?
Are all Ismailis the same?
How many kinds of Ismaili are there?
What is the difference between Nizari and Musta'li Ismailis?
Why did the Ismailis split into groups?
Which Ismaili branch is the Aga Khan's?
Are Bohras and Ismailis the same thing?
What divided the Ismaili community historically?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies (IIS) traces the Ismailis to 148 AH / 765 CE and the death of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and describes a community that over that long history subdivided into a number of branches and smaller groups, mostly through disputes over who should succeed a deceased Imam.

The two branches that survive as substantial communities today are the Nizaris and the Musta'lian Tayyibis. Both have their roots in the Fatimid period, and both stem from the major schism of 487 AH / 1094 CE over the succession to the Imam-caliph al-Mustansir. IIS says they differ above all over the Imamat: the Nizari branch believes in a living, physically present Imam, at present Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, named the 50th hereditary Imam in February 2025; the Musta'lian Tayyibis believe their Imams have remained in concealment since the time of al-Tayyib, and that in their absence the affairs of the community are administered by a da'i mutlaq, a supreme da'i with full authority.

Both branches divided again later. On the death of al-Musta'li's successor al-Amir in 524 AH / 1130 CE the Musta'lians split into Hafizis, who recognised the later Fatimid caliphs as their Imams and who disappeared completely after the fall of the Fatimid dynasty, and Tayyibis, who survived with strongholds in Yemen. From the sixteenth century CE the Tayyibis divided in turn into the Da'udi branch, whose members in India are known locally as Bohras, and the Sulaymani branch.

Other groups named in IIS writing are historical: among them the dissident Qarmatis of the third AH / ninth century CE. IIS records that the Nizari Ismailis survived the Mongol destruction of their state and long periods of persecution, without central leadership, in many parts of the Muslim world.

entries.title: The earliest divisions, before the Fatimids
questions: How did the Ismailis first separate from other Shia?
Who was Muhammad ibn Isma'il?
What was the Mubarakiyya?
Did early Ismailis disagree among themselves?
What is the dawr al-satr?
Why do some call the Ismailis 'Seveners'?
What happened after Ja'far al-Sadiq died?
entries.answer:
IIS traces the beginning of a separate Ismaili community to 148 AH / 765 CE, when Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq died. Most of his followers recognised his son Musa al-Kazim; other Imami Shi'i groups acknowledged Musa's older half-brother Isma'il, from whom the Isma'iliyya take their name, or Isma'il's son Muhammad ibn Isma'il.

Little is known of Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who went into hiding. This marked the start of the dawr al-satr, the period of concealment, which lasted until the Ismaili Imams appeared openly as Fatimid caliphs. On his death not long after 179 AH / 795 CE, his followers, then apparently known as the Mubarakiyya, divided. A majority refused to accept that he had died, recognised him as their seventh and last Imam, and awaited his return as the Mahdi. A smaller group accepted his death and traced the Imamat in his descendants. Almost nothing is known of these earliest groupings for roughly the next century.

IIS says that for about a hundred years a line of his descendants worked in secret to build a movement that would install an Imam from the Prophet's family as head of a new caliphate, spreading the message through a network of da'is and observing taqiyya, precautionary concealment of belief, to escape Abbasid persecution. The first of these leaders, 'Abdullah, settled in Salamiyya in central Syria, which became the secret headquarters of the da'wa.

Note that Nizari Ismailis do not accept the label 'Sevener'; the sources describe the belief in a seventh and final Imam as that of one early group, not of the tradition that continued.

entries.title: The Qarmatians (Qaramita)
questions: Who were the Qarmatians?
Are the Qarmatians Ismailis?
What was the Qarmati state of Bahrayn?
Why did the Qarmatians break away?
Did the Qarmatians fight the Fatimids?
Do Qarmatians still exist?
Why are Ismailis sometimes called Qarmatis?
entries.answer:
IIS describes the Qarmatians (Arabic Qaramita, older English 'Carmatians') as adherents of a branch of the Ismailis in the 3rd AH / 9th century CE, named after Hamdan Qarmat, who led the da'wa in the countryside around Kufa and in southern Iraq.

The break came in 286 AH / 899 CE. 'Abdullah al-Mahdi, the future first Fatimid caliph, had just succeeded to the leadership at Salamiyya and claimed the Imamat openly for himself and his ancestors, explaining that the name of Muhammad ibn Isma'il had served as a cover for concealed Imams. A loyalist faction, mainly in Yemen, Egypt, North Africa and Sind, accepted this. A dissident faction, led at first by Hamdan Qarmat, kept the older belief in the Mahdiship of Muhammad ibn Isma'il. From then on 'Qarmati' referred specifically to those who did not acknowledge 'Abdullah al-Mahdi or the Fatimid caliphs as Imams.

Their most important stronghold was the Qarmati state of Bahrayn, founded in 286 AH / 899 CE by the da'i Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi; it collapsed in 470 AH / 1077 CE. Relations with the Fatimids were hostile, and remained so under the caliph al-Hakim. In 290 AH / 903 CE rebellious Qarmatis led by the sons of the da'i Zikrawayh entered Salamiyya, massacred its inhabitants and destroyed Imam 'Abdullah's palace there.

Daftary adds that Sunni authors, generally ill-informed about divisions within Shi'ism, often could not distinguish Ismailis from Qarmatis and blamed the Ismaili movement for Qarmati atrocities.

entries.title: Hamdan Qarmat and the schism of 899
questions: Who was Hamdan Qarmat?
What does the name Qarmat mean?
Why did Hamdan Qarmat break with the Imam?
What happened to Hamdan Qarmat?
Who was 'Abdan?
What was the 899 schism about?
entries.answer:
Wilferd Madelung's article, published by IIS, describes Hamdan Qarmat b. al-As'at (d. 321 AH / 933 CE) as an Ismaili da'i and the founder of the movement in Iraq. He came from a village east of Kufa and was working as a carter when the da'i Husayn al-Ahwazi converted him, sometime between 260/873-74 and 264/877-78. He organised the da'wa in the Sawad, the countryside around Kufa, with his brother-in-law 'Abdan as chief propagandist. Together they appointed and trained da'is, including men sent to Bahrayn, Yemen and, by way of Yemen, the Maghrib.

The name 'Qarmat' is explained variously, perhaps from an Aramaic word meaning red-eyed, or as meaning short in stature or short-legged.

In line with the leadership at Salamiyya, Hamdan and 'Abdan had summoned people to the Imamat of Muhammad b. Isma'il and predicted his early advent as the Mahdi. When 'Abdullah, the future Fatimid al-Mahdi, claimed the Imamat for himself around 286/899, they suspended their missionary work. Hamdan then disappeared from Kalwada; 'Abdan was murdered.

Madelung reports a different possibility drawn from Ibn Hawqal: that Hamdan later rejoined the Fatimid Imam under a new identity as the da'i Abu 'Ali, serving in Egypt, Anatolia and finally the Maghrib as chief da'i, and dying in 321/933. He notes the main account, which says nothing of Hamdan after his disappearance, traces back to anti-Fatimid Iraqi sources, while Ibn Hawqal was a Fatimid sympathiser who knew Abu 'Ali's son.

entries.title: The split of 1094: Nizar and al-Musta'li
questions: Why did the Ismailis divide into Nizaris and Musta'lis?
Who were Nizar and al-Musta'li?
What happened when al-Mustansir died?
When did the Ismaili community split in two?
Which line does the Aga Khan descend from?
Who was al-Afdal?
What was the 487 AH schism?
entries.answer:
IIS describes the division of 487 AH / 1094 CE as the permanent schism in Ismaili history. On the death of the Imam-caliph al-Mustansir, the eighth Fatimid caliph and eighteenth Ismaili Imam, the succession was disputed between his sons Nizar, the original heir designate, and al-Musta'li, who was installed on the Fatimid throne by the powerful vizier al-Afdal.

The da'wa headquarters in Cairo and the Ismaili communities of Egypt, Yemen and western India recognised al-Musta'li. The Ismailis of Persia and neighbouring lands supported Nizar. Nizar revolted, was defeated and was killed in 488 AH / 1095 CE. From then on the Imamat was handed down in two parallel lines among al-Mustansir's descendants, later designated Nizari and Musta'li (or Musta'lawi).

In Persia, the da'i Hasan-i Sabbah had taken the fortress of Alamut in 483 AH / 1090 CE. He supported Nizar, severed relations with Cairo, and so founded a Nizari da'wa independent of the Fatimid regime, together with what became the Nizari state in Persia with a subsidiary in Syria.

Daftary notes that after the schism relations ceased between the Ismailis of Persia and the later Fatimid caliphs, and that hostility developed between the Nizaris and the Musta'lians. The Nizari Imams of modern times, who carry the hereditary title Aga Khan, trace their descent to Imam Nizar.

entries.title: The Musta'li Ismailis
questions: Who are the Musta'li Ismailis?
What do Musta'lians believe about the Imam?
Where do Musta'li Ismailis live?
Are Musta'lis still Ismailis?
What is the difference between Musta'li and Nizari belief?
Do Musta'lis follow the Aga Khan?
What is a Musta'lian Tayyibi?
entries.answer:
The Musta'li Ismailis are the branch that in 1094 recognised al-Musta'li as the Imam after al-Mustansir. IIS describes them as one of the two main Ismaili branches surviving today, alongside the Nizaris, with both rooted in the Fatimid period.

After a further split in 524 AH / 1130 CE, Musta'li Ismailism survived only in its Tayyibi form. IIS therefore usually writes of the 'Musta'lian Tayyibi Ismailis'. Their distinguishing belief, as IIS presents it, concerns the Imamat: they hold that their twenty-first Imam, al-Tayyib, went into physical concealment (satr), and that while the Imamat continues in his line, authority in his physical absence is exercised by a vicegerent, the da'i al-mutlaq, who acts on his behalf. Nizaris, by contrast, believe in a living, physically present Imam. IIS says this difference has led the two communities to develop along different historical and institutional paths.

In doctrine, the Tayyibis maintained Fatimid traditions and preserved a substantial part of the Ismaili literature of the Fatimid period. Building particularly on the metaphysical system of the Fatimid da'i Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, they developed their own esoteric system with distinctive eschatological themes. Their law rests on the Da'a'im al-Islam of the Fatimid jurist al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 363 AH / 974 CE).

Today Musta'lian Tayyibis are found mainly in South Asia, with smaller numbers in Yemen, Saudi Arabia, and immigrant communities in Britain, North America and elsewhere.

entries.title: The Hafizi-Tayyibi split of 1130
questions: What was the Hafizi-Tayyibi split?
Who was al-Tayyib?
Who was al-Hafiz?
What happened after al-Amir died?
Do Hafizi Ismailis still exist?
Why did Musta'li Ismailism divide again?
What happened to Ismailism in Egypt after the Fatimids?
entries.answer:
IIS describes a second division within the Musta'li branch, on the death of al-Musta'li's son and successor al-Amir in 524 AH / 1130 CE.

The Musta'li da'wa headquarters in Cairo endorsed the Imamat of al-Amir's cousin and successor to the Fatimid throne, al-Hafiz. His Imamat was accepted by the Musta'li Ismailis of Egypt and Syria and by a portion of those in Yemen. Those who recognised al-Hafiz (d. 544 AH / 1149 CE) and the later Fatimid caliphs as their Imams became known as Hafizis.

The Musta'li Ismailis of the Sulayhid state in Yemen, and those of Gujarat in western India, instead recognised the Imamat of al-Amir's son al-Tayyib, and became known as Tayyibis.

Hafizi Ismailism, IIS says, disappeared completely soon after the Fatimid dynasty collapsed in 567 AH / 1171 CE, when Salah al-Din took control of Egypt and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. Daftary adds that the Ayyubids systematically destroyed the great Fatimid libraries, including the collections of the Dar al-'Ilm in Cairo, and persecuted the Ismailis of Egypt. From then on Musta'li Ismailism survived only in its Tayyibi form, with permanent strongholds in Yemen.

This is why the two Ismaili communities that exist today are the Nizaris and the Musta'lian Tayyibis: the Hafizi line did not outlive the state that sustained it.

entries.title: The Tayyibi da'wa in Yemen and the Da'i al-Mutlaq
questions: What is a Da'i al-Mutlaq?
Who leads the Musta'li Ismailis if the Imam is hidden?
Why did the Tayyibi da'wa move to Yemen?
What is the role of the da'i mutlaq?
When did the Tayyibi headquarters move to India?
Who was Idris 'Imad al-Din?
How is Tayyibi leadership different from Nizari leadership?
entries.answer:
IIS explains that after the Tayyibi branch formed, the Musta'li da'wa hierarchy inherited from Fatimid Cairo was transferred, after the dynasty's collapse, to Yemen, where it remained for several centuries and expanded into Gujarat.

Because the Tayyibis hold that their Imams have remained in concealment since al-Tayyib, the affairs of the community are administered by a da'i mutlaq, literally a da'i with absolute or unrestricted authority, who guides the community on behalf of the hidden Imam. IIS describes him as the executive head of the da'wa organisation and the community's spiritual leader, and elsewhere as a vicegerent acting on the Imam's behalf.

The Tayyibi da'wa spread successfully in the Haraz region of Yemen and in Gujarat. Nanji notes that despite occasional persecution, such as that inflicted by Zaydi rulers, the community preserved the rich esoteric tradition formulated in Fatimid times. Among the scholars it produced, the nineteenth da'i, Idris 'Imad al-Din (d. 1468 CE), was the most outstanding; his historical writings remain important sources.

In the early 16th century the headship passed to an Indian from Sidhpur, and in 1567 CE the headquarters of the Da'i al-Mutlaq were transferred from Yemen to Gujarat, first to Ahmadabad. By then the Ismaili Bohras of South Asia greatly outnumbered their Yemeni coreligionists.

This office is the structural difference between the two surviving branches: Nizaris follow a present, living Imam, while Tayyibis follow a da'i acting for an Imam in concealment.

entries.title: The Bohras
questions: Who are the Bohras?
Are Bohras Ismaili Muslims?
What is the difference between Daudi and Sulaymani Bohras?
Where did the Bohra community come from?
Who leads the Daudi Bohras?
Are Bohras and Khojas the same?
How many Bohras are there?
What is the Alavi Bohra group?
entries.answer:
IIS uses 'Bohras' for the Tayyibi Musta'li Ismailis of South Asia. The community grew from a da'wa founded in Gujarat in 1067 CE by missionaries sent from Yemen, spreading first among urban artisans and traders; converts became known as Bohras, with centres at Cambay, Patan, Sidhpur and later Ahmadabad.

In 997 AH / 1589 CE a dispute over the succession to the twenty-sixth da'i mutlaq, Da'ud ibn 'Ajabshah, split the Tayyibis into Da'udi and Sulaymani branches, each following a separate line of da'is. Daftary and Nanji note further subdivisions in India after periodic challenges to the da'i's authority, including a third group that appeared in 1624 under the name 'Aliyya, a small community centred in Baroda.

The Da'udi Bohras are the larger group, concentrated in South Asia, especially Gujarat, with communities in Yemen, Britain, North America and Sri Lanka. Since the 1920s Bombay (Mumbai) has been the permanent seat of the Da'udi da'i mutlaq and his central administration; Surat remains a centre of learning, home to the Jame'a Sayfiya seminary. IIS notes the community's strong tradition of Arabic scholarship and manuscript preservation, its majalis, and a reputation for entrepreneurship and charitable work.

The Sulaymani leadership has remained hereditary in the Makrami family, with headquarters at Najran; Sulaymanis are concentrated in northern Yemen and Saudi Arabia, with a few thousand in India.

Bohras are Musta'lian Tayyibis; Khojas are Nizaris. They are distinct communities.

entries.title: The Druze and their origins in the Fatimid period
questions: Where did the Druze come from?
Are the Druze Ismailis?
What is the connection between the Druze and al-Hakim?
Who was Hamza b. 'Ali?
Did the Fatimids support the Druze movement?
Why are the Druze called Druze?
Are Druze Muslims?
entries.answer:
IIS places the beginnings of the Druze religion in the reign of the Fatimid Imam-caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (r. 386-411 AH / 996-1021 CE).

Daftary writes that from around 408 AH / 1017 CE a number of da'is who had come to Cairo from Persia and Central Asia, prominent among them Hasan Akram, Hamza b. 'Ali and Muhammad Darzi (Darazi), propagated new doctrines attributing divinity to al-Hakim, effectively founding a new religious movement that proclaimed the end of the era of Islam. The movement, later named after Darzi, caused much unrest in the closing years of al-Hakim's caliphate.

Daftary is explicit on two points. Contrary to the claims of later Sunni authors, there is no evidence that al-Hakim himself encouraged them. And the leadership of the Fatimid da'wa was categorically opposed to the movement: the chief da'i Khatkin al-Dhayf invited the theologian Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani to Cairo to refute its doctrines, and Kirmani's works checked their spread within the da'wa.

A lecture hosted by IIS describes the founders as Ismaili missionaries whose writings, al-Hikma or the Rasa'il al-Hikma, set out a new doctrine that parted from mainstream Fatimid teaching; the movement was criticised for ghuluww (exaggeration), was banned from Cairo under the caliph al-Zahir, and developed thereafter in the mountains of Syria, where clan leaders converted between 1017 and 1043 and passed the doctrine on secretly.

These are Ismaili-institutional descriptions of another community. How the Druze describe themselves is not represented in these sources.

entries.title: The Qasim-Shahi and Muhammad-Shahi Nizari lines
questions: What are the Qasim-Shahi and Muhammad-Shahi lines?
Did the Nizaris split as well?
What happened to the Muhammad-Shahi Ismailis?
Which line do today's Ismailis follow?
Who was Shah Tahir al-Husayni?
Why did the Ismailis of Salamiyya change allegiance?
What is the full name of the Aga Khan's community?
entries.answer:
After the Mongols destroyed the Nizari state at Alamut in 654 AH / 1256 CE, the Imams entered a long period of concealment. IIS writing on the Nizaris records a further schism during this period, over the succession to Shams al-Din Muhammad.

Those who followed the line of Qasim Shah are the Ismailis who today acknowledge Prince Rahim Aga Khan V as the 50th hereditary Imam. He was named on 5 February 2025, designated by his late father, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, the 49th Imam, who had died in Lisbon the previous day. On this basis the community's precise designation can be given as the Nizari Qasim-Shahi Shi'i Ismaili Muslims.

The other branch is the Muhammad-Shahi line. Its most prominent figure was Shah Tahir al-Husayni (d. 1594), who propagated a form of Ismailism under the guise of Twelver Shi'ism; he served as a courtier to the Deccan ruler Burhan Nizam Shah. IIS says the line of Muhammad-Shahi Imams discontinued in the final decades of the 18th century, after which Muhammad-Shahi Ismailis either merged with the Qasim-Shahi line or were assimilated into Twelver Shi'ism.

A concrete instance is recorded in the IIS article on Salamiyya in Syria. In 1304 AH / 1887 CE the Ismailis of Salamiyya, who like most Syrian Ismailis had until then belonged to the Muhammad-Shahi branch, transferred their allegiance to the Qasim-Shahi line of Nizari Imams, then represented by Aga Khan III, who afterwards organised the community there and built schools and an agricultural institution. Salamiyya now holds the largest concentration of Ismailis in Syria and the Near East.

entries.title: The Imam-Shahis
questions: Who are the Imam-Shahis?
What is the Imam-Shahi group in Gujarat?
Why did some Khojas break away?
Who was Imam Shah?
Are Imam-Shahis Ismailis?
What happened after Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din?
entries.answer:
The Imam-Shahis are a group that separated from the Nizari Ismaili community in western India. IIS gives them only a brief notice.

The background is the Nizari da'wa in South Asia, led by preachers called pirs. Pir Sadr al-Din consolidated the community and gave the title Khoja to converts from the Lohana trading caste; the tradition that developed is known as Satpanth, the 'true path'. Sadr al-Din was succeeded by his son Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din, who settled at Ucch in Sind.

Daftary and Nanji write that after the death of Pir Hasan Kabir al-Din, a section of the community seceded and established itself in Gujarat, becoming known as Imam-Shahis. The majority continued to adhere to the authority of the Nizari Imams.

A separate IIS article on early Ismaili history in South Asia mentions Imam Shah in passing: Ismaili tradition credits Mahmud Begada, sultan of Gujarat (r. 1458-1511 CE), with granting the Ismaili preacher Imam Shah land near the capital, Ahmadabad. The same article notes that by the end of the 15th century Ismaili influence in Gujarat was in decline, partly because of the sultans' actions and partly because of local Sufi groups.

Beyond this the allowed sources say nothing: they do not describe Imam-Shahi beliefs, leadership, size or present-day existence.
