entries.notes: This is close to the limit of what the allowed sources contain on the Imam-Shahis: essentially one sentence in an encyclopaedia article plus a passing mention. Nothing about their doctrine or their situation today is available, and the two sources do not clearly establish whether the Imam Shah granted land is the same figure the group is named after.

entries.title: Ismailis and Twelver Shia Muslims
questions: How are Ismailis related to Twelver Shias?
What do Ismailis and Twelvers have in common?
Where do Ismailis and Twelvers differ?
Why did Ismailis and Twelvers separate?
Are Ismailis the same as the Shia in Iran?
Did Ismailis ever pass as Twelvers?
Which Shia group is bigger?
entries.answer:
IIS presents Ismailis and Twelvers as two communities that grew from a single Shi'i root. Both hold that the Prophet designated Imam 'Ali as his successor at Ghadir Khumm, and both trace authority through the Ahl al-Bayt by nass, designation by the Imam of the time.

The parting came after Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq died in 765 CE. A dispute over the succession produced the two main Shi'a communities: the Ithna'ashariyya or Twelvers, who followed Musa al-Kazim, and the Isma'iliyya, who followed the line through Isma'il and his son Muhammad ibn Isma'il. A third branch, the Zaydis, developed separately. IIS says the Ismailis are the second largest Shi'a community after the Twelvers.

IIS puts the shared inheritance plainly: for all Shi'a, the period up to the death of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq constitutes a shared legacy, including the traditions of the Prophet and the early Imams, the beginnings of Shi'i legal thought and the foundations of philosophical and esoteric interpretation. Twelvers hold that their twelfth Imam entered occultation, and that in his absence qualified scholars, mujtahids, exercise ijtihad; Ismailis follow a living Imam or, among Tayyibis, a da'i acting for a concealed Imam.

Relations also show up historically. After Twelver Shi'ism became the state religion of Iran under the Safavids in 907 AH / 1501 CE, the Nizaris of Persia practised taqiyya as Twelvers. IIS also records that Muhammad-Shahi Nizaris were eventually assimilated into Twelver Shi'ism.

sources.title: Ismailis (Medieval Islamic Civilization: An Encyclopedia)
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Medieval Islamic Civilization: An Encyclopedia, 2006

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography and Beliefs (Daryoush Mohammad Poor)

entries.notes: The allowed sources describe the historical relationship but say very little about present-day relations between Ismaili and Twelver communities, or about Twelver views of Ismailis. That gap is not filled here.

entries.title: Ismailis and Sunni Muslims
questions: How do Ismailis relate to Sunni Muslims?
What is the difference between Ismailis and Sunnis?
Have Ismailis and Sunnis ever cooperated?
Did Ismaili rulers treat Sunnis well?
Why were Sunnis hostile to Ismailis?
Did Ismailis ever live as Sunnis?
What was Jalal al-Din Hasan's policy?
entries.answer:
IIS frames the Sunni-Shi'a difference as one of interpretation, dating to the absence of consensus over succession after the Prophet's death in 632 CE: the Shi'at 'Ali held that the Prophet had designated 'Ali, while those who followed the caliphs coalesced into the majoritarian Sunni branch, the Ahl al-Sunna wa al-Jama'a.

The historical record IIS presents runs in both directions. Daftary writes that the Ismailis, as a movement aiming to replace the Abbasid caliphate with an 'Alid one, aroused hostility from the Sunni majority early on, and that after 909 CE the Abbasid caliphs and Sunni 'ulama launched what amounted to an official anti-Ismaili campaign. Under the Saljuqs, the 12th century saw a series of massacres of Ismailis.

But IIS also stresses periods of accommodation. It describes Fatimid policy as marked by deference to religious plurality: mosques and endowments of different legal schools were patronised, merit governed appointments, and al-Hakim elevated a Sunni jurist to the office of chief qadi. One Fatimid edict is paraphrased as leaving each Muslim to find his own solution within his religion. At Alamut, the Nizari Imam Jalal al-Din Hasan (r. 1210-1221 CE) pursued rapprochement with Sunni rulers and jurists; the Abbasid caliph al-Nasir acknowledged the legitimacy of his rule, and IIS reads this as an affirmation that what unites Muslims matters more than differences of interpretation.

After Alamut fell, Nizaris in Iran adopted Sunni and Sufi guises to survive; Sufi orders, though largely Sunni, held Imam 'Ali in high esteem and often gave them shelter.

Ismailis (Medieval Islamic Civilization: An Encyclopedia)

entries.notes: This is the Ismaili institutional account of a shared history. Sunni accounts of the same events are outside the allowed sources and are not represented. IIS also notes that Jalal al-Din Hasan's order to follow the shari'a in its Sunni form was later explained as a form of taqiyya.

entries.title: Are Ismailis Muslims?
questions: Are Ismailis Muslims?
Are Ismailis part of Islam?
Do Ismailis consider themselves Muslim?
Is Ismailism a separate religion?
What is a tariqah of Islam?
Where do Ismailis fit within Islam?
Why do some people say Ismailis are not Muslims?
entries.answer:
The community's own institutions state the position directly. The Ismaili Imamat and the community's official material describe Ismailis as the Shia Imami Ismaili Muslims, who belong to the Shia branch of Islam, with the Shia and Sunni forming the two major branches. They describe the Ismaili interpretation as a major, historical part of the faith of Islam, with a credal tradition reaching back to the early seventh century and a school of jurisprudence first promulgated during the Fatimid caliphate. IIS refers to the Ismaili tariqah of Islam, tariqah meaning a path within the faith.

IIS adds the theological grounding: the Shi'a, like other Muslim groups, affirm the shahada, belief in the unity of God and in the Prophet Muhammad as God's Messenger, while holding that God instructed the Prophet to designate a figure of authority to succeed him in guiding the community.

The question is asked because the claim has been denied historically. Daftary describes a sustained anti-Ismaili campaign by the Abbasid caliphs and Sunni 'ulama from the 10th century onward, whose object was to have the Ismailis condemned as heretics or deviators; this included the 'Baghdad manifesto' of 402 AH / 1011 CE, in which the Abbasid caliph assembled Sunni and Twelver scholars to declare in writing that the Fatimid caliphs lacked 'Alid ancestry.

Formal recognition in the modern period is discussed in a separate entry on the Amman Message of 2005.

sources.title: The Shia Ismaili Muslims (background on the Ismaili Muslim community)

al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (Farhad Daftary)

entries.notes: This entry states the community's own position and the historical record of its denial, both from the community's institutions. It is not a neutral survey of what other Muslim authorities say today, because the allowed sources do not contain one.

entries.title: The Amman Message and recognition of Ismailis
questions: What is the Amman Message?
Are Ismailis officially recognised as Muslims?
What are the eight schools of Islamic jurisprudence?
Did the Aga Khan take part in the Amman conference?
What did the Amman conference say about takfir?
Who can issue a fatwa according to the Amman Message?
When was the international Islamic conference in Jordan?
entries.answer:
IIS reports on the International Islamic Conference held in Amman, Jordan, opened by King Abdullah II, which brought together more than 170 religious leaders and scholars from some 40 countries. IIS describes it as an unusually broad gathering, and says the Institute sent delegates, including Farhad Daftary.

The conference forged a consensus on the mutual acceptance of the legitimacy of different Muslim denominations. It affirmed that whoever adheres to one of the eight schools of Muslim jurisprudence is a Muslim who cannot be declared or treated as an apostate or infidel, and whose life, honour and property are inviolable. The eight named schools include the four Sunni schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali), the Shia schools (Ithna Ashari, Ismaili, Zaidi), and the Ibadi and Zahiri traditions.

The declaration also condemned the practice among extremists of issuing religious opinions that encourage violence against Muslims, rejected terrorism as illegitimate and an affront to Islam, and resolved that only those qualified within their respective schools of jurisprudence have the authority to issue fatwas.

IIS notes that His Highness the Aga Khan, the 49th hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims, sent a message in advance in support of the conference's goals.

This matters for the question of recognition: it is the clearest instance the allowed sources give of Ismailism being formally affirmed as a legitimate school within Islam by a broad body of Muslim authorities.

sources.title: The International Islamic Conference, Amman, Jordan

entries.notes: The IIS page says the full text of the Aga Khan's message follows the report, but that text does not appear on the page as it loads, so its contents are not summarised here. The page is dated 2006 and does not state the conference date precisely; the Amman Message process is usually dated to 2004-2005. Only one allowed source covers this event.

entries.title: The anti-Ismaili 'black legend'
questions: What is the anti-Ismaili black legend?
Why were Ismailis accused of heresy?
Who wrote polemics against the Ismailis?
Who were Ibn Rizam and Akhu Muhsin?
Were the Fatimids really descended from the Prophet?
What was the Baghdad manifesto?
Why is so much written about Ismailis unreliable?
entries.answer:
Daftary uses the term 'black legend' for a body of anti-Ismaili writing produced by Muslim polemicists. He describes it as the product of a systematic campaign: after the Fatimid state was founded in 909 CE the Abbasid caliphs and Sunni 'ulama launched what amounted to official anti-Ismaili propaganda, aimed at discrediting the whole movement so the Ismailis could be condemned as heretics.

By spreading defamations and even forged accounts, these authors produced, in the course of the 10th century, a portrait of Ismailism as the arch-heresy of Islam (ilhad), designed by non-'Alid impostors, or even by a Jewish magician disguised as a Muslim, to destroy Islam from within. By the 11th century this account, complete with elaborate stages of initiation, was accepted as an accurate description of Ismaili beliefs and practices, and fed further polemics and heresiographical accusations. Anti-Ismaili polemical writing supplied a major source for Sunni heresiographers such as al-Baghdadi (d. 1037).

The IIS article on the da'i notes that many Sunni authors drew on the polemics of Ibn Rizam and Akhu Muhsin for a supposed system of seven or nine named stages of initiation, and adds that there is no evidence of such stages in surviving Ismaili literature.

A connected charge was that the Fatimid Imam-caliphs falsely claimed descent from Fatima and 'Ali. In 402 AH / 1011 CE the Abbasid caliph al-Qadir assembled Sunni and Twelver Imami scholars to declare this in writing; the 'Baghdad manifesto' was read in Friday mosques across Abbasid lands.

Da'i (Encyclopaedia article)

Nanji makes the related point that treating Ismailism as a 'heresy' assumes an original orthodoxy from which others departed, an assumption he regards as debatable.

entries.title: The 'Assassin' legends
questions: Why are Ismailis called Assassins?
Is the Assassin story about Ismailis true?
Who was the Old Man of the Mountain?
Did Ismailis use hashish?
Where did the assassin legends come from?
What did Marco Polo say about the Ismailis?
Why do Ismailis object to the word Assassin?
entries.answer:
Daftary treats the 'Assassin' legends as European fabrications about the Nizari Ismailis, and his purpose is to invalidate the scholarly and popular legitimacy they acquired.

The western habit of calling the Nizaris 'Assassins' goes back to the Crusaders and their Latin chroniclers in the Levant. The name derived, under obscure circumstances, from variants of the Arabic word hashish, and in European languages it became a common noun meaning murderer, so the label is doubly pejorative and, Daftary says, a misnomer.

From the later 12th century, interlinked tales circulated in the Latin East and Europe about a mysterious sect whose members obeyed their leader, the 'Old Man of the Mountain', a title applied to the Syrian Nizari leader Rashid al-Din Sinan (d. 1193). Their willingness to undertake dangerous missions was explained by an intoxicating drug, and then by a secret 'garden of paradise' where drugged devotees tasted bliss. Daftary separates these into the 'paradise legend', the 'hashish legend' and the 'deathleap legend', which developed in stages and culminated in the version popularised by Marco Polo.

He argues the legends were formulated by western observers, not Muslims: similar stories are absent from medieval Islamic sources, including contemporary histories of Syria, and educated Muslim historians, though hostile, did not fantasise about Nizari secret practices. Well-informed westerners such as William of Tyre also did not contribute to them. Nineteenth-century orientalists, notably Silvestre de Sacy and von Hammer-Purgstall, then lent them scholarly authority.

sources.title: Ismaili Studies: A Summary Review (Farhad Daftary)

entries.notes: Daftary's argument that the legends were European inventions rooted in Muslim hostility is an interpretation advanced from within an Ismaili research institute; he presents it as the contention of his study. The allowed sources do not set out what the Nizaris of Alamut did or did not do in terms of targeted killings.

entries.title: Persecution of Ismailis
questions: Were Ismailis persecuted?
What happened to Ismailis under the Saljuqs?
Did the Mongols kill Ismailis?
What did the Ayyubids do to the Ismailis?
Were Bohras persecuted in India?
Why did Ismailis have to hide their faith?
Which dynasties attacked the Ismailis?
entries.answer:
IIS sources describe repeated persecution. Daftary writes that in the Middle Ages the Ismailis were perhaps the most severely persecuted community within the Muslim world, subjected to massacres in many localities, and that this was a principal reason they guarded their literature and doctrines.

Specific episodes named in these sources include: the forces of Mahmud of Ghazna, described as fiercely anti-Ismaili, causing destruction in Sind where large numbers of Ismailis were massacred; a rebellion in Ifriqiya in favour of the Abbasids accompanied by the massacre of several Ismaili communities; massacres of Ismaili communities in North Africa under al-Hakim, led by Sunni mobs; the Ayyubids' systematic destruction of the Fatimid libraries, including the Dar al-'Ilm collections in Cairo, and persecution of the Ismailis of Egypt; an escalation of Saljuq hostility in the early 12th century, with a series of brutal massacres, and Ismailis or their sympathisers caught in Saljuq-ruled towns tortured and killed; the Mongol demolition of Alamut and other strongholds in 1256 CE, with a general and widespread massacre and the killing of Imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah; Mamluk persecution of the Syrian Ismailis; occasional persecution of the Musta'li community in Yemen by Zaydi rulers; and periodic persecution of the Bohras in South Asia, with many converting to Sunni Islam, the religion of the region's Muslim rulers, until British rule ended official persecution in the early 19th century.

This history is why taqiyya, the precautionary concealment of belief, is a recurring theme in Ismaili history.

sources.title: Ismaili Historiography (Farhad Daftary)
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 176-178, 2007

sources.title: Ismaili Communities - South Asia
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopedia of Modern Asia, Vol. 3, pp. 185-187, 2002

entries.notes: The allowed sources discuss persecution almost entirely in the medieval and early modern periods. They say very little about persecution of Ismailis in the modern era; the Modern Ismaili Communities article mentions only that the Sulaymani community of Najran has often found it difficult to practise its faith openly, and that Ismailis faced dislocation and refugee crises in East Africa, Tajikistan, Iran, Syria and Afghanistan without characterising these as religious persecution.

entries.title: Taqiyya, Sufi guises and survival
questions: What is taqiyya?
Why did Ismailis hide their beliefs?
Did Ismailis pretend to be Sufis?
Did Ismailis pretend to be Sunni or Twelver?
Why is Ismaili history hard to reconstruct?
What was the Anjudan revival?
How did the Ismailis survive after Alamut?
entries.answer:
Taqiyya is the precautionary concealment of one's religious belief in the face of danger, a Shi'i principle. IIS sources treat it as central to how Ismaili communities survived long stretches of hostility.

Daftary writes that, with the major exception of the Fatimid period when Ismaili doctrines were preached openly, Ismailism developed in secrecy and the Ismailis were coerced into a clandestine existence, which in turn gave their adversaries the opportunity to misrepresent their beliefs. Nanji adds that this secrecy is itself an obstacle to writing Ismaili history.

After the Mongols destroyed the Nizari state in 1256 CE, the community was left without central leadership for around two centuries, and various Nizari communities developed independently, adopting Sunni and Sufi guises to protect themselves. IIS notes that the Sufi orders then common in the Iranian lands, though predominantly Sunni, all held Imam 'Ali in high esteem, and often offered hospitality to Ismailis; in Iran the movement's organisation came in some ways to resemble that of a Sufi tariqa. By the mid-9th AH / 15th century CE the Nizari Imams emerged at Anjudan in central Persia, beginning a revival of the da'wa and of literary activity. After Twelver Shi'ism became the Safavid state religion in 907 AH / 1501 CE, the Nizaris of Persia practised taqiyya as Twelvers.

One IIS writer notes that Ismaili thought became so intermingled with Sufism and Twelver Shi'ism that until the time of Aga Khan III it can be difficult to distinguish Ismaili identity from that of Sufis or Twelvers.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography and Beliefs (Daryoush Mohammad Poor)

entries.notes: Scholars quoted by IIS differ on how far Ismaili-Sufi interaction was disguise and how far genuine convergence; Nanji describes a 'real coalescence' of Ismaili and Sufi dimensions after Alamut, while also citing taqiyya as a contributory factor.

entries.title: How Ismaili rulers treated other Muslims and non-Muslims
questions: How did the Fatimids treat Sunnis?
Were the Fatimids tolerant?
How did Ismaili states treat Christians and Jews?
Did Fatimid law apply to everyone?
What was Fatimid policy on religious difference?
Did Ismaili rulers appoint non-Ismailis?
entries.answer:
IIS presents the conduct of Ismaili states towards other communities as part of the Ismaili account of relations with other Muslims.

Of the Fatimid caliphate it says that law was formulated and implemented with deference to a philosophy of religious tolerance and respect for difference, and paraphrases a Fatimid edict to the effect that each Muslim may seek his own solution within his religion. The Fatimids encouraged private patronage of mosques and pious endowments by Muslims of different legal schools, a policy IIS reads as reflecting a plurality of pious ways rather than a single monolithic interpretation.

In appointments, including the judiciary, merit was a primary criterion. IIS gives as an example the Imam-caliph al-Hakim elevating a Sunni jurist to the position of chief qadi, praising his sense of justice and intellectual calibre. Al-Hakim's foundation of the Dar al-'Ilm in Cairo in 395 AH / 1005 CE, teaching subjects from Qur'an and hadith to philosophy and astronomy, is described as making access to education available to the public.

IIS also notes Fatimid support for Christians and Jews: many Coptic and Armenian Christians and Jews attained important positions and took an active part in social, cultural, intellectual and economic life, a policy IIS grounds in the Qur'anic principle of respect for the Ahl al-Kitab, the People of the Book.

At Alamut, IIS says the Nizaris maintained patronage of learning that benefited Muslim and non-Muslim scholars alike, and that their settlements sheltered refugees regardless of creed.

sources.title: al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (Farhad Daftary)
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. 11, pp. 572-573, 2003

entries.notes: This is the Ismaili institutions' own account of their historical states and is framed approvingly; it is not a critical assessment. Daftary notes separately that Sunni historiographers portrayed al-Hakim as persecuting non-Muslims, and that modern scholarship is revising that picture, so the record here is contested.

entries.title: Why accounts of Ismailis were unreliable, and what changed
questions: Why is so much written about Ismailis wrong?
When did scholars start using Ismaili sources?
Who was Wladimir Ivanow?
How were Ismaili manuscripts recovered?
Did Bohra scholars help Ismaili studies?
Why did orientalists misunderstand the Ismailis?
Where can reliable information on Ismailis be found?
entries.answer:
Daftary argues that until the middle of the 20th century the Ismailis were studied almost entirely on the basis of evidence collected, or often fabricated, by their enemies.

He traces the problem in stages. Medieval Muslim polemicists produced the 'black legend'. Crusader-era Europeans produced the 'Assassin' legends. Nineteenth-century orientalists, led by Silvestre de Sacy, worked from Arabic manuscripts written largely by Sunni authors, and so studied Islam from a Sunni viewpoint, borrowing classifications from Christian contexts that treated Sunnism as orthodoxy and Shi'ism as heterodoxy. On that basis, misrepresentation and plain fiction permeated von Hammer-Purgstall's 1818 book on the Nizaris of Alamut, which was treated as standard until the 1930s. Daftary allows exceptions, naming Charles Defrémery on the Nizaris and Michael de Goeje on the Qarmatis.

The breakthrough came with the recovery of genuine Ismaili texts preserved secretly in private collections. Manuscripts from Yemen and Central Asia surfaced in the early 20th century; Nizari texts were collected in Badakhshan and studied by Aleksandr Semenov. Modern Ismaili studies began in the 1930s in India, drawing on the significant manuscript collections preserved in the Tayyibi Ismaili Bohra community, through the work of Wladimir Ivanow (1886-1970) and Bohra scholars including Asaf A. A. Fyzee, Husayn F. al-Hamdani and Zahid 'Ali.

Nanji adds that Ismaili sources have their own limitations: later writings, like all retrospective traditions, project a post facto image onto the earlier past.

sources.title: Ismaili Studies: A Summary Review (Farhad Daftary)
Ismaili Historiography (Farhad Daftary)
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 176-178, 2007

entries.notes: Worth noting for balance: this account of the field's development is itself written by scholars of the Institute of Ismaili Studies, which is an institution of the Ismaili Imamat. It also records that the modern recovery of Musta'lian Tayyibi manuscripts was largely the work of Bohra scholars.

entries.title: Where the branches live today, and how many
questions: How many Ismailis are there?
Where do Ismailis live?
How many Bohras are there?
Which Ismaili branch is largest?
Are Ismailis spread around the world?
How many countries have Ismaili communities?
entries.answer:
The two surviving branches differ greatly in size and distribution, though the figures in the allowed sources vary and are dated.

For the Nizaris, Daftary writes that they number several millions, account for the bulk of the world's Ismaili population, and are scattered across more than twenty-five countries in Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Europe and North America. IIS elsewhere gives around thirty countries, including Iran, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Syria, Tajikistan and several African countries. The community's own official material gives a figure of approximately 20 million across over 25 countries. The heritages represented are Central Asian, Persian, Arab and South Asian; the Nizaris of Badakhshan, now divided between Tajikistan and Afghanistan, preserved many Persian Ismaili texts.

For the Musta'lian Tayyibis, IIS gives a total Da'udi Bohra population of around 700,000 to 800,000, more than half in Gujarat, with communities in Yemen, Britain, North America and Sri Lanka; and around 60,000 to 70,000 Sulaymanis, concentrated in northern Yemen and Najran in Saudi Arabia, with a few thousand in India. A small 'Aliyya community of about 8,000 is centred in Baroda.

Both Khojas and Bohras were among the earliest Asian communities to settle in East Africa in the 19th century; in the 1970s the bulk of East African Ismailis moved to the West. Migration from Tajikistan and Afghanistan after the Soviet collapse has since reshaped the Nizari communities of Europe and North America.

The Bohra figures come from IIS articles of the early 2000s. No allowed source gives a figure for the Druze, and none exists here for Imam-Shahis.

entries.title: Who are the Ismailis?
questions: Who are the Ismailis?
What does Ismaili mean?
Who are the Shia Imami Ismaili Muslims?
What is the Ismaili community?
Where does the name Ismaili come from?
Are Ismailis an ethnic group or a religious community?
What do Ismailis call themselves?
Is Ismaili a nationality?
entries.answer:
The Ismailis - more formally the Shia Imami Ismaili Muslims - are a community within the Shia branch of Islam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them as adherents of a branch of Shia Islam that upholds Ismail, the eldest son of the Shia Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 765), as his father's successor; the community's name derives from him.

Ismailis are not a single ethnicity or nationality. The community's own institutions describe it as richly diverse, made up of people from many cultures, languages and countries. The Institute of Ismaili Studies groups Ismaili traditions into four broad geographic and ethnographic families - Arab, Persian, Central Asian and South Asian - noting that communities in Africa are predominantly of South Asian origin and that settlement in the West draws on all of these traditions.

What unites them, according to the Ismaili Imamat, is allegiance to a living, hereditary Imam descended from the Prophet Muhammad. The Ismaili Imamat states that the Ismailis are today the only Shia Muslims led by a living hereditary Imam, and that this allegiance has fostered an ethos of self-reliance, unity and common identity.

The community describes itself as espousing an esoteric, spiritual vision of Islam, and as active in civil society wherever it lives, contributing time, knowledge and material resources to the wider society. A local Ismaili community is called a Jamat.

entries.title: Are Ismailis Muslim?
questions: Are Ismailis Muslim?
Do Ismailis consider themselves Muslims?
Is Ismailism a separate religion from Islam?
Do Ismailis believe in one God?
Do Ismailis accept Prophet Muhammad?
Do Ismailis recite the shahada?
Is the Ismaili faith part of Islam?
entries.answer:
Yes. The community's own institutions describe Ismailis as Muslims, and specifically as Shia Imami Ismaili Muslims. The Ismaili states that Sunni and Shia Muslims share many central beliefs, including belief in the Oneness of God (tawhid) and that Prophet Muhammad was the final Messenger of God, who received the revelations recorded in the Holy Qur'an. Ismailis hold those beliefs.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that the shahada, the declaration of faith, has two parts: that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; Shia Muslims often add an affirmation of Imam Ali as Commander of the Faithful. The Ismaili notes that affirming the shahada is among the practices observed in jamatkhanas.

The Ismaili also addresses a common misunderstanding directly. In a 1985 interview reproduced on the community's site, the 49th Imam was asked about the claim that he is regarded as a living god; he replied that this is not true and would be blasphemous, since Islam prohibits all forms of idolatry. The same article explains that when Ismailis invoke the Prophet and the Imams in prayer, they are seeking intercession - asking those close to God to plead on their behalf - not equating anyone with God.

sources.title: Shia and Sunni: Understanding different Muslim interpretations
Why do Ismailis seek help from Hazrat Ali and the Imams?
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Are Ismailis Sunni or Shia?
questions: Are Ismailis Sunni or Shia?
What is the difference between Sunni and Shia?
How do Ismailis relate to other Shia Muslims?
Are Ismailis the same as Twelvers?
What is Shia Islam?
Why did Muslims divide into Sunni and Shia?
Where do Ismailis fit within Shia Islam?
entries.answer:
Ismailis are Shia. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines the Shia as those who, in addition to following the sunna of the Prophet Muhammad, believe in the Imamat of Ali ibn Abi Talib and his descendants through Fatima, and names the three primary Shia groups as the Ithna'asharis (Twelvers), the Ismailis and the Zaydis.

The Ismaili explains that the core difference between Sunni and Shia Muslims is whether the Prophet explicitly designated a successor. Sunnis hold that he did not, and regard the caliphs as his immediate successors; over time the caliphs came to be seen mainly as political rulers while the scholars (ulama) became the religious authorities. The Shia hold that the Prophet publicly designated his cousin and son-in-law Hazrat Ali - most famously at Ghadir Khumm - as the first of a line of hereditary Imams from his family.

The Ismailis and the Twelvers parted after the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq: the Twelvers recognised his younger son Musa al-Kazim, while the Ismailis recognised his eldest son Ismail. Farhad Daftary and Azim Nanji, writing for the Institute, encourage readers to see these not as sects in a narrow sense but as different communities of interpretation within the wider Muslim umma, and to reject the idea that there is one authentic Islam from which Shiism is a departure.

sources.title: Shia and Sunni: Understanding different Muslim interpretations
What is Shi'a Islam? by Farhad Daftary and Azim Nanji

entries.title: How many Ismailis are there, and where do they live?
questions: How many Ismailis are there?
Where do Ismailis live?
Which countries have Ismaili communities?
How big is the Ismaili population?
Are there Ismailis in Canada and the United States?
Is the Ismaili community worldwide?
How many countries do Ismailis live in?
entries.answer:
The community's own institutions give a range rather than a precise figure, and their published counts differ.

The Ismaili Imamat states that the Ismailis live in over 35 countries and number approximately 12 to 15 million. The Ismaili, the community's official site, says Ismailis live in more than 70 countries, mainly in Central, East and South Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, North America, Australia and New Zealand. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the community as settled in over 25 countries across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, North America and Australia, and calls it the second-largest Shia community in the world after the Twelvers.

The Institute groups Ismaili traditions into four broad geographic and ethnographic families - Arab, Persian, Central Asian and South Asian. Communities in Africa are primarily of South Asian origin, while more recent settlement in Europe and North America draws on all of these traditions.

Because these figures come from different pages and were written at different times, a newcomer should treat them as approximate. The sources agree on the shape of the picture - a global, plural community concentrated historically in Asia, Africa and the Middle East, with substantial more recent communities in the West - rather than on a single number.
entries.notes: The three official sources give different country counts (over 35, more than 70, over 25) and only the Imamat site gives a population range. The discrepancy is reported rather than resolved.

entries.title: Who is the Aga Khan?
questions: Who is the Aga Khan?
Who is the current Ismaili Imam?
What does the title Aga Khan mean?
Who is Prince Rahim Aga Khan V?
Who was Aga Khan IV?
Is the Aga Khan a king or a religious leader?
How did the Aga Khan title begin?
Who is the 50th Imam?
entries.answer:
Aga Khan is a hereditary title. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that it was granted by the Shah of Persia to the Ismaili Imam of the day in 1818 and has been inherited by each of his successors to the Imamat ever since. It is a title borne by the Imam, not a separate office.

Sir Sultan Mahomed Shah, Aga Khan III, was the 48th Imam and died in 1957. He was succeeded by his grandson, Shah Karim al-Husayni, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, the 49th Imam, who led the community for 67 years until his death on 4 February 2025.

On 5 February 2025, following the unsealing of his father's will, Prince Rahim al-Hussaini Aga Khan V was named the 50th hereditary Imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims. The Ismaili Imamat records that he was born on 12 October 1971, studied at Brown University, and had long served on the boards of Aga Khan Development Network agencies, chairing its Environment and Climate Committee. In his Takht-nishini Farman of 11 February 2025 he pledged to dedicate his life to the spiritual and material well-being of the Ismaili Jamat.

Ismailis usually refer to the Imam of their own time as Mawlana Hazar Imam rather than by the title Aga Khan.

sources.title: Glossary: His Highness Prince Karim Aga Khan IV

entries.title: What is the Imamat?
questions: What is the Imamat?
What is the Ismaili Imamat?
What does the Imam do?
Is the Imamat a political office?
Where is the seat of the Ismaili Imamat?
What is the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat?
Why do Ismailis need a living Imam?
What authority does the Imam have?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines Imamat as the institution of hereditary spiritual leadership in Shia Islam. The Ismaili Imamat describes itself as a supra-national entity representing the succession of Imams since the time of the Prophet Muhammad.

In Shia belief, the Prophet was the last Messenger of God, and upon his passing revelation ceased - but the community's need for spiritual and moral guidance continued. The Imamat exists, in Azim Nanji's words for the Institute, to complement prophethood, enabling Muslims to contextualise the practice of their faith and to understand both the outward and inner dimensions of the Qur'an.

The Imamat's own site is explicit that the role is spiritual and its authority is that of religious interpretation, not a political one: the Imams do not govern any land. At the same time it holds that in Islam the spiritual and material worlds are inextricably connected, so the Imam's responsibilities extend to improving the quality of life of the community and of the societies among whom Ismailis live. Ismailis are expected to be loyal, law-abiding citizens of their countries.

In 2015 Portugal and the Ismaili Imamat signed an agreement recognising the Imamat as an international entity with legal personality. In July 2018 the Henrique de Mendonca Palace in Lisbon was designated the Seat of the Ismaili Imamat, to be known as the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat.

sources.title: The Imamate in Ismailism by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 210-212

entries.title: What is a Hazir Imam, or Imam-of-the-Time?
questions: What is a Hazir Imam?
What does Mawlana Hazar Imam mean?
What is the Imam-of-the-Time?
Why do Ismailis have a living Imam?
What is the difference between a living Imam and a hidden Imam?
What does Hazar mean?
Who do Ismailis mean by Hazar Imam?
entries.answer:
Hazir (or Hazar) Imam means the present Imam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies glosses Mawlana Hazar Imam - in Arabic Mawlana al-Imam al-Hadir - as "our lord, the present Imam", the designation Nizari Ismailis use for their contemporary Imam.

The emphasis on presence matters. The Ismaili Imamat states that the Ismailis are today the only Shia Muslims led by a living, hereditary Imam in direct descent from the Prophet. Other Shia traditions hold that their Imam is in concealment; Ismailis hold that theirs is physically present and accessible in each generation.

What that presence is for is set out by the community's institutions in consistent terms: the Imam-of-the-Time interprets the faith for changing historical contexts, and works to improve the quality of life of the Jamat and of the wider society. The Ismaili describes the relationship between the Imam and each follower (murid) as a permanent spiritual bond, accepted through the pledge of allegiance known as bay'a, and reaffirmed daily in prayer.

Since 4 February 2025, Mawlana Hazar Imam for Ismailis is His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, the 50th hereditary Imam. Ismailis normally use this title rather than a personal name when speaking of the Imam of their own time.

entries.title: How is the next Imam chosen?
questions: How is the next Ismaili Imam chosen?
What is nass?
Who decides who becomes Imam?
Can a woman be the Ismaili Imam?
Does the eldest son always become Imam?
When does the new Imam take office?
How was Aga Khan V designated?
entries.answer:
Succession is by designation, not election. The Ismaili explains that each Imam designates his successor during his lifetime, and that the appointment takes effect immediately on the Imam's death. The technical term is nass: an explicit designation made before witnesses, understood to be divinely inspired, through which knowledge and authority pass from one Imam to the next.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the concept of nass was developed in the early decades of Shiism, particularly under the Imams Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq, at a time when several people were claiming the Imamat. Shia Muslims understand the Prophet's own designation of Hazrat Ali at Ghadir Khumm as the first instance of it.

The Preamble of the Ismaili Constitution, ordained in 1986, states that succession to the Imamat is by way of nass, it being the absolute prerogative of the Imam of the time to appoint his successor from among any of his male descendants, whether sons or remoter male issue. The Ismaili Imamat states the same principle.

In practice the designation is not announced in advance. Aga Khan IV said in a 1985 interview that he alone knew who the next Imam would be, and that his successor would become Imam when he died. Prince Rahim Aga Khan V was named on 5 February 2025 after his father's will was unsealed.

sources.title: How does the Ismaili Imam designate his successor?

entries.title: What is a Jamatkhana?
questions: What is a Jamatkhana?
Is a Jamatkhana a mosque?
What does jamatkhana mean?
Where do Ismailis worship?
Do only Ismailis use jamatkhanas?
Do men and women sit together in a jamatkhana?
What is the difference between a jamatkhana and a masjid?
entries.answer:
Jamatkhana means "house of the community". The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains the word as a compound of the Arabic jama'a (group or community), or its Persian form jama'at, and the Persian khana (house).

The Ismaili notes that spaces called jamatkhanas have been used across Muslim history by a number of Sunni and Shia communities, including Sunni Memons, Shia Bohras and Chishti Sufis, and that Mughal complexes in South Asia - the Taj Mahal among them - often included a jamatkhana. So the term is not exclusive to Ismailis, though today Shia Ismaili Muslims use jamatkhanas as their main space of worship and gathering.

A jamatkhana is not a mosque. The Ismaili describes non-denominational masjids as public places, while the jamatkhana is a private space under the authority of the Imam-of-the-Time, who alone determines what practices take place there. Karim Jiwani, writing for the Institute, situates it among the many diverse spaces of gathering and worship that Muslim societies have developed.

Ismaili jamatkhanas are described by the community as inclusive of ethnicity and gender, with men and women sitting in separate but side-by-side sections during ritual prayers and ceremonies. They are also described as places where values such as humility, generosity, pluralism and service are put into practice, and they are largely run by volunteers.

sources.title: Muslim Spaces of Piety and Worship by Karim Jiwani
Ismaili Jamatkhanas, Congregational Practice and Privacy

entries.title: Can a non-Ismaili visit a Jamatkhana?
questions: Can a non-Ismaili visit a jamatkhana?
Why can't I attend Ismaili prayers?
Are jamatkhanas open to the public?
Can my Ismaili friend take me to jamatkhana?
Why are Ismaili prayers private?
Can non-Muslims enter an Ismaili Centre?
Is the jamatkhana closed to visitors?
entries.answer:
Formal congregational prayers in a jamatkhana are reserved for Ismailis. The Ismaili explains that participation is limited to those who have pledged their allegiance - bay'a - to the Imam-of-the-Time, because the practices performed there are expressions of the bond between the Imam and his followers, and because determining those practices is the sole prerogative of the Imam.

The community's own explanation frames this as a boundary between public and private rather than as exclusion. Jamatkhanas are described as private tariqa spaces, in contrast to non-denominational mosques, which are public. The Ismaili notes that many religious communities restrict certain spaces and rites to initiated members, and offers parallels in other traditions, and points out that Ismailis have kept such private spaces throughout their history - the Fatimid majalis al-hikma, or sessions of wisdom, were likewise reserved for those who had taken the oath of allegiance.

That is not the whole picture. Outside formal prayer times, many jamatkhanas - and especially the Ismaili Centres - welcome multi-faith family members and the wider public to educational, cultural and social programmes, which the community describes as part of a deliberate effort to build bridges with the societies in which Ismailis live. If you have been invited, the practical answer is to ask your host which parts of the building and which occasions are open.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?
Ismaili Jamatkhanas, Congregational Practice and Privacy

entries.title: Do Ismailis pray five times a day?
questions: Do Ismailis pray five times a day?
How do Ismailis pray?
What is dua?
What happens during prayers in jamatkhana?
Do Ismailis perform salat?
How often do Ismailis pray?
What prayers do Ismailis recite?
entries.answer:
The community's own institutions describe the forms of Ismaili prayer, and are explicit that these are determined by the Imam-of-the-Time. They do not publish a simple count of daily prayers, so this answer describes what the sources do say.

The Ismaili states that Ismaili practices in jamatkhana include a variety of prayers recommended in the Holy Qur'an: du'a (supplication), tasbih (glorification), dhikr (remembrance) and salawat (seeking blessings on the Prophet and his progeny). They also include recitation of verses of the Qur'an, affirming the shahada, reciting devotional poetry such as qasidas, nashids and ginans, and the reading of farmans, which is guidance from the Imam. Special prayers may be observed at festivals, in times of difficulty, and at rites of passage, particularly deaths.

The same source says the pledge of allegiance to the Imam is reaffirmed daily in various prayers and jamatkhana practices, which indicates a daily rhythm of prayer without specifying a number of occasions.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines salat as a Qur'anic term for prayer in general that later came to be used for the daily ritual prayer, and notes that some Ismaili authors, such as Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, set outward acts of worship alongside an inner, esoteric worship of knowledge. The emphasis on both the outward form and its inner meaning is characteristic of the tradition.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The allowed sources describe the forms and content of Ismaili prayer but do not state how many times a day Ismailis pray, and jamatkhana practices are described as the Imam's sole prerogative. The specific numerical question is left unanswered rather than filled in.

entries.title: Do Ismailis fast during Ramadan?
questions: Do Ismailis fast?
Do Ismailis fast during Ramadan?
What is the purpose of fasting in Islam?
Do Ismailis observe Ramadan?
What is sawm?
Is fasting compulsory for Ismailis?
What is Shukarvari Beej?
entries.answer:
Yes - and the community's own explanation emphasises that fasting takes more than one form.

The Ismaili describes Ramadan as the holy month in which the Prophet Muhammad received the first revelation of the Qur'an, and says Ismailis celebrate it together with other Muslims as a month of special felicity. It then explains that Muslims have different ways of fasting, including all forms of self-restraint: not eating and drinking, but also feeding a poor person, absorption in the remembrance of God, avoiding gossip or unkind speech, restraint of the eyes and mouth, humility, and self-purification.

The stated purpose is the cultivation of taqwa, God-consciousness, and of spiritual and moral character - living by the ethics of Islam at all times, without forsaking the good things of this world. The Ismaili notes that individuals may participate in fasting in whatever way they choose, since it is not meant to cause undue hardship, and that those who are elderly, ill, pregnant or nursing are encouraged to feed the poor and needy instead.

The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, which the community describes as both a personal and a social festivity and an occasion to reaffirm generosity and compassion through charity.

Other fasts are observed in particular traditions within the community: when Chandraat, the new moon, falls on a Friday, the day is called Shukarvari Beej, and members of the Jamat in the Pir Sadardin tradition usually fast.

sources.title: What is the purpose of fasting in Ramadan?
On the occasion of Shukarvari Beej

entries.title: What about hajj and the other practices of Islam?
questions: Do Ismailis go on hajj?
What is hajj?
Do Ismailis follow the five pillars?
Do Ismailis give zakat?
What are the pillars of Islam?
Do Ismailis make pilgrimage to Mecca?
How do Ismailis understand religious duties?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines the terms. Hajj is the annual pilgrimage to the Ka'ba in Mecca, the Great Pilgrimage, distinguished from the lesser pilgrimage or umra; it takes place over five days in the twelfth lunar month, Dhu'l-Hijja, and on the tenth day pilgrims offer a sacrifice commemorating Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son - the day Muslims worldwide keep as Eid al-Adha. Zakat is defined as obligatory alms for Muslims, and the shahada as one of the key principles of Islam.

On how religious duties are framed, the Institute notes a distinction drawn by some Ismaili authors, such as Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani (d. after 1020), between al-ibadat al-amaliyya - worship performed through bodily actions and good deeds - and ibadat batina ilmiyya, an inner, esoteric worship of knowledge. This pairing of outward form and inner meaning runs through Ismaili thought, where the outward (zahir) and the inner (batin) are held together rather than set against each other.

What these sources do not do is describe contemporary Ismaili practice of the hajj, or set out a list of pillars as Ismailis observe them. The community's public material on practice concentrates instead on jamatkhana prayer, on Ramadan and on the ethics of charity. A newcomer should not assume either that Ismailis do or do not perform the hajj on the basis of what is published here.
entries.notes: The allowed sources define hajj and zakat in general Islamic terms but do not describe Ismaili observance of the hajj or publish an account of the pillars as practised by Ismailis. That gap is stated in the answer rather than filled from outside sources.

entries.title: Can someone become Ismaili?
questions: Can someone become Ismaili?
How do you convert to Ismailism?
Can I join the Ismaili community?
Do Ismailis accept converts?
What is bay'a?
Can you marry into the Ismaili community?
Is the Ismaili community open to newcomers?
entries.answer:
The community's own institutions describe what membership consists of, but do not publish a procedure for joining.

What they are clear about is the bond at the centre of it. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines bay'a as an oath of allegiance by which people recognise the authority of an individual; in many Muslim traditions it means offering oneself to a spiritual master in exchange for spiritual knowledge and guidance, and in the Shia Ismaili tradition it is the acceptance of the permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and the murid, uniting Ismailis worldwide in loyalty, devotion and obedience to the Imam. The Ismaili states that participation in formal jamatkhana prayers is restricted to those who have pledged this bay'a.

Historically, the tradition did receive people. The Institute's glossary describes the da'wa - the summons or invitation to the cause of the Imamat - and the da'i, the summoner who carried it, and uses the term mustajib, "respondent", for an initiate at the lowest rank of the Fatimid religious hierarchy. In South Asia, the Institute notes, the Khojas were those who converted to Nizari Ismaili Islam from about the thirteenth century onward.

The present-day process - who to approach, what is asked, how long it takes - is not set out on these sites. Anyone seriously interested would need to contact a local Ismaili institution directly.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?
Khojas by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia of Islam and the Muslim World, Vol. II, p. 393, 2003

entries.notes: No allowed source describes a contemporary procedure for becoming Ismaili. The answer reports what membership means and that the process is not published, rather than inferring one.

entries.title: How are religious dues and offerings used?
questions: Do Ismailis pay religious dues?
What is nazrana?
Where does Ismaili money go?
How are Ismaili offerings used?
Do Ismailis tithe?
What is Time and Knowledge Nazrana?
What happens to offerings made in jamatkhana?
entries.answer:
The community's material describes offerings in terms of devotion and purification rather than as a membership fee.

The Ismaili explains that it is customary for Ismailis to give freewill offerings out of love and devotion to the Imam-of-the-Time, as a means of purifying themselves and of receiving blessings and prayers for forgiveness through the Imam's intercession. It grounds this in the Qur'anic instruction to the Prophet to take a freewill offering (sadaqa) from believers to purify them and to pray for them. Because the Imam cannot always be physically present, this is usually done in jamatkhanas through his appointed representatives.

A nazrana is described as an unconditional gift or offering presented to the Imam-of-the-Time on special occasions, which may be material or may be a gift of time and knowledge. The Ismaili states that the Imams have invested nazrana for the betterment of the community by creating and strengthening institutions.

The Time and Knowledge Nazrana (TKN) is presented as combining two traditions: offering the Imam an unconditional gift to mark epochal events, and offering one's own intellectual capacity to the Imamat's work for the Jamat and the societies it lives among. Voluntary service is itself treated as a form of offering: the community notes that its institutions, including jamatkhanas, are largely run by volunteers.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies separately defines zakat as obligatory alms for Muslims.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The allowed sources do not describe dasond or any fixed percentage of income, and do not publish accounts of how offerings are allocated. Only the general purposes stated by the institutions are reported here.

entries.title: What is the place of women in the Ismaili community?
questions: What is the role of women in the Ismaili community?
Do Ismaili women work?
Do Ismaili women pray with men?
Are Ismaili women educated?
Can Ismaili women be community leaders?
How does the Imamat view women's education?
Are there famous Ismaili women in history?
entries.answer:
The community's institutions present the education and participation of women as a long-standing commitment rather than a recent adjustment.

The Ismaili records that during the Fatimid era both women and men could attend public lectures on religious learning at what is now al-Azhar, and that the majalis al-hikma, the sessions of wisdom, were held for women and men who had pledged allegiance to the Imam. It notes that Aga Khan III advised his Jamat that if financial constraints forced a choice, the education of daughters should be prioritised over that of sons - a policy he justified both practically and on the grounds that a woman's own happiness and welfare were reason enough. The Aga Khan Development Network's schools in northern Pakistan are cited as a result, along with the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery in Karachi.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies has published accounts of women who shaped Ismaili history: Sitt al-Mulk, the Fatimid princess who acted as regent for the Imam-Caliph al-Zahir; Mata Salamat, who petitioned the Qajar court after the murder of the 45th Imam, was given the title of Pir and delivered sermons to the Jamat; and Sayyida Imam Begum, the only known female composer in the ginan tradition.

In jamatkhana, The Ismaili describes men and women as sitting in separate but side-by-side sections, and the spaces as inclusive of ethnicity and gender. Women serve as mukhiani, among the functionaries appointed by the Imam to officiate at religious ceremonies.

sources.title: Empowering women: A legacy of the Ismaili Imamat
Women Who Have Impacted Ismaili History

entries.title: How do Ismailis view other faiths and pluralism?
questions: How do Ismailis view other religions?
What do Ismailis think of Christians and Jews?
What is pluralism in Ismaili thought?
Do Ismailis do interfaith work?
Why does the Aga Khan talk about pluralism?
Are Ismailis tolerant of other beliefs?
What is the Global Centre for Pluralism?
entries.answer:
Pluralism is presented by the community's institutions as an ethic drawn from the faith, not a diplomatic posture.

The Ismaili grounds it in the Qur'an: that God created all humans from a single soul (4:1), and that "among His wonders is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your languages and colours" (30:22). It argues that a pluralistic outlook requires real knowledge of others - quoting Mawlana Hazar Imam's remark that a secure pluralistic society needs communities confident both in their own traditions and in those of their neighbours - and that this means learning honestly about histories of conflict and the persecution of minorities.

Writing for the Institute of Ismaili Studies, Reza Shah-Kazemi begins from the Prophet's invitation to a group of Christians in 631 CE to perform their rites in his own mosque, and argues that the Qur'an's universal message invites Muslims to respect and revere the essence residing at the core of the revealed religions.

Farhad Daftary's work for the Institute applies a similar openness within Islam itself, urging readers to see Sunni and Shia as different communities of interpretation rather than as orthodoxy and deviation.

Institutionally, the Ismaili Imamat describes its engagement with governments and international agencies as driven by the ethics of Islam and directed towards human dignity, pluralistic engagement and peace building, and its development agencies as non-denominational.

sources.title: Pluralism and the Qur'an by Reza Shah-Kazemi
Diversity in Islam: Communities of Interpretation by Farhad Daftary
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, 2006

entries.title: What festivals do Ismailis observe?
questions: What festivals do Ismailis celebrate?
What is Imamat Day?
What is Salgirah?
Do Ismailis celebrate Eid?
What is Navroz?
What is Yawm-e Ali?
When is Imamat Day?
What holidays are important to Ismailis?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili describes festivals as times of communal gathering and celebration, and also moments for reflection, gratitude and charitable offerings, which reinforce unity and a sense of belonging among Ismailis worldwide.

The festivals listed on the community's own site include Navroz, Salgirah, Imamat Day, Milad-un-Nabi, Yawm-e Ali, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Eid al-Ghadir, Ramadan, Laylat al-Qadr and Muharram.

Two are particular to the Imamat. Imamat Day marks the anniversary of the present Imam's accession; for Mawlana Hazar Imam Prince Rahim Aga Khan V this is 4 February, the day in 2025 on which the Imamat passed from his father. The Ismaili describes it as an occasion to reaffirm allegiance and gratitude and to give thanks for the continuity of the Imamat. Salgirah is the Imam's birthday - 12 October - which the community describes as an occasion to reflect on the spiritual bond linking each murid to the Imam and to express love, loyalty and devotion.

Navroz marks the new year and the first day of spring, a day of renewal and fresh start when families and communities come together. Eid al-Fitr ends the month of Ramadan and is described as both personal and social - a time to maintain prayer and self-restraint, and to reaffirm generosity and compassion through acts of charity.

entries.title: What place does the Quran have in Ismaili belief?
questions: Do Ismailis believe in the Quran?
What is the Quran to Ismailis?
Do Ismailis read the Quran?
What is ta'wil?
What are zahir and batin?
Do Ismailis interpret the Quran differently?
Is the Quran recited in jamatkhana?
entries.answer:
Ismailis, like all Muslims, hold the Qur'an to be divine revelation. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as containing the revelations received by the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca and Medina over some twenty-three years, comprising 114 suras of varying length, and playing a central role in ritual, law, theology, literature, art and spirituality. The Ismaili Imamat records the Shia affirmation that the Prophet left behind two weighty legacies to guide future generations: the Holy Qur'an and his progeny.

What is distinctive in the Ismaili reading is the relationship between the outward and the inner. The Institute defines zahir as the outward, apparent or exoteric meaning of a sacred text, ritual or prescription, and batin as its inner or esoteric meaning; ta'wil is the drawing out of that inner meaning from the literal wording. Azim Nanji, writing for the Institute, presents the Imamat as existing so that Muslims can contextualise the practice of their faith and understand fully both the exoteric and esoteric dimensions of the Qur'an.

In practice, The Ismaili lists recitation of verses of the Holy Qur'an among the practices observed in jamatkhana, alongside du'a, tasbih, dhikr, salawat and the affirmation of the shahada. Qur'anic verses are also quoted throughout the community's own teaching material on fasting, charity, pluralism and prayer.

sources.title: The Imamate in Ismailism by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 210-212

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: What are ginans?
questions: What are ginans?
What language are ginans in?
Who wrote the ginans?
Are ginans scripture?
What is the difference between a ginan and a qasida?
Where are ginans recited?
What is Satpanth?
entries.answer:
Ginans are devotional poems belonging to the South Asian Ismaili tradition. The Institute of Ismaili Studies traces the word to the Sanskrit jnan, contemplative or reflective knowledge, and describes a ginan as a poetic composition in an Indian language - Sindhi, Punjabi, Gujarati, Hindi or Multani - with both didactic and mystical elements, preserved orally before being written down in the Khojki script.

Authorship is traditionally ascribed to the Pirs, the figures who led the Khoja community from at least the thirteenth to the nineteenth centuries. The Institute records that community historiography attributes the ginans to a series of Nizari Ismaili missionary-preachers, known as Pirs and Sayyids, believed to have been designated by the Imams from as early as the eleventh and twelfth centuries to propagate the teaching of Satpanth, the "True Path", in the Indian subcontinent. Through these compositions they highlighted the significance of accepting the authority of the living Imam.

One named female composer is recorded: Sayyida Imam Begum, active in the time of Aga Khan I, described as the last of the ginan composers and the only woman in the tradition, whose verses on love, devotion and yearning are still recited.

Ginans are recited today in jamatkhana as part of devotional practice, alongside qasidas - the chanted poem of the Arabic and Persian-speaking Nizari tradition - and nashids.

sources.title: Ginans by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in The Oxford Dictionary of Islam, 2004

sources.title: Women Who Have Impacted Ismaili History
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: How do Ismailis greet one another, and what etiquette should a guest know?
questions: How do Ismailis greet each other?
What does Ya Ali Madad mean?
What is Mawla Ali Madad?
How should I greet an Ismaili friend?
What is salawat?
What should I know before visiting an Ismaili Centre?
What do Ismailis say instead of salaam?
entries.answer:
The greetings Ismailis use among themselves are Ya Ali Madad and Mawla Ali Madad. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes a children's book in its own series built entirely around a young boy learning the meaning of these two greetings as he moves through the Ismaili Centre in Toronto. The Ismaili presents a song of the same name in which young members of the Jamat greet one another across the world, describing it as an illustration of a shared sense of community regardless of where people come from.

Salawat - seeking blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, and for Ismailis on the hereditary Imams descended from him - is recited on many occasions and is among the practices observed in jamatkhana.

Festival greetings follow the familiar Muslim pattern: Navroz Mubarak, Eid Mubarak, Salgirah Khushiali Mubarak.

For a visitor, the main point of etiquette that the community itself states clearly concerns access rather than manners: formal congregational prayers in the jamatkhana are for Ismailis, while many jamatkhanas and especially the Ismaili Centres welcome members of the wider society to educational, cultural and social programmes outside prayer times. Detailed guidance on dress, shoes, photography or seating for guests is not published on these sites, so the practical course is to ask your host or the centre directly.

sources.title: What is the significance of Salawat?
Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.notes: The allowed sources confirm the greetings and the public/private distinction, but publish no visitor etiquette guide (dress, shoes, photography). That gap is stated rather than filled.

entries.title: How is the Ismaili community organised?
questions: How is the Ismaili community organised?
What is the Ismaili Constitution?
What are the Ismaili Councils?
What is ITREB?
Who runs the Ismaili community?
What is social governance in the Ismaili community?
What boards serve the Jamat?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili Imamat explains that, historically and according to the needs of the time, the Imams have given rules of conduct and constitutions for the community's social governance. On succeeding to the Imamat in 1957, Aga Khan IV adapted the modern system first pioneered by his grandfather Aga Khan III, and in 1986 ordained an Ismaili Constitution that for the first time brought the global community's social governance under a common framework.

Under that Constitution, National, Regional and Local Councils are responsible for overall social governance, while Central Institutions provide services in education, health, social welfare, housing, economic welfare, cultural and women's activities, and youth and sports development. The Constitution also incorporates Religious Education Boards, and contains provisions for resolving conflict through impartial conciliation and arbitration - provisions that the Imamat notes are increasingly used in some countries by non-Ismailis as well.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines the Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs) as local and international boards, ultimately accountable to the Imam, responsible for religious instruction and for supervising details of religious practice in their jurisdictions. A published ITREB mandate describes duties including implementing religious education curricula, training waezeen and religion teachers, publishing materials, and serving as a point of reference for Mukhis and Kamadias on religious rites.

Shams Vellani, writing for the Institute, describes the Constitution as an expression of the community's Shia ethics that helped consolidate a shared identity while recognising its pluralism.

sources.title: Glossary: The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs)
Meet the Institutions - Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
The Institutions of the Ismaili Muslim Community by Shams Vellani

entries.title: What is the Aga Khan Development Network, and why does a religious leader run one?
questions: What is the AKDN?
What is the Aga Khan Development Network?
Why does the Aga Khan build hospitals and schools?
Is AKDN only for Ismailis?
What does AKDN do?
How is development connected to Ismaili faith?
Who funds AKDN?
entries.answer:
The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the Aga Khan Development Network as a contemporary endeavour of the Ismaili Imamat to realise the ethics and social conscience of Islam through institutional action. It brings together agencies whose mandates range across health, education, architecture, rural development and private sector enterprise.

The Ismaili Imamat describes AKDN as a group of private, international, non-denominational agencies working to improve living conditions and opportunities in some of the poorest parts of the developing world - in Central Asia, South Asia, Africa and the Middle East - with mandates spanning education from pre-school to university, health from primary to tertiary care, culture, rural development, human habitat, crisis response, microfinance, economic development and the strengthening of civil society.

The reasoning the Imamat gives for a spiritual office undertaking this work is theological rather than incidental. Its site states that the Imam's role is spiritual and not political, but that Islam holds the spiritual and material worlds to be inextricably connected - a pairing the Imams have described as din and dunya, faith and world. On that view, faith deepens rather than removes concern for the conditions of human life, and "quality of life" is understood to encompass the whole ethical and social context in which people live, not only material well-being.

Because the agencies are non-denominational, their programmes serve whole populations regardless of faith or background.

entries.title: What are the Ismaili Centres?
questions: What are Ismaili Centres?
Where are the Ismaili Centres?
Can I visit an Ismaili Centre?
What is the difference between an Ismaili Centre and a jamatkhana?
What happens at an Ismaili Centre?
Is the Ismaili Centre open to the public?
entries.answer:
The Ismaili describes the Ismaili Centres as high-profile buildings representing the pluralist ethos, traditions and values of the community. Each centre incorporates a jamatkhana, together with spaces for welcoming people from the wider society to social, cultural and educational programmes.

The community's own listing names centres in London, Vancouver, Lisbon, Dubai, Dushanbe and Toronto, with a further centre in Houston. The Ismaili Imamat's site also records the Delegation of the Ismaili Imamat in Ottawa, inaugurated during the Golden Jubilee, among the Imamat's buildings.

The centres illustrate the distinction the community draws between private and public space. Speaking at the foundation ceremony of the Ismaili Jamatkhana and Centre in Khorog, Tajikistan, in 2008, Mawlana Hazar Imam described the jamatkhana as reserved for traditions and practices specific to the Shia Ismaili tariqah of Islam, while the Centre would be a symbol of the confluence between the spiritual and the secular in Islam.

In practice this means that the prayer hall is for Ismailis during congregational practice, while the other spaces in the complex function as religious, educational and social centres promoting dialogue, discussion and community building, and are open to the wider community. The Ismaili describes welcoming members of wider society to these spaces as part of a deliberate effort to build bridges.

sources.title: Ismaili Jamatkhanas, Congregational Practice and Privacy

entries.title: Why is voluntary service so central in the Ismaili community?
questions: Why do Ismailis volunteer so much?
What is khidma?
What is seva in the Ismaili context?
Who runs Ismaili jamatkhanas?
What is the Ismaili Volunteer Corps?
What is Time and Knowledge Nazrana?
Is volunteering a religious act for Ismailis?
entries.answer:
Service is presented by the community as a form of devotional offering rather than as optional extra-curricular work.

The Ismaili states that its institutions, jamatkhanas included, are largely run by dedicated volunteers who offer their time and knowledge out of love and devotion to the Imam and the community, and lists voluntary service alongside material offerings as a type of offering made in jamatkhana. The Ismaili Volunteers - uniformed volunteers who, the community notes, have served for over a century in all Jamati geographies - take as their motto khidma, which The Ismaili glosses as the notion of unconditional service.

The Time and Knowledge Nazrana, established during the Golden Jubilee, is described as combining two traditions: presenting the Imam with an unconditional gift to mark epochal events, and offering one's intellectual capacity to the Imamat's work for the Jamat and the wider society.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies places this in a longer frame, describing the personal and communal sharing of time, knowledge, skills and experience as a deeply ingrained tradition of the Ismaili community worldwide, and as a reflection of the Qur'anic ethic of upholding the dignity of humankind. The Ismaili Imamat likewise describes Ismailis as active in civil society in every country where they live, contributing to the betterment of the societies among whom they live.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Where can I learn more from the community's own institutions?
questions: Where can I learn more about Ismailis?
What should I read about the Ismaili community?
What is the Institute of Ismaili Studies?
Are there official Ismaili websites?
Where can I find reliable information on Ismailism?
What books does IIS publish?
What is the Ta'lim curriculum?
entries.answer:
Four of the community's own sites carry most of what a newcomer needs.

The Institute of Ismaili Studies (iis.ac.uk) is the community's research and education institution in London. It publishes scholarly articles and books by authors such as Farhad Daftary, Azim Nanji, Ali Asani and Shafique Virani, maintains an extensive glossary of Islamic and Ismaili terms, and runs the Aga Khan Library. Its Department of Education develops the international Ta'lim curriculum used in religious education programmes organised by ITREBs, covering pre-primary to secondary ages, produced in ten or more languages and used in over twenty-five countries. It has also begun a Children's Series of illustrated books for families.

The Ismaili (the.ismaili) is the community's official site, carrying news, festival explainers and the What Ismailis Believe series of short articles and videos written in accessible language for people beginning to ask questions about the faith.

The Ismaili Imamat (ismaili.imamat) sets out the Imamat's history, the present Imam's biography, the Seat in Lisbon, the Ismaili Constitution and the Imamat's international relations.

The Aga Khan Development Network (akdn.org) documents the Imamat's development agencies and their work in health, education, culture, habitat and economic development.

entries.title: Imam
questions: What is an Imam?
What does Imam mean in Shia Islam?
Is an Imam the same as a prayer leader?
Who can be an Imam?
What does the Ismaili Imam do?
Is Imam a title or a role?
entries.answer: In general Muslim usage, an imam is a leader of prayers or a religious leader. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the Shia restrict the term to their spiritual leaders descended from Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Prophet's daughter Fatima. In the Ismaili tradition the Imam both leads the interpretation of the faith and works to improve the quality of life of the community and the societies in which it lives.

entries.title: Imamat (Imama, Imamate)
questions: What is the Imamat?
What does Imamate mean?
Is the Imamat hereditary?
What is the Ismaili Imamat?
Is the Imamat political?
Where is the Imamat based?
entries.answer: A noun formed from Imam, referring to the institution of hereditary spiritual leadership in Shia Islam. The Ismaili Imamat describes itself as a supra-national entity representing the succession of Imams since the time of the Prophet Muhammad, whose authority is that of religious interpretation rather than political rule. Its Seat, designated in 2018, is the Henrique de Mendonca Palace in Lisbon, known as the Diwan of the Ismaili Imamat.

entries.title: Hazir Imam
questions: What is a Hazir Imam?
What does Hazir mean?
What is the Imam-of-the-Time?
Why is the Imam called present?
Do Ismailis have a living Imam?
Who is the Hazir Imam today?
entries.answer: Hazir, or Hazar, means present. The Hazir Imam is the Imam of the present time, as distinct from Imams of the past. The Ismaili Imamat states that the Ismailis are today the only Shia Muslims led by a living, hereditary Imam in direct descent from the Prophet. English-language community material usually renders the term as Imam-of-the-Time. Since February 2025 the Hazir Imam is Prince Rahim Aga Khan V, the 50th Imam.

entries.title: Mawlana Hazar Imam
questions: What does Mawlana Hazar Imam mean?
Why do Ismailis say Mawlana Hazar Imam?
Who is Mawlana Hazar Imam?
Is Mawlana Hazar Imam the Aga Khan?
What is the Arabic form of this title?
How do Ismailis refer to their Imam?
entries.answer: Literally "our lord, the present Imam" - in Arabic Mawlana al-Imam al-Hadir. The Institute of Ismaili Studies identifies it as the designation Nizari Ismailis use for their contemporary Imam, currently His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan. Ismailis generally use this title, rather than the hereditary title Aga Khan, when speaking of the Imam of their own time, and the community's own publications follow that usage.

entries.title: Jamat
questions: What is a Jamat?
What does Jamat mean?
Is Jamat the same as congregation?
What is the global Jamat?
How do Ismailis use the word Jamat?
What does Jamati mean?
entries.answer: An assembly or religious congregation. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that Nizari Ismailis also use the term for their individual communities. In everyday community usage a Jamat can mean the people gathered in a particular jamatkhana, the Ismailis of a country or jurisdiction, or - in the phrase "the global Jamat" - Ismailis worldwide. The word is Arabic in origin, from jama'a, meaning group or community.

entries.title: Jamatkhana
questions: What is a jamatkhana?
What does jamatkhana mean?
Is a jamatkhana a mosque?
Who may enter a jamatkhana?
Do other Muslims use jamatkhanas?
Where do Ismailis gather to pray?
entries.answer: "House of the community", from the Arabic jama'a (group) and the Persian khana (house). The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that certain Sunni and Shia communities have used spaces of this name for prayer and communal gathering, particularly Sufi groups. Today the jamatkhana is the primary space of worship and gathering for Shia Ismaili Muslims. It is a private tariqa space; formal congregational practice within it is reserved for those who have pledged bay'a to the Imam-of-the-Time.

entries.title: Mukhi (and Mukhiani)
questions: What is a Mukhi?
What does a Mukhi do?
What is a Mukhiani?
Who appoints the Mukhi?
Can a woman be a Mukhi?
Is the Mukhi like a priest?
entries.answer: A functionary designated by the Ismaili Imamat to officiate at ceremonies in a jamatkhana. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the Mukhi as holding this office for a particular jamatkhana, and the Mukhiani as one of usually four functionaries at each jamatkhana appointed at the discretion of the Imam to officiate over religious ceremonies - a role held by women. ITREB serves as a point of reference for Mukhis on matters of religious rites and practice.

sources.title: In memoriam: Aitmadi Dr Aziz Kurwa
Meet the Institutions - Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board

entries.notes: The allowed sources define the office in passing rather than in a dedicated entry; terms of appointment and the full range of duties are not published there.

entries.title: Kamadia
questions: What is a Kamadia?
What does a Kamadia do?
Is a Kamadia the same as a Mukhi?
Who appoints the Kamadia?
What is a Kamadiani?
What is Kamadia Saheb?
entries.answer: An office in a jamatkhana held alongside that of the Mukhi. The Ismaili records that ITREB acts as a point of reference and consultation for Mukhis and Kamadias in matters of religious rites and practices of the Ismaili Tariqah, and community announcements are addressed to Mukhi and Kamadia Sahebaan together. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes usually four functionaries at each jamatkhana, appointed at the Imam's discretion, who officiate over religious ceremonies.

sources.title: Meet the Institutions - Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
