entries.notes: The allowed sources name the office but do not define its duties separately from those of the Mukhi. The distinction between the two roles is not described there.

entries.title: Du'a
questions: What is dua?
What does du'a mean?
Is dua the same as salat?
When do Ismailis recite dua?
What kind of prayer is dua?
Is dua said in Arabic?
entries.answer: A prayer of supplication. The Ismaili lists du'a first among the forms of prayer observed in jamatkhana, alongside tasbih (glorification), dhikr (remembrance) and salawat (seeking blessings on the Prophet and his progeny), describing them as prayers recommended in the Holy Qur'an. The Institute of Ismaili Studies separately defines salat as the Qur'anic term for prayer in general, which later came to denote the daily ritual prayer.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The allowed sources identify du'a as a form of jamatkhana prayer but do not publish its text, structure or frequency.

entries.title: Ginan
questions: What is a ginan?
What language are ginans in?
Who composed the ginans?
Are ginans sung?
What is Khojki?
What does ginan mean?
entries.answer: From the Sanskrit for knowledge. A ginan is a devotional poem in an Indian language - Sindhi, Punjabi, Gujarati, Hindi or Multani - ascribed to one of the Pirs who founded and led the Khoja Ismaili community between the thirteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes ginans as combining didactic and mystical poetry, preserved orally before being written down in the Khojki script, and recognised for preserving the devotional spirit of Islam in local languages.

sources.title: Ginans by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in The Oxford Dictionary of Islam, 2004

entries.title: Qasida
questions: What is a qasida?
How is a qasida different from a ginan?
Are qasidas recited in jamatkhana?
What language are qasidas in?
What does qasida mean?
Who composes qasidas?
entries.answer: A polythematic poem originating in pre-Islamic Arabia, later used for any poem of a certain length in Arabic, Persian and Turkish literature, often including praise of a person. Persian qasidas are also composed to celebrate festivals. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the chanted qasida is part of the religious tradition of Arabic and Persian-speaking Nizari Ismailis, and The Ismaili lists qasidas among the devotional poetry recited in jamatkhana.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Farman
questions: What is a farman?
What does farman mean?
Who gives farmans?
Are farmans written or spoken?
What is a Takht-nishini Farman?
Are farmans published?
entries.answer: From Persian, meaning command, authority, will or permission; under the Ottomans it denoted a written order of the sultan. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that in the Shia Ismaili context it refers to an address by the Imam to his community. The Ismaili lists the reading of farmans - described as guidance from the Imam - among jamatkhana practices. Prince Rahim Aga Khan V delivered his Takht-nishini Farman on 11 February 2025.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Didar
questions: What is didar?
What does didar mean?
What is a physical didar?
What is spiritual didar?
Why is didar important to Ismailis?
Is didar the same as mulaqat?
entries.answer: A word for seeing or beholding. The Ismaili explains that in the Shia Ismaili tradition didar can be experienced both physically and spiritually. Physical didar refers to occasions when Ismailis are graced with the opportunity to see and be in the presence of the hereditary Imam-of-the-Time. Spiritual didar refers to an experience in which, through the guidance of the Imam, one internally experiences the presence of God's light.

entries.title: Tariqah (tariqa)
questions: What is a tariqah?
What does tariqa mean?
Is the Ismaili tradition a tariqah?
Are Sufi orders tariqas?
Why is the jamatkhana called a tariqa space?
What is the Shia Imami Ismaili tariqah?
entries.answer: Arabic for way or path. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines it as the path followed by mystical schools of interpretation in Islam. The Ismaili describes tariqas as communities of Muslims following a path guided by a spiritual leader - a Shia Imam or a Sufi murshid - who guides their interpretation and practice as part of an inward search for spiritual enlightenment. Ismailis describe their own tradition as the Shia Imami Ismaili tariqah of Islam.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.title: Batin
questions: What is batin?
What does batin mean?
What is the esoteric meaning of scripture?
How is batin related to zahir?
Why do Ismailis emphasise the inner meaning?
Is batin secret knowledge?
entries.answer: The inner or esoteric meaning of a sacred text, ritual or religious prescription, usually contrasted with the zahir, its outward form. The Institute of Ismaili Studies treats the pair as complementary rather than opposed: the batin is drawn out from the zahir by ta'wil, esoteric interpretation. The holding together of outward practice and inner meaning is characteristic of Ismaili thought, which also speaks of an inner, knowledge-based worship alongside worship performed through bodily acts.

entries.title: Zahir
questions: What is zahir?
What does zahir mean?
What is the exoteric meaning?
How does zahir relate to batin?
Is the outward form of religion important?
Do Ismailis reject outward practice?
entries.answer: The outward, apparent or exoteric meaning of a sacred text, ritual or religious prescription, from which the batin - its inner meaning - is drawn out. The Institute of Ismaili Studies defines the term in exactly this relational way, and the pairing zahir/batin runs throughout Ismaili literature. Neither is dispensable: the outward form is the vehicle through which the inner meaning is reached by ta'wil.

entries.title: Ta'wil
questions: What is ta'wil?
What does tawil mean?
How do Ismailis interpret the Quran?
Is ta'wil the same as tafsir?
What is esoteric interpretation?
Who performs ta'wil?
entries.answer: The elucidation of the inner or esoteric meaning - the batin - from the literal wording or apparent meaning of a text, ritual or religious prescription. The Institute of Ismaili Studies gives this definition, and notes the related term batini ta'wil. Azim Nanji describes the Imamat as existing so that Muslims may understand fully both the exoteric and esoteric dimensions of the Qur'an, which places ta'wil at the centre of the Imam's interpretive role.

sources.title: The Imamate in Ismailism by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 210-212

entries.title: Da'i
questions: What is a da'i?
What does dai mean?
Who were the Ismaili da'is?
What did a da'i do?
Is a da'i a missionary?
What is a da'i al-mutlaq?
entries.answer: Literally "summoner". The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the da'i as a figure comparable to a missionary among various Muslim communities, a term used especially among the Ismailis before and during the Fatimid period and in the Alamut period. Fatimid da'is were expected to possess encyclopaedic knowledge - of the Qur'an and hadith, but also history, theology, philosophy, languages and the natural sciences. The plural is du'at.

entries.title: Da'wa
questions: What is da'wa?
What does dawa mean?
What was the Ismaili da'wa?
Is da'wa the same as preaching?
What were the ranks of the da'wa?
Does da'wa still exist today?
entries.answer: Literally summons, mission or invitation to Islam. Among Shia Muslims it meant the invitation to adopt the cause of the Imamat. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the term also refers more specifically to the hierarchy of the Ismaili religious organisation in the pre-Fatimid, Fatimid and Alamut periods. That hierarchy was known as the hudud al-din; a new initiate at its lowest rank was called a mustajib, a "respondent".

entries.title: Pir
questions: What is a Pir?
What does pir mean?
Who were the Ismaili Pirs?
Did Pirs write the ginans?
Is a pir the same as a shaykh?
Was there a female Pir?
entries.answer: Literally "elder", equivalent to the Arabic shaykh: a spiritual director or murshid, who in Sufism may found a tariqa. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the earliest Qasim Shahi Imams were referred to as pirs; that in the post-Alamut period the term designated local leaders of Nizari communities, some hereditary; and that in Indian Satpanth Ismailism the Pirs led the Khoja community from at least the thirteenth to the nineteenth centuries and are credited with the ginans.

sources.title: Women Who Have Impacted Ismaili History

entries.title: Satpanth
questions: What is Satpanth?
What does Satpanth mean?
Who taught Satpanth?
Is Satpanth the same as Ismailism?
What is Satpanthi literature?
How did Ismailism spread in India?
entries.answer: Satpanth means "True Path". The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that community historiography attributes the ginans to a series of Nizari Ismaili missionary-preachers, the Pirs and Sayyids, believed to have been designated by the Imams from as early as the eleventh and twelfth centuries with the mission of propagating the teaching of Satpanth in the Indian subcontinent. Their devotional compositions emphasised accepting the authority of the living Ismaili Imam. Satpanthi literature is a field of continuing scholarly research.

sources.title: Women Who Have Impacted Ismaili History
Religious Traditions and Early Ismaili History in South Asia by Samira Sheikh

entries.title: Khoja
questions: Who are the Khojas?
What does Khoja mean?
Are all Khojas Ismaili?
Where do Khojas live?
What is the origin of the Khoja community?
What is the difference between Khoja Ismailis and Khoja Ithna'asharis?
entries.answer: From the Persian khwaja, lord or master. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes the Khojas as one of the Ismaili communities originating in the Indian subcontinent and now living in many countries. Azim Nanji notes that the name referred to those converted to Nizari Ismaili Islam from about the thirteenth century, predominantly from Gujarat and Kutch. In the nineteenth century most remained Ismaili, while one group became Ithna'ashari and a smaller group adopted Sunnism.

sources.title: Khojas by Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia of Islam and the Muslim World, Vol. II, p. 393, 2003

entries.title: Nizari
questions: Who are the Nizari Ismailis?
What does Nizari mean?
Why are they called Nizari?
Are the Aga Khan's followers Nizari?
How did the Nizari branch begin?
Are Nizaris the largest Ismaili group?
entries.answer: Adherents of the branch of the Ismailis who gave allegiance to Nizar, the eldest son of the Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mustansir (d. 1094), as his successor. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the dispute over al-Mustansir's succession is effectively where Nizari history begins. The Nizaris later subdivided further; the line followed today by the Ismailis who acknowledge the Aga Khans is the Qasim Shahi branch.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.title: Musta'li
questions: Who are the Musta'li Ismailis?
What does Musta'li mean?
How do Musta'lis differ from Nizaris?
Are the Bohras Musta'li?
Who is the da'i al-mutlaq?
Where do Musta'li Ismailis live?
entries.answer: Adherents of the branch of the Ismailis who supported al-Musta'li, the younger son of the Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mustansir (d. 1094), as his successor. Zulfikar Hirji and Azim Nanji explain that the Musta'li-Tayyibi Ismailis hold that their twenty-first Imam, al-Tayyib, went into concealment, and that while the Imamat continues in his line, authority in his physical absence is exercised by a vicegerent, the da'i al-mutlaq. The Bohras are an Indian Musta'li community.

sources.title: Modern Ismaili Communities by Zulfikar Hirji and Azim Nanji
sources.provenance: IIS edition of an article first published in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIV, pp. 208-210

entries.title: Fatimid
questions: Who were the Fatimids?
What was the Fatimid caliphate?
Why are they called Fatimid?
Did Ismailis rule Egypt?
What did the Fatimids found?
When did the Fatimid dynasty end?
entries.answer: A major Muslim dynasty of Ismaili caliphs in North Africa from 909 and later in Egypt (973-1171), who claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad through Ali and took their name from the Prophet's daughter Fatima. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the apogee of Ismaili power was reached under the Fatimid Imam-Caliphs, and that institutions of learning founded under their patronage included al-Azhar in Cairo and the Dar al-Ilm, the Academy of Knowledge.

entries.title: Alamut
questions: What was Alamut?
Where is Alamut?
What happened at Alamut?
When did Alamut fall?
What was the Alamut period?
Who was Hasan-i Sabbah?
entries.answer: A fortress of the Nizari Ismailis in northern Iran, which fell to the Mongols in 654 AH / 1256 CE. The Institute of Ismaili Studies treats the Alamut period (roughly 1090-1256) as a distinct era of Ismaili history, associated with Hasan-i Sabbah and his doctrine of ta'lim, with the declaration of qiyamat, and with the scholarship of figures such as Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. Libraries at Ismaili centres in Iran and Syria drew visiting scholars.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.title: Nur
questions: What is nur?
What does nur mean?
What is the verse of light?
How is nur connected to the Imams?
Why is light important in Ismaili thought?
What is the light of the Imams?
entries.answer: Light. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the term is used for God, who is defined as light in the Qur'an's "verse of light" (24:35): God is the light of the heavens and the earth. In Shiism the term is also taken to mean the light believed to have passed through Adam, via Muhammad, into the family of Ali and his successors, the Imams. The Ismaili connects this transmission of light to the concept of nass.

sources.title: How does the Ismaili Imam designate his successor?

entries.title: Walaya (and wilaya)
questions: What is walaya?
What does wilaya mean?
What is devotion to the Imam?
What authority does the Imam have?
Is walaya the same as sainthood?
What is the difference between walaya and wilaya?
entries.answer: Walaya means friendship or assistance; in Sufism it denotes qualities roughly translatable as sainthood, and in Islam more specifically devotion to the Imam. The closely related term wilaya is defined by the Institute of Ismaili Studies as authority - in Shia Islam, the authority the Imam has over the believers. The two words are often discussed together because they express the reciprocal sides of the same bond: the follower's devotion and the Imam's authority.

entries.title: Bay'a (bayah)
questions: What is bay'a?
What does bayah mean?
What is the oath of allegiance?
Why do Ismailis give bay'a to the Imam?
Is bay'a in the Quran?
What does bay'a mean for daily practice?
entries.answer: An oath of allegiance: the act by which people, individually or collectively, recognise the authority of an individual. The Institute of Ismaili Studies traces the practice to Arab tradition and the practice of the Prophet, and to the Qur'an (48:10, 48:18, 60:12). In the Shia Ismaili tradition it is the acceptance of the permanent spiritual bond between the Imam and the murid, uniting Ismailis worldwide in loyalty, devotion and obedience. It is reaffirmed daily in prayer.

sources.title: Why are prayers in jamatkhana only for Ismailis?

entries.title: Taqiyya
questions: What is taqiyya?
What does taqiyya mean?
Why did Ismailis practise taqiyya?
Is taqiyya lying?
When was taqiyya used?
Do Ismailis still practise taqiyya?
entries.answer: Precautionary dissimulation of one's religious beliefs, especially in times of persecution or danger - a practice particularly associated with Shia Muslims. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that after the Mongol conquest of Alamut, Nizari Imams and their followers lived at times under taqiyya, the Imams appearing outwardly as Sufi masters and their followers as murids. Twenty-six of the first forty-nine Imams resided in Persia, at times openly and at times concealed.

sources.title: Women Who Have Impacted Ismaili History

entries.title: Satr (sitr)
questions: What is satr?
What is dawr al-satr?
What does satr mean?
Were the Imams ever hidden?
Is satr the same as occultation?
How did hidden Imams communicate?
entries.answer: From the Arabic root meaning to veil or conceal. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that in Ismaili history the term is used in the phrase dawr al-satr, a period when the Imams remained hidden from public view because of the political climate. The Imam remained physically present but was not readily identifiable or accessible to followers or detractors; communication with the community was maintained through a small number of religious officials, the du'at.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.title: Qiyama (qiyamat)
questions: What is qiyama?
What is the Day of Resurrection in Islam?
What was the declaration of qiyamat at Alamut?
What does qa'im mean?
Who was Khudavand-i Qiyamat?
Is qiyamat the end of the world?
entries.answer: Al-qiyama is the Arabic term for the Last Day, the Day of Resurrection, a concept prominent in the Qur'an and part of the Islamic creed. In Nizari history the word has a further sense: the Imam Hasan, known as Khudavand-i Qiyamat, proclaimed the qiyamat in the Alamut period. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that critics read this as a rejection of outward religious practice, while a prevailing Ismaili tradition interprets it as a spiritual revelation of truth.
entries.notes: The Institute states plainly that the meaning of the Alamut declaration of qiyamat is contested between critics and the community's own interpretation.

entries.title: Navroz (Nawruz)
questions: What is Navroz?
When is Navroz?
What does Nawruz mean?
Do Ismailis celebrate the Persian new year?
How is Navroz celebrated?
Is Navroz religious or cultural?
entries.answer: The new year festival marking the first day of spring. The Ismaili describes Nawruz as a day, like new year traditions in other cultures, when families and communities come together - a reminder of renewal and a fresh start, and a chance to reflect on the past year's achievements and failures and to make resolutions. It is listed among the festivals the community observes each year, occasions the community frames as times for reflection, gratitude and charitable offering.

entries.title: Salgirah
questions: What is Salgirah?
When is Salgirah?
Why do Ismailis celebrate the Imam's birthday?
What does Salgirah mean?
What is Khushiali?
What do Ismailis say on Salgirah?
entries.answer: The birthday of the Imam-of-the-Time, observed by Ismailis worldwide. The Ismaili describes it as an occasion for Ismailis to reflect on the unique spiritual bond that links each murid to the Imam, and to express love, loyalty and devotion to the Imamat that binds the community together. Mawlana Hazar Imam Prince Rahim Aga Khan V was born on 12 October 1971. The festival greeting is Salgirah Khushiali Mubarak.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis celebrate their Imam's birthday?

entries.title: Imamat Day
questions: What is Imamat Day?
When is Imamat Day?
Why do Ismailis observe Imamat Day?
What is celebrated on Imamat Day?
Has the date of Imamat Day changed?
What do Ismailis do on Imamat Day?
entries.answer: The anniversary of the present Imam's accession to the Imamat. For Mawlana Hazar Imam Prince Rahim Aga Khan V this is 4 February, the day in 2025 on which the Imamat passed to him. The Ismaili describes it as an occasion to reaffirm allegiance and gratitude to the Imam for his guidance, to renew commitment to the ethics of the faith, and to give thanks for the continuity of the Imamat.

entries.title: Chandraat
questions: What is Chandraat?
What does Chandraat mean?
What is the Chandraat majlis?
What is Shukarvari Beej?
Why is the new moon marked?
Do all Ismailis observe Chandraat?
entries.answer: The night of the new moon, which in Islam marks the beginning of each lunar month. The Ismaili records that in the Pir Sadardin tradition a Chandraat majlis was established in Bombay over a century ago by Imam Sultan Mahomed Shah, its aim being to seek spiritual strength together through special prayers of supplication. When Chandraat falls on a Friday the day is called Shukarvari Beej, and members of the Jamat in that tradition usually fast.

sources.title: On the occasion of Shukarvari Beej

entries.notes: The only allowed source found describes Chandraat within the Pir Sadardin tradition; practice elsewhere in the community is not described.

entries.title: Seva / Khidmat
questions: What is khidma?
What is seva in the Ismaili community?
Why do Ismailis volunteer?
What is the Ismaili Volunteer Corps?
Is service a religious duty?
What is TKN?
entries.answer: Voluntary service offered to the community and the Imam. The Ismaili Volunteers take as their motto khidma, which The Ismaili glosses as the notion of unconditional service; uniformed volunteers have served in all Jamati geographies for over a century. Community institutions, jamatkhanas included, are described as largely run by volunteers offering time and knowledge out of love and devotion. The Ismaili treats voluntary service as itself a type of offering made in jamatkhana.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.notes: The allowed sources use khidma/khidmat; the South Asian term seva is not defined on them.

entries.title: Waez (waezeen)
questions: What is a waez?
Who are the waezeen?
How does someone become a waez?
What is an al-Waez?
Who trains waezeen?
Is a waez a preacher?
entries.answer: A trained religious speaker in the Ismaili community; the plural is waezeen, and individuals are addressed as al-Waez or al-Waeza. The Institute of Ismaili Studies runs an International Training Programme for Waezeen, open to members of the Jamat with an undergraduate degree or equivalent who commit to at least three years of service through ITREB after completing the training. ITREB's own mandate includes implementing programmes for the training and upgrading of waezeen and religion teachers.

sources.title: Meet the Institutions - Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board

entries.title: ITREB
questions: What is ITREB?
What does ITREB stand for?
What does ITREB do?
Who does ITREB report to?
Is ITREB the same as a Council?
Who teaches Ismaili religious education?
keywords: Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board
entries.answer: The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards - more fully, the Shia Imami Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes them as local and international boards, ultimately accountable to the Imam, responsible for religious instruction and for supervising details of religious practice in their jurisdictions. A published ITREB mandate lists implementing religious education curricula, training waezeen and teachers, supporting research and publication, and advising Mukhis and Kamadias on religious rites.

sources.title: Glossary: The Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Boards (ITREBs)
Meet the Institutions - Ismaili Tariqah and Religious Education Board

entries.title: AKDN
questions: What is AKDN?
What does the Aga Khan Development Network do?
Is AKDN a charity?
Does AKDN help only Ismailis?
Which agencies make up AKDN?
Who leads AKDN?
entries.answer: The Aga Khan Development Network. The Institute of Ismaili Studies describes it as a contemporary endeavour of the Ismaili Imamat to realise the ethics and social conscience of Islam through institutional action, bringing together agencies whose mandates span health, education, architecture, rural development and private enterprise. The Ismaili Imamat describes its agencies as private, international and non-denominational, working to improve living conditions in some of the poorest parts of the developing world.

entries.title: Ya Ali Madad
questions: What does Ya Ali Madad mean?
How do Ismailis greet each other?
What is Mawla Ali Madad?
How do I reply to Ya Ali Madad?
Is Ya Ali Madad a prayer?
Can a non-Ismaili say Ya Ali Madad?
entries.answer: A greeting used among Ismailis, invoking the help of Hazrat Ali. The Institute of Ismaili Studies has published a children's book built around a young boy learning the meaning of the greetings Ya Ali Madad and Mawla Ali Madad. The Ismaili presents a song of the same name in which young members of the Jamat greet one another across the world, describing it as an illustration of a shared sense of community regardless of where people come from.
entries.notes: The allowed sources confirm the greetings and their context but do not give a word-by-word translation or a prescribed reply.

entries.title: Shahada
questions: What is the shahada?
What is the Islamic declaration of faith?
Do Shia Muslims add to the shahada?
What does la ilaha illa'llah mean?
Is the shahada recited in jamatkhana?
How many parts does the shahada have?
entries.answer: From the Arabic root meaning to bear witness: the public declaration of belief, and among the key principles of Islam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies explains that it has two parts - that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God - and that the second part distinguishes Muslims from followers of other monotheistic religions. Shia Muslims often add an affirmation of Imam Ali as Commander of the Faithful. The Ismaili lists affirming the shahada among jamatkhana practices.

sources.title: What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Salawat
questions: What is salawat?
What does salawat mean?
Why do Ismailis recite salawat?
Is salawat the same as salat?
When is salawat recited?
What is the plural of salat?
entries.answer: In Islam, salawat means seeking blessings upon the Prophet Muhammad. The Ismaili explains that for Shia Ismaili Muslims salawat is recited for the Prophet and also for the hereditary Imams descended from him, and lists it among the forms of prayer observed in jamatkhana. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that salat, of which salawat is the plural, is a Qur'anic term for prayer in general that later came to denote the daily ritual prayer.

sources.title: What is the significance of Salawat?

entries.title: Tasbih
questions: What is tasbih?
What is the tasbih of Bibi Fatima?
What words are used in tasbih?
Is tasbih the same as dhikr?
Why is it named after Bibi Fatima?
How many times is tasbih repeated?
entries.answer: Glorification of God through the repetition of set formulae. The Ismaili recounts that the Prophet taught his daughter Hazrat Bibi Fatima to say, after every prayer, Allahu Akbar, Al-hamdu lil-lah and Subhan Allah thirty-three times each, concluding with la ilaha illa'l-lah; she made this a fixed practice, and the prayer came to be named after her. Shia Muslims continue the practice today. The Ismaili lists tasbih among the prayers observed in jamatkhana.

sources.title: The history of Bibi Fatima's Tasbih and its practice today
What practices do Ismailis observe in jamatkhanas?

entries.title: Aql
questions: What is aql?
What does aql mean?
How do Muslims value reason?
What is aql-i kull?
Is intellect important in Ismaili thought?
What is the role of reason in Islam?
entries.answer: Reason, intellect, mind. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that the noun does not itself appear in the Qur'an, though the related verb aqala does - as in "Do you not understand?" (2:44) - and cross-references aql-i kull, the universal intellect of Ismaili cosmology. The Institute describes the pursuit and patronage of intellectual enquiry as a hallmark of Ismaili history, doctrine and practice.

entries.title: Ahl al-Bayt
questions: What is ahl al-bayt?
Who are the people of the house?
Which family members are included?
Why is the Prophet's family important to Shia Muslims?
Does the Quran mention ahl al-bayt?
What does ahl al-bayt mean literally?
entries.answer: Literally "the people of the house": the Prophet Muhammad and the members of his household, especially his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib, his daughter Fatima, his grandsons al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and their progeny. The Ismaili notes the Shia understanding of the Qur'anic verse in which God expresses the wish to purify the ahl al-bayt (33:33), and the Shia belief that the Imams from the Prophet's family hold a higher spiritual status.

sources.title: Shia and Sunni: Understanding different Muslim interpretations

entries.title: Ghadir Khumm
questions: What is Ghadir Khumm?
What happened at Ghadir Khumm?
What did the Prophet say at Ghadir Khumm?
What is Eid al-Ghadir?
Why is Ghadir Khumm important to Shia Muslims?
When is Eid al-Ghadir?
entries.answer: A pool or marsh between Mecca and Medina where, returning from his farewell pilgrimage in 632 CE, the Prophet Muhammad stopped to deliver a sermon. The Institute of Ismaili Studies records that he there declared Imam Ali the mawla of the believers - preserved in hadith as "he whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla". Shia Muslims read this as the public designation of Ali as successor. The event falls on 18 Dhu'l-Hijja and is commemorated as Eid al-Ghadir.

sources.title: Shia and Sunni: Understanding different Muslim interpretations

entries.notes: The Ismaili notes that the word mawla can mean friend, client or master, and that the Shia read it as master; the interpretation of the phrase is where Sunni and Shia readings diverge.

entries.title: Hujja
questions: What is a hujja?
What does hujjat mean?
Who is called a proof of God?
What rank was the hujja in the da'wa?
Was Hasan-i Sabbah a hujja?
What is the plural of hujja?
entries.answer: A Qur'anic term meaning both proof and the presentation of proof. The Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that in Shia Islam it designates Prophets and Imams as proofs of God's presence on earth; that in the pre-Fatimid and Fatimid da'wa it was also applied to senior da'is; and that in the Alamut period it came to denote those representing the Imam. Hasan-i Sabbah held the title, indicating the highest rank immediately after the Imam.

sources.title: Nizari Ismailis: History, Geography, and Beliefs

entries.title: Ismaili Constitution
questions: What is the Ismaili Constitution?
When was the Ismaili Constitution ordained?
What does the Constitution cover?
Who wrote the Ismaili Constitution?
Does the Constitution cover succession?
What is conciliation and arbitration?
entries.answer: The constitution of the Ismaili community's social governance, ordained by Aga Khan IV in 1986. The Ismaili Imamat states that it brought the global community's social governance under a common aegis for the first time, providing for National, Regional and Local Councils, Central Institutions and Religious Education Boards, and for resolving conflict through impartial conciliation and arbitration. Its Preamble states that succession to the Imamat is by way of nass, the Imam's absolute prerogative.

sources.title: How does the Ismaili Imam designate his successor?

entries.title: Council
questions: What is an Ismaili Council?
What does a National Council do?
Who appoints the Councils?
What is social governance?
What are the Central Institutions?
Is the Council religious or administrative?
entries.answer: Under the Ismaili Constitution, National, Regional and Local Councils are responsible for the overall social governance of the community, while Central Institutions provide services in education, health, social welfare, housing, economic welfare, cultural and women's activities, and youth and sports development. Shams Vellani, writing for the Institute of Ismaili Studies, describes this constitutional framework as an expression of the community's Shia ethics, consolidating a shared identity while recognising the community's own pluralism.

sources.title: The Institutions of the Ismaili Muslim Community by Shams Vellani

entries.title: Mawla
questions: What does mawla mean?
Why is Ali called mawla?
Is mawla the same as master?
What is Mawlana?
How do Shia and Sunni read the word mawla?
What is the root meaning of mawla?
entries.answer: Lord or master, often used as an honorific; the Institute of Ismaili Studies notes that in early Islam it could also mean client. The word is central to the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir Khumm - "he whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla". The Ismaili notes it can be read as friend, client or master, and that the Shia accepted the sense of master. Mawlana, "our lord", is the form used in Mawlana Hazar Imam.

sources.title: Shia and Sunni: Understanding different Muslim interpretations

entries.title: Tawhid
questions: What is tawhid?
Do Ismailis believe in one God?
What does tawhid mean?
Is tawhid part of Ismaili belief?
What is the Oneness of God?
Is tawhid shared by all Muslims?
entries.answer: The Oneness of God, or belief in Divine Unity - the Institute of Ismaili Studies calls it one of the fundamental tenets of Islam. The Ismaili states that Ismailis, like all Muslims, believe in the oneness of God as professed in the first part of the shahada, la ilaha illa'llah, "there is no god but Allah", and uses this to explain why terms of honour applied to the Imam must not be confused with references to God.

sources.title: Why do Ismailis call their Imam Khudavind?

entries.title: Sharia
questions: What is sharia?
What does shari'a mean?
Is sharia the same as Islamic law?
How do Ismailis relate to sharia?
What is Ismaili jurisprudence?
Does sharia only mean law?
entries.answer: Literally "the path to be followed": the standard term for Muslim law and, more broadly, the totality of the Islamic way of life. The Institute of Ismaili Studies gives this definition, and elsewhere notes the classical distinction within religious practice between al-ibadat al-amaliyya, worship performed through bodily actions and good deeds, and mu'amalat, worldly activities - with some Ismaili authors setting outward worship alongside an inner, knowledge-based worship.
entries.notes: The allowed sources define sharia in general Islamic terms; they do not publish an account of how sharia is applied in contemporary Ismaili practice.
